papers.abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.
authors: Yueh-Cheng Liu, Snehal Jauhri, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner, Angela Dai
bullets: Covers household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces with detailed geometry, physically based materials, and curated layouts.
Provides object- and part-level semantic annotations for joint visual and embodied learning.
Supports inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation, improving state-of-the-art methods over alternative synthetic datasets.
Introduces a mobile manipulation benchmark for vision-language-action models, scoring both pick-and-place success and grasp location.
The dataset is intended for public release to support research in visual and embodied AI.

papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $\pi_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
authors: Xuanchen Liu, Hejun Zhang, Boxuan Dong, Ying Wu, Heshuai Li, Wen Gao, Yonghong Tian, Weihao Yu
bullets: Introduces RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark comparing mirror-free tasks with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions.
Across five policy types, all mirror settings reduce success; average drops range from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points, reaching 62.5 points on mirrored tabletops.
Matched non-reflective panels show that collisions alone do not explain failures: 50–88% of mirror-specific failures involve no recorded robot–panel contact.
Analyses indicate phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real objects, with additional diagnostics for grasping, pushing, and occlusion.
Real-robot tests with π₀.₅ and FastWAM also show reduced success, motivating reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/
authors: Hanzhao Xi, Zhonghao Li, Suxuan Liu, Shanghan Zhou, Zesheng Chen, Qiufeng Wang, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets VLM errors in exact Part IDs, unsupported parts, and inconsistent cross-step assignments.
PartGround links manual evidence with product-specific inventory and references, representing assignments in an Assembly IR.
PlanRefine audits assignments against available inventory and removes the lowest-confidence conflicts while flagging uncertainty for review.
On the IAW dataset, CAPER achieved 83.33% finite-inventory consistency with zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences.
It reduced inventory-overuse pairs from 9 to 0 and excess units from 51 to 0.

papers.abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
authors: Maximilian Xiling Li, Nils Blank, Paul Mattes, Pankhuri Vanjani, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Discrete skill policies can fail because of their vocabulary, selector, or execution, but joint training makes these causes hard to separate.
MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with a nearest demonstrated motion, then boundedly corrects it toward the prediction without training new parameters.
Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped reference policy is statistically equivalent to the original.
On LIBERO-90, quantization has no measurable cost and skill choice costs at most 2 points; selector placement and correction explain nearly all remaining gaps, up to 12 points.
Offline reconstruction fails to predict these effects or reliably assess library size, design, and transfer across benchmark suites.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes skill-vocabulary policies and closed-loop attribution for robot policies, including a 7B VLA model on LIBERO-90; directly relevant to robot skill learning and VLA.
papers.title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
papers.tldr: MPQ turns a demonstrated-motion library into a parameter-free post-policy wrapper that isolates whether closed-loop failures come from skill choice or skill execution.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy/
authors: Kaidi Zhang, Pengyuan Guo, Zhengtong Xu, Caiyi Zhang, Huayi Gou, Guanlin Huang, Aaron Lim, Anas Rafei, Yu She
bullets: Targets the challenge of translating ambiguous task goals into changing physical interactions.
Uses a VLM for symbolic state and goal estimation, followed by PDDL-based skill planning.
Steers atomic manipulation skills with language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies outcomes for replanning.
Provides a common phase-level interface for specialized policies and generalist action models.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show improved task following and recovery in complex long-horizon tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Atomic Policy architecture, shown with point-steered skills for Tabletop Manipulation. The planner combines VLM state and goal estimation with PDDL planning. For the active pick blue cube phase, the grounder (MolmoPoint) supplies a 2D image point pk. The selected skill generates an action chunk At using a diffusion U-Net conditioned on images, proprioception qt, and pk. The VLM checker evaluates the outcome against a phase-specific checklist: done advances the plan, not_done continues the phase, and replan requests a new plan. Blue arrows indicate execution and phase transitions; the red arrow indicates replanning.

Figure 5. Real-robot trial outcomes. Top: in-distribution (ID); bottom: out-of-distribution (OOD). Boxes show the interquartile range (IQR), dark lines mark medians, and whiskers extend to the outermost observations within 1.5 IQR of the box edges. White diamonds mark means, and dots show individual trials (n = 10 per method, task, and condition). Tasks are arranged by increasing language-grounding and compositional demands, from Multi-drawer to Stacking to Crossword. The language-only end-to-end baselines show wide trial-to-trial variation on Stacking and poor performance on Crossword, suggesting limited steerability as language-conditioning demands increase. Atomic + MolmoBot improves over fine-tuned MolmoBot on OOD Stacking and Crossword, supporting the combined benefit of point guidance and atomic-phase execution. Atomic + π0.5 also improves on these tasks without point inputs, showing that high-level planning and checker-controlled execution can improve OOD performance through language-based phase guidance alone.

Figure 6. Completion time of successful real-robot trials. Top: ID; bottom: OOD. Only trials with a task score of 1 are included. Large dots show the mean completion time, vertical lines show ± one sample standard deviation, and faint dots show individual trials; n is the number of successful trials for each method. Fine-tuned MolmoBot completes no Crossword trial, and fine-tuned π0.5 completes a single ID Crossword trial. Completion time for Atomic Policy includes planning, verification, and replanning by the VLM, so successful Atomic Policy trials take longer than successful end-to-end trials; for example, Atomic + π0.5 averages 128.6 s on ID Stacking versus 61.6 s for fine-tuned π0.5. Means based on few successes, such as n ≤ 2, should be interpreted with caution.

Figure 3. Task instructions and phase execution. Each row pairs an instruction with selected observations from execution. Bold labels name atomic phases, and the text after each colon identifies the point target; n/a denotes a phase without point conditioning. Blue boxes mark replanning after a detected failure or uncertain task state, such as a fallen cube in Stacking. The checker uses phase-specific completion criteria to continue execution, advance the phase, or request a new plan. Ellipses omit repeated or previously illustrated phases.

Figure 7. Failure modes on Multi-drawer. Each panel traces the 20 trials of one method (10 ID and 10 OOD) from execution to outcome. Trials either proceed without a recorded failure or encounter an error that is recovered through replanning or remains unresolved. Outcomes are SUCCESS (task score 1), PARTIAL (0 < task score < 1), and FAIL (task score 0). Failure types are wrong object or order (incorrect object, sequence, word, target recognition, or plan), reach or stuck (target or receptacle not reached, drawer not opened, or robot motion stalls), grasp, and place. Recovery is counted only when explicitly recorded in the evaluation notes. No method produces a zero-score trial on Multi-drawer. The Atomic Policy variants fail mainly through grasp and place errors, with one planning error for Atomic + MolmoBot. For fine-tuned MolmoBot, 7 of its 11 unsuccessful trials involve failure to reach the OOD receptacle during placement: the policy fails to guide the grasped object to the white bowl, suggesting difficulty grounding the unfamiliar receptacle’s location.

Figure 4. Learning curves on MolmoSpaces PnP Next-To. MolmoBot and π0.5 are evaluated during task-specific fine-tuning. Solid curves show success averaged over the ten most recent checkpoint evaluations. For the first nine checkpoints, the average uses all checkpoints evaluated so far. Dashed horizontal lines indicate each model’s zero-shot success rate.

Figure 8. Failure modes on Stacking. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. All 17 unrecovered failures of Atomic + DP and 9 of 10 of Atomic + MolmoBot are grasp or place errors, while Atomic + π0.5 fails in only 3 of 20 trials. Atomic + DP struggles with the fine-grained alignment required for stacking, suggesting that its low-level visuomotor policy has not learned sufficient placement precision from the available demonstrations. High-level replanning can retry these actions but cannot ensure accurate execution. In contrast, wrong object or order accounts for 8 of 11 failed trials of fine-tuned MolmoBot and 3 of 4 of fine-tuned π0.5, which together produce 11 zero-score trials.

Figure 9. Failure modes on Crossword. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. Wrong object, order, or place accounts for 36 of 39 unsuccessful trials of the fine-tuned baselines, whose rollouts often follow the training word or misorder letters. In contrast, 25 of 31 unrecovered failures across the Atomic Policy variants are grasp or place errors, and four trials succeed after recovery. Together with Tab. 4, these results support the benefit of explicit guidance and closed-loop planning for both ID execution and OOD generalization: Atomic + MolmoBot raises task score from 30.0 to 82.5 on ID trials and from 0.0 to 72.5 on OOD trials. Atomic + DP achieves the highest task scores in both conditions (91.3 ID and 90.0 OOD), showing that a point-guided policy can perform well on a task with strong language-grounding and sequencing demands.

papers.title: Atomic Policy: Composing Atomic Manipulation Skills with Agentic Reasoning
papers.tldr: Atomic Policy combines VLM reasoning, symbolic planning, and feedback-guided skill execution to enable recovery-aware long-horizon robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module. Without any external plugin module adopted, our end-to-end framework with the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance boosts the accuracy and efficiency of WAMs. Without using any private embodied training data, our AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple public robotic manipulation benchmarks including LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency.
authors: Hongcheng Zhang, Lei Sun, Songxuan Liu, Tengteng Pan, Yuqiang Zhai, Xianglong Xu, Jianya Guo, Xiao Song
bullets: Existing WAMs rely on implicit attention, limiting action-relevant prediction and control.
AG-WAM introduces three plug-and-play modules: content-adaptive predictive, guidance-point visual, and state-conditioned text attention.
The framework is end-to-end and requires no external plugin modules or private embodied training data.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, with improved training and inference efficiency.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable simultaneous processing of egocentric video and textual target descriptions to produce action commands for embodied tracking platforms. However, these platforms rarely move exactly as commanded, in part due to unexpected environmental disturbances such as wind, unleveled terrain, and road bumps. Here we study how such models handle uncommanded egomotion. First, we explore performance across diverse disturbances by benchmarking three tracking VLAs on three datasets. We find that models differ in which environmental disturbances hurt them most, but all are sensitive to sudden target loss. Tracing egomotion from pixels to emitted actions, we identify two gaps. In representation, motion is reliably recovered through explicit relations between frames, but aggressive compression of past frames weakens small-motion readouts. In action, large rotations do reach the decision state, yet the decoded direction carries only a few percent of a mirrored rotation's effect on the turn. Targeting both gaps, we fine-tune one model, Uni-NaVid, on data amounting to just 1.7% of its original training set in a ladder of analysis-motivated variants. These gain 5-22 points after target-loss without degrading clean success; after a smooth loss, the best one improves success by 72% (relative), recovering 76% of its gap to clean. We also show that targeted fine-tuning improves recovery partly via a text-mediated action dependency, without new architecture, large-scale data collection or training from scratch.
authors: Dan Zlotnikov, Nadav Alali, Ohad Ben-Shahar
bullets: Benchmarks three tracking VLAs across three datasets and diverse disturbances.
All models are sensitive to sudden target loss, though disturbance susceptibility varies.
Explicit cross-frame relations recover motion, while aggressive frame compression weakens small-motion perception.
Large rotations reach the decision state, but their decoded turn direction has little effect relative to mirrored rotations.
Analysis-driven fine-tuning on 1.7% of original training data improves target-loss recovery while preserving clean performance; gains are strongest after smooth loss.

papers.abstract: Robot teams can split workloads or combine complementary bodies, but only if each robot leaves the shared world in a state its teammate can use. Existing multi-robot benchmarks emphasize task allocation and skill sequencing, rarely testing whether the resulting physical states are usable. To evaluate collective physical capability, we introduce DeCoNav-Act, a benchmark for language-guided multi-robot mobile manipulation in a shared physics simulation. Its 350 homogeneous and 150 heterogeneous tasks, each verified by joint reference execution, span two coordination mechanisms: parallel workloads in shared space and physical dependencies in which one robot establishes a condition for a teammate to use. Beyond team success, DeCoNav-Act measures path efficiency and handoff coverage and success, and adds a diagnostic from verified pre-handoff states. Evaluating sensor-grounded adaptations of ASPIRE and RAX and our agent CoMoMa, we find that with GPT-5.6-luna no method completes a task, at most 8.8% of dependencies are reached, and even from pre-handoff states no handoff is completed; with GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa establishes the condition in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% succeed.
authors: Yunzi Wu, Sunyao Zhou, Xiaotao Zhang, Yucheng Deng, Yuehao Huang, Lin Qian, Xuanrui Cui, Xinhai Li, Chenjia Bai, Hongqing Chu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Introduces 500 language-guided mobile-manipulation tasks: 350 homogeneous and 150 heterogeneous.
Covers parallel workloads in shared spaces and physical dependencies where one robot prepares a condition for another.
Measures team success, path efficiency, handoff coverage and success, plus verified pre-handoff-state diagnostics.
Evaluations show no complete tasks with GPT-5.6-luna; dependencies were reached in at most 8.8% of cases and no handoffs succeeded.
With GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa established dependency conditions in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% resulted in successful handoffs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.
authors: Sichen Wu, Qian Sun, Mengfan Liu, Weikai Qin, Bike Zhu, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level motion generation and physical execution in humanoid whole-body control.

On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, average success rises from 59.2% to 71.7%, a 12.5-point improvement over the supervised base VLA.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.

Adapts the world model and critic on real rollouts, then improves the actor with imagined-rollout PPO or critic-guided best-of-N selection.
Outperforms large-scale VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and reaches 75% average success on two real-world tasks versus 45% for π₀.₅.
World-model accuracy and speed, plus ablations, support jointly learning dynamics and value for better policies.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$. papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.
authors: Jialong Peng, Shihao Zhou, Feng Yan, Wen Xiao, Haozheng Wang, Wenqi Ren, Wenyuan Sheng, Jian Qiao, Jiaxu Miao, Lin Ma, Chao Yang
bullets: Addresses the data and annotation costs that limit existing robotic in-context learning methods.
Encodes demonstrated and completed interaction action–effect sequences into reusable visual-action memories.
Predicts the upcoming execution intent to retrieve relevant experience from memory.
Conditions a vision-language-action model with retrieved experience tokens and gated cross-attention.
Reports gains over a baseline across RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-robot experiments, including stronger improvements on unseen tasks.

Backbone outputs support action generation and next-step intent prediction. The intention decoder and intention predictor use residual MLPs. papers.tldr: MXI-MemICL enables robots to improve in-context manipulation by retrieving and using memories of prior demonstrations and interactions without extra pretraining or specialized annotations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) planners inherit semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models, but their reasoning is rarely grounded in 3D scene structure and its evolution over time. We introduce GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework for 3D spatiotemporal reasoning and planning. Multi-layer features from a 3D foundation model augment the vision-language backbone through gated cross-attention. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions into ordered, separately supervised latent states. An action expert generates trajectory proposals from these states and multi-layer scene features, and ranks them using scene-grounded, interacting score tokens. We also introduce NAVSIM 3DQA to train and evaluate metric 3D spatial and motion understanding. GeoVLDrive achieves 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. On NAVSIM 3DQA, the geometry-grounded backbone scores 89.2% overall, 4.6 percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. On LingoQA, the backbone achieves 68.6% Lingo-Judge accuracy.
authors: JiaHui Huang, Songyan Zhang, Hanbing Li, Hanchao Leng, Kuiyuan Yang, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the lack of 3D spatiotemporal grounding in vision-language-action planners.
Uses gated cross-attention to integrate multi-layer 3D foundation-model features with a vision-language backbone.
Structures reasoning into supervised latent states covering future geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions.
Generates and ranks trajectory proposals with an action expert and scene-grounded interacting score tokens.
Reports 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 89.2% on the proposed NAVSIM 3DQA benchmark.

papers.abstract: Robot in-context learning (ICL) enables a policy to perform unseen tasks by following contextual demonstrations, without task-specific fine-tuning. This is increasingly valuable as large language models reasoning at low frequency can specify tasks through demonstrations and delegate high-frequency execution to such a policy. However, methods conditioned on human videos are bounded by scarce human-robot pairs, while those conditioned on robot demonstrations accept only one or two source types at limited scale. We present Any2Act, a foundation model for robot ICL. Our key insight is that a demonstration should be expressed in the camera layout and action space of the robot that performs it (the executor), not of whoever provided it (the demonstrator). This unified embodiment-grounded representation decouples learning to follow from admitting a new source. Any2Act learns to follow once, from robot-to-robot pairs that already take this form in 1.2M real trajectories spanning 10K tasks. Human videos, simulation, UMI, and other robots are then translated into this representation, and source-routed adapters trained on only a few hundred pairs each absorb the residual gap while the pretrained model stays frozen. For long horizons, a training-free tracker feeds only the demonstration window around the executor's progress, bounding the context and rolling back to redo failed steps. From a single demonstration, Any2Act achieves 57.5% success on unseen tasks without fine-tuning, exceeding VLAs fine-tuned on 50 demonstrations per task; other demonstrators retain 74-91% of the success achieved with the executor's own demonstrations.
authors: Ziang Ren, Zifan Wang, Zhuoyang Li, Benhao Qin, Haoyang Li, Qingtao Liu, Xuchuan Chen, Zekun Qi, He Wang, Yanchao Yang, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses limited scalability of robot ICL from scarce human–robot pairs and narrowly supported demonstration sources.
Represents every demonstration according to the executor’s camera layout and action space, decoupling task following from demonstration-source integration.
Pretrains on 1.2M real trajectories spanning 10K tasks, then uses source-routed adapters trained on a few hundred pairs per source while freezing the base model.
Uses a training-free progress tracker to provide bounded demonstration windows and roll back failed long-horizon steps.
Achieves 57.5% success from a single demonstration on unseen tasks; other sources retain 74–91% of executor-demonstration performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Model overview. Bottom left: progress tracking advances the window along the execution and rolls it back to an earlier phase after a failure. Bottom middle: source-routed adapters (SRA) act only on demonstration tokens, leaving the pretrained model unchanged.

Figure 2. Demonstration sources. Top: robot-to-robot pairs from routine data collection supply pretraining; recordings of the same task are VLM-filtered and grouped, and any two form a pair. Bottom: human videos (via agentic ego2sim), UMI, and other robots are translated into the unified embodiment-grounded representation and read through source-routed adapters.

papers.title: Any2Act: Scaling In-Context Robot Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrations
papers.tldr: Any2Act is a robot in-context learning foundation model that unifies heterogeneous demonstrations in the executor robot’s viewpoint and action space, achieving strong zero-fine-tuning performance on unseen tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than behavior-disrupting attacks: rather than merely causing task failures or local action deviations, they must sustain closed-loop redirection to complete an attacker-specified multi-step task. To reliably induce such behaviors, existing methods typically rely on high poisoning rates to obtain sufficient target-trajectory supervision. However, high poisoning rates may compromise clean-task performance, whereas low rates leave target-trajectory supervision scarce and backdoor learning vulnerable to interference from dominant clean-task updates. To resolve this trade-off at low poisoning rates, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action. Stage I freezes the policy and uses differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision to optimize a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale, strengthening trigger-target associations from limited poisoned demonstrations. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II applies source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to decouple clean and backdoor updates and mitigate their interference, followed by learned column-wise calibration and analytic fusion into a unified policy. Experiments on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_0$, and $\pi_{0.5}$ across four LIBERO suites show consistent gains over all evaluated attack baselines. With only 1% poisoned data, our method achieves 86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial. Real-robot trials also demonstrate trajectory-level hijacking.
authors: Simin Huang, Jiawei Chen, Shaolong Zhu, Qiwei Liang, Zhaoxia Yin
bullets: Targets trajectory-level backdoors that redirect robots through attacker-specified multi-step tasks, rather than causing isolated failures.
Stage I optimizes a 3D trigger’s texture, position, and scale using differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision.
Stage II uses source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation, column-wise calibration, and analytic fusion to reduce interference between clean and backdoor learning.
Across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, π0, and π0.5 on four LIBERO suites, the method outperforms evaluated attack baselines.
On OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial with 1% poisoning, it reaches 86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success; real-robot trials also show trajectory hijacking.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our two-stage framework. Stage I (top): With the VLA policy frozen, we optimize a 3D trigger’s texture, translation, and scale through differentiable rendering, guided by visual attention, language attention, and target-action supervision. Stage II (bottom): With the optimized trigger fixed, clean and poisoned demonstrations selectively update serial Clean-LoRA and Trigger-LoRA adapters, respectively. Clean-reference gradient projection mitigates conflicting Trigger-LoRA updates. Learned column-wise coefficients calibrate Trigger-LoRA before both adaptations are analytically fused into a single dense VLA policy.

Figure 1. Trajectory-level backdoor attacks under limited poisoning. (a,b) Target success rate (TSR) and clean success rate (CSR) across poisoning rates on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBEROSpatial. At 1% poisoning, Ours achieves 86.4% TSR and 95.2% CSR, exceeding the strongest baseline by 71.6 and 3.6 percentage points, respectively. (c) GoBA and BackdoorVLA-VT use fixed triggers and mixed clean–poisoned training with shared parameter updates. (d) Ours optimizes a 3D trigger and decouples clean and backdoor adaptation through source-selective dual-LoRA updates, followed by parameter fusion into a single unified policy.

Figure 5. Simulated trajectory redirection. Each clean/triggered pair uses the same task instruction. Filmstrips show successive frames; right panels show 3D end-effector paths (green: clean; red: triggered). Attack targets: a cup (top) and a can (bottom).

Figure 4. Cumulative stage completion on LIBERO-Spatial at 1% poisoning: (a) OpenVLA-OFT; (b) π0. Curves give the percentage of 500 triggered episodes completing each successive stage. Stableplacement success is strict TSR.

Figure 3. Gradient conflict and interference (OpenVLA-OFT, LIBERO-Spatial, 1% poisoning). (a) Clean–trigger gradient cosine distributions: shared Single-LoRA (Original) vs. Ours; negative values indicate conflict. (b) Clean-to-trigger (Hc→t) and reverse (Ht→c) interference rates (%; lower is better). Error bars in (b): standard error of the mean (SEM).

papers.title: Sparse Poison, Strong Hijack: Efficient Trajectory-Level Backdoors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Only 1\% Poisoning
papers.tldr: A two-stage vision-language-action backdoor method enables sustained multi-step trajectory hijacking with only 1% poisoned demonstrations while largely preserving clean-task performance.

papers.abstract: Training humanoid vision-language-action (VLA) models relies heavily on costly real-robot teleoperation. Recent efforts convert egocentric human demonstrations into humanoid training data. However, most methods still require wearable motion trackers and leave important hand-object interaction cues implicit. Many also mix in real-robot teleoperation data for VLA post-training. These dependencies limit scalable data collection, while implicit interaction cues make precise contact harder to learn. To overcome these limitations, we propose EgoLoAF, the first paradigm to derive all training data for humanoid loco-manipulation directly from egocentric demonstrations without wearable motion trackers. We post-train the VLA on the converted data alone, without real-robot teleoperation demonstrations, and use explicit hand-object interaction cues to guide action generation. Specifically, to obtain humanoid action targets, we estimate torso motion from recorded camera poses and reconstruct both hand trajectories from video. From the same recording, we use each hand's current pose relative to the object to represent hand-object affordances. During post-training, we inject these affordances into the action expert through cross-attention while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen. Additionally, we release 128,400 egocentric demonstration episodes spanning 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, together with converted humanoid action trajectories and rendered robot-view observations. Across four real-world tasks, EgoLoAF nearly achieves teleoperation performance (73.1 vs. 74.4 in mean Task Progress Score), while achieving a mean 4.03 times improvement in data-collection efficiency.
authors: Yiming Zeng, Jiangyuxuan Dai, Yuheng Na, Tan Zhu Xuan, Zihan Lin, Xinfang Qi, Shijian Zhang, Chengqi Shi, Yihan Kuang, Zhide Zhong, Junjie He, Junfeng Li, Zimu Han, Naipeng Li, Haoang Li
bullets: Addresses costly teleoperation, wearable motion-tracker requirements, and implicit hand-object interaction cues in humanoid VLA training.
Estimates torso motion and reconstructs both hand trajectories from egocentric video to create humanoid action targets.
Encodes each hand’s pose relative to objects as affordances and injects them into the action expert via cross-attention while freezing the vision-language backbone.
Releases 128,400 episodes covering 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, including converted trajectories and rendered robot-view observations.
Across four real-world tasks, reaches a mean Task Progress Score of 73.1 versus 74.4 for teleoperation and improves data-collection efficiency by 4.03×.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of EgoLoAF, a novel data collection paradigm for humanoids. Top: We release 128,400 egocentric demonstration episodes spanning 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, collected without wearable motion trackers. Bottom left: We convert these demonstrations into rendered robot-view observations, torso and hand action targets, and current hand–object affordances. The action targets supervise the action expert, while the affordances condition action generation. Post-training uses no real-robot teleoperation demonstrations, and the vision-language model (VLM) remains frozen. Bottom right: Across four real-world tasks, EgoLoAF nearly matches the teleoperation-trained baseline in mean Task Progress Score (TPS; 73.1 vs. 74.4), while more than quadrupling data-collection efficiency on average (4.03×).

Figure 2 Pipeline of EgoLoAF. (a) Hand reconstruction and camera-to-torso mapping produce future torso and hand action targets in the current torso frame. (b) Monocular depth is scale-aligned with reconstructed hand geometry for object-pose estimation. Current entity poses and object-relative hand poses are encoded as hand–object affordance (HOA) tokens. (c) Human hands and forearms are replaced with rendered robot counterparts. (d) With the VLM frozen, the trainable action expert predicts action chunks from rendered observations, instructions, and current state, conditioned on HOA tokens through cross-attention. The targets in (a) provide action supervision.

Figure 5 Comparison with teleoperation. a Mean TPS (0–100, ↑), aggregated across evaluation batches of 20 trials per task. EgoLoAF uses 150 egocentric human demonstrations per task; robot training data match their frame counts. Both methods use spatial feedback; the teleoperation baseline has no affordance input. b Acquisition person-hours at matched training-frame budgets (↓): one collector for ego data and two for teleoperation. Arrow labels give the teleoperation/ego person-hour ratio for each task.

Figure 4 Real-world humanoid loco-manipulation. Task 1 tests grasping, torso turning, and precise placement of a tissue pack into a box. Task 2 combines turning, squatting, and bending to place a tissue pack into a low bin. Task 3 tests bimanual coordination and turning when placing both plush toys into a tray. Task 4 combines walking, half-squatting, placement inside a cabinet, and closing both doors. Each evaluation batch contains 20 trials per task for each policy.

papers.title: EgoLoAF: Learning Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations with Hand-Object Affordances
papers.tldr: EgoLoAF trains humanoid loco-manipulation VLA models solely from egocentric videos by reconstructing robot actions and explicitly modeling hand-object affordances, achieving near-teleoperation performance with substantially more efficient data collection.

papers.abstract: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.
authors: Kaipeng Fang, Yuhao Wang, Ji Zhang, Yunsong Zhou, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
bullets: Targets failures when agents invoke policies outside their reliable start-state region, termed the policy’s handoff boundary.
Boundary-Explicit Training uses contact segments with diverse start poses to create a wider, well-defined boundary communicated through a simple protocol.
Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement uses successful system rollouts to extend the boundary to earlier task stages, enabling earlier handoffs.
Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, the system improves success by over 26 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes.
It also reduces API cost by 41.3% and execution time by 37.5%.

One episode of placing a cup on a coaster for (a) Harness VLA and for our system (b) before and (c) after self-improvement, where (b) and (c) start from the same scene and (a) shows another seed. The bar above each row shows who controls the robot over time on a shared time axis: gray for the agent, with darker strips for planner motions, white for the policy, and circles for handoffs. (a) Before and after self-improvement on all 50 tasks. (b) A second round on 30 randomly selected tasks. Percentages are relative to the previous stage.

Figure 3. Illustration of Boundary-Aware Policy Learning. (a) Boundary-Explicit Training collects contact-segment demonstrations D0 from diverse start poses near the target object and fine-tunes the policy on these segments. A simple handoff protocol then guides the agent to enter the policy’s reliable region, invoke it for one contact segment, and verify the outcome. (b) Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement collects successful system rollouts, removes suboptimal behaviors through curation, and re-executes the tasks to construct D1. Retraining the policy on D0 ∪ D1 expands its handoff boundary toward earlier task stages, enabling earlier handoffs with fewer language-model calls.
Figure 2. Illustration of agent-orchestrated robot manipulation, with the components of our method highlighted in color.

Figure 6. Ablations on the policy and the handoff protocol. + handoff protocol equips Harness VLA with our handoff protocol while keeping its whole-task policy, and + our policy equips it with our policy. Success rates on all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0 (C2R). Error bars show 95% Wilson intervals. The success axis starts at 60%.

papers.abstract: Time is a fundamental dimension of robotic intelligence: a robot may fail despite physically correct actions if it acts outside a valid time window, responds too slowly to an event, or fails to meet required throughput. Yet existing robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize spatial correctness and logical task completion, largely overlooking the temporal constraints of real-world applications. We present RoboClock, a unified benchmark for time-aware robotic manipulation featuring 60 tasks across five application domains. Mirroring these failure modes, RoboClock structures tasks around three types of temporal constraints: Temporal Window, Event-Reactive, and Throughput. Furthermore, RoboClock incorporates a Latency-Aligned evaluation protocol that continuously advances environment time during model inference and control-interface delays, paired with time-sensitive metrics. Evaluating over 30 methods, we find that the best-performing approach is the trained VLA, yet it achieves only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy-level tasks, with persistent challenges in generalization and transfer. These findings reveal fundamental limitations in current robotic systems and highlight the need to jointly optimize physical competence, temporal reasoning, and execution latency.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires semantic understanding and fine-grained scene perception for precise action prediction. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic priors, but low-dimensional action labels provide limited structural supervision. Some studies extend VLAs with visual generation tasks or adopt video-based world-action models (WAMs), but both approaches introduce appearance-reconstruction overhead, which is less relevant to planning. Native multimodal models offer an alternative to unify understanding and generation within one backbone. On this basis, we propose NativeDrive, a native encoder-free multimodal driving framework adapting the unified backbone for policy learning and introduce a dense supervision task tailored to driving. The Native Action Interface reuses the understanding expert's token-prediction interface for the discrete policy and adapts the generation expert for continuous policy. Driving Semantic Editing reuses the generation expert's editing capability for dense scene-structure supervision during training, while inference runs only the selected planning policy. NativeDrive achieves competitive planning performance among unified understanding-and-generation models on NAVSIM v1 and v2, with ablations validating its components' effectiveness. Code will be released.
authors: Zehua Fan, Qi Jiang, Wei Li, Kai Tang, Yue Jiang, Yujian Li, Bailin Li, Feng Gao, Yan Wang, Kun Zhan
bullets: Targets limited structural supervision from low-dimensional action labels in vision-language-action models.

Runs only the selected planning policy at inference, avoiding unnecessary visual reconstruction.
Achieves competitive planning performance among unified understanding-and-generation models on NAVSIM v1 and v2; ablations support its components.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are expected to inherit visual grounding from vision-language models, yet often reach for an object's training location after it has been moved. Across six VLAs, we identify two shortcuts: a scene shortcut, where the arm follows the scene's original task despite a new instruction, and an instruction shortcut, where the instruction retrieves the requested object's training location. In $\pi_{0.5}$, the instruction shortcut persists even though object-name attention follows the moved target. We call this Seeing Is Not Reaching. To determine whether this grounding is unused or overridden, we separately mask an image-mediated grounding pathway and a direct instruction-to-action pathway. Masking the grounding pathway eliminates reaches to moved targets, whereas masking the direct pathway increases them. Thus, grounding already guides action but is often overridden by the instruction shortcut, which acts through the direct pathway. We introduce Pathway-Separated Guidance (PSG), which amplifies grounding and suppresses the shortcut without training or external target locations. On LIBERO-PRO Object under Position perturbations, PSG raises the target-reaching rate from 22.0% to 52.6% and task success from 16.6% to 40.8%, while largely preserving performance on the original tasks.
authors: Qing Zhang, Xuesong Li, Zhaoyuan Yang, Changlin Song, Xinyu Tian, Jing Zhang
bullets: Across six VLAs, two shortcuts appear: scene-based behavior and instruction-based retrieval of an object’s original location.

Pathway-Separated Guidance (PSG) amplifies grounding and suppresses the instruction shortcut without external target locations or training.
On LIBERO-PRO Object position perturbations, PSG improves target-reaching from 22.0% to 52.6% and task success from 16.6% to 40.8%, while largely preserving original-task performance.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents translate user instructions and screenshots into executable actions. To learn executable actions, existing approaches often rely on explicit reasoning during training, which encourage over-reliance on specific reasoning patterns rather than generalizable action-relevant information. In this paper, we propose an implicit framework, RISE, which integrates action-relevant reasoning into implicit state representations to guide GUI action prediction. To this end, action-relevant reasoning is captured through three complementary supervision objectives: full-CoT state alignment preserves information across the reasoning process, action-distribution alignment encodes action preferences, and reasoning-to-action boundary alignment captures the representation immediately before action generation. In this case, our RISE effectively learns informative implicit representations, thereby improving the accuracy of next-action token prediction. RISE achieves 70.6\% accuracy on OSWorld-G, establishing state-of-the-art performance among compared 8B models with a 4.3-point gain over its backbone. Results across two distinct backbones and six diverse benchmarks further demonstrate its effectiveness in GUI grounding and action prediction. Our code is available on our project page.
authors: Enqi Liu, Zhi Gao, Liu Liu, Lifeng Fan, Liyuan Pan
bullets: Targets the limited generalization of GUI agents trained with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning.

Effectiveness is supported across two backbones and six diverse benchmarks for GUI grounding and action prediction.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents translate screenshots and user instructions into executable actions. Most existing approaches rely on vision-language models to generate actions as text, often leading to substantial inference latency due to autoregressive decoding. To address this inefficiency, we propose GUI-PRISM, a hybrid action decoder that directly predicts action types and structured arguments while retaining language generation for open-ended text. Unlike existing spatial decoding methods that primarily focus on target localization, GUI-PRISM extends direct prediction to action types and their associated arguments, enabling complete GUI action prediction. Specifically, GUI-PRISM employs field-specific queries to extract action-relevant semantic and spatial information from a shared multimodal feature bank. It further models dependencies among action components through conditional queries. Gated residual cross-attention refines these predictions using fine-grained multimodal information. GUI-PRISM achieves 95.1\% accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2, outperforming the strongest head-based spatial decoding method by 2.0 percentage points while delivering a 3.8$\times$ inference speedup over the baseline. On AndroidControl-v2 and MM-Mind2Web-v2, it improves complete-action accuracy by 4.8 and 0.7 percentage points while achieving 2.7$\times$ and 3.9$\times$ inference speedups over the baseline, respectively. Our code is available on our project page.
authors: Enqi Liu, Zhi Gao, Liu Liu, Lifeng Fan, Liyuan Pan
bullets: Targets the high latency of autoregressive text-based action decoding in GUI agents.
Uses field-specific queries over shared multimodal features to predict action types and arguments directly.
Models dependencies between action components with conditional queries and refines them using gated residual cross-attention.
Reports 95.1% ScreenSpot-v2 accuracy, with 2.0 percentage-point improvement and 3.8× speedup over the strongest baseline.
Also improves complete-action accuracy and achieves 2.7×–3.9× speedups on AndroidControl-v2 and MM-Mind2Web-v2.

figures.caption: Figure 2. GUI-PRISM architecture. (a) Given a screenshot I and instruction u, the shared VLM processes the input prefix P . The action head predicts the action type c, target coordinate p, and finite-valued arguments, while the LM generates open-ended text values when required. These outputs form the complete action a = (c, v,p). (b) The PRISM feature bank projects visual, contextual, and actionrelevant states into shared memory M . Field-specific suffixes Qk produce queries that incorporate preceding predictions and memory summaries, yielding memory-conditioned queries q̃k. (c) Each query reads M to produce base logits. Gated residuals derived from actionrelevant features MA and visual features MV refine them into final type and coordinate logits ℓc, ℓx, ℓy for field decoding.

papers.abstract: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/RoboHarness-RL/

Uses supervised fine-tuning on successful demonstrations, followed by task-outcome-rewarded multi-turn RL without VLA or world action models.
Introduces LiteHarness, a hierarchical-memory system that keeps multi-turn contexts compact while preserving task performance.
With Qwen3.5-9B, RL improves success on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Pro, and randomized unseen RoboTwin scenes.
RL reduces repetitive tool calls, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.

papers.abstract: Affordance grounding localizes where an agent should interact with an object to perform a task. Many everyday manipulation tasks, however, require bimanual affordance, in which two hands assume complementary and cooperative roles to accomplish a shared goal. Existing 3D affordance datasets primarily ground single interaction regions, and manually annotating dual-hand, cooperative contacts does not scale. To address this gap, we introduce DUALingo, a large-scale dataset for task-conditioned, role-aware bimanual 3D affordance grounding on diverse everyday objects. DUALingo represents each task as two cooperative, hand-agnostic roles, each grounded as a heatmap on the object surface. It contains 271K free-form tasks on 71K objects, generated by a fully automated pipeline of open-weight foundation models without human labeling. Expert ratings and a validated LLM judge confirm the quality of the resulting annotations. Trained on DUALingo, existing 3D affordance models learn to ground both cooperative roles from natural-language instructions, with the best-performing model achieving a more than threefold improvement in aIoU over the zero-shot baseline, from 10.3 to 37.8. Robotic manipulation demonstrations illustrate the actionability of the predicted bimanual affordances in performing cooperative tasks. These results position DUALingo as a scalable foundation for learning everyday bimanual affordances. Project page: https://nycu-pair-labs.github.io/DUALingo/
authors: Ming-Lun Lee, Yi-En Li, Feng-Dian Su, Ming-Han Lee, Kun-Ru Wu, Krzysztof Czarnecki, Yu-Chee Tseng

Expert ratings and a validated LLM judge support the quality of the generated annotations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new manipulation skills while retaining the ability to follow previously learned instructions. Experience replay (ER) can mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but retaining only a small number of historical expert frames per task leaves many old-instruction responses without direct supervision. Under limited replay, we observe a structured failure mode in which an earlier instruction can trigger a subsequently learned, competing goal. To address this gap, we propose Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA), which supplements expert replay with instruction-conditioned response preservation. At each task boundary, XIA freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions paired with current observations. This extends supervision beyond stored historical examples without requiring additional expert replay data. Experiments across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites demonstrate improved success rates and reduced forgetting compared with ER under identical historical expert-data budgets. Additional RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support the effectiveness of XIA.

bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when continual VLA learning uses only small historical expert-data budgets.

RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support its effectiveness.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.

It predicts action chunks in 25.1 ms on an A100, reported as 12.3–41.5× faster than representative WAMs.

papers.abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.
bullets: Targets recognizable, recurring stuck states in robot foundation models rather than random failures.
A language-model agent reads and writes the policy’s parameters, repurposing near-silent action-expert neurons as failure-triggered corrective switches.
Applied to the simulated pi0.5 policy, edits to roughly 0.0002% of parameters improved success on recurring failures, including after task fine-tuning.
Reversed and random edits support that improvements came from the intended corrective behavior.
Works best when failures are internally recognizable and a simple correction can resolve them.

papers.abstract: While recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate 3D geometry, how to effectively exploit it for precise and generalizable action prediction remains a central challenge. We introduce Hi3R-VLA, a 3D policy that grounds heterogeneous modalities - vision, language, and action - in explicit 3D geometry for robotic manipulation. Our model integrates spatially-aligned visual features and language conditioning into point cloud representations, enriching scene geometry with fine-grained, task-relevant semantics. It then anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D coordinate frame and uses 3D-RoPE enhanced action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine point features to model geometric relationships between action targets and observed points. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of semantic fusion within 3D and spatial alignment between observations and actions. With fewer than 250M trainable parameters, Hi3R-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa, RLBench, RoboTwin2, DexJoCo and DexSuite across diverse manipulation tasks and embodiments, from single-arm and dual-arm grippers to dexterous hands. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate its effectiveness in the physical world. The model, code and dataset are publicly released at https://cshizhe.github.io/projects/hi3r_vla.html.
authors: Shizhe Chen, Paul Pacaud, Cordelia Schmid
bullets: Addresses the challenge of effectively using 3D geometry for precise and generalizable action prediction in vision-language-action models.
Fuses spatially aligned visual features and language conditioning into point-cloud representations with task-relevant semantics.
Anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D frame and applies 3D-RoPE action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine features.
Analysis highlights the importance of 3D semantic fusion and spatial alignment between observations and actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across five manipulation benchmarks and effectiveness in real-robot evaluations, using fewer than 250M trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.
authors: Adri\`a Ruiz, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski, Tinne Tuytelaars, Sergi Masip
bullets: Studies Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under continual learning on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus.
Finds that OOD performance on previously learned tasks rapidly collapses despite stable in-domain performance.
Identifies shared representational drift across domain shifts, concentrated in multimodal and action features.
Linear probes show OOD features retain task-relevant information but become difficult to read, suggesting representation misalignment.
Shows that ID stability alone is insufficient for assessing continual-learning robustness.

papers.abstract: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) end-to-end systems have driven major progress in robot learning, yet they still face persistent barriers to dependable real-world deployment. In practice, these models often exhibit brittle generalization under distribution shift (i.e., novel objects, layouts, lighting, or contact conditions), limited physical and causal reasoning, and inconsistent fine-grained motor control. Critically, many VLA pipelines offer limited ways to express and audit what a robot must not do, making it difficult to provide assurance in safety-critical settings. These limitations constrain scalability, maintainability, and trust when robots move beyond controlled demonstrations. We propose Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI: a deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning and control with explicit, machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints. By combining knowledge-guided perception, constraint-aware symbolic planning, and hybrid learning, Embodied NeSy AI enables robots to reason about their environment, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements, thus supporting scalable, trustworthy robot deployment.
authors: Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Jonathan Francis, Alessandro Oltramari
bullets: End-to-end vision-language-action systems can be brittle under distribution shifts and weak in physical, causal, and fine-grained motor reasoning.
They provide limited mechanisms for specifying and auditing prohibited behavior, hindering safety-critical deployment.
The proposed paradigm integrates learned perception, planning, and control with machine-readable knowledge and formal constraints.
Knowledge-guided perception, constraint-aware symbolic planning, and hybrid learning support adaptation, compliance checking, and scalable deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models effectively learn action policies from robot demonstrations, but struggle to generalize to changes in object positions and task goals. General multimodal foundation models (MFMs) offer complementary scene understanding and spatial reasoning, but remain slow and unreliable for direct fine-grained control. To understand how MFMs can improve VLA spatial generalization, we conduct a systematic capability analysis across multiple VLA architectures using atomic-stage interventions, revealing that many failures stem from poor target grounding and global spatial routing, while local manipulation skills remain largely usable. Based on these findings, we propose MFM-VLA, a selective collaboration framework in which an MFM provides target grounding and spatial guidance, controllers execute free-space motion, and the VLA retains control over fine-grained manipulation. We fine-tune the VLA with action-chunk-level dense geometric captions and perturbed-state recovery data to improve local guidance following and recovery from unfamiliar handoff states. A development-calibrated capability router selects between direct VLA execution and MFM-assisted execution to avoid unnecessary intervention. Across LIBERO-PRO, ALOHA-Sim-PRO, RoboCasa365, and real-world chemistry tasks, MFM-VLA improves success rates by 14.9, 74.0, 3.6, and 30.9 percentage points, respectively, over the corresponding base VLA. The project page is available at https://tom-zgt.github.io/MFM-VLA
authors: Guangting Zheng, Shaoxuan Wang, Yu Yuan, Zhipeng Tang, Jiajun Deng, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: VLA failures often arise from inaccurate target grounding and global spatial routing, while local manipulation skills remain usable.
The framework selectively combines MFM guidance, controller-based free-space motion, and VLA fine-grained control.
Dense geometric captions and perturbed-state recovery data strengthen local guidance and recovery from unfamiliar handoff states.
A calibrated router invokes MFM assistance only when needed.
Success rates improve over base VLAs across simulated and real-world chemistry tasks, with gains ranging from 3.6 to 74.0 percentage points.
