papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of repeatedly collecting physical robot experience for policy improvement.
Uses a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that learns from logged data while ranking newly generated actions without assigning artificial returns.
Freezes the critic to provide group-relative value signals for optimizing fresh action candidates from the current flow policy.
Improves the initial VLA across RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, LIBERO, and a real-robot dexterous manipulation task.
Scope: relies on offline robot experience and generative resampling from flow-based VLA policies.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agent Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks whether these requirements are fulfilled, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Experiments on three spatial reasoning benchmarks and four VLM backbones show that PEPS improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that knowing what a query requires before execution makes tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more efficient.
bullets: Addresses under-committed query compilation, where systems execute before fully specifying what must be resolved.
Uses a typed FESM schema covering Frame, Entity, State, and Metric.
A Parser defines executable requirements; an Executor grounds only needed primitives via fixed geometric APIs; a Verifier enables early termination or targeted repair.
Across three benchmarks and four VLM backbones, PEPS improves accuracy while reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and latency.
The approach is training-free and focused on spatial reasoning with explicit geometric computation.

papers.abstract: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
bullets: Introduces 112 expert-authored tasks covering feature implementation, bug repair, and application generation.
Uses held-out scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions on consumer XR hardware.
Its test suite matches blinded expert judgments with 96.5% accuracy across 124 candidate applications.
Across 10 models, the strongest configuration reaches 50.9% overall Pass@1.
Common failures involve asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
authors: Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Reasoning and trajectory objectives prioritize different VLM structures, so pruning based on either alone can damage performance.
Action-expert MLP channels have more stable importance across denoising steps than query heads, with a small subset carrying most importance.
MoOP combines both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select expert MLP channels.
At 24.0% parameter reduction, it retains 94.0% of dense-model LingoQA performance and matches or slightly exceeds strong driving baselines.
At 39.4% reduction, it achieves 1.37× faster inference and 36.6% lower peak memory without post-pruning fine-tuning, while preserving competitive driving performance.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.
authors: Xiao-Ming Wu, Kang Liao, Yuexiao Ma, Taolin Zhang, Mingqian Zhou, Nuo Chen, Ziming Li, Yihang Luo, Rui Li, Zhonghua Wu, Tianyu Xie, Xiawu Zheng, Zhongang Cai, Zhi Hou, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Analyzes prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use in frontier-model robotic harnesses.
Finds that interfaces leveraging native visual reasoning and tool use outperform reliance on handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors.
Provides guidance on action representation and chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement.
Achieves 83.3% success on RoboLab-120 and succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot real-world manipulation trials.
Interventions suggest performance depends more on accurate spatial target estimation than explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the Robotic Agentic Loop. A robotic harness consists of four key dimensions: 1) Prompting, including task instructions and visual observations; 2) Planning, including context management, planning strategies, and model and reasoning effort selection; 3) Tool Use, including acting tools and policy models; and 4) Action Execution, including action formats, action chunking, and asynchronous execution. These dimensions operate within a closed-loop framework and form the design space systematically explored in Embo-Harness.

Figure 4. Overview of Embo-Harness. Embo-Harness is designed to leverage the model’s native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, failure-derived skills, or action priors. The harness takes task instructions and high-resolution visual observations as inputs to GPT-6-Astra with xhigh reasoning effort. The frontier model produces short, fixed-length chunks of absolute end-effector (EEF) actions. Short multi-action sequences and VLA refinement are further integrated as tools to enhance manipulation performance. Zoom in for best view of the demos.

Figure 2. Typical Robotic Harness Paradigms. (1) Tool/code-aspolicy harnesses leverage frontier models for high-level planning while relying on predefined tools or generated code for action execution. (2) Model-as-policy harnesses delegate action generation to specialized policy models. (3) Frontier-model-as-policy harnesses directly generate robot actions using frontier models. All three paradigms operate within a closed-loop framework, differing primarily in how robot actions are generated.

Figure 5. Real-world robotic setup for Embo-Harness. Our setup consists of a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot arm equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, a wrist-mounted ZED Mini camera, and an external ZED 2 camera. We illustrate the objects and workspace used for real-world tabletop manipulation tasks.

GPT Harness exhibits a broader trajectory distribution than π0.5 in the PCA projection, suggesting distinct motion patterns.

Figure 7. Trajectory Distribution Comparison between EEF Absolute and EEF Destination Control (20 tasks, 3 runs in RoboLab benchmark). We compare the distributions of (a) translation speed, (b) angular speed, and (c) acceleration magnitude, along with (d) PCA projections of rollout trajectories. Despite differences in motion magnitudes caused by their execution rules, the two strategies exhibit broadly similar distributional patterns and overlapping trajectory projections, suggesting shared spatial motion characteristics.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{WeaveVLA}, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.

Adds an auxiliary geometry-reconstruction objective to preserve spatial structure.
Achieves over 98% average success on LIBERO and improves performance on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world tasks, including under OOD perturbations.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $\pi_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.
bullets: Token approximation error is a poor routing signal: it can be 1.3–1.7× worse for action deviation than input novelty.
Novelty is measured by whether a token falls outside the calibration subspace, favoring action-relevant views such as the wrist camera.
The training-free method routes each token once per layer to either a low-rank or original MLP, enabling static-shape CUDA-graph execution.
On LIBERO, it accelerates the π₀.₅ prefix by up to 1.61× and remains 2.7–2.9× closer to the original policy than competing compression methods at equal compute.
Closed-loop task success is preserved.

(b) Eager execution, same score and exact fraction: deciding once per token and layer instead of once per product moves the whole front to the right.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token routing for VLA prefix compute directly targets embodied vision-language-action efficiency.
papers.title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
papers.tldr: NoveltyGate speeds up VLA prefix computation by routing novel tokens through the exact MLP, outperforming error-based token selection while preserving task success.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $\pi_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.
authors: Hengzhi Jiang, Haixu Liu, Jindou Jia, Tinglan Wang, Shaobo Chen, Yiren Zhao, Ziyang Rao, Laiyuan Cui, Jiaxin Dong, Yin Ma, Hai Wei, Jiaqi Bai, Tuo An, Xinyu Zhou, Hao Ban, Hongdong Zhu, Yanqi Wang, Jiaqi Dou, Nuo Qian, Qi Liu, Bin Jin, Chang Wu, Qingfeng Li, Hui Yang, Weiyu Guo, Dicong Qiu, Qi Gao, Jianwei Niu, Kai Wen, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of unimodal, time-factorized Gaussian initialization for diverse manipulation tasks.
Uses a conditional Boltzmann machine to assign energies to binary source states, trained with an offline listwise objective based on resulting action quality.
Decodes the learned energy landscape through an Ising solver into continuous noise, followed by standard flow integration; the base VLA remains unchanged.
Improves π₀.₅ across three benchmarks, outperforming compared baselines and noise-optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, and ranking second to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus.
Also shows gains with noise-adapted fine-tuning, action-to-action warm starts, and the SmolVLA backbone.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Boltz-Flow. Right. A conditioning module replaces the Gaussian source of a frozen flow-matching policy. It maps the robot observation and instruction to a flow source, which the frozen flow heads integrate into an action chunk for the robot. Left. The CIM searches the hidden layer for low-energy binary states. A midpoint-Gaussian-quantile mapping then decodes these states (0-1 embedding) into the continuous flow source.

papers.abstract: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

papers.abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.
bullets: Benchmarks 11 laboratory and household tasks across six embodiment settings, from imagined-robot chat to simulated robot-arm control.
Pairs benign instructions with latent hazards and includes benign controls, safe alternatives, and operator pushback.
Across six VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates increase from 14% in chat to 47% in simulation; the rise is largely driven by open-weight models.
Models identify hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and respond to pushback more often in robot-control settings than in chat.
The safest models can also be overcautious on benign tasks, and text-only safety evaluations do not predict robot-controller behavior.

papers.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
authors: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Addresses learning actions from diverse videos that lack actions or share no common action space.
Uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse- and forward-dynamics models, connected by learnable dynamics registers.
Trains on counterfactual video pairs differing only in motion to distill compact latent actions without video generation.
Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on LARY for action classification and control, and transfer motion across robots, scenes, and human-to-robot settings.
The PAWlicy pretraining paradigm achieves a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over pi_0.5 on both evaluated real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.
authors: Le Yang, Haoyang Lyu, Honglei Jin, Wenshuo Chen, Jiawei Liang, Wenqiang Wang, Yutao Yue, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Multi-skill integration is difficult because joint fine-tuning and parameter merging can degrade individual skills during closed-loop control.
The method analyzes task-conditioned expert updates and identifies dominant, sometimes opposing directions in a shared response subspace.
GeoMerge-OPD combines response-space regularization via G-isometry, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation from independently fine-tuned task experts.
Experiments across two VLA backbones show balanced skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, including under perturbations.
The approach is evaluated on the reported benchmarks and focuses on mitigating behavioral interference during skill integration.

papers.abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
authors: Jiawei Guo, Yu Huang, Dijiang Dong, Yue Liu, Peiran Ren, Wei Shen
bullets: Evaluates instruction fidelity across eight manipulation tasks with 6–12 instruction branches per task, while keeping the initial scene and robot state fixed.
Branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation details to isolate behavioral adaptation to language changes.
Task-specific checkers assess terminal outcomes and execution compliance using trajectories, contacts, and event sequences.
RoboInF-4K contains 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived motion and contact annotations.
Evaluations of four manipulation or inference-only agents reveal a gap between task success and faithful instruction execution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.

The same fixed supervision rules improved four other frozen policies by 8–10 percentage points on a shared 50-scene subset.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
authors: Hyeonjae Kim, Jeongsol Kim, Sunwoo Park, Chanyu Moon, Yoojin Oh, Youngjun Jun, Kyumin Choi, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Asynchronous action generation reduces latency but stale observations cause performance degradation, especially during failed policy rollouts.
DelayOPSD compares a synchronous teacher using the current observation with a delayed student using an earlier observation and in-progress actions.
The student imitates the teacher throughout the iterative denoising process, with training performed on the policy’s own delayed rollouts.

DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among compared methods across LIBERO and Kinetix and improves real-robot success from 46% to 62%, without extra deployment modules.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.

papers.abstract: Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments. A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control. We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction. CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data. A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both. To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller. Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions. In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings. In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.

papers.abstract: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception which and further introduces spatial distance perception where and geometric structure perception how with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance when to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA.

An adaptive spatial-geometric guidance mechanism determines when these cues should influence action prediction.
Experiments in real-world and simulated settings demonstrate its effectiveness and superior performance.

papers.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

papers.abstract: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
authors: Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Ye Lu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Mean-instruction and task-conditioned velocities align strongly (cosine ≈0.94–0.95), so references are not pure harmful bias.
Averaging eight completed-state references leaves 98.3% of the individual mean norm, indicating a large shared transport component.
The proposed diagnostic and shrinkage analysis link correction strength to reference signal-to-noise.
Geometry-calibrated correction removes only the component orthogonal to task velocity and predicts a task-dependent scale.
In controlled RoboTwin experiments, centered orthogonal correction achieved 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one sweep; gains were non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.
authors: Wenhao Li, Yu Han, Xiu Su, Dehao Wu, Keke Huang, Shan You, Fei Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses WAM failures in challenging scenes and the high latency and cost of invoking System 2 at every step.
Trains a lightweight judgment token with cross-fitted temporal-difference learning from binary rollout success/failure signals.
Uses calibrated success probabilities to switch between WAM control and System 2 assistance chunk by chunk.
Distills System 2 takeover trajectories into the WAM to repair capability gaps and support later standalone operation.
Mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating aim to preserve existing capabilities during self-evolution.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL) framework. (1) Non-Invasive Calibrated Self-Assessment (Sec. 3.2): A lightweight judgment token J attends to the frozen WAM’s internal video and action streams through a causal mask and token-gated adapters, predicting calibrated success probability qθ via our proposed cross-fitted TD learning without affecting action predictions. (2) Adaptive System 1 & 2 Takeover (Sec. 3.3): At each decision step, qθ schedules control chunk by chunk; the WAM hands control to a GPT-6-Astra-based agent when qθ < τ and reclaims execution once confidence recovers above τback. (3) Capability-Gap Consolidation (Sec. 3.4): Keeping πbase frozen, successful agent takeovers (Dhelp) are combined with mastered-skill anchor data—the WAM’s own confident successes (Down) and pre-training replay (Dreplay)—into Dmix to train a separate repaired action expert πrep, distilling System 2’s recovery skills into System 1. (4) Erosion-Free Confidence-Gated Deployment (Sec. 3.5): During standalone deployment, πbase dynamically switches to πrep when base confidence qbase drops below τ and reclaims control once confidence recovers, repairing hard states without degrading mastered skills or invoking System 2 (scores shown: Fast-WAM on RoboTwin 2.0, 1 round).

Figure 4. System 1 & 2 success across agent call budgets (Fast-WAM on RoboTwin 2.0), plugging our judgment token vs. Spotter Screener [24], Sentinel (STAC) [1], FAVOR Verifier [32], SAFE [11], and Random Invocation into the same pipeline.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $\pi_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $\pi_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
authors: Yanlong Chen, Thongthornpatch Chamadol, Yichen Guo, Yunfei Gao, Mohan Liu, Addison Lin Wang, Yawei Li
bullets: Standard PTQ fails at ≤2 bits because static calibration misses quantization-induced state drift and layer-wise reconstruction does not reflect action-generation needs.
LoopQ uses on-policy rollouts from the quantized policy for drift-aware calibration.
Readout-aligned fine-tuning updates lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors while keeping trellis codes fixed.
At 2-bit weights, LoopQ reaches 60.4% on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7 versus 61.8% full precision; 1-bit π₀.₅ completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks.
The 2-bit π₀.₅ model uses integer kernels on Jetson AGX Thor, reducing weight storage by 4.1× and memory by 44%, and remains close to full precision on three real-arm tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of LoopQ. Format. A 16-bit window slides over the frozen trellis code stream and indexes a 512-entry table T . A row scale s multiplies each output. Step 1. Closed-loop calibration adds trace-normalized lighting, crop and on-policy statistics to Hdemo. Step 2. Readout-aligned fine-tuning trains only T , s and the normalization weights to match the teacher’s readout o and velocity v.

Figure 2. The two failure causes of 2-bit VLAs and their correction. (a) Decomposition of the deployment input shift across modules, indicating that on-policy states outweigh visual perturbations. (b) Layer-wise effect of closed-loop calibration relative to demonstration calibration. On-policy error decreases across the action head (top) and in 427 of 432 layers. Each 1% added on demonstrations removes 4.6% on on-policy states in the head (bottom). (c) Action-expert readout error on identical inputs from the pictured rollout, in the two leading directions of both models’ errors (top) and over policy calls (bottom). LoopQ halves the mean distance to full precision.

Full precision and LoopQ succeed, whereas the 2-bit post-training baseline fails. (b) Cause 1: quantization drift. End-effector trajectories on the initial frame. The 2-bit baseline departs from the fullprecision trajectory and halts, while LoopQ tracks it to completion. (c) Cause 2: readout corruption. (d) LIBERO-Plus success with linear layers at 2 bits per weight. (e) Storage and memory of π0.5 with 8-bit activations on Jetson AGX Thor.

Figure 4. LoopQ (2-bit π0.5) on an AgileX Piper arm. papers.abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/
authors: Tianle Zeng, Hanjing Ye, Bingyi Xia, Yuchen Zhou, Zibo Zhang, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling route execution with continuous follower- and scene-aware adaptation.
Uses a structured multimodal policy with an explicit Path, learned Pace for route progress, and Residual for local adaptation.
Introduces LeadInfra for closed-loop Unreal Engine data generation and LeadBench with 108 held-out episodes.
Trains on an approximately 4M-sample corpus and reaches 39.6% task success, the highest among evaluated policies on LeadBench.
Transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Overview of LeadInfra. LeadInfra compositionally combines route geometry, scenes, follower behaviors, appearances, and target–distractor configurations to generate diverse closed-loop robot-leading episodes. A causal expert converts realized interaction consequences into robot-action supervision without directly observing hidden behavior programs.

Figure 3 Overview of LeadVLA. Temporal front/rear observations, language, and route context produce 24 shared action queries. The route is also retained as an explicit Path reference. Pace regulates route progress, Residual provides local adaptation, and selected follower semantics couple only to Residual. A deterministic Path Composer outputs the final robot-local waypoints.

Figure 5 Progressive LeadBench evaluation. Columns increase route-execution difficulty from clean conditions (Core) to moderate (Easy) and stronger interference (Constrained); rows compare single-person leading with multiperson cases containing distractors. The progression increasingly couples local route recovery with follower-aware control.

Figure 1 Keep the route, adapt the execution. A robot leads a language-designated tourist to the departure terminal along a planned route. The sequence shows (1) normal leading, (2) slowing down as the follower pauses for a phone call, (3) waiting while the follower briefly disengages to interact with another pedestrian, and (4) resuming afterward. The nominal route remains unchanged, while the robot adapts how it executes the route to the follower’s evolving behavior.

Figure 6 Real-world evaluation settings. The physical experiments retain the core interaction structure of LeadBench: Core evaluates clean route execution, Easy adds local route interference, and multi-person settings include a distractor.

Figure 7 Representative assets in LeadInfra. LeadInfra combines diverse indoor and outdoor environments with multiple robot embodiments, compositional human appearances, sensing modalities, and physical scene assets. These assets support the route, interaction, and scene variations introduced in the following sections.

Figure 9 LeadInfra scene composition and episode generation. Starting from diverse environments (Sec. B.1), LeadInfra samples a nominal route (Sec. B.2), instantiates robot and human actors, composes follower-interaction programs and local scene variation (Secs. B.3 and B.4), and executes the resulting task in closed loop. A causal expert (Sec. B.5) generates robot supervision from realized interaction evidence rather than directly from hidden follower programs.

Figure 10 Human-expert teleoperation interface. Operators control the robot online while observing the same front/rear visual inputs, language instruction, and nominal route information available to evaluated policies. No simulator-privileged state is exposed through the interface.

Figure 8 Dynamic referent reassignment in LeadInfra. The designated follower changes from Target A to Target B while both people remain in the scene and the nominal route is unchanged. After reassignment, subsequent robot behavior should depend on the newly designated follower. Colored boxes and identity labels are shown only for visualization and are never provided to the policy.

Figure 12 Representative real-world closed-loop sequences. Rows correspond to Core-S, Core-M, Easy-S, and Easy-M. The overlaid speed gauge visualizes changes in the robot’s execution response over time. Across settings, LeadVLA largely preserves route-level progress while adapting its execution to the designated follower and local route conditions.

Figure 14 Ignoring distractor behavior during real-world leading. Target A remains the designated follower throughout the sequence. papers.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
authors: Yiheng Du, Jingqi Tian, Xu Jiang, Jiexuan Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Zecheng Tang, Jian Zhang
bullets: Maintains task state and subgoals across visual updates so remembered object identities and progress guide current actions.
At each update, infers an event, revises the task state, grounds a subgoal in the current scene, and generates an action.
Jointly trains one VLA to reason and act without an external reasoning model.
Uses exact likelihoods of memory text tokens for GRPO refinement from rollout rewards while keeping action generation deterministic.
Reports 66.46% on RoboMME, 79.83% on its Reference category, and 90.08% on LIBERO-Mem; it doubles RoboMME success versus an otherwise identical non-recurrent model.

papers.abstract: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user says "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Janet Wang, Xingchen Zhao, Zhenyu Zhang, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses failures from unknown motion drift, mid-task instruction changes, and misheard requests that ordinary policy instructions cannot fix.
Uses separate instruction and feedback channels, agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens, and counterfactual feedback; only the policy’s action module reads the feedback.
On LIBERO, success improves from 0.09 to 0.87 under constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under random drift.
The system handles changed or misheard requests in 0.91–1.00 of episodes while using 55 seconds and 8k tokens per success, versus 2.1 minutes and over 1M tokens for an acting agent.
Transfers across policies, agents, robots, and multi-arm tasks; agent replacement or improvement requires no policy retraining.

papers.abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
authors: Zikang Wen, Yuning Zhang, Dong Yuan
bullets: Shared-GPU inference reduces the cost of deploying many task-specific VLA policies, especially with LoRA adapters sharing a frozen backbone.
MotionExec triggers observations using motion structure in predicted action chunks to overlap inference with buffered execution.
SlackBatch uses per-robot slack and estimated GPU workload to decide when to wait, batch requests, or dispatch them.
With up to 96 simulated robots, it reduces mean episode stall by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points across evaluated settings.
Backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

papers.abstract: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.
authors: Jinlin Liu, Yumeng He, Qihan Huang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Han Peng
bullets: Skill-removed fine-tuning causes context misalignment (CoMi), with agents referencing removed skills across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1.
CGSI detects unsupported references in demonstration trajectories and masks or rewrites the affected sentences before fine-tuning.
CGSI reduces test-time CoMi by 72.5–94.6% while preserving task success.
It matches reinforcement-learning-based internalization baselines with substantially less training time and lowers processing costs versus large-scale trajectory auditing.
Scope: results are demonstrated on the three evaluated benchmarks and focus on sentence-level reference correction.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.
authors: Yue Huang, Tianshan Zhang, Zeyu Zhang, Jayeon Kang, Akide Liu, Sungjoon Choi, Dacheng Tao, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses limited long-range history and high inference cost in autoregressive diffusion motion generation.
Uses a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture with local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory.
Persistent content memory converts compressed motion history, state changes, and text features into dynamically updated content slots.

Optimized execution with CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and simplified flow reduces reported median latency from 1685.35 ms to 276.14 ms, with a 6.138× paired speedup and identical tested outputs and states.
Evaluations cover long-horizon terminal control, short-horizon spatial and text-motion matching, and real-world interactive control on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.
authors: Aditya Makineni, Amitesh Sahoo, Qing Tian
bullets: Addresses the loss of inference-time deliberation when VLA backbones are made lightweight.
Uses fast low-level and slow high-level latent states, updated from motor/proprioceptive and visual/instruction signals, respectively.
Performs nested reasoning cycles after one backbone pass, avoiding increases to backbone size.
A 22.5M-parameter head achieves 97.0% success on LIBERO and 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC→D.
Reports the lowest latency among compared methods and gains over a parameter-matched single-state head.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH). The VLM backbone extracts multimodal features from a deep layer (hviz, ha) and the embedding layer (hemb viz ). Inside the HR-AH, iterative latent reasoning is performed over S segments, each comprising KH hierarchical reasoning cycles. Within each cycle, the executor (fL) attends to concise action and proprioceptive context for frequent updates of the detailed motor commands, while the planner (fH ) processes the larger vision context and the instruction-informed compact zL at a slower rate to maintain an abstract task representation. The refinement module (fR) feeds the updated plan back into the action state, closing the bidirectional loop. All three modules share the same UBAttn block architecture (Sec. 3.3) with different context inputs. After each segment s, the action state is projected to a candidate action chunk Âs, and the reasoning halts once the relative change δs between consecutive predictions falls below a threshold τ (Sec. 3.5). The final prediction is executed as Â ∈ RNact×7.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_0,\pi_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
authors: Jiyong Kwon, Yikun Bai, Amirhossein Mollaali, Guang Lin
bullets: Existing Flow-GRPO-style methods reweight stochastic denoising transitions by advantages but ignore distances between sampled actions.
JKO-GRPO treats actions sampled at each state as an empirical distribution and formulates policy improvement as a Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto step.
A soft discrete c-transform converts group-relative advantages into transport targets, trained via shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler.
The method combines these updates with clipped Flow-GRPO without KL regularization.
Random-time branching extends the approach to sequential VLA control by applying independent group-level JKO updates at selected action-chunk states.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of JKO-GRPO. (a) Along each trajectory of the old policy πold, we select M random chunk indices, restore the simulator state st at each, and form an independent group of G continuations; their returns give group-relative advantages. (b) The first action chunks of a group share the state st. Flow-GRPO reweights them by advantage. The added JKO step constructs soft c-transform targets yi that trade advantage against action distance. (c) On the first branch chunk, the masked transport loss fits the deterministic ODE sampler to stop-gradient targets, reusing each sample’s initial noise ϵi. The clipped Flow-GRPO objective acts on the post-branch segment. Both terms train the same velocity field, and the transport loss requires neither a critic nor a policy density.
