papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
bullets: VLA policies can violate safety constraints despite strong benchmark performance, motivating safety filtering over sampled action chunks.
An exact-simulator lookahead filter improves safety rates by 11.5–25.7 points across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and selected RoboCasa tasks.
Learned critics detect dangerous states well (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates nearly at chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551–0.560).
Safety-selection gains degrade substantially when the world model’s state is perturbed; median position error can remove most of the benefit.
Evaluation should emphasize within-state ranking and state accuracy in tail cases and on handled objects, not just median error.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes what a world model must do to keep VLA policies safe via action-conditioned lookahead prediction, matching interactive world models and VLA safety.
papers.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
papers.tldr: A safety world model for VLA policies must accurately rank candidate actions within each state—not merely detect dangerous states—and remain reliable under state-estimation errors.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
authors: Rongze Tang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianjie Fang, Ziming Liu, Zhaolu Wang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses multi-robot manipulation requiring spatial-temporal coordination, role awareness, and embodiment awareness.
Expands a single-agent world action model across an agent dimension using shared weights and an agent-axis curriculum.
Uses joint self-attention, hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks to coordinate agent-specific behavior.
Introduces MA-Task Harness and MA-Bench, covering seven tasks with joint success, role, and collaboration metrics.
Achieves 82.7% mean joint success on MA-Bench and real-time closed-loop collaboration on a heterogeneous robot team.

papers.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $\pi_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
authors: Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Hexin Wang, Hanyu Zhou, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Pengfei Zhou
bullets: Across 14 vision encoders and 16 manipulation tasks, off-the-shelf teachers provided little clean-task benefit and substantially reduced robustness to perturbations.
Common teacher-selection criteria such as global semantics and spatial structure did not predict VLA performance.
Behavioral Structure Metric (BSM) measures whether nearby teacher representations lead to similar expert actions and strongly correlates with perturbation success.
Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA) selects teachers with higher BSM than the student and ends alignment based on the student’s BSM.
On SmolVLA, BAVA matched continuous alignment using one-third of the alignment budget and improved average success by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).
authors: Jeff Duan, Arjun Sharma, Jennifer Cruden, Vansh Tibrewal
bullets: Flow-based VLA models can produce different action trajectories from different noise samples, leading to variable outcomes.
The work adapts Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement method originally developed for video generation, to robot action sampling.
P&P requires robotics-specific changes because action data differ structurally from video data.
On 400 LIBERO episodes with SmolVLA, P&P improves the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points.
Episode-level P&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure, with AUC 0.851.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yushuo Hou, Anqi Zhao, Moyun Liu, Xingwei Zhao, Bo Tao, Jiawei Du, Joey Tianyi Zhou
bullets: Visual foresight is important for action prediction, but frame-aligned latents overfit to training-scene appearance.
The method separates semantic latents, which determine what and how to accomplish, from motion-oriented latents that predict future interactions.
Motion reasoning progresses from the global scene to the object–destination interaction region and then to the robot state.
Compared with LaST₀, it improves success across simulated and real dual-arm settings, including out-of-distribution environments.
The approach targets scene-change robustness; its scope is demonstrated on the reported SimplerEnv-WidowX and AgileX Piper tasks.

Each latent is conditioned on all its predecessors, and the action expert generates an action chunk conditioned on the observation, the instruction, and the latents. The inset (Motion over steps) overlays the interaction regions at t+8, t+16, and t+24 with the end-effector path: the regions contract toward the destination and trace how the robot moves rather than what the scene looks like. Top right: Each semantic latent encodes one stage of embodied chain-of-thought. Bottom right: The global and regional targets pool future-frame features from the frozen SigLIP encoder over the whole frame and within the interaction region, respectively. All targets are used only during training.

papers.selection_reason: Motion-oriented latent reasoning for VLA robot manipulation; directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning improves VLA robot manipulation by modeling how scenes evolve during an action rather than predicting isolated future-frame appearances, boosting generalization under environmental changes.

papers.abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.
authors: Meng-Hao Guo, Yi Zhang, Zhe-Han Mo, Han-Zheng Wang, Jia-Jun Wang, Xin-Sheng Chen, Jiaxi Song, Yi-Xuan Deng, Jia-Ning Li, Xuanyu Chu, Hengrui Zhang, Huan-ang Gao, Yongming Rao, Shi-Min Hu

Trained with over 5,000 hours of robot data plus general VQA data; nanoAstra-9B reaches 17.8% zero-shot success on RoboTwin 2.0’s randomized benchmark.

papers.abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.
authors: Kun Dai, Tianqi Wang, Haibo Lei, Chaoyang Li, Kai Zhang, Fuyuan Qiu, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li, Chuqing Cao, Tao Xie, Wenming Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic visual-language features and physical force-tactile measurements.
Uses a two-stage design: semantic-physical alignment and subsequent VLA integration.

Employs a gated cross-attention bridge to incorporate physical features into action generation.
Outperforms the PI05 baseline across three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks.

In Stage II, A2I-VLA integrates the hierarchical tactile and wrench features learned in the first stage into the VLA framework through a gated cross-attention bridge module.

papers.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $\zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $\zeta_0$ built on $\Psi_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. authors: Yizhi Chen, Zhanxiang Cao, Yitong Wang, Junyu Liu, Hongchu Zeng, Xinyi Peng, Chuxuan Huang, Yicheng Su, Zihao Zhou, Shengcheng Fu, Haoyang Li, Liyun Yan, Tianyue Zhan, Jianming Ma, Yang Zhang, Keqi Zhu, Xiaxi Si, Jinming Yao, Qiao Sun, Shizeng Zhang, Jiangwei Zhong, Yue Gao
bullets: Addresses the gap between visual foresight and accurate body-response prediction in humanoid interaction.
Transforms vision-language-action policies into World Action Models with shared-latent visual and joint-trajectory foresight.
Uses a future-conditioned teacher and dual-response transfer to train causal predictions without requiring future observations at deployment.
Improves mean success on seven HumanoidArena tasks to 63.6% and 79.5%, and on six real-world tasks to 78.3% and 85.0%, depending on the base policy.
Scope: evaluation covers seven simulated and six real-world humanoid tasks.

papers.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.
authors: Jingxiang Qu, Tian Xie, Youngjin Hong, Changhyun Choi, Yang Katie Zhao, Yi Liu

Figure 2. Predictive fine-tuning and asynchronous execution with JEPA-Tuner. During fine-tuning (bottom), the cross-modal adapter, JEPA predictor, and action expert are trained jointly while the VLM encoder stays frozen. The adapter fuses visual, language, and state embeddings into policy guidance. Given this guidance, the current robot state, and d intervening demonstrated actions, the predictor estimates visual guidance and robot state at t + d. The encoded future observation and measured future state supervise these predictions, while demonstrated action chunks supervise the expert under both observed and predicted guidance. During asynchronous execution (top), the same predictor anticipates guidance at the next chunk boundary. For instance, with chunk size H = 12, execution horizon E = 8, and latency ∆ = 4, inference starts from o5 and uses the committed actions a5, . . . , a8 to predict guidance for step 9. The expert decodes Chunk 2 from this guidance. Its first eight actions, a9, . . . , a16, follow the Chunk 1 immediately without overlap correction.

Figure 1. Latency-induced discrepancy in asynchronous execution. papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) leverage the world knowledge of video generation models to improve action generation by aligning visual prediction with action prediction. However, their prediction overhead prevents real-time deployment on edge devices, and they usually lack an effective long-term memory. We introduce SANA-Robot, a 4.5B WAM with minute-level memory that runs in real time on edge devices, built on the following core designs: (1) hybrid memory at constant cost: our WAM relies on linear attention to maintain a global memory with a fixed-size state, and on sliding window softmax attention layers that propagate previous information, enabling high success rates on tasks requiring whole-episode memory while keeping an efficient and constant inference speed; (2) a unified model: by dynamically applying different noise levels to action and video tokens, SANA-Robot can serve not only as a policy but also as a world simulator; (3) a full-stack infrastructure for both memory training and inference, including efficient data packing and shuffling as well as memory-phase-based asynchronous execution. SANA-Robot achieves the best performance on the memory dimension of RoboDojo among models of medium size (about 5B) and the highest success rates on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro and LIBERO-Max. In real-world deployment, SANA-Robot takes 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 with FP8 GEMMs and 115 ms with NVFP4 GEMMs, and achieves closed-loop, real-time asynchronous robot control at 30 Hz on edge devices, demonstrating both the efficiency and the effectiveness of SANA-Robot. Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Robot/
authors: Yuyang Zhao, Zekai Li, Yicheng Pan, Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Jiaxu Xing, Moritz Reuss, Quanquan Peng, Junsong Chen, Enze Xie, Zhijian Liu, Song Han

Reports strong memory-task performance and real-time deployment: 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 and 30 Hz control on edge devices.

papers.abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.
authors: Ahad Jawaid, Alexander Swerdlow, Yu Xiang
bullets: Trained on 49k hours spanning real robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and human motion.
Its causal decoder executes actions as tokens are generated, reducing latency for first actions.
Outperforms FAST and prior neural tokenizers across four simulation benchmarks, including unseen embodiments.
Improves vision-language-action models over FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot.
Human-hand-motion-only training performs close to robot-data-trained tokenizers, suggesting robot data may not be essential.

papers.abstract: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.
authors: Rulin Zhou, Yujie Ma, Rui Tang, Qiujie Song, Wanhao Liu, Guoheng Ma, Liangjing Shao, An Wang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the missing link between instrument motion, localized tissue response, and interaction history in surgical world models.
Uses a flow-matching policy to predict joint trajectories from interaction state, robot configuration, and task instructions.
Converts trajectories into geometry-aligned motion tokens and instrument renderings via calibrated URDF kinematics.
Maintains interaction history through recurrent geometry-guided dynamics and guides video generation with state and geometric residuals.
Introduces dVRK-Chole5.2k with 5,255 videos across 17 tasks; reports improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines, with ablations supporting state preservation and transport.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.
authors: Qihang Chen, Tengjie Li, Hongwei Lu, Jason Wu, Chyna Qu, Shikui Tu, Lei Xu
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-aware perception and predictive action selection in precise manipulation.
Distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens using a frozen spatial teacher.
Learns a compact, current-conditioned latent representing actionable near-future information without future observations at inference.
Fuses the predicted latent into the Action Expert through zero-initialized residual connections.
Shows improvements across LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.
authors: Chendong Xiang, Chengwen Zhang, Ruowen Zhao, Zeyuan Wang, Shuhe Huang, Rongxu Cui, Min Zhao, Fan Bao, Hengkai Tan, Jun Zhu
bullets: Addresses temporal misalignment between human demonstrations and robot actions, plus shortcut reliance on scene or task identity.
Generates matched human contexts from recorded robot videos and supplements them with real paired recordings.
Uses variable-length video windows and intra-task contrastive learning to make actions track the provided human context.
Achieves 83.5/100 across six unseen Astribot S1 tasks and 69.5% success on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, surpassing Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points.
Transfers context-specified behaviors to rearranged layouts and substituted tools despite training only on scene-aligned pairs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
authors: Tamoghno Das, Keyon Jazayeri, Yerin Cho, Nazmul Takbir, Arshia Aravinthan, Nikil Dutt
bullets: Addresses reliability failures when objects move during robot execution and policy switching causes stalls or stale observations.
Uses a learned trigger to selectively escalate from a lightweight policy to a higher-compute policy based on recovery potential and intervention risk.
Runs the incoming policy asynchronously alongside outgoing actions and aligns its context with the expected takeover state.
On LIBERO-Long, perturbed-task success rises from 69.5% to 77.1%, with 84.9% overall success—comparable to synchronous switching at 84.5%.
Reduces median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms and generalizes to unseen perturbations without retraining or recalibration.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Weisong Shi
bullets: Addresses the gap between oracle-based evaluation and the risk of the single trajectory actually executed.
Uses the frozen VLA’s last prompt-prefill hidden token with each candidate trajectory to predict relative quality and collision/offroad risk.
Filters candidates dominated on both risk predictions, then selects the highest-scoring remaining trajectory.
On 525 AlpaSim scenes, improves selected regret and top-1 agreement over first-sample and uniform-random selection.
Reduces collision-at-fault or offroad rate to 4.93%, from 6.41% and 6.10%; adds 1.7M parameters and 0.75 ms per decision.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. AlpaSafe overview. (a) One forward pass of the frozen Alpamayo-1.5 generator yields the K=8 candidate trajectories and the prompt-prefill hidden states H; the selector reads only the last token h = H[−1]. (b) The selector head encodes each candidate, fuses it with h through one cross-attention block with a residual connection, and outputs a bounded relative score si and collision/offroad logits (ci, oi); the group-mean, future-trajectory, and progress heads supervise training only. (c) Candidates dominated on the two risk logits are removed, and the highest si among the survivors is executed. Camera frames, candidates, scores, and logits are recorded data from one decision group of the evaluation pool (LASTTOKEN).

Orange (light gray in grayscale print) marks the executed trajectory and green (mid gray) the navigation route and, in the top-down view, the recorded human drive. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a risk-aware trajectory selector for VLA models in autonomous driving that reuses internal VLA states to select safe trajectories without rollouts.
papers.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: AlpaSafe selects safer trajectories from VLA-generated candidates using existing scene features, reducing collision/offroad risk without extra rollouts or VLA retraining.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.
authors: Jiahao Wang, Ming F. Li, Han Xu
bullets: Transferable adversarial attacks can disrupt a VLA model’s perception of the robot itself across tasks.
The method compares the robot’s visually inferred location with a spatial reference derived from proprioceptive states.
Perception–proprioception discrepancies serve as an attack-detection signal and guide mitigation.
Experiments show effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance.
Real-robot evaluations demonstrate effectiveness on real-world robotic tasks.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).
authors: Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Actuation changes such as controller retuning, latency, payload, or drift can severely reduce robot success without altering camera observations.
Before each episode, the robot performs short, axis-wise probes with known commands to reveal gain, delay, and drift.
A closed-form identifier estimates these effects, and PEA compensates subsequent commands without retraining the policy.
For combined visual and actuation shifts, a removable low-rank adapter adjusts the frozen policy to visible visual changes.
On LIBERO with a WAM and VLA, PEA recovered much of the lost performance and generalized to unseen actuation shifts, including 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PEA. Actuation shifts are invisible in images but revealed by motion, so PEA moves before it acts. (1) Probe: before each episode, the robot executes a 30-step probe that pushes one arm axis at a time with zero-sum commands, so that each gain, the delay and a constant drift leave separable traces. (2) Estimate: a closed-form identifier (orange), calibrated once offline and requiring no policy training, reads per-axis gain ĝ, delay d̂ and drift correction b̂ from the response (curves: logged x motion under gain 1.6 and a 1-step delay). (3) Act: every command of the frozen policy (gray) is rescaled and offset, and the arm holds for d̂ steps after each chunk; a lightweight LoRA adapter (blue) on the frozen weights, conditioned on the probe, handles visual shifts such as a moved camera.

Figure 4. Rollouts from the same initial state (Cosmos-Policy; last frame of each episode with the end-effector path, dot: start). Left, coupled camera and gain shift: the identifier alone corrects the gains but not the view, and the adapter completes the task. Right, 3× stiffer controller: each command moves the arm too far and the released model overshoots; the identifier reads effective gains of 1.5–1.9 and scales the commands down.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.
authors: Tzu-Yuan Huang, Shao-Hsuan Chang, Dai-Jie Wu, Ralf R\"omer, Yung-Hui Li, Stefan Sosnowski, Angela P. Schoellig, Kenneth Marino, Sandra Hirche
bullets: Safety filters can prevent unsafe actions but may push robots into states poorly represented in training data, reducing task performance.
InteR-VLA broadens task-relevant state coverage with diverse demonstrations under the same data budget.
The framework aligns training data with safety-filtered deployment to mitigate intervention-induced distribution shift.
Real-world experiments cover in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings across two evaluated VLAs.
InteR-VLA maintains safety and raises Safe Success Rate up to 90%, compared with 0% for nominal policies.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
bullets: Targets high latency and memory use that hinder VLA deployment on edge devices.
Combines trajectory-aware token propagation, contiguous spatial token selection, and flow-conditioned action-block refresh.
Aligns computation with both scene motion and hardware locality to reduce wasted compute and KV-cache fragmentation.
Closed-loop LIBERO evaluations report a 2.13× end-to-end speedup over dense inference with 30% visual-token retention and essentially unchanged success rate.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.
authors: Mark Zhao, Pengcheng Wang, Rui Yang, Jiarui Yao, Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Bingxuan Li, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang, Manling Li, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang
bullets: Real-time games expose a harness limitation: agents may fail because the game continues while the model is deciding.
AutoPILOT supports primitive actions, open-loop macros, and closed-loop controllers that act until control is returned.
The authors introduce AFK-Bench, a suite of 120 diverse browser games playable with either real-time or paused clocks.
With GPT-6.1 Sol, AutoPILOT achieves 68.6% real-time success versus 38.3% for VISTA and matches VISTA’s final success at one-fifth the API cost.
Results across models suggest that converting model outputs into temporally extended actions is a central part of agent design.

papers.selection_reason: Presents AutoPILOT, a visual agent harness that enables models to generate actions, open-loop macros, and closed-loop controllers within a single call, significantly improving real-time performance in games.
papers.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
papers.tldr: AutoPILOT improves multimodal game-playing agents in real-time settings by letting each model call produce sustained, screen-based controllers rather than only one action.

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.abstract: Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.

Provides eight evaluation tracks covering instruction following, reasoning, manipulation, robustness, coordination, precision, and cross-embodiment execution.

Results show substantial variation across evaluation tracks, highlighting the need for capability-oriented assessment.

papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.
authors: Yun Yan, Shizhi Hu, Zhichao Li, Yang Guan, Shiqi Liu, Jiaxin Gao, Xiangteng Zhang, Wenbo Ding, Jiuhua Zhao, Hui Guo, Xintao Yan, Keqiang Li, Shengbo Eben Li

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.

papers.abstract: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.
authors: Zian Deng, Tianyi Zhang, Zilong Zheng, Ziyu Liu, Tao Zhang, Yao Lyu, Shengbo Eben Li
bullets: Motivation: Future visual prediction is often retained during training even though it is unnecessary at inference, adding cost and complexity.

Architecture: A shared image-editing interface supports current-scene perception, future prediction, and combinations without task-specific perception heads.
Results: Achieves 99.10% success on LIBERO, 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus, and strong robustness on real-world manipulation tasks.
Efficiency: Uses one backbone forward pass and reaches 20.9 ms per action chunk on an H100, with reported 1.7–3.4× speedups over VLA and WAM baselines.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$\Delta$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.
authors: Bokai Ji, Jiapeng Chen, Yi Zhang, Zeyuan Ding, Yong Dai, Xiaozhu Ju, Jian Tang, Lemao Liu, Dejing Dou, Yong Li
bullets: Non-following models encode target information, but it is less linearly decodable than in instruction-following models.

A prior-instruction competition mechanism explains failures as prior signals dominating instruction signals.
Training-free interventions and broader evaluations support the mechanism and show LDS transfers across manipulation tasks and visual domains.

(c) Why LDS works. Counterfactual grounding supervision amplifies the existing instruction signal I while largely preserving its direction.

papers.abstract: Completing a manipulation task does not establish that a robot follows the requested goal rather than a familiar routine. ManipScope is an evaluation-only diagnostic benchmark for robotic instruction following under changed task requirements. Built on RoboTwin 2.0's simulation resources, it specifies 48 held-out scenes across six task families with explicit source-task links; policies are trained on unmodified RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrations, and no demonstrations of the scenes are provided, so success requires reusing skills under a changed request rather than fitting supplied examples. Beyond task success, ManipScope provides a chain of diagnostics in which each step tests one explanation of a failure. For twelve policy checkpoints, 84.6% of failures in 13,200 episodes on eleven selection scenes displace a distractor, and gripper records show that failed episodes usually grasp a non-target. When the target is reassigned among the candidates on identical initial states, ten checkpoints follow every instruction on 3.9% of 1,000 states, below the 16% of an instruction-blind chooser, while a GPT-6 agent run as positive control reaches 88%. The failure recurs on unmodified training tasks and is not explained by missing manipulation skills, so success in these scenes largely reflects instruction-independent preferences; two checkpoints trained on the same data nevertheless follow color instructions. In a feasibility test, letting an agent select the target and the policy execute partly restores instruction following. Case studies with future-video and internal-intervention probes further show that forecasts and execution can agree on the wrong target and that action changes need not transfer the goal. Success, consistency, and sensitivity must each be checked against the requested goal.
authors: Jiacheng Li, Yaping Li, Congsheng Xu, Qingchen Liu, Haonan Wang, Zhijie Deng, Jiahu Qin
bullets: Evaluation-only benchmark with 48 held-out scenes across six task families, using changed requirements and no demonstrations of test scenes.
A diagnostic chain separates task failure explanations, including distractor displacement, target selection, execution, and internal decision processes.
Across 13,200 episodes, 84.6% of failures displaced a distractor; target reassignment showed only 3.9% instruction-following across 1,000 states for the tested checkpoints.
The issue persists on unmodified training tasks and is not simply missing manipulation skill; some checkpoints trained on the same data do follow color instructions.
Results indicate that success, consistency, and sensitivity should each be evaluated against the specified goal; target selection before policy execution partly improves following.

papers.abstract: Single-modality action-expert pretraining controls competition from visual shortcuts before vision--language--action (VLA) adaptation. Yet single-modality pretraining can impair the vision--language interactions needed for subsequent joint prediction. We construct a diagnostic model in which VA or LA pretraining can disable an initially active pathway for joint vision--language modeling. In this model, subsequent training with complete visual and language inputs cannot restore the pathway, even with unlimited adaptation. We therefore introduce Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP), a new action-expert pretraining stage that precedes full-input training. During this stage, visual and text tokens are randomly masked before entering the VLM. In this unified diagnostic model, SCAP can preserve the joint vision--language modeling pathway during pretraining and subsequent full-input training. Compared with direct full-input training, it can also reduce reliance on visual shortcuts and increase reliance on language instructions. SCAP consistently improves performance across four different VLA architectures. In real-robot experiments, it achieves 76.67% average success across three instruction-conditioned manipulation tasks, outperforming full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.
authors: Xiao Lin, Yaoxu Lyu, Ronghao Dang, Zhili Liu, Kaijing Ma, Yang Zhou, Dingning Liu, Runzhe Teng, Jun Cen, Shanghang Zhang, Chengju Liu, Qijun Chen
bullets: Single-modality pretraining can disable pathways needed for later joint vision–language prediction, and full-input adaptation may not recover them.

The method preserves joint modeling while encouraging greater reliance on language instructions instead of visual shortcuts.
SCAP improves performance across four VLA architectures and reaches 76.67% average success on three real-robot manipulation tasks.
Its reported success is 25 percentage points higher than full-input pretraining in those experiments.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/
authors: Zhiyuan Li, Charles Eret, Dingsheng Liu, Xuan Zhao, Joshua Choi, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Covers 80 bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished environments, with 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K language instructions.
Varies distractor density from clean scenes to dense visual and operational clutter.
Introduces safety-aware metrics for collisions with the environment and non-target objects, beyond task success rate.
Evaluates visual, linguistic, and object-level perturbations through per-factor analysis.
Experiments show clutter reduces success and increases non-target collisions, while perturbation type and training-data composition affect performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.
authors: Stefan de Lasa, Mohammadreza Mofayezi, Gennady Pekhimenko, Nandita Vijaykumar
bullets: VLAs support generalizable robot control but can leave serving hardware under-utilized.
Multi-client serving may improve hardware utilization by processing requests concurrently.
The study evaluates batching and co-execution across latency, throughput, power, and utilization.
Results highlight trade-offs and challenges for designing future multi-VLA serving systems.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.
authors: Junde Li, Wei-Han Yu, Xiangyi Chu, Yaoxin Li, Jiawei Xu, Ka-Fai Un, Pui-In Mak
bullets: Addresses three grounding failures: lost contact geometry, misaligned token-level gradients, and optimization collapse from discrete indicators.
Uses a forward-only tactile encoder, token-parallel zeroth-order activation updates, and SlipGuard for continuous incipient-slip verification.
On an elasto-plastic shell, its closed-loop gate reached 29× lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp and avoided permanent deformation.
Achieved 97.6% average success across three evaluated LIBERO suites while reducing peak activation memory 7.12× versus a backpropagated step.

papers.abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch where identical joint values yield different spatial configurations across robot embodiments.
Uses a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that reconstructs both joint angles and link poses.
Generates scalable kinematic supervision with MorphGen and pretrains on 40 million morphology-state pairs.
Evaluated with a frozen tokenizer in a vision-language-action policy on RoboTwin 2.0 and the ten-task EmbodiBench benchmark.
Link-pose supervision is important: removing it lowers EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.
authors: Yiyang Du, Yuxuan Kuang, Qitao Zhao, Yixuan Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Yi Xu, Xin Li, Wenbin He, Liu Ren, Chenyan Xiong

Identifies bottlenecks in grasping and alignment, with uneven recovery across failure types.
Releases 12,844 annotated actions and a fine-tuned open-source critic; failure-mode accuracy improves from 32.58% to 74.24% on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark.
