papers.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx
authors: Kai Lu, Chenyang Ma, Ioannis Havoutis
bullets: Targets failures caused by tightly coupled temporal structure, skill execution, and precision in monolithic VLA models.

Applies world-coordinate locking for base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and anchored contact targets.
Experiments on three simulated tasks and one real Unitree G1 task show improved stage progression and task success rates.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.
authors: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, Pham Tri Quang, Sreevenkata Anjani Tishita Godavarthi, Nghi D. Q. Bui, Daniel Sonntag, Chase Rainwater, Duy Minh Ho Nguyen, Anh Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Evaluates dynamic extrinsic dexterity involving gravity, friction, inertia, mass, and center of mass—not just gripper–object contact.
Introduces nine throwing tasks across 100 scenes, with uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects and varied destinations.
Uses 35K trajectories generated by an automatic pipeline combining grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization.
Three evaluated VLAs achieve success rates below 3%, with failures driven by poor robustness before throwing and limited physical understanding.
Providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success; similar failure patterns appear on a humanoid robot and in real-world tests.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the PhyDEX data generation pipeline. (a) Environment construction: given a task template, we retrieve a target object, a destination, and a scene from the asset library to create a new task. (b) Domain randomization: we diversify each task visually (camera views, lighting, scene layout), in its trajectories (grasp pose, object pose, robot state), and in its physical properties (mass, CoM, friction). (c) Trajectory generation: GraspGen-X proposes grasp poses, cuRobo plans a collision-free approach, and an SLSQP-based optimizer computes the throwing trajectory q(t) from the initial joint state (q0, q̇0), the object properties (m,CoM, µ), and the target p∗, refining it in a closed loop until the throw succeeds. (d) Data storage: each successful episode is saved in LeRobot format with multi-view RGB, force/torque signals, and actions.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.
authors: Zixuan Liu, Hashem Haghbayan, Zizhan Zheng, Siavash Khajavi
bullets: Addresses failures where VLA models cannot effectively use relevant retrieved expert demonstrations.
Learns an uncertainty predictor over actions conditioned on retrieved demonstrations to guide assistance requests.
Calibrates an uncertainty threshold with task-level risk control to meet a specified success-rate requirement.
Continually adds expert corrections to retrieval memory while preserving the risk guarantee.
Across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO suites, improves average task success by 9.2–11.2 percentage points with fewer expert requests.

This error leads to continued execution in the wrong direction and ultimately task failure. papers.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

More human pretraining data lowers held-out robot action prediction error and improves downstream real-robot success.
After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, the policy reaches a 93.75% mean success rate across eight tasks and generalizes to unseen objects and object–destination pairings.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent benefits from adding tactile sensing to vision-language-action models.
A tokenizer conditioned on visual observations and executed actions compresses future tactile changes into discrete innovation codes.
TacInno-VLA predicts these codes as an auxiliary training target, adding no deployment-time tactile module.
Achieves 87.5% average success across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks.
Outperforms the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively; ablations support visual/action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary prediction.

During training, two auxiliary heads predict the tactile innovation code from the code queries and the current contact state from the tactile tokens. The attention mask (left) prevents all other tokens from attending to the code queries. At deployment (top left), the TacInno tokenizer and both auxiliary heads are removed.

papers.abstract: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4 points, and replacing their value directions with those of another observation lowers it by 3.2 to 7.2 points across three donors, whereas the same replacement on two non-endpoint tokens in the executed prefix lowers it by 28.4 points. The token that does fit the sink profile on mass and value norm is the prefix BOS; on this checkpoint, zeroing its value raises success in two paired runs, by +13.2 points (95% CI [+7.0, +19.4]) and +6.0 points ([+0.2, +11.8]). Inside the action chunk, a relative-offset routing profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps closed-loop success on three held-out tasks (42.7% against a 38.7% baseline), while uniform or shuffled routing drops success to 3-4%. High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does.
authors: Yuxi Zheng, Yueqian Lin, Yudong Liu, Zijia Tang, Junyu Pan, Yiheng Wang, Hai Helen Li, Yiran Chen

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes attention structure in flow-based VLA policies for robot manipulation.
papers.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Endpoint action tokens in a flow-based VLA policy attract slightly elevated attention but do not behave like attention sinks; their functional role is better explained by positional routing.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across benchmarks and hardware. We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared skillset for robot manipulation? We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration policy that guides their selection and composition, without any demonstrations or model weight updates. We interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model. During training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks by 9-28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8-13.3 on RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1-14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1-3). After training, with the learned skills frozen, UniCraft demonstrates zero-shot transfer across 4 new robot embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo.

papers.abstract: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.
authors: Changtao Zhao, Yingxue Guan, Li Wang, Shijie Zhao, Yuhang Zhang, Shengkai Zhang, Qing Wang, Ziying Song
bullets: Addresses the cost of frequent multimodal inference and the risk that reused commands become misaligned with vehicle motion.
Uses a training-free action buffer that aligns speed-curvature commands with measured motion, advances execution, and preserves corrections across updates.
Refreshes plans using a bounded rule based on plan roughness, without backbone features or an additional learned driving policy.
Over a 3 s horizon, it reports lower trajectory errors across four backbones on ORAD-3D and RELLIS-3D, with FDE reductions of 18.0% and 36.7% at the evaluated request rates.
Reduces Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by 16.6× and 20.8× under serial replay; controls attribute the accuracy gains mainly to persistent state correction.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.
authors: Zheyuan Liu, Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang, Xiangchi Yuan, Ningshan Ma, Meng Jiang
bullets: Initial-state refusal may fail after takeover during task execution, and simply failing to complete a task can still cause physical incidents such as dropping objects.
State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) constructs stationary arm and consistent gripper targets for prohibited-task demonstrations.
Joint policy adaptation learns these fallback targets while preserving actions for retained tasks.
On evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduced post-takeover target success to 1.3% with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while maintaining high retained-task success.
The method targets settings where holding is an appropriate fallback response and is evaluated with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid agents in everyday environments are expected to react to diverse cues as humans do, with semantically appropriate and physically executable behaviors. Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support only a narrow range of cue modalities and are limited to purely kinematic generation, leaving the resulting reactions susceptible to physical artifacts. To this end, we present MixReact, the first unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues, integrating a Discrete--Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT) for state prediction with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for physical execution. DisCo-MoT couples a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention within a MoT architecture. Guidance from discrete context mitigates collapse into averaged behaviors in one-to-many reaction generation, while direct prediction in continuous state space bypasses the decoding bottleneck of discrete representations. HAT then maps the predicted next state and observed execution history to executable actions, enabling robust closed-loop control in physics-based simulation. Experiments across all three modalities demonstrate consistent improvements over the baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, while ablations validate the complementary contributions of the components. Our code will be released to facilitate future research. Project page: https://binlee26.github.io/MixReact_Page/
authors: Bin Li, Xing Zhu, Jingya Wang
bullets: Addresses limited cue modalities and physically implausible artifacts in existing reactive humanoid generation methods.
Uses DisCo-MoT to combine discrete masked modeling with continuous autoregressive diffusion for multimodal next-state prediction.
Employs HAT to convert predicted states and execution history into actions for robust closed-loop physics-based control.
Experiments across text, audio, and video show improved fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency over baselines.
Ablations support the complementary roles of the framework’s components.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MixReact. MCA maps a text, audio, or video cue to the semantic memory C. Within DisCo-MoT, discrete masked modeling samples a complete reaction once, providing cached intermediate keys and values that guide history-conditioned autoregressive diffusion through one-way mixture attention. HAT converts each predicted next state and observed execution history into an executable action, while simulator feedback updates both prediction and control histories.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework with three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills the explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.
authors: Wei Dai, Jinkun Liu, Jiayi Chen, Han Liu, Wenbo Ding, Shaolun Huang
bullets: Addresses failures in tool-contract following, limited access to frontier teacher internals, and imitation degradation under rollout distribution shift.
Synthesizes and filters teacher trajectories, distills explanation-and-code targets into a trainable 9B VLM, then optimizes student rollouts with runtime-error-penalized rewards.
Uses the same primitive-free Python tool throughout, exposing only visual observations and seven-dimensional end-effector control.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks, held-out success improves from 0/100 for the base model to 14/100 after SFT and 84/100 after RL; median calls per episode fall from 36 to 11.
Finds and mitigates a self-reinforcing runtime-error failure mode through failure monitoring and sampling-side curation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The EmbodyAgent full-pipeline post-training framework; the photographs are LIBERO Spatial frames. Left: the single output contract shared verbatim across all stages—at every turn the VLM emits a forced explanation et followed by an executable program ct over two raw runtime operations, shown for two turns of the episode below. Center: the three-stage pipeline. Stage 1 (black-box data synthesis) queries Astra Medium on training-split initial states without accessing teacher weights and filters successful think-then-code episodes into 1,475 targets; Stage 2 (multimodal SFT) distills these targets into an open-weight 9B VLM; Stage 3 (online RL) optimizes the student’s own rollouts via group-relative outcome credit. Bottom: a successful held-out episode from the post-trained 9B VLM (RL round 64), pairing each frame with its verbatim explanation and program through grasp, lift, lower, and place.

Figure 2: Stage 3 RL progression across ten LIBERO Spatial tasks. Left: greedy success on the 100 held-out test states after each round alongside temperature-one training rollout success (round 0 is the Stage 2 SFT checkpoint). The purple dashed line indicates the black-box Astra Medium teacher’s collection acceptance rate (32%, validated episodes over valid attempts, averaged over tasks); under RL, student rollout success rises from 8.4% to 87.7%, surpassing the teacher’s collection rate. The shaded band marks rounds 21–33, where runtime-error episodes dominated failures. Right: median model calls per test episode, inflating briefly during the error wave (rounds 31–33) and compressing to 10–14 calls once the wave subsides.

Stage 2 SFT lifts the same VLM to 14/100 (117 s/episode), and Stage 3 RL advances it to 84/100 (136 s/episode, simulation included). The dashed line marks the black-box teacher’s 1,887 s of frontier-API inference per episode, paid once offline during Stage 1 synthesis across 1,620 attempts.

papers.abstract: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $\pi_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
authors: Jinxi Liu, Ruifeng Zhai, Hao Liu, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Addresses viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts in multi-view vision-language-action models.
Predicts actions in each camera frame, providing observation-aligned supervision for the same physical motion.
Jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific experts with two directed attention graphs.
Uses Cross Graph Consistency to align the graphs’ base-frame predictions.
Achieves 88.1% full-inference and 85.7% base-only success on LIBERO-Plus; real-world base-only success reaches 58.3% under spatial shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of OVOA-VLA.(a) Each view-specific action expert attends to its own view and predicts camera-frame actions, jointly trained with the base expert. CGC encourages consistency between the two base-frame predictions. (c) Full Inference uses R → B; Base-only Inference uses B → R, omitting view-specific experts while retaining all input views. Both execute base-frame actions.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.
authors: Yukun Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
bullets: Targets world action models with one shared ℓ∞-bounded (4/255) perturbation across frames, tasks, and camera views.
Across eight models on LIBERO and RoboTwin, the attack drives task success near zero and shifts actions toward the chosen target; control attacks cause little target-direction shift.
Restoring future tokens removes 61–94% of the targeted effect in five models, while constrained attacks can make current-frame tokens more important.
Restoring only 0.36% of FFN neurons in layers 10–29 removes 72–96% of the effect in six models.

papers.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
papers.tldr: SteerTrace shows that tiny universal perturbations can reliably steer world action models toward attacker-chosen actions and identifies the internal tokens, neurons, and residual directions responsible.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.
authors: Jun Xia, Shangwen Wang, Jun Ma, Ruichao Ren, Zhouyang Jia, Xin Zhao, Huijun Liu, Jie Yu
bullets: Targets the vulnerability of VLA policies that continuously depend on visual feedback during manipulation.
Searches a frozen text-conditioned diffusion model’s latent space for task-disruptive, natural-looking object textures.
Uses a gradient-free gray-box attack with an eight-expert latent proposal network refined through rollout feedback.
Evaluated on pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites, achieving 57.9% cASR versus 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures.
Produces higher scene similarity and a lower detector flag rate than optimized patch baselines, motivating defenses that assess appearance and task behavior jointly.

papers.abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.
authors: Xudi Ge, Yepeng Liu, Haifeng Liu, Enze Shi, Liangqi Zhang, Yongchao Xu
bullets: Addresses action drift caused by illumination changes despite unchanged physical states.
VASE estimates visual action reliability from a frozen policy’s sensitivity to illumination perturbations.
TACE compares predicted and measured touch during execution to detect discrepancies.
Combines visual reliability and tactile discrepancies to gate bounded corrections for unexecuted actions.
Trained only in normal lighting, it achieves 87.5% success under normal and 73.8% under challenging unseen lighting across four real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.
authors: Xu Pan, Chubin Zhang, Xingrui Yu, Runmin Lan, Zihao Wang, Wenkai Guo, Bofang Jia, Bo An, Ziwei Wang
bullets: Addresses stale visual memory and disconnected action chunks caused by overlapping perception and execution.
Uses a Causal Latent World Model to predict current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history.
Applies action-sensitive distillation to preserve the frozen expert’s control behavior.
Uses Predictive Flow Warm-Starting for single-step correction of the remaining action horizon without additional training.
On LIBERO-10, achieves 93.8% success with 5.04× inference throughput, alongside improved robustness and motion smoothness.

papers.abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Chenyuan Zhou, Chaoyi Huang, Zibo Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Yong-Lu Li
bullets: Addresses cross-tool manipulation by identifying geometric features shared across tools with similar functions.
Uses an embodied agent to reconstruct demonstrations in simulation, form and test affordance hypotheses, and refine extraction skills.
Encodes discovered functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone for training and inference.
Builds a reusable affordance-extraction skill library for unseen tools.
Achieves 86.1% simulated cross-tool trajectory-retargeting success and improves real-robot task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$ across three tasks.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the failure of robot policies to compose reliable atomic skills over long-horizon tasks.
A VLM observes camera images and provides the next step in the policy’s instruction format; successful rollouts are relabeled and used for fine-tuning.
On stalled states, next-step coaching increases subgoal completion by 4.6× over the original task instruction.
Unassisted success on unseen long-horizon scenes improves from 47.4% to 59.3%, outperforming human-demonstration and self-collected-success fine-tuning at equal data budgets.
The action backbone remains frozen; the approach is scoped to leveraging existing skills through language guidance.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.
authors: Qiman Wu, Hanlin Chen, Yuhua Wei, Mingyuan Wang, Shaman Tang, Minghao Li, Rui Xin, Xingye Liu, Zhichao Yang, Yiqi Yu, Hongyan Pei, Xiaowen Tian, YingYing Liu, Shiwen Liu, Jiahui Hu, Yizhao Wang, Yuheng Zhang, Anhua Liu, Yue He, Shuang Su, Da Zhu, Hua Zhou, Pengfei Diao, Haojie Yang, Weichao Huang, Hang Zhang, Honggou Yang, Xianming Liu

Provides a shared initialization for TuringPAI-Drive and TuringPAI-Embodied, supporting driving and manipulation applications.
TuringPAI-Drive stays within 1.2% of a full-token baseline on evaluated ADE/FDE metrics and runs at 12 Hz on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC.
TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
authors: Linfeng Dong, Jianwei Niu, Jiuyi Zhao, Ruibing Feng, Xinghao Wu, Wu Yang, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu, Mu Li
bullets: Addresses memory-augmented VLA models that either retrieve past observations without reasoning or let long histories interfere with current perception.

A flow-matching action expert uses the latent memory while Perception Attention directly grounds actions in the current view.

Achieves strong simulated and real-world performance, including 68.8% average success on real-world memory tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ActMem. (a) A pretrained vision-language backbone (Qwen3-VL) encodes the instruction, the timestamped historical frames, and the current perception, and performs latent memory reasoning inside the backbone to produce the subtask together with its Latent Memory CoT states Ct, which condition a flow-matching action expert; Perception Attention additionally routes the current visual features to the action expert. (b) Inside the backbone, the subtask tokens that form Memory CoT follow the history and the current view in the sequence, so under the causal mask they read both, and their hidden states become Ct; the action expert receives only Ct, not the history tokens. (c) Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Consecutive decisions usually share the same subtask, so the previous subtask is reused as a draft and verified against the updated context in a single parallel pass. If it is accepted, its hidden states are recomputed to give the new Ct, with no token-by-token decoding.

papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and fragmented, model-specific training stacks of embodied models.
Uses a common abstraction layer to share infrastructure without restricting model architectures or execution requirements.
Combines reusable and hardware-aware optimizations spanning computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8 communication for DDP/FSDP.
Also provides unified data infrastructure, egocentric-to-robot data synthesis, and concurrent simulator evaluation.
Reports 1.47×–4.38× higher training throughput and 4.1×–23.2× faster evaluation than corresponding open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoongForge-Embodied system architecture. The framework unifies heterogeneous VLA and WAM models under a single native-PyTorch training stack, combining an integrated data pipeline (Ego2Robot, unified data loaders, and composable transforms), an acceleration toolkit of shared optimizations with model-specific execution paths, distributed training with FP8 communication, and an integrated evaluation orchestrator. The right-hand panels preview representative results on training speedup, trainingloss consistency, and benchmark success rates (Section 8).

Figure 3: Training-aligned evaluation architecture. A unified entry point launches a benchmark client process and a model inference server process, which exchange only model inputs and predicted actions over WebSocket RPC. Numbered markers denote the four pipeline stages: observation adaptation (1), payload construction (2), and action decoding (4) run in the client, whereas action prediction through the shared training-side predict_action interface (3) runs in the server, which also hosts the model registry/factory and the action-chunk cache. The client loop returns from each environment step to observation adaptation until the episode terminates.

Figure 2: Unified data architecture of LoongForge-Embodied. Heterogeneous embodied datasets are integrated through a format abstraction layer that exposes a common sample contract. Model-specific data processing is supported through extensible registries for transformations, preprocessing, collation, and sampling, enabling diverse VLA and WAM models to share the same data infrastructure.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.

papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
bullets: Addresses the lack of grounded scene-change reasoning in VLM-generated multi-step manipulation plans and the inefficiency and drift of pixel-level world models.
Imagines candidate plans in DINOv2 feature space using a flow-matching world model with action cross-attention and causal temporal history.
A dual-head critic evaluates imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before robot execution.
On six language-conditioned tasks, it achieved 83.3% success, outperforming the reported latent-world-model, VLM-only, and pixel-diffusion baselines.

All executed plans were verified successfully; remaining failures came from low-level grasp or placement slips, while simulation results showed strong CALVIN and cluttered nut-assembly performance with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.
authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna, Julia Richter, Julian Nubert, Joonho Lee, Matthias M\"uller, Marco Hutter
bullets: Targets robust autonomous navigation in diverse, unstructured real-world terrain.
Uses a VLM to interpret scenes, assess risks, understand signs, and assign navigation costs.
Converts semantic outputs into a real-time dense risk map through open-vocabulary segmentation.
Conditions pre-trained RL policies for agile locomotion and local navigation.
Real-world trials achieved kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, while exposing limits in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the ROAM pipeline. The proposed system bridges high-level reasoning from vision-language models (VLMs) with low-level actuator commands for autonomous robot control. It processes RGB images and robot descriptions through a VLM to generate object labels enriched with risk, preferred area, and steppable values. These labels are converted into semantic images using open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, which operates at a higher frequency than the VLM analysis. The semantic images are then fused with elevation maps to create an environmental representation that reinforcement learning (RL) policies utilize for fast and robust robot control.

Fig. 2. Deployment of ROAM across diverse environments. These include natural outdoor settings such as mountain trails (A to E), forests (F), and grassy areas (G), as well as urban environments such as university campuses (H) and roads (I). The system was also tested in indoor settings (J to L). Additionally, we evaluated its performance in the presence of various challenges, such as smoke (M), train tracks (N), and signage (O).

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce \textbf{HINT-WAM}, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline expert-trajectory training and reliable execution on a model’s self-generated states.
Uses the demonstration’s future video as privileged hindsight for a teacher, while the student receives only deployment-time observations.
Applies on-policy self-distillation along the student’s denoising trajectories to provide dense action targets.
Uses an energy-score, distribution-level objective to transfer the teacher’s action distribution to a flow-matching action expert.
The abstract presents the framework and motivation but reports no quantitative experimental results or explicit limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HINT-WAM. Stage 0 (top left): the action expert is fine-tuned with flow matching on demonstrations, conditioned on the key/value cache of the frozen video expert, giving the student initialization. Stage A (top right): with the SFT model frozen, a hindsight encoder compresses the demonstration’s future observations into hindsight tokens, which the action expert reads through gated cross-attention adapters; only the encoder and adapters are trained. Stage B (bottom): the student integrates its own ODE without gradients, and its implied actions at selected denoising points are matched to a single sample from the frozen hindsight teacher with the energy score, together with a behavior-cloning anchor. Only the student is deployed.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.
bullets: Human recordings provide useful visual and action information but lack robot joint positions and actuator commands.
A VLA backbone predicts discrete EEF action chunks, while a shared flow-matching expert produces executable EEF and joint streams.
Discrete supervision drives informative cross-domain representations and improves learning from human data.
Joint readout is effective for fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, while IK-based EEF readout better supports human-to-robot transfer.
The method can learn new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.

papers.abstract: Reliable manipulation requires policies that generalize across tasks, layouts, and object interactions. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained multimodal understanding with learned control, but their performance remains limited on unfamiliar task compositions. We present Axiom-0, a VLA policy that addresses both the quality of its representations and their use in action generation through hierarchical self-refinement. Intra-VLM Representation Refinement (IVRR) strengthens selected intermediate features through consistency supervision with learned feature projections during training. VLM-Action Interface Refinement (VAIR) recursively updates the resulting conditioning before action generation. Joint optimization of the supervised VLM layers, VAIR, and the action generator connects the two components. On RoboCasa365, Axiom-0 achieves 62.32% overall success in our evaluation, exceeding the highest published leaderboard score (Paimon-0, 58.1%) by 4.22 percentage points and the Xiaomi-Robotics-1 reference by 4.92 points. Under the evaluated profiling setup, mean action-chunk generation latency increases by 1.7% over Xiaomi-Robotics-1. These results demonstrate improved task completion with modest inference overhead.
bullets: Targets poor generalization to unfamiliar task compositions, layouts, and object interactions.
Uses Intra-VLM Representation Refinement to improve selected intermediate features through consistency supervision.
Uses recursive VLM-Action Interface Refinement before action generation, jointly optimized with supervised VLM layers and the action generator.
Achieves 62.32% overall success on RoboCasa365, with 1.7% higher mean action-chunk latency than Xiaomi-Robotics-1 under the evaluated setup.
Scope: results are reported for RoboCasa365 and the specified profiling configuration.

(d) shows the refined cache and the DiT sampling path; the cache is computed once per observation and reused across five Euler sampling steps. Feature grids and Transformer internals are schematic.

papers.abstract: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale vision-language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{Region-Aware Interaction Networks (RAIN)}, which formulates a task as a sequence of goal-conditioned subtasks, each specified by an action type and a target-region mask. This formulation allows learned skills to be reused across different objects and scene layouts and composed into task sequences not seen during training. Its Target-adaptive Cross-View Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-view features on target masks and exchanges information across views, while PlanDiT predicts target-directed trajectories and actions. A Transition Head estimates subtask completion to enable automatic transitions. We also introduce a \textbf{Reference-based Retargeting Strategy (RRS)}, which uses recorded trajectories to synthesize smooth approaches to reference interactions with alternative target regions, without collecting additional data. Experiments on \textbf{LIBERO-Analogy}, our new benchmark for robotic task generalization, and real-world tabletop tasks demonstrate that RAIN generalizes more robustly than existing VLA baselines.
bullets: Addresses VLA models’ limited adaptation to new objects, layouts, and unseen task compositions.
Decomposes tasks into subtasks defined by an action type and target-region mask.
Uses a target-adaptive cross-view encoder, PlanDiT for target-directed actions, and a transition head for automatic subtask sequencing.
Reference-based retargeting synthesizes smooth approaches to new target regions from recorded trajectories without additional data.
Evaluations on LIBERO-Analogy and real tabletop tasks show more robust generalization than existing VLA baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture of RAIN. For each subtask, RAIN receives an action type and target masks. The Target-adaptive Cross-view Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-stage features from the third-person and wrist views on the target masks. The PlanDiT uses these stage-wise features to jointly predict future waypoints and action chunks. The Transition Head pools target-region features and fuses the views to predict subtask completion.

papers.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.
authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs, Aditya Dutt, Sasanka Nagavalli, Nassim A. Samad, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Yue Wang, Yuliang Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost of video-generative world models and the feature-space disconnect in existing latent policies.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers that couples the VLM with foresight and continuous action experts.
Predicts future spatial tokens directly in the VLM’s native visual-token space.
Trained on human videos and robot trajectories, it reports 81.9% success on SIMPLE and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk.
Also remains competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

Reaches 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials without real-test-environment fine-tuning, versus 47.50% for InternVLA-N1.

papers.abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/
authors: Emad Aghajanzadeh, Bethany Anne Wong, Leonhard Kunze, Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Forstenh\"ausler, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann

Projects intermediate driving representations into language-embedding space to support effective reasoning with a lightweight LM.

Uses an adjustable reasoning rate to balance computational cost and language-assisted planning.
Reports strong Bench2Drive performance and competitive NAVSIM and AlpaSim results at lower computational cost than VLM-based approaches.
