papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.
authors: Jiayou Zhu, Peng Guo, Litian Zhang, Xinze Shi, Yuting Zhang, Zelong Yu, Yize Tian, Jirong Liu, Zifeng Kang
bullets: Targets adversarial patches that corrupt vision-language-action policies and subsequent observations.
Uses attention changes from local visual edits to guide patch localization and select local purification treatments.
Revalidates and updates defenses as embodied actions change the observed scene.
Evaluated across four attack methods and multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control.
Succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of evaluated tasks, improving LIBERO-Object success from 0% to 70.0%, with 548.9 ms mean decision time per control step.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies implicitly assume that third-person cameras remain fixed at their data-collection poses; once a camera is bumped, remounted, or swapped at deployment, task success degrades precipitously even though the underlying task and robot remain unchanged. We present Homeward, a training-free, plug-and-play observation adapter that canonicalizes observations from an uncalibrated deployment camera back into the training view for frozen VLA policies. Our design stems from a closed-loop diagnostic paradox in simulation: while re-rendering perturbed views into the training camera with oracle geometry recovers much of the lost performance, substituting an off-the-shelf feed-forward 3D foundation model can leave the policy worse off than applying no correction at all. This degradation concentrates on the thin, articulated robot arm, which feed-forward depth prediction tears and scatters - yet the arm's exact 3D state is already known from robot kinematics. Homeward exploits this asymmetry: it estimates what is unknown - camera parameters and static scene depth - from the live RGB frame and a single training-view reference, and renders what is known - the moving robot links - directly from the kinematic model. Evaluated across $\sim$300,000 closed-loop episodes spanning four frozen VLAs, Homeward boosts success across all 1,599 camera variants of LIBERO-Plus from 62.5%, 76.5%, 68.0%, and 3.6% to 77.6%, 95.1%, 91.2%, and 26.4% for OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_{0.5}$, $\pi_0$, and OpenVLA, respectively. Without any scene fine-tuning or deployment camera calibration, Homeward extends to 6-DoF random placements, focal-length changes, and, with per-step pose estimation, continuous intra-episode camera drift, while matching or surpassing a calibrated, scene-trained view-synthesis baseline on three of four policies on LIBERO-Plus.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.
authors: Wenhao Li, Zhongyi Han, Yuhao Wei, Liang Han, Yilong Yin, Liqiang Nie
bullets: Problem: Standard few-shot VLA policies memorize camera-to-robot geometry and fail after camera bumps or robot re-docking.
Method: Uses the robot arm via forward kinematics as a metric calibration target and static scene geometry as a world anchor.

Evaluation: Introduces LIBERO-PoseShift and evaluates simulation plus four real-world UR5e tasks under camera, base, and compound shifts.
Results: Improves shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and 36.7 points on the real robot, without perturbed training data or test-time calibration.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses VLA model robustness to camera-base extrinsics with canonicalization and fine-tuning.
papers.title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: WACO makes few-shot vision-language-action policies robust to shifted cameras and robot bases by estimating and correcting camera-to-base changes from a single RGB-D frame.

papers.abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
authors: Haotian Xu, Yue Hu, Zhengqiu Zhu, Tuo Feng, Wenguan Wang, Quanjun Yin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting changing viewpoints with stable spatial evidence during long-range flight.
Builds a north-up navigation map from visual observations, geographic priors, and landmarks.
Uses instruction- and state-conditioned memory retrieval to predict map-frame targets, then converts them into body-frame commands.
Early goal commitment stabilizes long-horizon execution by fixing the target from the first K predictions.
On Test Unseen, it improves navigation error, success rate, and success-weighted path length, with efficient 0.68-second inference and 8.6 GB peak memory on one A100.

papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.
authors: Idan Ben-Ami, Arnon Netzer, Sarah Keren, Idit Diamant
bullets: Targets the inference cost and mixed uncertainty signals of sampling-based Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC).
Uses a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation and Jacobian-vector products to derive action-level uncertainty.
Measures local uncertainty around the selected execution trajectory, unlike AAC’s global dispersion across alternative chunks.
Correlates strongly with AAC while being less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid strategies.
Performs favorably across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, combining task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency.

papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps, the instruction drives the action; when an unreferenced screen region hijacks the step, the instruction loses control over the decision state or that region dictates it instead. We term this signature intent--evidence dominance inversion and propose IDEA (Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit) to detect backdoor activation at inference time for each step without trigger knowledge or attack data. Specifically, Intent Counterfactual Probing (ICP) measures how far redirected instructions move the decision state, and Region Causal Audit (RCA) quantifies how far ablating a candidate region moves it. A gated conformal score compares both displacements against clean steps at the same distance from the clean manifold, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families show that IDEA consistently detects backdoor activation under a controlled false-positive rate and outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods, while localizing the trigger region for every alarm and adding only modest inference overhead.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Sizai Hou, Jian Yang, Ge Sun, Junyu Luo, Wenkai Zhang, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses step-level backdoor detection for open-weight GUI agents, which existing image- and CLIP-focused detectors do not cover.
Uses Intent Counterfactual Probing to measure instruction influence and Region Causal Audit to measure candidate-region influence.
A gated conformal score compares these effects with clean steps at comparable manifold distances, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families report consistent detection at controlled false-positive rates, trigger localization, and modest overhead.
Scope: detection is performed per step without trigger knowledge or attack data; the abstract does not specify detailed quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.
authors: Shiwei Wu, Yuwen Pan, Zhi Li, Yaowen Li, Yan Zhou, Xuemiao Xu, Yu Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable human labels and reliable rule-based repairs for failures encountered during closed-loop UAV navigation.
Uses recursive self-improvement: the current policy anchors failures, proposes or samples repairs, evaluates them by flying onward, and distills verified repairs.
Renews supervision each round to uncover failures hidden behind earlier failures while preserving behavior elsewhere.
On TravelUAV, three rounds improve success from 46.4% to 67.5% and halve collisions, with no extra human labels or inference cost.
Scope: evaluated on a supervised 2B-parameter policy and the TravelUAV benchmark.

In each round, (1) AFA samples anchors from probes before every failure of πk; (2) CVR restores each anchor, lets πk continue the executed action a−, its sampled actions, and rule-based proposals, and accepts as the repair c⋆ the first candidate that qualifies again in a re-flight; and (3) RRL distills the verified repairs into a student copy of πk, keeping the outputs of πk on states that need no repair, to obtain πk+1.

papers.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.
bullets: The study evaluates two LIBERO-Spatial tasks that differ only in the landmark word identifying one of two bowls.
Unseen synonyms often direct the policy to the named bowl, unlike made-up words, but one task’s closed-loop completion falls to 67.6% versus 100% for the original wording.
Token-pasting tests suggest landmark information affects object choice before the connector, while coordinated information from landmark, instruction, and image tokens affects behavior after it.
Diversified landmark-word finetuning—and even connector-only training—can repair synonym completion; original-instruction finetuning does not.
Closed-loop evaluation should separately measure object choice and completion, with interventions on both sides of the connector; open-loop starting-frame scores can miss part of the repair.

papers.title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
papers.tldr: In GR00T N1.7, landmark synonyms can guide the correct object choice but still reduce task completion, with vulnerabilities spanning both sides of the vision-language/action connector.

papers.abstract: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yeqiang Wang, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Bingqian Wu, Fan Zhou, Jianjie Zhang, Chentao Shen, Wentao Yang, Rui Qian, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language-conditioned reference motions and controller-executed motions under balance and contact constraints.
Uses a differentiable world model with a fixed tracking controller to predict execution segments and assess the complete resulting trajectory against the instruction.
Backpropagates semantic feedback through inserted predicted segments to adapt the motion generator.
Adds an anchoring loss to keep adapted references close to those from the initial generator.
On BONES-SEED, it largely preserves reference-to-execution instruction retrieval accuracy and achieves the highest executed-motion retrieval accuracy among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.
authors: Xianhao Pan, Chi Li, Hanchao Li, Yunxin Liu, Jiankai Sun, Luhui Hu
bullets: Addresses the conflict between language-conditioned control and instruction-independent world dynamics.

Outperforms the authors’ task-ID-conditioned baseline, improving overall success from 76.0% to 84.9% and LIBERO-Goal success from 67.1% to 88.5%.
Instruction-switching tests show task and policy outputs change with language, while dynamics representations and predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and actions.

papers.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.
authors: Junlin Long, Xu Deng, Yiran Wang, Yue Yang, Yang Zhao, Zeyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses language-guided loco-manipulation for arm-free quadrupeds, including walking on three legs while using a front leg to manipulate.
Uses two stages: cross-morphology adaptation with on-policy self-distillation, followed by reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation.
The first student retains near-teacher performance (76.7% vs. 77.0%) while sampling 14× faster.
Task-specific RL and multi-teacher distillation improve performance to 85.0% on ten QLM-Bench simulated tasks.
The initial distilled student is also deployed on a real Unitree Go2 Air.

papers.abstract: In precision manipulation, small errors in alignment or force can cause jamming or deformation, making contact feedback essential for adapting pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models to these tasks. A single tactile observation leaves the response to recent actions ambiguous. Direct tactile fusion during post-training can also disperse the action expert's visual attention and reduce the share it allocates to contact regions. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA augments pretrained VLAs with lightweight tactile modules. A queryable action-response memory retrieves recent contact responses so that the action expert can combine them with immediate tactile feedback. Contact-guided gaze supervision concentrates the visual attention of the tactile semantic token on image regions corresponding to fingertip contact. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensor inputs. It also achieves 67% success on an optical-tactile task from the public UniVTAC benchmark and 66.7% mean success across three real-robot tasks. These results show that tactile post-training helps pretrained VLAs adjust to changing contact.

papers.abstract: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel's spatial location and force vector. Hand-object and object-object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.
authors: Xin Zhang, Shiqi Zhang, Siyuan Cao, Juncheng Cai, Yedong Shen, Yuxuan Gao, Dianlong Wen, Kaixue Long, Lu Zhang, Yao Li, Jiajun Deng, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and visually ambiguous contact states that make local geometry and object relations difficult to infer from vision alone.
Builds a shared robot-base-frame visuo-tactile representation from RGB-D points, dense five-finger tactile measurements, taxel locations, and force vectors.
Adds hand-object and object-object relations from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces to guide contact adjustment and object alignment.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with a UR7e and XHand, improving average success by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and 20 points over the strongest alternative.
Ablations show complementary benefits from scene geometry, spatial tactile feedback, shared spatial grounding, and explicit geometric relations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of 3DTouch. (a) 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG) back-projects RGB-D observations into scene point clouds and transforms taxel positions and force vectors into a shared robot-base frame using forward kinematics (FK). Separate encoders produce scene tokens and finger-level tactile tokens. (b) Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM) aligns reference object meshes using estimated poses and encodes relative displacements and distances between hand landmarks and nearby object surface points, and between representative regions of interacting objects, into hand–object (HO) and object–object (OO) tokens. The scene, tactile, and relation tokens jointly condition the action expert, while the original vision-language pathway and flow-matching objective are preserved.

Figure 1. Overview of 3DTouch. Compared with the 2D-only VLA shown on the left, 3DTouch augments a pretrained vision-languageaction policy with scene geometry, spatially grounded tactile feedback, and explicit geometric relations. Scene points and tactile measurements are represented in a shared robot-base coordinate frame, while hand–object and object–object relations describe task-relevant geometric configurations. These complementary representations jointly condition action generation, with the bottom panels illustrating five real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and their success-rate comparisons against baselines.

Figure 4. Overview of five contact-rich manipulation tasks performed on the UR7e robot equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. Each column shows the start and end states of a task, with red dashed arrows indicating the intended manipulation motions.

Figure 3. Pose Estimator. SAM2 generates object segmentation masks, which RGBTrack uses together with RGB-D observations and reconstructed reference meshes to obtain offline 6D pose annotations. These annotations supervise a lightweight pose estimator that predicts object poses directly from RGB-D observations and sampled reference surface points.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$\pi_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.
authors: Tianqi Gong, Haochen Niu, Yusheng Zhao, Lantao Zhang, Haoyu Liu, Rendong Ying, Peilin Liu
bullets: Uses current observations and execution history to localize the active subtask and phase.
Provides phase-specific visual targets for interaction/contact and local completion states.
Jointly conditions the VLA on local language instructions and the relevant visual target.
Monitors anomalies and recovers through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation.
Improves success across simulated benchmarks and real-robot tasks, including 21.7% to 59.2% mean full-task success in three real-world experiments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.
authors: Hanqi Mao, Jiajun Fan, Ruihan Guo, Shuaike Shen, Ziwen Wang, Hui Ren, Xianrui Zhong, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and cost of requiring a large model before every vision-language agent action.
A training-free judge scores candidate steps against the current screenshot in one forward pass; accepted drafts avoid invoking the large model.

The large model generates only a minority of steps, enabling more completed closed-loop episodes and faster, more accurate operation with a 27B target.
The calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and Vanguard also composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative step-level decoding judge for vision-language agents; relevant to embodied VLA and efficient inference.
papers.title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
papers.tldr: Vanguard uses screenshots to decide when a small model’s speculative action is trustworthy, reducing large-model calls while often improving agent accuracy.

papers.abstract: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.
authors: Manav Kulshrestha, Shreyans Jain, Apoorva Vashisth, Ankush Gupta, Damon Conover, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the need to choose grasps that are both physically feasible and suitable for the downstream task.
Introduces a dataset with 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations across 100,911 image-task pairs and 17 object categories.
Generates task-independent grasp proposals, then uses a language-conditioned re-ranker to jointly evaluate them.
Outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points and is validated on real objects with a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of LAGR. Given multimodal visual observations, a task-independent proposal generator extracts fused visual features and predicts physically plausible grasp candidates with associated confidence scores. A language-conditioned re-ranker combines proposal geometry, multi-scale visual features, and task instruction embeddings, then applies a proposal-context transformer to jointly evaluate candidate suitability. The final grasp is selected by combining task-compatibility predictions with physical confidence, without modifying the proposed grasp geometry.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
authors: Apoorva Vashisth, Manav Kulshrestha, Damon Conover, Zachary Kingston, Aniket Bera
bullets: Targets performance degradation in long-horizon tasks involving interdependent manipulations.
Uses an execution-aware, VLA-agnostic framework that evaluates motion progress and revises future plans from observed outcomes.
Leaves the underlying VLA policy unchanged and requires no additional fine-tuning.
Improves success rates by 21.9% on RoboCasa365 and 10.4% on CALVIN over the next strongest baseline.
Also demonstrates real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RePlan-VLA. Given a long-horizon language instruction and visually grounded scene observations, the planner decomposes the task into executable short-horizon subtasks, which are sequentially executed by a frozen VLA policy. A separate progress estimator monitors execution at the manipulation-primitive level, detects deviations from the intended subtask, and generates naturallanguage failure feedback. Upon failure, the planner uses the updated scene observations and diagnostic feedback to revise the remaining subtask sequence. The bottom panel illustrates this closed-loop process: after successfully placing a croissant on the cutting board, the robot approaches an incorrect object while retrieving a jam jar. RePlan-VLA detects the mismatch and replans, enabling the robot to recover and complete the remaining manipulation.

papers.abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.
authors: Jinhao Zhang, Yushen Zuo, Ke Rui, Weitao Zhou, Haibao Yu, Honglong Tian, Xiaoheng Ma, Jie Mei, Jiawei Wang, Minglei Li
bullets: Addresses WAMs’ limited open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning.
Uses a learnable embedding to exchange intent information between the VLM and WAM, supervised by text and goal images.
Introduces a two-stage training strategy for effective joint optimization and collaboration.
Reports leading performance across LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro, and improved long-horizon planning on RoboCasa365.
Real-world experiments support the method’s practical effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.
authors: Keke Tang, Guolin Qiu, Tianyu Hao, Daizong Liu, Yikai Zhang, Peican Zhu, Zhihong Tian
bullets: Targets the gap between VLA-predicted task-space commands and their downstream physical execution.

Uses these directions to optimize an adversarial patch that degrades command realization and task completion.
Simulation across multiple VLA policies shows greater command–execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks.
Real-robot experiments validate execution degradation on physical platforms.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

bullets: Dexterous manipulation is difficult because most VLA training data targets parallel-jaw grippers, while multi-finger teleoperation data is scarce.
The study combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL) for adapting VLAs to a LEAP hand.
Across five fine-tuning recipes and two simulation tasks, SFT rollout success poorly predicts post-DSRL performance.
Freezing the VLM and tuning only the action expert yields the most steerable policy, including for out-of-distribution placements.
LoRA is reported as the least steerable adaptation approach.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $\pi_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.
bullets: LIBERO-trained VLA policies often fail on LIBERO-PRO when objects move or instructions change.
The method augments demonstrations by relocating and rotating objects, transferring tasks across environments and surfaces, and paraphrasing instructions.
A perception module using frozen DINOv3 features provides object positions and gripper-state information alongside TinyCLIP image and instruction embeddings.
A from-scratch flow-matching diffusion transformer predicts actions from this decoupled representation.
RageVLA achieves 0.72 on LIBERO-PRO, compared with 0.53 for the best published model; performance remains strong under object displacement tests.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
authors: Xuanwei Liu, Guipu Cao, Zhongyi Luo, Jiafei Duan
bullets: Existing tokenizers concatenate both arms’ actions, leaving shared motions and cross-arm dependencies for the policy to learn implicitly.
BiCAT uses a shared motion representation, symmetric cross-arm attention, and a joint decoder to condition each arm on its partner.
It predicts each arm’s tokens in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it.
Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among compared tokenizers.
It improves simulated mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with 40.5 ms per action chunk; gains are largest for tightly coordinated tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).
authors: Anas Anwarul Haq Khan, Amrin Kareem, Muhammad Umer Sheikh, Biplab Banerjee, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Problem: 2D visual encoders and unreliable monocular depth struggle with long-range distances, altitude selection, and coordinating forward/downward views.
Method: Lift depth from both cameras into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame, while aligning visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training.
The two components address complementary failure modes: explicit 3D lifting reduces collisions, while implicit geometry alignment improves target completion.
GRID raises target-reaching from 61.5% to 69.5% and task completion after reaching the target from 57.7% to 61.4%, with reported statistical significance.
On TravelUAV, GRID achieves the best success rate across all splits, with relative gains of 9.5%–25.4% over the prior state of the art.

The frozen depth model Φ predicts range maps Dc (on the flat ground below the UAV, range grows radially). The token keeps four depth samples di,s, whose mean would land in empty space. The samples are back-projected along their viewing rays into the UAV’s body frame, encoded, and added to the token. Middle: the policy (Sec. 3.1). Bottom: implicit alignment (Sec. 3.3), used during training only (dashed). The standard VGGT aggregator [35], unmodified and frozen, alternates frame attention within each view and global attention across both views 24 times (lines are schematic). Its last-layer features are resampled per view to one target yc,i per token, and the hidden states zc,i at LLM layer ℓ=24 are aligned with these targets.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
bullets: Pixel-level future generation contains many visually plausible but planning-irrelevant details.
The model represents each surrounding agent with discrete tokens encoding identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context.
Agent tokens are learned through geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning.
Open- and closed-loop experiments across diverse driving scenarios show stronger planning, better use of visual and dynamic information, and interpretable world states.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AgentWorld. Given multi-view observations, ego-status, navigation goals, and language prompts, AgentWorld constructs an agent-centric world state by grounding discrete agent tokens with 4D geometry and 2D visual features through multimodal routed anchoring. The grounded agent tokens are then used by the policy model for reasoning, action, and planning through grounding, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning stages.
Figure 4: The pipeline of the multimodal routed anchoring. Agent queries are routed to geometry and vision branches, and fused through cross-attention to produce grounded agent tokens.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison between VLA-World [30] and AgentWorld. For each scene, the left panels visualize the future ego trajectories of VLA-World (top) and AgentWorld (bottom), with AgentWorld additionally showing the traffic participants aligned with the special tokens ⟨agent_i⟩. The right panels present the corresponding perception, reasoning, and planning results.

Figure 1: (a) VLA models output actions from observations and prompts, lacking explicit spatiotemporal modeling and interaction awareness. (b) World models learn predictive latent futures, yet their imagined states fail to align with causal reasoning. (c) VLA World models integrate imagination and language reasoning, but reason over generated frames rather than interactive agents for driving decisions. (d) By contrast, AgentWorld models futures via discrete latent agent states, enabling VLA reasoning over physically grounded 3D geometry, motion dynamics and agent interactions.
Figure 2: Visual grounding results (UniAD metric) and token efficiency of VLA models.
Figure 8: Prompt design for reasoning with agent data generation.
Figure 6: Ablation studies on agent-centric world states. (a) Perception and (b) planning performance with varying numbers of agent tokens. (c) Performance comparisons of w/ and w/o ego-status.

Figure 11: Visualization of trajectories across VLA-World and our AgentWorld on the nuScenes validation dataset. The predicted and ground-truth trajectories are depicted in red and green, respectively.

Figure 7: Example of the Stage-1 agent grounding QA template. Given multi-view driving observations and a grounding instruction, AgentWorld outputs a fixed set of <agent_i> tokens inside the <perception> field. These tokens act as latent agent slots: active slots are supervised to align with physical traffic participants through 3D box and future trajectory targets, while unused slots are trained as no-object.

Figure 9: Example of the Stage-2 reasoning-oriented SFT template. Given multi-view driving observations, ego-state instructions, and the fixed <agent_i> slots in the <perception> field, AgentWorld learns to generate a structured response consisting of concise agent-grounded reasoning in <think>, a high-level driving command in <action>, and future ego waypoints in <answer>. The rationale explicitly references decision-relevant agent tokens, encouraging the policy to plan based on surrounding-agent interactions rather than shortcut cues.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? We propose LeapBot-JAC, which allocates sparse future-control references and dense execution targets within one shared action expert. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and jointly denoised at aligned physical-time positions. Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host's visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host's world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3% success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0% and 97.3%. On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5% to 70.4% and from 73.1% to 77.3%, respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between predicting long action chunks and executing only a prefix before replanning.
Uses one shared action expert to jointly denoise sparse future-control references and dense execution targets at aligned physical times.
Directed attention lets execution tokens use reference tokens while respecting visibility constraints.
Adds no action tokens or parameters and preserves the host world-modeling process; only the execution chain controls the robot.
Improves LIBERO success to 98.3% and zero-shot LIBERO-Plus success to 70.4% for FastWAM, with additional RoboTwin and real-world evaluations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of LeapBot-JAC. A shared action expert jointly denoises a sparse reference chain R and a dense execution chain A within a fixed action-token budget. Physical-time encoding aligns the two chains, while a directed attention mask allows A to attend to R and blocks direct reverse access, subject to the host’s visibility constraints. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls, and only the execution prefix drives the robot. The illustrated K = 10 is used on LIBERO/LIBERO-Plus; RoboTwin uses K = 16. The host’s world-modeling objectives and sampling schedule are preserved.

papers.abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation, with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation, where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model, lifting monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views, producing consistent left-right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io
bullets: Addresses the shortage of large-scale real-world stereo datasets for vision-language-action manipulation models.
Warps monocular left-view video into a right view using estimated depth and video-diffusion inpainting for disocclusions.
Alternatively, jointly renders photorealistic, left-right-consistent stereo views from simulation.
Produces higher-quality synthetic stereo data than existing baselines, according to the abstract.
Using the generated data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves bimanual manipulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Method Overview. StereoEngine-L applies when a ground-truth left video is available. The warping module (1) moves every left pixel to its position in the right view, giving a warped right video and a mask marking the pixels no left pixel could reach. A video diffusion model (2) fills the masked region from these and a language prompt ℓ, giving a right video (3) that pairs with the original left. StereoEngine-S applies when no real video exists. We render (1) the episode in simulation from two cameras, convert both renders to Canny edges, and (2) pass the edge videos to the model with two reference images and the instruction ℓ. The edge map defines the scene geometry, while the reference images supply the appearance of the real workspace such as background, lighting, and surface texture. Then (3) a video generation model generates the synthetic video. In both methods, the resulting stereo pairs can be used to train a downstream bimanual stereo-conditioned policy.

Fig. 4: Real-world rollouts. Each row shows a successful policy rollout by ExStereo [24] trained on StereoEngine data, from top to bottom: Stack Two Bowls, Lift Transparent Bottles, Close Door, Lift Two Bottles, and Container Plate. Both StereoEngine methods test Stack Two Bowls, while the other four tasks are tested on one of our methods. Columns show the progression of time (left to right).

Fig. 3: Warping Module. (1) the ground truth left view is abstracted into a grid of pixels, where A to N label the background and O1 to O4 label the object, and each pixel is given the disparity it must move by, d = 4 for the object and d = 1 for the background. (2) every pixel moves left by its own disparity, since the camera translates right. The object moves further and covers C,D,E, and the nearer pixel is kept, so only B survives. (3) the background G,H, I was hidden behind the object and never observed, so nothing can fill the gap it leaves and those columns become the mask. (4) the rest of the background shifts left by one, leaving the right border without any source. (5) the grid is mapped back to pixels to give the warped right view, correct where a pixel arrived and empty where the left camera never saw the surface.

Fig. 6: Comparison of RealSense and stereo. Top: an American football captured with a standard RGB camera. Bottom left: the 3D point cloud from an Intel RealSense D405 depth sensor where the red region shows geometric deformation of the ball’s surface. Bottom right: the point cloud recovered by FoundationStereo [25] from a stereo pair captured with a ZED Mini 2 where the same green region shows minimal deformation of the object.

Fig. 5: Synthetic episode generation. The top three rows show synthetic episodes generated by StereoEngine-S, one per task, from top to bottom: Stack Two Bowls, Lift Two Bottles, and Container Plate. Below the dashed line, the last row (Fold Clothes) shows a largescale data generation example from StereoEngine-L, where a real monocular demonstration is lifted into stereo. Within each row, adjacent columns form a left–right stereo pair, and successive pairs show the progression of time from left to right.
Fig. 7: Real-World Setup. Our real-world platform uses two AgileX PiPER arms. The pink dashed circle marks the ZED Mini 2 stereo camera that captures the stereo pairs.

Video Gen.: operates on videos instead of single images. No Stereo Pairs: requires no real stereo correspondences for training. TABLE III: Stereo generation quality for StereoEngine-L, on 50 heldout real stereo clips. These clips are different from the demonstrations used for training. Each method synthesizes a right view from the same groundtruth left video. CTC measures temporal consistency across generated frames. StereoEngine achieves the best score on every metric. Here, ↑ means higher is better, and ↓ means lower is better.

TABLE II: Real-world results. Success rate over 20 trials (higher is better). The Base Policy is the stereo-conditioned policy being trained (ExStereo [24] or StereoVLA [5]), and each column is a different training condition. In StereoEngine-L, each column is a different mid-training condition: No Mid. trains the policy directly with no stereo mid-training, and the remaining columns mid-train it on stereo data from SVG [15] and StereoCrafter [14] (baselines) or our StereoEngine (highlighted in green); all conditions share the same real fine-tuning data per task. In StereoEngine-S, no real demonstrations are used for training, so each column is a different source of task-specific training data: simulated point clouds versus our StereoEngine synthetic stereo. Across both, StereoEngine (Ours) gives the best performance.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
authors: Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
bullets: Recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3), gripper states, scene geometry, and camera parameters from RGB videos with initial 2D TCP queries.
Uses a shared 4D scene representation for both tracking observed motion and generating future TCP trajectories conditioned on robot observations and language.
Introduces cross-embodiment augmentation by retargeting recovered motions and synthesizing observations without source-robot state recordings.
Reports 7.60 mm and 16.07 mm absolute trajectory errors on DROID and RoboLab, respectively, and 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin.
Joint training with source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TCP4D. 1⃝ TCP4D Tracker takes a monocular video as input and constructs a 4D scene representation. Given the TCP’s 2D location in the initial frame as a query, it decodes the scene geometry, the TCP’s SE(3) motion, and the gripper state. 2⃝ TCP4D Generator extracts local features along the TCP tracks to form queries and incorporates the robot states. Conditioned on the current 4D scene representation, the wrist RGB view, and language instruction, it predicts the TCP motion and gripper state over the next h steps.

papers.abstract: Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~\footnote{https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/}, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.\footnote{We will release our code and data upon publication.}
authors: Junseong Pyo, Hyeongjin Kim, Jongwook Han, Seungwon Kook, Sungjib Lim, Yohan Jo

papers.abstract: Recent world action models (WAMs) drop future prediction at inference, assuming that representations learned through auxiliary future supervision still benefit action generation. However, our layerwise analysis of Fast-WAM reveals a depth-dependent mismatch: while probes decode future state transitions more accurately from deeper visual layers, the gradients and visual focuses of the future and action objectives increasingly diverge with depth, leaving much of this predictive information unused by the action pathway. To address this issue, we introduce RelayWAM, which adds an explicit transition space between the video and action backbones. Conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant predictive cues across depth and relay them directly into the action attention, without generating future frames at inference. Experiments show that RelayWAM substantially amplifies the benefit of future supervision, translating into stronger generalization under distribution shifts in both simulation and real-world robot tasks. On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM achieves 72.03% mean success, compared to 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.
authors: Fangchuan Wang, Hao Zhang, Qiyan Zhao, Huanqi Zhao, Guanting Ye, Xu-Yao Zhang, Yuqing Gao
bullets: Future information becomes more decodable in deeper visual layers, but its gradients and visual focus increasingly diverge from the action objective.
RelayWAM inserts instruction-, robot-state-, and action-conditioned recurrent transition layers between video and action backbones.
These layers extract predictive cues across depth and feed them into action attention without predicting future frames at inference.
The method strengthens the practical value of future supervision in simulated and real-world robot tasks.
On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM reaches 72.03% mean success, versus 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of RelayWAM and the representation–utilization gap. Left: Training-focus attribution reveals that existing futuresupervised WAMs suffer from an objective mismatch—action relies on local gripper–object regions while future prediction attends to the whole scene—whereas RelayWAM aligns both focuses. Top right: Linear probing shows that future supervision writes rich predictive cues (∆R2) into deeper Video DiT layers. Bottom right: RelayWAM introduces an explicit transition space to relay these cues to the Action DiT without test-time future generation, reaching 72.03% success on LIBERO-Plus.

Figure 4. Architecture of RelayWAM. Attached to selected intermediate and deep layers of the Video DiT, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant future information from visual representations conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, current action estimate, and flow time. The extracted cues are progressively accumulated across depth into action-aligned transition tokens Tl, projected into transition keys and values (K̂l, V̂l), and injected directly into the native Action DiT attention. This enables action generation to leverage multi-depth predictive representations without generating future observations at inference time.

Figure 3. Action and future supervision diverge across depth in Fast-WAM. Top left: gradient energy projected onto top-k action and future directions shows that the two objectives share subspaces in shallow layers (layer 4) but become nearly orthogonal in deep layers (layer 28). Top right: held-out future R2 decoded from action-sensitive subspaces drops well below random subspaces of equal dimension as depth increases. Bottom: training-focus maps on “open the middle drawer” and top-10% focus concentration averaged over five tasks. Unlike Fast-WAM (solid), RelayWAM (dashed) keeps both objectives focused on task-relevant regions.

Figure 5. Real-world apple picking on a Piper robotic arm. Left: qualitative rollouts under out-of-distribution apple placements with leaf occlusion (top) and colored ambient lighting perturbations (bottom). Right: success rates (%) across 20 trials per setting. Without any large-scale embodied pretraining (unlike DM0.5), RelayWAM outperforms Fast-WAM across all settings and maintains strong robustness under severe illumination shifts (70% vs. 15%).

Figure 6. Controlled 2×2 ablation of future supervision and the transition space. LIBERO-Plus success rate (%) versus layer20 future predictability (R2) across all four controlled variants. Adding future supervision alone (w/o transition space) raises R2 but yields only a +5.2-point success gain over the base model (w/o both), whereas introducing the transition space unlocks the utility of predictive features and amplifies the gain to +15.6 points (72.03% overall).

Figure 2. Causal erasure of future information in Fast-WAM vs. RelayWAM. We erase residual future directions from a sliding window of 4 consecutive Video DiT layers read by the action pathway, leaving the video backbone unchanged. Top: held-out R2 of the residual future decoded after future erasure (solid red) versus variance-matched random erasure of the same rank (dashed blue). Bottom: resulting action shift normalized by noise-resampling variance, plotted at the center of each erased window. While FastWAM (left) is insensitive to future erasure, RelayWAM (right) shows a pronounced action shift across intermediate-to-deep layers (layers 12–20), confirming active utilization of predictive cues. Shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals over episodes.
