papers.abstract: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.
authors: Ran Qi, Yixin Xiao, Dawei Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Jinbang Huang, Xuan Zhao, Yintao Ma, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited gains from improving robot agents and models independently.
Uses code-as-policy so agents create reusable programs for failure detection and recovery.
Converts corrective experiences into end-to-end policy updates for vision-language-action models.
Uses the updated model’s changing failure distribution to guide further agent-program refinement.
Experiments across BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin show sustained performance gains over successive rounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RoboCoEvo. The co-evolution framework of agent and policy improving each other over successive rounds. (a) Policy-Guided Agent Evolution: the agent locates failures in the policy’s failed rollouts and groups recurring failures into failure modes (FMs), shown at the top for each round. For each FM, it writes a detector that identifies the failure state in a rollout (red) and a recovery program that completes the failed subtask from this state in simulation (green). As the policy improves, its rollouts expose FMs that did not occur in earlier rounds. In each subsequent round, the agent writes detectors and recovery programs for the newly identified FMs and refines those of persisting FMs to improve detection accuracy and recovery success. (b) Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion: the policy is fine-tuned on the corrective experience together with the original demonstrations, which enables the policy itself to avoid or recover from the targeted failures. The rollouts of the updated policy initiate the next round, and its task success increases over successive rounds. The scores compare the base policy with the policy after RoboCoEvo.

Figure 2: The RoboCoEvo pipeline. Each round proceeds clockwise, starting with rollouts of the current policy πi. Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (right): the agent identifies failure modes (FMs) from K sampled failures and writes a detector dm for each FM. The detectors localize failure states in all failed rollouts, from which the agent writes a recovery program ρm for each FM. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion (left): failure-conditioned augmentation perturbs each localized state s into J states s̃j of the same FM, and ρm completes the failed subtask from both the original and the perturbed states, which yields the corrective experience Ri. The policy is then post-trained on D0 and the accumulated corrective experience to obtain πi+1, whose rollouts start the next round. Steps marked with circular arrows are updated in every round.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of the base policy and RoboCoEvo on targeted failure modes. Each row shows one failure mode on one benchmark. Left: the base policy π0 enters the failure mode and fails to recover. Right: after RoboCoEvo, π1 enters the same failure mode and recovers without the agent. Frames are aligned by stage.

Figure 3: Failure-conditioned augmentation on two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. From an observed failure state s (left), the agent edits the robot and object states in the simulator to obtain perturbed states s̃1, s̃2, . . . (right) that preserve the same FM. Each perturbed state serves as an additional initial state for the recovery program, so a single observed failure yields multiple recovery runs.

papers.abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.
bullets: Studies deployment-time compute allocation for a frozen chunked robot policy: more denoising per call versus more frequent replanning.
Evaluates both nominal compute rate and total compute per completed attempt, using discovery and held-out task comparisons.

In synchronous LIBERO simulation with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint and chunk length K=50, d=2 with h=2 achieved 139/160 successes versus 122/160 for d=5, while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step.
Increasing replanning from h=2 to h=5 at d=2 used 60.7% less arithmetic per attempt but produced nearly identical successes; equivalence was not established.
Findings are a scoped case study, not a universal deployment recommendation; arithmetic and latency characterize costs differently.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
authors: Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, Nicolas Thome
bullets: VLA fine-tuning on robot demonstrations can cause catastrophic forgetting of the original VLM’s language and visual grounding.
The method decomposes the VLA–VLM task vector with SVD and learns per-component mixing coefficients.
Coefficients are optimized to balance action prediction with vision-language capabilities.
Experiments show strong performance on both capabilities and consistent gains over established merging baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our VLM–VLA merging method. (a) The task vector ∆(l) is extracted by subtracting the VLM weights from the VLA weights for each layer l. (b) ∆(l) is decomposed via Singular Value Decomposition, revealing the orthogonal directions of adaptation introduced during VLA fine-tuning. (c) A scalar mixing coefficient α (l) k is assigned to each singular component, controlling how much of each direction is retained in the merged model. The coefficients α are optimised by minimising a composite objective that jointly penalises degradation of language generation quality and action prediction accuracy with respect to both source models.

Figure 1: (Left) Given the same visual scene, a VLM responds accurately to descriptive language prompts but produces no action output. Fine-tuning into a VLA enables action prediction from a task goal, but at the cost of language grounding — the VLA generates incoherent text when prompted with the same descriptive query. Our merged model recovers both capabilities, producing coherent language responses while retaining the ability to predict actions. (Right) The VLM achieves strong language performance but cannot act, while VLAs excel at manipulation but lose language capability. Our merged models are the only ones that achieve the best of both worlds, reaching the upper-right region of the trade-off space.

Figure 6: Per-layer similarity to source models. (Top) Oursπ0Fast . (Bottom) Oursπ0.5 . For each of the 602 weight matrices, we compute the cosine similarity between the VLM and VLA weights (blue), between the merged model and the VLM (orange), and between the merged model and the VLA (green). In both cases, the merged model is consistently closer to the VLA than to the VLM across all layers, while remaining well above the VLM–VLA baseline throughout.

Figure 8: Qualitative captioning examples. Given the same visual observation, the VLM produces coherent scene descriptions, the VLA (π0.5) generates fragmented or incomplete text due to catastrophic forgetting, and Oursπ0.5 merged model recovers meaningful captions while retaining action capabilities.

Figure 5: Effect of SVD rank. (Left) Training losses for varying rank r ∈ {4, 16, 64, 256, 1024, full}: Ltext is largely insensitive to rank, while Lact improves markedly with higher rank, indicating that the VLA adaptation is diffuse across many singular components. (Right) Downstream evaluation confirms this asymmetry: ROUGE-L saturates from r = 16, while LIBERO success rate requires r ≥ 1024 to exceed 90% — language recovery needs far fewer singular directions than action preservation.

Figure 7: Mean α vs. rank index. (Top) Oursπ0.5 . (Bottom) Oursπ0Fast . For each rank index k, we average α (l) k across all 602 layers. Both VLA variants show the same overall pattern: mean α is near 0 for the most dominant directions and rises monotonically toward the tail of the spectrum, confirming that this asymmetry is not specific to a single action decoding strategy.

Figure 3: Qualitative captioning examples. Given the same visual observation, the VLM produces coherent scene descriptions, the VLA (π0.5) generates fragmented or incomplete text due to catastrophic forgetting, and Oursπ0.5 merged model recovers meaningful captions while retaining action capabilities.

Figure 4: Granularity of mixing coefficients. We compare two levels of granularity for α — per-layer and per-component (ours) — and report the evolution of Ltext, Lact, DKL(πα∥πVLM) and DKL(πα∥πVLA) over training. Per-component α converges to substantially lower values on every metric, confirming that fine-grained SVD-based control is essential to simultaneously preserve language and action capabilities.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.
authors: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of screenshot-and-action learning, which discards tutorials’ audio-visual information.
Uses a watch–act–rewatch paradigm to combine external demonstrations with reflection on agent behavior.
Introduces video-SALMONN-VEX, an audio-visual computer-use agent, and AGGO to optimize video-derived guidance for action prediction.
Augments AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with more than 24K real-world tutorial videos.
Reports a 22% relative OSWorld success increase over the Qwen3.5 backbone; generated guidance also improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong capabilities as generalist agents that perceive, reason, and act in interactive environments. Yet real-time environments such as video games demand both deliberate control for exploration and split-second reactions to fast-moving hazards. Existing agents struggle to handle both: relying solely on direct VLM actions is too slow for sudden events, whereas delegating execution to fixed scripts leaves the agent blind at the moment of action, leading to frequent misfires whenever the scene shifts. Humans overcome this by pairing normal conscious control with conditioned reflexes-while the mind handles deliberate actions and shapes reflex rules, the reflex itself still relies on live vision to make the final instant decision. Emulating this mechanism, we propose ViCoR (Visual Conditioned Reflex). Alongside normal gameplay actions, the main VLM defines and updates lightweight situational guidance for recurring events, while a fast visual reflex branch (invoking the VLM in no-thinking mode) inspects live local views with motion cues to make the final sub-second action decisions. By offloading 67.8% of high-frequency reactions to the reflex branch (680 ms per check), ViCoR reduces average per-action decision latency by 2.6x (from 14.0 s to 5.4 s) and cuts token consumption by 36.9%. Across 17 diverse 2D and 3D games in the GameWorld benchmark, ViCoR achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving task success rate by +11.8% (from 52.9% to 64.7%) and average normalized progress by +13.9% (from 66.5% to 80.4%) over the strongest deliberative VLM and script baselines. In fast-paced real-time games, ViCoR refines its reflexes across episodes to boost progress by 1.67x, and even with a low-effort main planner, surpasses high-effort deliberative baselines by +8.1% at one-third of the token cost.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between slow deliberative VLM actions and brittle fixed scripts in fast-changing environments.
Uses a main VLM to guide recurring situations and a fast visual reflex branch to make final, sub-second decisions from live views and motion cues.
Offloads 67.8% of high-frequency reactions, reducing average decision latency 2.6× and token use by 36.9%.
Across 17 GameWorld games, improves task success from 52.9% to 64.7% and normalized progress from 66.5% to 80.4%.
Reflexes improve across episodes, increasing progress 1.67× in fast-paced games.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.
authors: Jinquan Zhang, Run Yang, Dongfu Yin, Qiang Lai, Yufeng Yan, Pengshuai Yin, F. Richard Yu
bullets: A single source-task defense update already improves robustness on held-out target tasks.
SN-TRV combines source defense updates by preserving their mean direction while calibrating update magnitude from source norms.
The transferred update modifies only the target visual encoder and requires no target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or inference modules.
Across three VLA backbones and fixed/adaptive attacks, SN-TRV outperforms naive averaging, though attack coverage remains a limitation.
Physical PiPER trials raise average success against printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

papers.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
authors: Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, Guiyu Ma, Tianyu Fan, Longze Chen, Hao Sun, Jiaming Li, Jiaming Yang, Xiaohao Liu, Tao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Hangtian Jia, Shuai Yuan, Lvdi Wang, Xiao Liu, Chao Ma, Yuting Zou, Yinhe Zheng, Xiaobo Xia, Dawei Jiang, Shaoqing Ren

Employs a cloud-edge inference engine for concurrent environment interaction, unbounded-context execution, and low online latency.
Shows solid generalization and operational efficiency across challenging 3D open-world games, with competitive performance on 2D game benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of Gamer. A generalist game agent framework operates across a broad range of visually and mechanically diverse games. At each step, the agent uses the current screen, task context, recent interaction history, long-term memory, and reasoning to generate native keyboard and mouse actions in real time. The agent interacts continuously through this loop. Cross-game training, multi-level supervision, and persistent memory support transferable control and sustained task execution.

Figure 6 Streaming-vLLM for persistent multi-environment inference. Each game client maintains separate short-term history, long-term memory, and logical KV-cache state. Paged allocation and memory-aware KV-cache reuse avoid repeated context processing, while incremental rotary position embedding (RoPE) refresh corrects retained keys after compaction. The runtime combines architecture-aware execution, BF16-verified FSM speculation, and early action dispatch to serve concurrent real-time interactions.

Figure 5 Memory-linked long-horizon optimization with TA-GRPO. A long interaction may exceed the model’s context budget (top). Memory compaction divides online rollouts into finite segments whose task states remain connected by generated summaries (bottom). Segments at corresponding stages are compared using environmentverifiable outcomes, and temporal credit assignment distributes their group-relative advantage across decisions. The figure is schematic, and model execution uses the real-time serving backend in Sec. 5.

Figure 4 Sparse reasoning and cross-context memory in supervised fine-tuning. The shared autoregressive policy integrates visual observations, task memory, optional reasoning, and executable keyboard-mouse actions. Context memory compaction preserves task progress across long interactions, while adaptive reasoning allows the policy to act directly at routine steps and generate explicit reasoning when needed.

Figure 2 CPT for unified keyboard-mouse control. Synchronized gameplay observations and device events are mapped to a shared action representation. Random key remapping reduces reliance on key identity, while repeat-aware loss decay reweights temporally persistent actions. The resulting control prior is used by the subsequent task-conditioned training stages.

Figure 7 Bottom-up construction of multi-level task supervision. The diagram illustrates the organization of aligned gameplay segments into local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages. Trajectories with aligned action annotations are further used to construct SFT examples at three levels: short-horizon operations, medium-horizon subgoals, and long-horizon tasks. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($\pi_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

papers.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
authors: Grid Robotics, :, Qingfeng Lan, Duo Li, Siyao Li, Yiheng Lyu, Shijian Lu, Zhenghao Qi, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang, Ming Yang, Zhiqin Yang, Zuhao Yang, Tao Yu
bullets: Frames agentic robots as open-world systems that observe, interpret intent, reason, use skills and tools, verify outcomes, and adapt.
Defines “Embodied System 2” as a foundation model plus an embodied harness for physical decision-making.
Highlights the challenge of converting general reasoning into safe actions under time, mechanical, environmental, and irreversibility constraints.
Proposes evaluating both foundation-model capabilities and end-to-end closed-loop robotic performance.
Outlines a roadmap from executing individual primitives toward safely fulfilling sustained roles with broader responsibility.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | A reference framework for agentic robotics. An Embodied S2 consists of a foundation model and an embodied harness, whose five core parts manage context, tools, planning, memory, and verification. S2 runs on demand or in response to events, whereas S1 and S0 execute at their own rates. A real-time event monitor outside the three systems watches the user, the robot body, and the physical world at a high rate. It interrupts S2 when an event may change the task and, under predefined safety rules, triggers an immediate reaction in S0 without waiting for S2. S2 may call S0 directly through the tool interface; S0 keeps its own real-time loop.

Figure 2 | Two paradigms. (a) An action policy maps the task instruction and observation to action targets. It might include reasoning, subtask prediction, or in-context adaptation. (b) S2 combines a foundation model with an embodied harness. Together, they interpret intent, orchestrate skills and tools, verify outcomes, and adapt subsequent decisions. S1 provides callable skills and tools. S0 performs body control. The S1 path is illustrative; S2 may also call S0 or external tools.

Figure 4 | Three typical execution paths. One system may use all three paths within a single task. For simplicity, the robot body is omitted. (a) Layered orchestration: S2 invokes S1 skills and tools, which produce control targets that S0 executes. (b) Direct control: S2 controls S0 directly through an action interface; S0 still runs its own real-time control loop. (c) Code as policy: S2 writes code that a runtime interpreter executes in the role of S1.

Figure 6 | Core abilities of Embodied S2. These abilities are necessary for Embodied S2 to perform successfully and reliably in the physical world; some reside in the foundation model, while others emerge from its integration with the embodied harness.

Figure 8 | How long each layer takes per decision or control update. All values are given as times, with the equivalent rate in parentheses (time = 1/rate). The S0 and S1 bands are indicative ranges. The S1 band covers control skills only, since the perception and planning modules of S1 are invoked on demand and have no fixed rate. S2 is event-driven rather than periodic, so we plot time per decision; the S2 band is a target for dynamic manipulation, not a requirement for every task. Helix’s “System 2” is a vendor label: its output is a latent representation, so our criterion does not classify it as S2 (Section 3.1); we include it as the fastest upper-level module plotted. The Astra measurements come from different tasks and settings and are not directly comparable with one another.

Figure 11 | What physical agents must rebuild. Foundations replace the four enabling conditions of Figure 10; runtime constraints, which follow from time, irreversibility, and a changing body, govern how the system operates; and evaluation in the running world validates its claims.

Figure 5 | The agentic loop. Top: one cycle comprises six steps. S2 interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints to decide how to proceed, and invokes an S1 skill, an S0 interface, or an external tool as needed. The invoked capability executes under its contract. S2 then observes and verifies the outcome by answering four questions (whether the request was accepted, whether execution terminated, whether the physical effect holds, and whether the user’s intent is satisfied). Based on the verification, it continues, recovers, asks, or reports. The real-time event monitor, which watches the user, the body, and the scene, can interrupt S2 at any point. Bottom: the same steps on a schematic time axis, labeled with their step numbers and colors. S2 deliberates on demand, S1 runs while a tool executes, and S0 runs continuously; after an interruption, S2 cancels the running tool call and replans while S0 keeps the body stable; the hatched segment marks the canceled execution.

Figure 1 | A vision for agentic robotics: from executing tasks to fulfilling roles. A home breakfast scenario illustrates progressively broader responsibility entrusted to robots: from executing a primitive (L1), completing a task (L2), coordinating a workflow (L3), to fulfilling a standing role (L4).

Figure 9 | The S2 evaluation recipe at a glance: the 9 dimensions (inner ring) and their 53 sub-dimensions (outer ring). Darker cells mark the 29 embodiment-related sub-dimensions: those specific to embodiment or strongly dependent on it; standard evaluations of general language models rarely cover these sub-dimensions.

Figure 7 | Capped scaling. Frontier models scale monotonically: greater capability comes with longer latency. Embodied S2 must instead become more capable within a fixed decision deadline. A decision that arrives after the deadline is usually too late, even if it is correct: the situation has already changed, so acting on it could fail the task or create a hazard. Note that the curves are schematic: they illustrate the qualitative relationship, not measured data.

papers.abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.

papers.abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $\pi_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

Combines generated demonstrations with successful VLA rollouts, producing an updated policy that no longer requires coding-agent assistance.
In simulation, raises success from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the poor cross-embodiment alignment caused by learning latent actions primarily from video reconstruction.
Uses language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and create soft neighborhood supervision.

Enables unified training on human and robot videos without requiring paired data.
Scaling general human video reduces downstream robot action prediction error, while task-specific human video improves real-world task success.

papers.abstract: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.
authors: Donglin Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Yantong Zhong, Wenhao Zheng, Zihan Ding, Yue Liao, Hongsheng Li, Ke Xu, Si Liu
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of converting concise language, egocentric vision, and UAV dynamics into continuous object-relative flight actions.
UAV-Flow includes 30,692 real-world expert trajectories across eight motion categories and 10,109 simulation trajectories with task-specific completion criteria.
FlowVLA uses mixed real-simulation imitation pretraining followed by Tail-Aware GRPO online post-training.
On 273 held-out simulation episodes, FlowVLA reaches 75.58% mean success after pretraining and 93.16% after TGRPO post-training.
Real-world indoor and outdoor experiments show robust execution of object-relative commands.

papers.abstract: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
authors: Shengtao Wu, Zichao Dong, Weixuan Qiao, Xiaolu Liu, Xin Zhan, Junbo Chen, Jianke Zhu
bullets: General VLMs transfer well to diverse driving tasks, but precise metric depth is the main limitation.

Evaluation covers 3D perception, driving language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding.
The method reportedly surpasses existing driving VLMs, approaches expert models in 3D perception, and retains general reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Planning for a heterogeneous robot team from a scene image and an instruction involves two kinds of decisions. Some must be judged from the scene: which goals are already met, how the task splits, and which robot does what. Others follow from these and can be computed: prerequisite actions, handoffs between robots, and timing. We argue that each kind should go to the component suited to it: a small vision-language model learns the first, and a deterministic solver computes the second. In NSDL (Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor), the trained model writes its judgments as a plan sketch, which lists the goals that still need action and the intended steps in order, each with a robot. The solver expands the sketch into an executable joint plan. The model calls two tools, a detector for evidence and the solver, and is trained with the solver in the loop. We evaluate on the public VIKI-L2 benchmark and on LOCUS-Bench, a new benchmark that grades the two kinds of difficulty separately. NSDL outperforms end-to-end planners and formalize-then-plan baselines on both benchmarks and with three backbones from 3B to 8B; the 7B model reaches 97.0% out-of-distribution accuracy on VIKI-L2. Ordering and scheduling errors nearly disappear once the solver writes the structure; the remaining failures are misjudged states, and most goals the model misses are ones it never lists. Code, model weights, and LOCUS-Bench are publicly available at https://github.com/Xincheng-Tan/NSDL.
authors: Xincheng Tan, Ke Wang, Yining Di, Minfeng Zhu
bullets: Targets heterogeneous robot teams planning from a scene image and instruction.
The model creates a plan sketch identifying unmet goals, ordered steps, and robot assignments.
A solver derives prerequisites, handoffs, timing, and the final joint plan; a detector supplies visual evidence.
Evaluated on VIKI-L2 and the new LOCUS-Bench, NSDL outperforms the compared end-to-end and formalize-then-plan baselines.
On VIKI-L2, its 7B model achieves 97.0% out-of-distribution accuracy; remaining errors mainly involve misjudged scene states or omitted goals.

papers.abstract: Frontier models such as GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 can now plan and call tools, yet they still struggle to drive real robots through long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, blind while the arm moves and while they think. We present Reins, a harness in which an off-the-shelf model operates a dual-arm robot with 3D perception tools and atomic actions that report contact and grip. The model chains actions in one call, each with a condition that must hold, stopping at the first that fails; a second instance, the narrator, watches the cameras continuously and reports what changed with every result. From images, Reins also builds a simulation-ready twin of the scene for continual policy learning. With natural-language prompts and no task-specific code, GPT-6.1 Sol succeeds in 88% of real episodes on five tasks; without the harness, it fails every shell game, taking 8 times as long. Three frontier models perform alike but differ in tracking a scene that changes while the actor thinks. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Pengfei Ye, Zhiyang Dou, Yuxiang Ma, Haonan Chen, Heng Yang, Edward H. Adelson

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}
authors: Zhuo Han, Yeqiang Wang, Xinran Wang, Hongwei Han, Yi Xiong, Zunian Wan, Jianbo Mao, Huan Peng, Yongcheng Liu, Wei Shan, Maoqing Yao
bullets: Addresses VLA policies that overlook spatial structure and task history when making action decisions.
Adds features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model to temporal memory alongside visual representations.
Uses a principled scoring rule to select history that is relevant to the current observation and complementary to existing memory.
Achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods across LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge.
Improves real-world success over π₀.₅ by 58.33, 30.00, and 35.00 percentage points on block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, respectively.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.
authors: Xiangyi Jia, Kaixian Qu, Shengzhi Wang, Chenyu Yang, Robert Katzschmann, Marco Hutter
bullets: Frames operator intent prediction hierarchically as atomic action plus overarching mission from short visual histories.
Introduces VI AMO, containing 6,600 episodes, 13,653 action annotations, and 9,702 mission annotations from eleven robot sources.
The resulting Vision-Intention Model substantially improves intent similarity over GPT-4o and GPT-5.6 Luna, including on many labels unseen during training.
In a downstream real-world takeover task, predicted missions reduce human teleoperation time and intent-prediction latency relative to the proprietary baselines.
Scope: the approach is evaluated on teleoperation histories and a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of the integrated technologies developed for the Open Platform League at RoboCup@Home 2026 in Incheon. A vision system integrated with learning-based, training-free models enables robust object recognition for both known and unknown objects. We introduce a RoomPlan-based method that semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to generate semantic maps. Additionally, a large language model-based planner interprets the instructions recognized by Whisper and generates primitive skill sequences for execution. A reservoir-computing framework serves as a lightweight temporal-processing model for action recognition. Its field-programmable gate array-based implementation enables low-power, real-time operation. This is key to removing operational time constraints for service robots. Open-source releases, including task environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks, enhance reproducibility, reuse, and continuous progress within the RoboCup@Home community.

A RoomPlan-based tool semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to create semantic maps.

An FPGA-based reservoir-computing framework enables lightweight, low-power, real-time action recognition.
Open-source environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks support reproducibility and reuse.

papers.abstract: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.
authors: Jinze Tao, Yuxiao Han, Kangkang Dong, Yancong Wei, Xiaojun Zhu, Bokui Chen, Houde Liu
bullets: Motivation: Calling an LLM planner at every episode adds cost and delay.
Method: Convert planner-driven motions, sub-instructions, detours, and resulting poses into VLA training data under the original task instruction.
Training: Mask losses for goal-averse steps, label states within 1 m of the goal as stops, and update the VLA with low-rank adaptation.
Result: The VLA learns to stop at goals and reach goals the base model misses, across all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces H2E, a method to distill task-level experience from an LLM planner into a VLA model for embodied navigation, directly fitting the 'Vision-Language-Action' subtopic.
papers.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
papers.tldr: H2E distills successful LLM-planner navigation experience into a VLA so it can navigate independently, improving success from 35.0% to 44.9% on REVERIE-CE val-unseen.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.
authors: Zefan Wang, Yufan Dang, Xuanwei Shi, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yin, SikYuen Tam, Hanyu Liu, Yasheng Wang, Yaxi Lu, Songyang Zhang, Xin Cong, Yuan Yao
bullets: Provides a controlled comparison of harness design, action interface, experience reuse, and scene geometry.
Finds that retaining full episode history and terminating motions early are especially effective design choices.
Experience reuse changes behavior but does not provide universally free improvements.
Scene geometry is highly beneficial, including when depth is predicted from RGB alone.
Raises RoboDojo performance from 29.7 to 50.3 without a learned policy, self-improvement loop, or task-specific tuning.

papers.title: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents
papers.tldr: JustRUA shows that a carefully simplified robot-use harness can substantially improve GPT-6 Astra’s simulated robot-arm performance without task-specific training.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: https://mmahdavian.github.io/MOSAIC/
authors: Richard Shi, Mohammad Mahdavian, Mehrdad Momeni Zadeh, Mohammed Elmahgiubi, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Addresses the weakness of primarily 2D VLA models in reasoning about geometry and obstacle relationships.
Uses auxiliary semantic grounding to predict masks for the target, destination, and surrounding obstacles.
Builds role-specific geometric tokens from masks and reconstructed depth, injecting them into the action expert.
Adds obstacle-aware attention supervision focused on obstacles near the robot during execution.
Improves success by 5.1% in cluttered scenes and 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains up to 25.0% in the hardest environment; also validates real-world manipulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: MOSAIC Model Structure. (a) A vision–language backbone encodes observations, instructions, and robot state, with role tokens supporting semantic mask prediction. (b) The action expert attends to the shared prefix and produces learned attention maps. (c) Object-level depth is extracted using the VGGT-Ω combined with the predicted masks. The depth tokens are generated and injected into the action expert final layers. (d) Contact-relevant expert targets supervise attention through forward KL divergence during training. (e) Predicted attention maps are averaged, detached, and injected through residual cross-attention into late action layers. (f) Flow matching generates actions for robot execution.
Fig. 1: MOSAIC overview. A pretrained VLA is augmented with role-specific masks, object-level depth tokens, and obstacle-focused attention guidance.

Fig. 5: Average attention maps from the first three action-expert layers for the RoboPRO-finetuned base π0.5 model (top) and our final model (bottom) across two manipulation actions. Blue regions indicate higher attention. Our model consistently focuses on potential collision regions, while the base π0.5 exhibits less obstacle-aware attention.

Fig. 3: The pipeline for groundtruth attention map generation. (a) The original RGB countertop camera view. (b) Per-object contact disk generation. The closest point of each object’s bounding box is projected onto pixel space. Disks are centered at these points to highlight potential contact zones. (c) Proximity weight map β. Higher weight for objects closer to the robot body, less weight for farther objects, zero weight for very distant objects. (d) Obstacle contact mask. Using the proximity weight map β to filter out irrelevant objects. (e) Groundtruth attention heatmap H. Obstacle contact mask convolved with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation σ to represent the spatial distribution of visual attention. (f) Patch-wise distributed groundtruth attention map. Matches the granularity of the action expert’s attention modules.

Fig. 4: Task-conditioned visual annotations for (a) Simulation and (b) Real-world data. In (a), rows show RGB images, mask overlays, and binary target (T), destination (D), and obstacle (O) masks. Examples illustrate an object destination (a-1), anchor-relative placement (a-2), a table-region destination with 5 cm clearance (a-3), and pick-only manipulation without a destination (a-4). Simulation overlays use red/green/blue for T/D/O. In (b), examples (b-1) to (b-4) show four real-world tasks with one to four added distractors.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MOSAIC, a framework that augments VLA policies with geometric tokens and obstacle-aware attention to improve manipulation success in cluttered scenes.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
papers.tldr: MOSAIC enhances pretrained vision-language-action policies with explicit object, destination, depth, and obstacle cues to improve manipulation in cluttered and visually perturbed scenes.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
authors: Miao Pan, Kaixiang Yao, Xiaohe Zhou, Xu Wang, Qinfeng Li, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Targets three missing abilities: causal failure localization, capability-aware adaptation, and experience-driven decision revision.
Builds recovery data by perturbing successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and retaining observable, recoverable failures.
Uses Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision with evaluation-first SFT to structure failure diagnosis before recovery planning.
Applies OPD to reduce errors from self-generated planning prefixes without adding a deployment-time branch.
Improves composite task success by 6.1 points with a frozen VLA and manipulation/navigation success by 13.9 points with fixed GPT-5.5 execution.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of Embodied-Corrector training. Training proceeds from execution evaluation to recovery planning, followed by NEPO optimization that reduces the mismatch between verified evaluation prefixes used during training and model-generated prefixes used at deployment.

Figure 4 Architecture and closed-loop workflow of the Embodied-Corrector Harness. Separating execution evaluation, recovery planning, fixed code/VLA realization, and environment-validated memory turns failure evidence into executable correction while preserving prior progress.

Figure 2 Controlled failure-data construction. Successful trajectories are branched through controlled perturbations and replayed to produce aligned supervision for outcome judgment, cause diagnosis, recovery-subtask selection, and fine-grained planning.
Figure 7 Piper task success (%; 20 episodes per task and method). Gray and purple markers show each frozen VLA without and with Embodied-Corrector. Macro averages weight the five tasks equally.

Figure 1 Failure diagnosis and feedback controls on EB-ALFRED. (a) Frozen multimodal models struggle to identify the physical cause of failed execution. (b) With the model and action interface fixed, cause-level feedback improves replanning more than repeating the failed outcome.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.
authors: Zhuoyue Li, Zhendong Han, Pankhuri Vanjani, Wenting Li, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Dynamic objects can make predicted action chunks stale before execution.
The study varies prediction/execution horizons, inference synchronization, action delivery, motion cues, and latent-space reinforcement learning.
A prediction horizon of about one second performs best, while the optimal execution horizon depends on the model checkpoint.
Shorter horizons benefit asynchronous execution, and trajectory-continuity methods outperform latency-only approaches.
Policy adaptation repairs targeted failures, but changing the execution horizon can provide comparable gains on some tasks.

papers.abstract: Most action tokenizers for autoregressive vision language action (VLA) models compress motion into chunks that must be decoded in full before their actions become executable. We introduce ActionCodec2, a non-neural streaming tokenizer that releases actions incrementally while keeping trajectory reconstruction error within a prescribed tolerance. Its encoder quantizes each step relative to the decoder's reconstructed state, so the selected motion primitive corrects residual error rather than allowing errors from independently quantized increments to accumulate. Finding the smallest such primitive set is a geometric covering problem; we derive the exact minimum for translation and constant-factor-tight bounds for rotation. Set-BPE then losslessly merges co-occurring primitive symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, without a fixed coordinate ordering. A universal version fitted on 20k hours of data from 24 embodiments averages 8.8 tokens per second for 15 Hz end-effector motion on this corpus. With the same VLA backbone, ActionCodec2 outperforms the compared tokenizers on three simulation benchmarks and in zero-shot real-robot evaluation. Its streaming representation allows policies to incorporate state feedback within an action chunk, substantially improving performance over open-loop execution under randomized dynamics, external disturbances, and moving objects. The same tokens also can serve as a direct control interface for VLM agents, which compose successful action sequences into reusable macros. These agent-built macros reduce control decisions and thinking-token usage across attempts and transfer to a held-out task. More results are available at https://zibindong.github.io/actioncodec2-page/
authors: Zibin Dong, Yicheng Liu, Shiduo Zhang, Tianyuan Yuan, Baijun Ye, Jinqiu Wang, Hang Zhao
bullets: Releases actions incrementally instead of requiring full chunk decoding.
Quantizes relative to the reconstructed state to correct residual errors and maintain a target reconstruction tolerance.

A universal version averages 8.8 tokens/s for 15 Hz end-effector motion across 20k hours and 24 embodiments.
Improves compared-tokenizer performance in simulation and zero-shot real-robot settings, especially under feedback-demanding disturbances and moving objects.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities for robot manipulation, but their performance on accessible mobile bimanual platforms remains underexplored. We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual platform integrating two LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot 4 and a LeRobot-ROS 2 software stack. Using long-horizon toilet cleaning as a case study, we collect 250 real-world demonstrations and evaluate $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, and GR00T under the same embodiment and task conditions. We further evaluate variants using SARM-derived task-progress signals and short-term MEM observation history. Among the evaluated models, $\pi_0$ performs best, achieving 60% strict and 70% relaxed autonomous success, increasing to 90% with limited human intervention. In contrast, the evaluated progress- and memory-augmented variants do not improve their corresponding baselines. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of long-horizon mobile bimanual manipulation on accessible hardware while highlighting remaining challenges in reliable VLA deployment. Project website: https://so101-turtlebot4.github.io/mobile-bimanual-cleaning/

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring multimodal understanding and world knowledge to end-to-end autonomous driving. To further improve the quality of predicted trajectories, existing studies introduce candidate refinement, residual denoising, and token correction. However, these methods typically focus on unified refinement of the entire trajectory, paying limited attention to the distinct physical quantities and their interactions. We further investigate physical specialization and coordination in trajectory refinement, centering on position and heading for simpler and more intuitive correction modeling. To this end, we propose CARE-Drive (Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories), which decomposes trajectory refinement into waypoint residual correction and position-conditioned heading generation. Through imitation learning and a future-token auxiliary task, the backbone provides predictive representations and a base trajectory. The position expert predicts bounded metric waypoint residuals, while the heading expert reconstructs vehicle orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on the corrected path. With the backbone frozen, the two experts are optimized alternately through supervised initialization and reinforcement fine-tuning. This design simplifies refinement through clear physical specialization while preserving conditional coupling during prediction and optimization. On NAVSIM v1, CARE-Drive achieves 88.8 PDMS, improving by 2.4 points over the unrefined base trajectories generated by the same backbone. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of specialized experts and staged training.
authors: Xiao Ma, Yijun Chen, Zhiquan Hu, Jicheng Zhao, Yuming Li, Chuang Dai
bullets: Targets limitations of unified trajectory refinement, which often overlooks interactions between physical quantities.
Separates refinement into bounded waypoint residual correction and position-conditioned heading generation.
Uses a frozen VLA backbone with imitation learning, a future-token auxiliary task, supervised initialization, and reinforcement fine-tuning.
Achieves 88.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, a 2.4-point improvement over the same backbone’s unrefined trajectories.
Ablations support the value of specialized experts and staged training.
