papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.
authors: Shunming Liu, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Addresses domain gaps when transferring discrete diffusion generation to autonomous driving.
Optimizes planning representations during supervised fine-tuning to reduce hallucinations.
Uses metric-guided diversity filtering during reinforcement learning to improve exploration.
Introduces Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding, which adapts decoding to scene complexity.
Reports a 29.7% improvement over the unoptimized model and stronger performance than same-architecture autoregressive baselines across closed- and open-loop benchmarks.

During the processing of training samples, the planning components are discretized and replaced with corresponding special tokens to facilitate supervised learning. Reinforcement Learning: Checkpoints of varying maturity levels are screened based on diversity and accuracy metrics, after which they are fed into the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training process. Inference: dVLM exhibits distinct confidence trends across different driving scenarios. DAD mechanism transforms these trends into specialized inference sequences to optimize output quality.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.
bullets: Addresses why identifying causally sensitive components alone may not enable reliable finite-scale control.
Uses a frozen VLM framework that separates localization, actuation geometry and gain, target reachability, target selection, and gating.
Magnitude-normalized actuation converts a low-energy causal subspace into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy by 8.00 percentage points on untouched procedural data.
Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation reaches 81.25% of oracle targets, compared with 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched budgets.
On a new natural cohort, targeted actuation improves the frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% while editing only 63 inputs; gains are modest overall.

figures.caption: Figure 7. From low-rank sensitivity to independently confirmed control. (a) Same-α rank-4 CSA severely underactuates; magnitude normalization restores and slightly exceeds whole-head accuracy on the v3 development intervention subset. (b) The learned Top-4 subspace exceeds every one of 20 frozen random rank-4 controls; random mean is 27.18% and random maximum is 30.78%, versus 52.53% for Top-4. (c) After the CSA method is closed, a newly generated v4 confirmation set yields 50.25% baseline, 57.25% whole-head, and 58.25% MN-CSA. (d) MN-CSA obtains 174 repairs and 14 breaks versus 150 repairs and 10 breaks for whole-head, producing 20 additional net repairs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.
authors: Wen-Han Hsieh, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chia-Chien Chen, David M. Chan, Trevor Darrell
bullets: Addresses ineffective sampled action sequences and the latency of computationally expensive action verification.
Collects autonomous rollouts from the frozen VLA and trains a compact verifier to predict task-success scores for action chunks.
At inference, the verifier scores candidate actions and selects the highest-scoring one for execution.
Achieves 82.3% average success across four LIBERO-10 tasks and improves average success by 22.6% over the baseline on three real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models to deployment-time distribution shifts is important for reliable robotic operation, but conventional first-order adaptation can exceed the memory budget of inference-oriented deployment platforms. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a forward-only alternative with inference-level memory, but accurate gradient estimation requires many perturbation queries, making naive ZO prohibitively slow for large VLA models. We present VLA-ZO, a framework for fast ZO adaptation that exploits the structure of VLA computation. By confining adaptation to the action side, VLA-ZO keeps the expensive vision-language prefix frozen and reuses its conditioning states across perturbation queries and optimizer steps, while schedule-aware prefetching hides state-transfer overhead. On LIBERO camera-viewpoint shifts, VLA-ZO reduces end-to-end adaptation time by 25.59$\times$ at $q=16$ and 32.54$\times$ at $q=64$ relative to baseline ZO, while improving average task success from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% and 63.58%, respectively. These results show that making ZO faster can make larger query budgets practical, providing a promising path toward resource-efficient VLA adaptation on deployment platforms.
bullets: Targets deployment-time adaptation to camera-viewpoint distribution shifts without the memory cost of first-order optimization.
Adapts only the action component while freezing and reusing the expensive vision-language prefix across queries and optimizer steps.
Uses schedule-aware prefetching to hide conditioning-state transfer overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 25.59× and 32.54× faster adaptation than baseline ZO at query budgets of 16 and 64, respectively.
Average task success improves from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% at q=16 and 63.58% at q=64.

papers.abstract: Expressive humanoid interaction requires speech, facial animation, and body gestures to form a coherent response. However, many full-body humanoid robots produce speech and gestures without a visually expressive face, while talking-face animation and robot gesture generation are typically developed separately. We present Talk, Render, Act (TRABot), an agent-based framework comprising specialized agents for motion-atom construction, dialogue generation, motion planning, and facial animation. First, to produce natural and semantically meaningful gestures, we construct Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms by segmenting long-form, G1-retargeted BEAT2 motion into units with natural gesture boundaries, human-verified communicative functions, and feasible trajectories. Second, to preserve semantic order and coordinate body motion with the spoken response, we introduce a Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner. Given an ordered semantic function sequence and an estimated response duration, the planner selects approved atoms to realize the longest feasible action sequence while accounting for transitions and neutral recovery. Finally, we deploy a Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration system on a physical G1 humanoid, combining streaming dialogue audio, audio-driven facial animation, and semantically planned body motion in a unified real-time interaction loop. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that TRAbot achieves the best overall performance among all compared conditions in terms of naturalness, expressiveness, and multimodal coherence.
bullets: Addresses the separation of talking-face animation and robot gesture generation, as well as limited facial expressiveness in many humanoid robots.
Builds Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms from retargeted motion, with communicative labels, natural boundaries, and feasible trajectories.
Uses a Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner to select gesture sequences aligned with semantic order, response duration, transitions, and recovery.
Integrates streaming dialogue audio, audio-driven facial animation, and planned body motion on a physical G1 humanoid.
Experiments report the best overall naturalness, expressiveness, and multimodal coherence among compared conditions.

The Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration System executes speech, facial animation, and robot body motion concurrently.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models currently demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of real-world robotics tasks. However, they often still lack the generalization ability to handle large visual out-of-distribution shifts. Post-training of VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to benefit robustness, but significant room for improvement remains. In this work, we systematically study the effect of image augmentation on VLA post-training. We find that it is crucial to augment only the critic module during RL updates, while leaving the actor's input clean during both rollouts and updates. For $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 this raises out-of-distribution success on LIBERO-Plus by $7.8$ and $10.0$ points respectively, while augmenting the actor collapses training entirely. We investigate a range of augmentation types and strengths, and provide practical recommendations for improving generalization in VLA post-training.
bullets: VLA models still struggle with large visual out-of-distribution shifts despite strong task performance.
Image augmentation should be applied exclusively to the critic during RL updates; the actor should receive clean inputs during rollouts and updates.
For π₀.₅ and GR00T N1.5, this improves LIBERO-Plus out-of-distribution success by 7.8 and 10.0 points, respectively.
Augmenting the actor causes training to collapse in the studied setting.
The study evaluates augmentation types and strengths and offers practical recommendations for VLA post-training.

papers.tldr: Augmenting only the critic—not the actor—during RL post-training substantially improves VLA robustness to visual distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.
bullets: On RoboMME counting tasks, brief pauses or wrist fidgets trigger phantom progress and sharply reduce success.
The failure comes from a temporal shortcut: steady-paced demonstrations make timestamps predictive of progress.
Changing timestamps alone induces early stopping with fast clocks and repetition with slow clocks.
Removing time encodings is insufficient because null-event frames still occupy sampled memory slots.
Event-based memory indexing restores at least half the lost performance without retraining; pause-injection training fails to fix the issue and harms counting.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-augmented VLA policies with temporal shortcuts and phantom progress directly relevant to embodied memory and VLA.
papers.title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Time-indexed memory in VLA policies can mistake elapsed time or idle motion for task progress, causing premature or repeated actions.

papers.abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
authors: Ilia Larchenko, Gleb Zarin, Atindra Nair, Keerti Manney, Vitaly Kleban, Mirko Kiefer, Anjana Yodaiken
bullets: Targets long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge.
Uses one π₀.₅-based vision-language-action checkpoint across all 100 tasks, with extended training and variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching.
Expanded from 50 to 100 tasks using semantic stages, warm-started task and stage embeddings, and a 21-dimensional teleoperation-aligned action space.
Routes 14 tasks to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent, whose mean Q was 0.639 versus 0.108 for the learned policy on those tasks.
The team placed 9th overall and was the only independent team in the top 10; the public submission scored 0.446 Q.

papers.abstract: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DexSeed/.
authors: Huaijin Pi, Zehong Shen, Yong Wang, Kechun Xu, Changpeng Wang, Dingkun Wei, Xueyang Wang, Wenjia Wang, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Taku Komura
bullets: Addresses the high cost of teleoperated demonstrations and the limited diversity of direct human-to-robot interaction transfer.
Expands human sequences across grasp modes, object geometries, and manipulation locations while preserving local hand–object relationships.
Uses InteractionMesh-based retargeting, arm trajectory augmentation, physics simulation, and RL-based finger control to generate executable rollouts.
Pairs successful simulated observations and actions with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA policy.
Experiments report better contact fidelity and whole-arm execution than evaluated baselines, with simulation and real-world demonstrations of language-specified grasps.

papers.abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.
authors: Lianlei Shan, Han Jin, Yaunchao Ma, Xinpeng Chen, Linhao Zhou, Xin Bin
bullets: Uses human gameplay recordings that pair observations, actions, and visual consequences for robot-policy pretraining.
Combines keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual foresight from a frozen video model.
Coverage-preserving anchor selection and attention masking create one-second targets while preventing teacher-forced future actions from affecting foresight queries.
On four LIBERO suites, success rises from 85.90% to 90.55% after the complete pretraining and fine-tuning pipeline.
Results are heterogeneous: 24 of 40 tasks improve, 10 decline, and 6 tie; the study does not isolate individual training components or variability.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $\pi_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.
authors: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Dongbin Zhang, Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Peng Jiao, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Aligns robot actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a common behavioral-intent space.
Uses an embodiment-conditioned decoder to translate shared intent into robot-specific actions and control interfaces.
Adapts to a new robot from a single recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only embodiment embeddings.
With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO reaches 76.7% average success on real SO-101 and Piper robots, versus 70.0% for fully finetuned π₀.
Reports 97.3% success on LIBERO, 52.7% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 80.8% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CIALLO. (A) During pretraining, three encoders map an action chunk with proprioception, a pair of current and future frames, and an instruction grounded in the current frame into a shared intent space. We align their outputs with contrastive losses and train a shared decoder to reconstruct the demonstrated actions from each intent, conditioned on the robot’s embodiment parameters. (B) To learn a policy, Qwen-CIALLO predicts intent from observations and instructions, using the frozen action encoder as a teacher and the demonstrated actions to supervise the decoder output. CS denotes cosine similarity loss. (C) To transfer the codec to a new robot, we first calibrate its essential vector and arm and axis embeddings while keeping the shared weights fixed, then train the policy with the calibrated codec frozen.

Figure 2. The action codec. The action encoder (middle) uses the essential vector E to map control signals into shared intent, incorporating context from the proprioceptive encoder (top). The decoder (bottom) combines this intent with the target action schema and current proprioception, remodulates the result for the target embodiment, and uses the TransConv Head to predict each control scalar on a shared basis of 256 ordered bins. The decoded action is the softmax expectation over the bin centers.

Figure 4. Evolution of bin weights under scalar supervision. Bars show the softmax weights at six training steps. The blue line indicates the predicted scalar, computed as their expectation, and the red cross marks the nominal target of 0.75. The prediction approaches the target as the weights change, although no loss is applied directly to the bin weights.

Figure 3. Vision and text paths. The vision encoder compares current and future observations with a shared frozen DINOv2 backbone and an E-conditioned local interaction encoder, then pools valid tokens from multiple cameras into chunk-level intent. The text codec compresses the instruction into a task-level intent, grounds it using features reused from the current frame to form the same K ×D intent interface, and reconstructs masked instruction tokens from the task-level intent.

Figure 5. Intent geometry at the final pretraining checkpoint. Color identifies the embodiment and marker shape identifies the input modality. A shared three-dimensional t-SNE embedding is fitted after reducing the flattened intents to 50 dimensions with PCA. The projection emphasizes local neighborhood structure, while global distances should not be interpreted quantitatively.

Figure 6. Demonstration sequences for the three real robot tasks on SO-101 and single-arm Piper. Each row shows front camera observations at 15%, 50%, and 85% of one demonstration, ordered from left to right. These examples illustrate the recorded trajectories and do not indicate evaluation success.

papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani
bullets: Reads experiment steps from a photo of a printed protocol.
Identifies identical containers by reading labels from multiple camera views, without fixed positions or fiducial markers.
Relocates target containers before every step and adapts execution settings, including speed, to the handled material.
Completed 5/5 runs of one protocol and 4/5 of another without human intervention; correctly identified all containers in 160 localization trials.
Demonstrated on a Franka Panda arm and two children’s chemistry-kit protocols, so scope is limited to the tested setup and procedures.

Once per run, the instruction parser reads the steps from a photo of the sheet, the scene agent names the objects on the bench, and the planner orders the sub-tasks. For each sub-task, the skill-call agent produces one skill call, and the skill locates its target again before it acts. Red markers show where P1–P5 are implemented.

Fig. 1. Curie’s Jarvis workflow. (A) A vision-language model reads the protocol photo. The LLM orders subtasks and replans after failures. (B) Votes across four camera views identify vessels from paper labels. (C) A 3D point cloud reconstructs the bench; multi-view geometry locates the target vessel. (D) The LLM selects predefined skills and their parameters for the Franka Panda. Shown: Magic Beaker.

Fig. 3. One locate on the real bench. (a) SAM 3 masks for the prompt in each of the four camera views. (b) The label read on the container in each view and the vote across cameras. (c) The container’s position from multi-view geometry, which the skill then uses.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
authors: Denis Grachev, Damien LaRocque, Omar Moured
bullets: Retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks performs strongly without policy training.
Retrieval experiences the smallest performance drop among evaluated policies under LIBERO-Plus perturbations.
Across nine public VLAs, fine-tuning mainly improves the vision-language backbone as a retrieval key; predicted actions remain close to demonstrations.
The proposed Local Action Consistency (LAC) metric correlates with retrieval success and can guide retrieval-key training.

papers.abstract: Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention. We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor. We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $\pi_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.
authors: Zequan Zeng, Kai Wang, Delvin Ce Zhang, Huaping Liu, Zhipeng Yuan, Junqin Yang, YunLong Zhang
bullets: Targets failures from confusing similar workflow stages and stalling after human intervention.
Uses a vision–language planner to create ordered atomic skills from the protocol and workspace view.
A multiframe monitor detects skill completion or infeasibility, triggering progression or replanning.
A skill-conditioned vision–language–action policy generates trajectories, coordinated asynchronously with monitoring.
Achieves 82% success in blood gas analysis and 70% in tube sorting; it also replans after sample removal and continues processing.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of Robo-MLT. A frozen Qwen3.7-Max planner maps a user command, the instrument protocol, and an initial scene observation to an ordered sequence of atomic skills. System 2 tracks the plan with a dual-head execution monitor and invokes replanning once the active skill can no longer be completed; System 1 executes the active skill with a Qwen3-VL-conditioned flow-matching policy.

Fig. 3. Architecture of the System 2 execution monitor. Frozen SigLIP2 encoders embed a sliding window of M multiview observations and the active skill instruction lt; a causal temporal encoder and cross-attention blocks ground the observation history in the instruction to form the feature vt, from which two MLP heads predict the completion and recovery probabilities γ̂t and β̂t.

Fig. 1. Perceptual aliasing in medical laboratory automation, and the proposed Robo-MLT framework. (Top) In a reversible workflow, visually similar observations can require opposite actions; a policy without explicit workflow state may therefore act at the wrong stage. (Bottom) System 2 tracks the active skill from temporal observations; System 1 maps that skill and the current observation to fine-grained trajectories.

Fig. 6. Representative execution timeline of Robo-MLT on Blood Gas Analysis. The completion and recovery probabilities predicted by System 2 are shown over a continuous execution, with the active skills indicated above each plot. The timeline illustrates skill transitions and workflow recovery following an operator-induced interruption.

Fig. 5. Real-world performance on the nominal suite. (a) Task success rate SR, (b) sample completion rate SCR, and (c) completion time. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals in (a)–(b) and ±1 SD in (c).

Fig. 7. Representative perceptual-aliasing failure of end-to-end IL and VLA baselines on Blood Gas Analysis. Visually similar observations during insertion and withdrawal can cause the policy to confuse workflow stages, leading to repeated insertion attempts and ultimately stalling the procedure.

Fig. 4. The two real-world medical laboratory tasks. (Top) Blood Gas Analysis with its |S|=7 atomic skills. (Bottom) Blood Sample Tube Sorting: clotting and routine tubes are randomly placed on the rack and sorted into their designated plates (|S|=5).

papers.abstract: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.
authors: Delin Zhao, Zhengrong Yue, Junlin He, Yali Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed practice sources, which may fail to expose new weaknesses as capabilities change.
Alternates updates to a curriculum harness that proposes informative challenges and an execution harness that develops reusable revisions.
Uses admitted challenge snapshots to compare execution revisions while keeping the other component fixed.
Starting from compact LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting deployment outperformed evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels.

On LIBERO-PRO, it achieved 74.0% success, improving over the initial deployment and direct VLA-controller execution; case studies cover practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

figures.caption: Figure 3 The final deployment improves across all four evaluation panels. Bar labels give success counts on a 200-episode scale. Model baselines use checkpoints fine-tuned on original LIBERO and evaluated without further training on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X.

Figure 1 From fixed practice to adversarial co-evolution. (a) Fixed practice improves execution against an unchanged challenge source. (b) In RoboACE, the curriculum exposes current execution weaknesses, while execution expands its capabilities through reusable harness revisions. As capabilities grow, the curriculum targets new weaknesses, sustaining adversarial coevolution. The blue and orange robots represent the execution and curriculum harnesses, respectively.

Figure 2 Alternating revisions connect challenge production and execution. The curriculum side uses prior capability evidence to probe a fixed execution deployment. Admitted conditions form a fixed snapshot for comparing execution revisions, whose outcomes inform the next round. Independent agents run the harnesses, external optimizers revise them, and the Strategic Advisor periodically reviews the longer history.

Figure 4 Reusable revisions address concrete gaps in both harnesses. Each row follows a case from its starting point to a reusable revision and the recorded follow-up. (a) The curriculum revision changes how the agent retrieves past execution feedback to select practice. A subsequent independent run uses the reader to create a valid 30-condition course with two agent-selected replacements. (b) Following new drawer practice selected by the curriculum, the execution revision distinguishes a front-panel reference point from the attached handle and requires target-drawer verification. Successes change from 48 to 50 on the same 54-condition snapshot. The frame is recorded, and the markers and rule summaries are explanatory.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.

Across five real-world tasks, reduces mean latency from 137.25 ms to 93.25 ms (1.47× speedup) while achieving 61% average success versus 60% unpruned.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.
bullets: Addresses the need to reduce reliance on expensive real-robot training data.
Existing video-based transfer methods are hindered by action representations entangled with scene-specific noise.
AIT first extracts and disentangles explicit and implicit action intents from human manipulation videos.
It then aligns human and robot domains in a shared intent space and decodes intents into executable robot actions.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show more effective and consistent transfer than prior baselines.

papers.abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.
bullets: Targets the challenge of handling objects with different materials, deformation, and contact dynamics.
Estimates physical parameters by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation.
Conditions a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy on the recovered physical properties.
Uses a physics memory bank for efficient retrieval without online simulation optimization.
Experiments in simulation and the real world report improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed training framework. Given multi-view images, we first estimate the physical properties of the manipulated object by combining feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF-3DGS) with MPM via a differentiable physical simulation. The simulator is coupled with a differentiable rasterizer and optimized under video guidance, where gradients are back-propagated through the simulation. Physics-based constraints, including Dirichlet boundary conditions for manipulation events and geometric consistency via temporal Chamfer distance, further regularize the estimated physical parameters by aligning simulated particle dynamics with demonstration videos. The learned physical parameters are then injected into a physical-aware diffusion policy as physics conditions, together with language instructions and visual observations, enabling the policy to predict physics-consistent robot actions and gripper states.

Fig. 3. Object preservation results on fragile objects. Among successful pick-and-place trials, the methods differ in their ability to preserve object integrity. We evaluate object preservation by measuring grape rupture and irreversible deformation of paper cups over 30 successful pick-andplace trials. A trial is considered successful only if the object remains intact, exhibiting neither grape rupture nor irreversible deformation. Our method achieves the highest object preservation success rate on both object categories.

Fig. 4. Visualization of learned material-aware routing weights in our MoE policy. Each row represents an object and each column corresponds to a physical-property expert. The bubble size and color indicate the routing weight assigned to each expert. The learned router discovers clear expert specialization, where objects with different physical characteristics are preferentially routed to their corresponding experts while maintaining adaptive soft assignments across experts.

papers.abstract: We introduce DreamFormer, a model-based agent that acquires language-conditioned, multi-task skills by imitating expert demonstrations within the latent imagination of a learned world model. DreamFormer first learns a task-agnostic Transformer world model from unstructured play data, then acquires task-specific behaviors by optimizing an intrinsic reward that aligns agent-generated rollouts with expert demonstrations in latent space. Since the policy is trained on-policy inside imagination, it is exposed to its own errors during training, mitigating the covariate shift inherent to offline behavioral cloning. To make long-horizon imagination affordable, DreamFormer encodes a high-resolution multi-view robotic observation into a single input token, avoiding both spatial downsampling and the multi-token representations used by prior Transformer world models. On the long-horizon CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer outperforms LUMOS, the comparable model-based agent, on single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs 2.34 average tasks completed per chain of five) while keeping imagination rollouts tractable. Against HULC, the behavior cloning baseline, it nearly doubles performance on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (1.30 vs 0.67), indicating that dynamics learned by the world model transfer more readily than a directly cloned policy. This is consistent with the role attributed to internal models in biological agents, where a model of environment dynamics supports behavior in situations not previously encountered.
bullets: Learns a task-agnostic world model from unstructured play data, then optimizes task behavior in imagined rollouts aligned with expert demonstrations.
On-policy training within imagination exposes the policy to its own errors, reducing offline behavioral-cloning covariate shift.
Compresses high-resolution multi-view observations into a single token to keep long-horizon Transformer imagination tractable.
On CALVIN, completes more tasks than LUMOS in single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs. 2.34) and nearly doubles HULC’s zero-shot transfer performance (1.30 vs. 0.67).

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual feedback degrades under closure occlusion. AgenticTactileVLA is presented as an execution-time supervisor that shifts part of object-specific adaptation from prediction to physical interaction. A fixed VLA provides the approach and hand targets; the supervisor decides whether to remain transparent, refine finger flexion, retain or release the corrected configuration, return control to the VLA for retry, or select a compliant hand-control regime. It uses finger-position and motor-effort feedback as proprioceptive contact evidence and requires neither tactile sensors nor VLA retraining. On a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand, a randomized matched-block evaluation on five objects held out from VLA training yields 61.3% completion for the base VLA, 72.0% for unconditional close-to-stall control, and 84.0% for the supervisor under a shared budget; the gain is positive on every object and persists under moderate pose perturbations. Ablations show the gain is not explained by extended closure alone, and that selective triggering reduces correction episodes by 65.7% with no detected change in completion. A retention audit shows acceptance predicts retention in 88.9% of held-out cases, while compliant objects expose conservative false rejection. A thin-walled-cup study demonstrates contextual routing to compliant control, matching an always-compliant reference. These results suggest that contact-guided execution-time adaptation can improve the object-level generalization of a fixed VLA to held-out objects by adapting physical realization without object-specific retraining.
bullets: Addresses failures caused by object-specific geometry, compliance, and visual occlusion during grasp execution.
Supervises a fixed VLA by selectively refining finger flexion, retaining or releasing corrections, retrying with VLA control, or routing to compliant hand control.
Uses finger position and motor-effort feedback as contact evidence, requiring no tactile sensors or VLA retraining.
On five held-out objects, completion improved from 61.3% for the base VLA to 84.0% with the supervisor under a shared budget; gains persisted under moderate pose perturbations.
Selective triggering reduced correction episodes by 65.7% without detected completion loss, while compliant objects revealed conservative false rejection as a limitation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.
bullets: Studies how dataset size, training updates, checkpoint selection, and simulation affect VLA adaptation for precise chess-piece manipulation.

In simulation, success improves with more data and updates; a short learning-rate cooldown adds up to 31 success-rate points.
Validation loss and action error are unreliable for selecting checkpoints.
Several rollout-based and reinforcement-learning refinements did not measurably outperform plain behavior cloning in this setting; simulator, expert, and demonstrations are released.

papers.abstract: Robots are increasingly expected to execute natural-language manipulation tasks in real-world environments. This is particularly relevant in household assistance and logistics, where clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and execution feasibility. This challenge becomes even more pronounced for bimanual humanoid platforms, where coordinating two manipulators introduces additional interaction and kinematic constraints. We present a zero-shot vision-language framework for execution-aware bimanual manipulation that jointly reasons about task objectives and physical feasibility. Planning is grounded in a structured scene representation that combines semantic object relations with execution constraints, enabling the selection of obstacle relocations and execution choices while preserving task semantics. Compatible actions are organised into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator evaluates these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history to support local recovery or targeted replanning. Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid robot across nine language-conditioned manipulation scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers from execution failures with fewer model queries than always replanning. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining execution reasoning directly into task planning. Videos and additional material are available on the Project Webpage: https://advrhumanoids.github.io/bridging-planning-execution/.
bullets: Targets household and logistics tasks where clutter, bimanual coordination, and kinematic constraints complicate execution.
Uses a structured scene representation combining semantic object relations with execution constraints to choose relocations and actions.

A hierarchical validator handles perceptual uncertainty and supports local recovery or targeted replanning using execution history.
On the CENTAURO robot, it achieves higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline and recovers failures with fewer model queries than always replanning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed language-conditioned bimanual manipulation pipeline. papers.abstract: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between action-oriented driving instructions and direct continuous ego-trajectory prediction.
Introduces TrajCond, a discrete 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory for conditioning VLA planning.
Uses two-stage training, followed by simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories.
Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show consistent gains in open- and closed-loop trajectory prediction.
Discrete trajectories are more effective as conditioning signals than as final planning outputs.

papers.abstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining progress across successive goals while producing stable, natural whole-body motion in confined spaces.
Coordinates three asynchronous roles: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body control.
Uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and execution.
Introduces a physics-grounded data engine for collision-aware, route-faithful motion demonstrations paired with visual observations.

In simulation, LHNav improves success and smoothness while reducing collisions and falls; it reaches 75.56% long-horizon success using only single-goal training, and transfers to real-world zero-shot execution on a Unitree G1.

An action buffer supplies the latest motion-token chunk to the Brainstem’s frozen SONIC controller, which combines it with proprioception to produce joint targets at 50 Hz for PD control. papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project website: https://j-x-chen.github.io/Thermo-VLA-web/
bullets: Addresses the limited temperature-aware relational reasoning of VLAs that treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs.
Introduces a ThermoRes Encoder that separates hot and cold representations and applies gated, language-conditioned residual modulation to RGB tokens.
Evaluates six real-world tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1, covering grounding and relational reasoning.
Achieves a 0.86 average success rate on four thermal-dependent tasks, 18 percentage points above the pi_0.5 RGB-thermal baseline.
Maintains a 0.78 average success rate under unseen objects and scene variations; the mechanism also improves color-attribute tasks in simulation and on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.
bullets: Motivation: Generalist robot policies may fail on a single interpretable step despite otherwise completing the task.
Method: Replays of 21 decisions under reworded instructions identify a misbinding, then copy the rewording’s per-layer effect into language-model MLP weights.
Result: Held-out success increased from 27 to 106 of 128 episodes, with 81 fixes and 2 regressions; random same-size edits had no effect.
Scope: Editing the language model worked best; edits to the action expert or head helped less or not at all, and unrelated failure-targeted edits did not help.
Caveat: Substantial outcome variability motivates paired reruns of the unedited policy and confirmation on held-out seeds.

papers.abstract: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient. Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.
bullets: Addresses the accuracy loss and computational cost of merging heterogeneous, privately trained driving experts.
Jointly decomposes expert weight updates with SVD into shared components and small domain-specific residuals.
Uses two clip-level blind routers for VLM reasoning and flow-matching dynamics, trained from soft labels on a small proxy set.
Across six diverse driving domains and vehicle types, it approaches per-domain expert accuracy and outperforms reported baselines near single-model cost.
New domains can be added by projecting their updates onto the shared basis, without end-to-end retraining; the model also generalizes to unseen domain combinations.

Composition is trained on a small proxy set, and a new domain opts in by projecting its delta onto the frozen basis.

papers.title: DeltaForge: A Post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts VLA for Multi-Domain Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DeltaForge efficiently consolidates independently fine-tuned driving VLA experts into one multi-domain model by routing only compact domain-specific weight components.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
bullets: Addresses stale observations and reduced control rates caused by placing large VLA backbones in the closed-loop control path.
Runs a slow vision-language model and fast flow-matching action head asynchronously via LCM.
Fuses stale semantic features with fresh visual input and uses desynchronized training plus adaptive temporal aggregation to handle latency.
Maintains 20 Hz control from 0.8B to 8B backbones, while the synchronous pipeline drops from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz on RoboTwin.
Achieves higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline on a real humanoid with dexterous hands.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. DASH architecture. The policy is split into a slow VLM (System 2) and a fast action head (System 1), deployed as three concurrent processes (environment, VLM server, and action server) coupled by a decentralized, non-blocking latest-value bus (LCM). The VLM runs off the control loop and publishes a context (the hidden states of the routed VLM layers) that the action head reads with latest-value semantics, so the control rate is set by the action head alone.

Fig. 7. Matched simulation episodes, synchronous inference (top) vs. DASH (bottom). Frames are sampled at equal intervals of simulated time up to the completion time of the successful run; done marks completion, and still running marks the run that later times out.

Fig. 2. (a) Uncertainty grows along the prediction horizon: the early portion of an action chunk is reliable, while its distant tail admits increasingly different future actions. (b) Frequent chunk updates curb divergence: synchronous inference executes the long, uncertain tail of each chunk, so a new prediction can trigger a large correction; DASH refreshes chunks often and stays on the reliable early portion.

Fig. 4. Desynchronized training data. The two visual channels are sampled at different times so the training inputs reproduce the staleness met at deployment, while the supervision target remains anchored at the action head’s timestamp.

Fig. 5. Adaptive interpolation for temporal aggregation. The fractional offset measured from the true chunk arrival interval is split into a whole-tick shift and a linear interpolation between adjacent entries, with the residual fractions accumulated so the alignment tracks elapsed execution time.

Fig. 6. Success rate by backbone size (Table I): synchronous inference, Async (w/o desynced training), and DASH. DASH is higher than synchronous inference at every size (+1.0/+2.7/+5.9/+3.2 pp) while its action path stays at 50ms.

papers.abstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: https://wrld.github.io/surgtap-3d/
bullets: Addresses limited scale, diversity, and interaction-aware 3D supervision in existing surgical datasets.
Provides 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from robotic and manual surgeries.
Uses contact-region prompting, tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement to convert monocular videos into structured annotations.
Includes temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks despite occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and fast motion.
Benchmarks instrument and tissue tracking, displacement estimation, deformable reconstruction, and surgical action understanding.

papers.abstract: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.
bullets: Frozen monitors degrade to near-chance failure ranking after task or policy changes.
SFF updates only the monitor’s last linear layer after each episode using its success/failure label; its threshold adapts after successes.
The method runs at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core.
Under unannounced drift, SFF outperformed a frozen monitor on 4 of 5 simulated test suites and a reset strategy on all suites.
Across 434 real-robot runs involving four VLAs, SFF outperformed the frozen monitor after task or policy switches and exceeded a full reset in an exploratory comparison.
