papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
bullets: Problem: Existing vision-language-action and world-action priors may not adequately capture humanoid robot motion structure.
Method: Kinematic Action Models pretrain directly on whole-body motion and condition generation on tasks, visual observations, and execution feedback.
Architecture: Kimodo-Policy combines a frozen text-to-motion backbone, lightweight ControlNet visual conditioning, hierarchical root-body-hand coordination, and motion-history-based action chunks.
Results: It reports 72.14% overall success on HumanoidArena, competitive SIMPLE performance, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence that motion generation can complement foundation models for humanoid action learning.

papers.abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
bullets: Builds traceable scene–factor–decision records with candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations to refine training data from critical events and verified failures.
Uses Xiaomi-Drive-o1, a shared vision-language model integrating perception, causation, action, world modeling, and value estimation.
Connects task blocks through candidate-specific latent evidence and predicted visual consequences, while a value-of-computation head allocates inference effort adaptively.
Reports strong benchmark results, including the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and broad metric improvements over Alpamayo 1.5 in AlpaSim.
Joint training improves 5 s minADE@6 for the 0.8B model by about 54%, and adaptive inference reaches full-reasoning performance with 28% of the tokens; real-vehicle tests support runtime feasibility.

figures.caption: Figure 5 Annotation pipeline for key factor–decision pairs and CoC, illustrated using a 20-second driving clip. papers.abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
bullets: Zero-shot, end-to-end robot control gives coding agents capabilities beyond earlier VLA and WAM systems.
Digital threats such as indirect prompt injection can propagate from webpages or emails to physical robot behavior.
ArmedAgent evaluates robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios.
The benchmark is tested in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm across several frontier models and agent frameworks.
Results indicate substantial safety risks in current coding-agent robot-control systems.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic gameplay in Minecraft and Roblox, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting gameplay demonstrations for vision-language-action models.
An LLM agent builds executable game environments and skill-targeted tasks.
Programmatic experts use privileged simulator state to produce instructions, visual observations, and keyboard/mouse actions.
Script2Play is behavior-cloned on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay.
It performs effectively on multiple public benchmarks and generalizes across game engines.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.
bullets: Models human activity as part of the manipulation task rather than background variation.
Covers four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence, with paired human-present task variants.
Includes a demonstration-generation pipeline and evaluates VLA, imitation-learning, and heuristic policies.
Human presence challenges current policies; manipulation and recovery are the dominant failure sources, and success does not consistently imply better safety.
HARP-Bench demonstrations improve simulated performance and help on real-world human contribution, but transfer to interruption remains limited.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.
bullets: Targets the high latency of autoregressive action generation on resource-constrained robots.
Uses a lightweight retrieval-augmented draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without an additional neural draft model.
Reduces verification overhead through kinematics-guided action acceptance and KV-cache-sharing attention.
Introduces the Zora core to accelerate irregular memory access during retrieval.
On four VLA models using LIBERO, it retains comparable accuracy and achieves up to 3.4× software-only and 7.6× hardware-supported speedup over GPUs.

figures.caption: Fig. 12. Overview of the ZORA core architecture. The core accelerates HNSW-based DG retrieval through a four-stage pipeline: fetch, compute, accumulation, and update. The PE array exploits node-level parallelism and embedding-level parallelism to compute partial similarity scores between the query embedding and neighbor embeddings. Partial similarity scores are accumulated and then consumed by either the reduction unit for greedy search in upper HNSW layers or the comparison units for top-k selection in the bottom layer. Lastly, the neighbor index fetch unit updates the search frontier for unvisited nodes.

Fig. 11. Overview of the ZORA accelerator architecture. The accelerator contains a ZORA core to accelerate DG retrieval, a checker unit, and a DNN accelerator. Yellow blocks highlight our key contributions.

Fig. 2. The HNSW-based retrieval process. The input is first encoded into a query embedding, which is used to search the vector database before selecting the top-K retrieved results for downstream VLA models. The search database is implemented with a HNSW graph, where search proceeds in a coarse-tofine manner, from the top layer to the bottom layer.

Fig. 1. Inference process of single-action autoregressive VLA models. With the visual observation ot and language instruction I, the model first performs a prefill step to encode the input context and generate the KV cache. During decoding, action tokens are generated autoregressively and appended to the KV cache. Once all action tokens are generated, including relative movement ∆xt+1, rotation change ∆rt+1, and gripper state gt+1, the VLA model then uses a small action detokenizer to decode the action and control the robot. Lastly, the execution updates the next observation for subsequent action generation.

papers.abstract: Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the high action-inference cost that slows vision-based robot execution.
Generates continuous target positions from discontinuous predictions using a tracking-control formulation.
Uses asynchronous inference and variance-based adaptive action skipping to improve execution speed.
Evaluated with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot.
Reports substantial speedups while maintaining high task success rates.

papers.abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io
bullets: Addresses VLA failures under shifts in viewpoint, background, object identity, and robot morphology.
Uses geometric calibration to warp source demonstrations toward the target setup.
Applies coarse-to-fine retrieval to select trajectories compatible with the base VLA.
Guides flow-matching inference without retraining the VLA or enlarging its context window.
Evaluated across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation; it outperforms related baselines in simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RAGu pipeline. (a) We filter real-world datasets using semantic keywords for broad task categories with similar kinematic profiles, such as pick-and-place via language instruction labels in the datasets. (b) Task-relevant objects in the target scene are identified using semantic bounding box detection to extract target waypoints W ′, allowing the source trajectories to be smoothly adapted despite visual shifts. (c) Retrieval candidates i are coarsely pruned to the top-N using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based matching. We then select the optimal trajectory i⋆ from pruned trajectories i ′ ∈ [N ] that minimizes the guidance gradient norm (||∇A0 Ci∗(Xt)||2), retrieving the demonstration best aligned with the VLA’s expected Cartesian trajectory Xt. (d) At test time, the chosen reference i⋆ defines an energy field (Lwarp ≈ ||Xt − i⋆||2), steering diffusion denoising for zero-shot adaptation.

Figure 4: Real-World Success Rates. Comparing RAGu against the base flow-matching policy (π0.5), retrieval-based in-context learning baseline (RICL) and a VLM-based goal steering baseline (Omniguide). We evaluate the models across 5 diverse manipulation tasks: Open Drawer, Open Cabinet, Close Microwave, Towel to Plate, & Wipe Table.

Figure 2: RAGu enables zero-shot adaptation across domains and embodiments. RAGu transfers manipulation knowledge across four settings: Real→Real, Real→Sim, Sim→Real with different morphologies with the base VLA’s weights completely frozen without any parameter update.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale. Project website: ember-center-berkeley.github.io/DreamVLA.
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of collecting extensive whole-body humanoid demonstrations and designing task-specific RL rewards.
Uses generated motion trajectories as references to guide reinforcement learning toward reliable task execution.
Introduces reference-conditioned DAgger distillation: failed learner rollouts are corrected by restarting an RL expert from sampled learner states with the same reference suffix.
Evaluates platform picking, drawer opening, button pressing, and walking-plus-picking tasks, with ablations on DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated-data scale.

Our DAgger loop restarts the privileged expert from a sampled state of a failed VLA rollout, follows the same reference suffix, and aggregates successful recoveries. papers.abstract: Search allows a robotic policy to evaluate candidate futures before committing to an action. Motivated by test-time planning for vision-language action (VLA) models, we study selective search over action chunks in PushT using a frozen Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy. Beam search generates perturbed alternatives around the policy prediction and scores them through rollouts from cloned simulator states. Across 50 evaluation episodes, beam search raises task success from 0% to 18% and increases average cumulative reward from 39.44 to 103.2. We introduce One Step Ahead (OSA), a gate that simulates the nominal policy chunk and invokes full search only when its predicted coverage drop exceeds a threshold. In the reported ablations, OSA preserves or improves success while reducing runtime by approximately 3x relative to full beam search. Ablations over tree depth, branching factor, beam width, and replanning frequency show that larger search budgets do not consistently improve performance. The results support selective test-time search for action-chunking policies; evaluation on language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots remains future work.
bullets: Beam search evaluates perturbed action-chunk candidates using rollouts from cloned simulator states.
Across 50 episodes, success increases from 0% to 18%, and average cumulative reward rises from 39.44 to 103.2.
One Step Ahead (OSA) triggers full search only when the nominal policy predicts a coverage drop.
Search-budget ablations show that larger tree depth, branching, beam width, or replanning frequency do not consistently help.
The study is limited to simulated PushT; language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots are not evaluated.

Figure 3. One Step Ahead ablation at D = 4, C = 8, and beam widths 2, 4, and 8. Blue: full beam search; green: OSA. Panels show success, average cumulative reward, and runtime. papers.abstract: A language model can repair a robot policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on $\pi_{0.5}$ all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3\% to 92.0\% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired $p=1.31\times10^{-10}$). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3\% to 87.5\%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor's own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0\% to 48.6\%, while the evaluated VLA's aggregate rate is unchanged. The evidence supports precise lexical repair, not general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.
authors: Jusheng Zhang, Keze Wang, Liang Lin
bullets: Three sessions improved success on 765 held-out paraphrases, with the best result rising from 86.3% to 92.0%.
Edits affected instructions containing the modified tokens; the other 430 episodes showed no outcome changes.
Random-direction edits did not help, supporting the specificity of the weight edits.
Full lexicon replacement achieved similar gains but caused more regressions; the direct difference was not statistically significant.
The evidence supports targeted lexical repair, not acquisition of broadly missing capabilities; most additional candidate edits were rejected.

papers.abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.
authors: Pranav Teegavarapu, Sriyash Poddar, Rico Qi, Cleah Winston, Krisha Khandelwal, Aykut Onyol, Natasha Jaques, Abhishek Gupta
bullets: Real users tend to intervene when robot progress stalls, and their corrective actions are often suboptimal—contrary to common simulation assumptions.

Decoupled critics stabilize learning by preventing intervention bonuses from propagating to pre-intervention states.
The method achieves 10–50% higher success than competitive baselines in simulation and on real robots, and improves pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving. We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space. In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving). The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model. Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference. This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning. These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual driving information and sparse language or trajectory supervision in VLA models.
Introduces a progressive chain of task-specific latent expert tokens within the VLA model.
Distills visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from DINOv3, SAM3, and DepthAnything3.
Uses curriculum-style supervision that progresses from representation to semantics and geometry while targeting efficient inference.
Experiments across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks report consistent improvements in object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning.

papers.abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. Website: https://pranjal2041.github.io/cua-embodied
bullets: Embodied tasks can be reframed as interaction with software that renders an environment and exposes controls.
A single computer-use agent design was reused across four ECCV workshop competitions without competition-specific tuning.
The agent earned first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place finishes across those competitions.
Software-learned skills such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration transferred to embodied tasks.
The authors argue this could support a single general model for embodied AI.

Figure 3: Computer use and embodied AI require much of the same from an agent. In both, it must see its surroundings, locate a target, act on it precisely, issue discrete commands, and explore. The main difference is time, as the screen often changes slowly while the physical world keeps moving.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SURE. (a) Given observations and a language instruction, an OpenVLA-7B backbone produces action tokens that are decoded into action chunks. (b) Our probabilistic action decoder models translation and rotation as discretized distributions and recovers continuous controls with expectation-based decoding, capturing spatial uncertainty and multimodality. (c) During training, Soft-DTW alignment supervision aligns predicted and demonstrated action chunks that progress at different speeds, addressing temporal uncertainty in robot demonstrations.

Figure 2: Architecture of the probabilistic action decoder. Action tokens Ht ∈ Rk×da×dV LM are first fused by a grouped 1 × 1 convolution and then split into translation, rotation, and gripper branches. Translation and rotation use two Deconv Blocks to upsample an ordered bin axis from 1 → R/4 → R. The resulting per-axis logits over R bins are normalized by softmax and decoded into continuous actions by expectation. Each Deconv Block combines depthwise transposed convolution with pointwise residual layers to encode local correlations among neighboring bins. The gripper action is decoded by a lightweight MLP.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically generate actions in chunks, organizing continuous robot execution into separately predicted segments and thus introducing potential discontinuities at action-chunk transitions. We propose ODEAction, a chunk-free action generation paradigm that replaces action-chunk prediction with Continuous Action Evolution. Given visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioceptive information, ODEAction learns an action transition field defined over action space, where a transition vector characterizes the evolution rate of the current action with respect to evolution time. During execution, the model takes the current action as its initial condition and integrates the learned field using an ordinary differential equation (ODE), recursively generating subsequent actions with explicit dependencies. ODEAction is implemented as an action head and does not depend on a specific vision-language backbone architecture. Experiments on LIBERO, EBench, RoboTwin, and real robots show that ODEAction improves both task performance and trajectory quality over matched action-chunking baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on fine manipulation tasks.

bullets: Addresses discontinuities caused by independently predicted action chunks in vision-language-action models.
Learns an action transition field conditioned on visual observations, language instructions, and proprioception.

Implemented as a backbone-agnostic action head.
Experiments across simulated and real-robot settings show improved task performance and trajectory quality, especially for fine manipulation.

papers.abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.
authors: Boran Zhao, Yanbin Hu, Jun Ye, Zhenxian Hu, Yuxin Zhai, Jin Cui, Pengju Ren
bullets: Addresses noisy, redundant episodic memories that obscure transferable manipulation principles in complex 3D scenes.

(C) Historical experiences retrieved from the Spatial and Object suites provide reusable manipulation priors for grasping, in-drawer placement, and drawer closure, enabling compositional experience transfer across subgoals.

Fig. 1. Illustration of memory noise and its effects on 3D manipulation. (b) Using ECHO [6] for manipulation execution, we group memories by target and subgoal and randomly remove 30% of redundant entries differing only in non-target object details while preserving task-relevant experiences. On LIBERO-Long, in-distribution success rates decrease slightly from 93.50% to 93.25%, whereas out-of-distribution success rates improve from 92.78% to 94.67%. These results suggest that removing redundant memory details can improve out-of-distribution generalization while largely preserving indistribution performance.

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.

figures.caption: Figure 7 Architecture of A2-WLA. A motion-aware history encoder converts six-frame multiview histories into visual tokens. A 2B Qwen3-VL backbone combines these tokens with the task instruction to produce current context and a latent action. The world model predicts future visual features, which a spatial compressor aggregates into future context. An 18-layer action expert uses both contexts to generate a 50-step action chunk through ten-step flow integration, while a separate head estimates per-step progress. During recovery, a correction adapter injects a code-conditioned residual after the ninth layer. The lower panel shows how adjacent differences between paired-frame representations provide motion features for gated cross-attention and residual fusion before visual token merging.

Figure 1 The A2-MEAS framework. The MetaBrain coordinates task reasoning and recovery. Grounding agents provide specialized evidence. The correction interface combines recovery language, spatial evidence, executed history, and a fresh base-action proposal to modulate A2-WLA. These agents cooperate to control one robot.

Figure 3 The correction interface within action generation. Language, spatial evidence, executed history and a fresh base proposal are encoded once per candidate. At every flow step, the adapter uses the current action hidden states to produce position-dependent residuals. Injection after the ninth of 18 action layers allows subsequent layers to convert the modified state into a corrected flow velocity. Orange modules are trained during correction learning while the base model is frozen. All parameters remain fixed during deployment.

Figure 6 Execution and recovery as one feedback loop. Ordinary action generation records the executed prefix and its observed outcome. An abnormal event invokes the MetaBrain and the required grounding agents. A fresh recovery state conditions both the base proposal and corrected generation. Failed attempts update the evidence and consume the remaining event budget. Verified recovery resumes execution toward the unfinished task goal. A timeout, exhausted budget or failed feasibility check exits recovery.

Figure 2 State progression during the closed-loop recovery of a misaligned filter placement. papers.abstract: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.
authors: Shengjun Deng, Yinghan Zhang, Chengrui Wei, Liu Liang, Songyuan Liu, Pengkun Zheng, Yajun Zheng, Ying Zhang, Yuan Tian, Xi Li, Teng Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of identifying and consistently following a described person from egocentric observations.
Uses complementary mask and bounding-box grounding supervision alongside investigated auxiliary tasks such as segmentation, spatial classification, and future prediction.
Introduces Q-identity, which compresses historical observations while preserving target-specific appearance and spatial cues.
A 0.8B-parameter model reaches a 77.9% average success rate on EVT-Bench, 16.9 percentage points above OmTrackVLA across three tasks.
Provides a quadruped-robot dataset with 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames; masks also yield bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels automatically.

Right: Q-identity aggregates target-region features and full-image context through joint query–target self-attention, full-image cross-attention, and feed-forward updates. The resulting compact historical tokens are fed back into the VLA’s visual input.

The dataset contains 33 target appearance profiles, including 24 female and 9 male profiles. (B) Representative qualitative examples from indoor STT, outdoor STT, and outdoor DT sequences. papers.selection_reason: Presents a target-grounded Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework for embodied person tracking, integrating auxiliary supervision and efficient temporal modeling, directly relevant to embodied AI and VLA research.
papers.title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
papers.tldr: DobotTrack improves language-guided embodied person tracking by combining target-grounded auxiliary supervision with efficient, identity-aware temporal memory.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.
bullets: Addresses the tension between real-time onboard inference, onboard-model failures, and limited server capacity.
Uses a small onboard VLA with failure prediction to selectively switch action generation to a large server VLA.
Formulates switching as minimizing server-request cost subject to a required success probability.
In simulation on three LIBERO suites, it improved success by 11–22 percentage points over the small VLA alone.
It used 49–77% fewer requests than server-only control, with a 2–4 percentage-point success-rate reduction and slower growth in completion time under latency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a failure-prediction-based handover between on-robot and server VLA models, directly relevant to embodied AI and vision-language-action.
papers.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
papers.tldr: VLA handover improves robot reliability by invoking a server-based large VLA only when the onboard model is predicted to fail, reducing remote requests and latency sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $\pi_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses skill retention and phase-dependent skill composition in vision-language-action policies.
Finds that per-skill low-rank updates occupy a distinguishable low-dimensional parameter subspace.
Stores each skill as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter, augmented with trainable residuals.
Uses a VLM-conditioned per-chunk router supervised by an action-derived oracle to select primitives based on task progress.
On RoboCasa365, reports 56.43% atomic-skill and 20.00% composite success, versus 17.86% and 17.50% for a two-stage π₀.₅-LoRA baseline; also validates on a real AgileX PIPER robot.

(3) Chunk-wise routed execution (inference): each LoRA-injected action-expert layer applies the routed mixture at the activation level (Eq. 5), producing an action chunk.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses VLA policy adaptation with skill retention and long-horizon composition via low-rank skill primitives and routing.
papers.title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation
papers.tldr: PRISM preserves reusable VLA skills as frozen low-rank primitives and routes among them in context to execute long-horizon composite tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.
authors: Ramy ElMallah, Marc Bishara, Hyegang Kim, Yuxi Zhang, Chongyu Zhu, Chi-Guhn Lee
bullets: Simulates robots, cameras, IoT devices, wearables, residents, visitors, faulty sensors, and time-evolving hazards in Isaac Sim.
Includes 20 tasks across five household-assistance and safety families, where identical alerts may have different causes.
Scores outcomes and action sequences using temporal-logic checks and predefined action costs.
Across six VLMs, the best family-balanced score is 61.9%; models over-reacted, with prohibited interventions occurring more than twice as often as missed required interventions.
Designed as an extensible platform for studying coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy–safety trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.
bullets: On LIBERO-Goal, negated instructions did not change the executed task: the forbidden task occurred in 79% of negated rollouts, versus 78% completion for plain tasks.
A goal probe produced similar representations for “not X” and “X,” indicating weak encoding of negation in the executed goal.
The first action depends mainly on instruction tokens before layer 12 and the final prompt token from layer 16 onward.
Steering instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12/18 rollouts; later prefill interventions failed, while patching every decoded action token at layer 24 redirected 15/18.
Layer-32 goal read-outs detected non-compliance during changing instructions, supporting external enforcement and monitoring of safety constraints.

papers.selection_reason: Localizes and edits goal representations in a VLA model, with implications for safety and interpretability.
papers.title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.tldr: OpenVLA largely ignores textual prohibitions, but probing and activation interventions reveal where its executed goal is represented and how to redirect or monitor it.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.
authors: Sungwon Moon, Minji Kim, Hyemin Boo, Daeun Song, Jiyoung Lee
bullets: Targets slow closed-loop robot response caused by expensive visual processing.
Training-free pruning uses the predicted prior action as a geometric prior before the vision encoder runs.
In the fixed third-person view, it keeps patches along the projected end-effector path and semantic anchors.
In the wrist view, it removes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for action-induced camera motion.
Evaluated in LIBERO, VLABench, and four real-robot tasks, achieving up to 1.61× speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction with negligible success-rate degradation.

papers.abstract: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.
authors: Xiaohan Sun, Vuk Radovanovic, Merce Alvarez, Carol O'Sullivan, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Panayiotis Charalambous
bullets: Addresses the inflexibility of handwritten rules and the latency, cost, and unsupported-action risks of per-tick LLM control.
Uses an LLM when instructions are added or changed, then validates referenced entities and actions against the current Unity scene.
A graph neural network selects each agent’s action and target at every simulation tick; Unity executes movement, interaction, and animation.
Evaluations found validator feasibility decisions aligned with human judgments more often than the LLM’s assessments.
On a behavioural benchmark, it followed instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CrowdDirector. (a) Offline policy training. In generated worlds, simulation rollouts and a constrained LLM ranking score the same set of available actions, giving 𝑞roll and 𝑞LLM. Averaging them yields the hybrid target 𝑞train, which trains the graph policy. Because both distributions cover the same candidates, the blend cannot introduce an unavailable action. (b) Runtime orchestration. An LLM interprets a new instruction once (1), and the scene validator checks it against the live scene, storing an accepted result as a directive and rejecting an unsupported target (2). The current scene and active directives are then rebuilt as a crowd graph with a candidate list for each agent (3), the trained policy selects one candidate per agent (4), and Unity executes the result (5).

Figure 3: Architecture of the graph policy. Type-specific encoders produce 64-dimensional node representations, which are updated by three relational GNN layers. A shared multilayer perceptron scores each candidate from its agent representation, target representation, their interaction, and the 34-dimensional candidate features.

papers.selection_reason: Connects natural-language directives to agent action selection in a simulated environment, transferable to embodied vision-language-action systems.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
authors: Mingjia Huo, Yao Fu, Bo Chang, Yaqing Wang, Dawei Zhu, Dylan Zhang, Xinyang Yi, Lichan Hong, Ed H. Chi, Hao Zhang, Jiaxi Tang
bullets: Benchmarks VLMs on 20 Atari 2600 games using high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams.
Separates in-game dynamics from inference speed to test spatiotemporal perception, reasoning, and action grounding.
Finds failures in tracking object motion and direction, brittle sequential decisions, and over-reliance on textual history over new visual feedback.
Analyzes which game scores reliably reflect competence and examines the effects of memory design and prompting.
Highlights a persistent gap between passive visual understanding and active decision-making in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. Project page with code, data and videos: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/
authors: Luca Macesanu, Tianluo Zhang, Aditya Patil, Archit Sharma, Kevin Angers, Christopher M. Clark, Chen Feng, Juexiao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting demonstrations that match the robot’s current execution stage during in-context learning.
Introduces an In-Context Value Function Estimator that estimates task-relative progress from a reference video, instruction, and current observation.
Uses progress-aligned demonstration chunks with a post-trained π₀.₅ policy for in-context action generation.
On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, success rises from 6.2% to 23.8%, while task progress increases from 28.9% to 55.5%.

This is then optionally fused with visual similarity, driving retrieval of a context chunk ct from the demonstration pool. The IC-VLA (θ) conditions on ct to predict the next action chunk, closing the loop without any parameter updates.

Fig. 6. VFE at deployment: task progress rate by value estimation method. All methods are evaluated using the same IC-VLA backbone using Robo-Dopamine annotations at training time. IC-VFE yields substantially higher OOD progress than the alternative online estimators, indicating that retrieval quality is sensitive to the value estimator used at deployment.

papers.abstract: We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training. We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $\pi_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90. Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.
bullets: Identifies a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is represented but has insufficient influence on trajectory generation.
Matched counterfactuals and driving replays show plans are driven mainly by ego-speed history and respond weakly to hazard proximity or reasoning traces.
The trajectory generator can brake, but does not reliably do so when hazards are present.
Injecting a hazard-conditioned energy into frozen Alpamayo-1.5 flow-matching sampling restores hazard-responsive control at generation time.
With exact obstacle geometry, footprint intrusion fell from 58.1% to 14.5% and collisions were eliminated in the braking-relevant closed-loop tests when stopping distance was sufficient.

papers.abstract: Integrating force awareness into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models involves not merely encoding wrench measurements as an additional modality, but determining when and how strongly physical interaction should influence robot action generation. Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action. This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway. FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation. In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed force-injection pathways in existing vision-language-action models.
Uses learnable force query tokens to infer force relevance from visual-language context.
Modulates an external tokenized force pathway according to the inferred force admission signal.
Evaluated on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, achieving the highest mean success rate over six stages.

(b) The VLM-based Implicit Force Reasoning Module grounds force query states with visual features through cross-attention and decodes them into motion phase inference, producing the admission signal that determines when force information becomes action-relevant. (c) The Force Tokenizer Module discretizes wrench histories into contact-semantic codes via a frozen VQ-Encoder and uses their Code Embeddings to FiLM-condition the force pathway.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/oopsierecover for videos.
bullets: Targets the need for large amounts of corrective data and poor generalization in deployed VLA models.
Uses abduction to infer the intent behind corrective demonstrations.
Represents inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs that steer actions away from undesirable regions.
Evaluated across 6 tasks with variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks.
Reports successful recovery across broad novel situations without new corrective data for each variation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: OOPSIERECOVER: From semantic interventions to reusable VLA corrections. In OOPSIERECOVER, a human monitors VLA execution and intervenes to provide semantic corrections: a corrective trajectory and a language description for some type of correction, ci, (orange). We then synthesize the collected set of interventions for each correction type into a Semantically Grounded Gated Cost by i) parsing the sensorimotor demonstration as temporal point sets tracked on semantic scene entities, ii) generating gated costs from the motion of the point sets, and iii) verifying these costs by evaluating their capability to explain all human corrections of the same type (blue). During deployment (green), these costs determine when steering is needed and rank candidate actions using the learned corrective programs. This separates the intended correction from its demonstrated trajectory, allowing correction programs to be used in the environment where they are collected and to generalize to new situations, while the base VLA remains frozen.

Fig. 3: Simulation and real-world tasks. We evaluate a diverse set of tasks that elicit different types of corrections; avoiding collisions, improving placement precision, and correctly articulating objects.

Fig. 1: Learning reusable corrections from human interventions with OOPSIERECOVER. A human corrects a lid-closure failure and describes the intended behavior. OOPSIERECOVER grounds this feedback in semantic point sets, and uses abduction – finding a simple explanation consistent with the observed intervention – to synthesize a gated correction cost that steers a frozen VLA. (Right) The synthesized correction programs generalize: they can be reused under changed object poses and scene layouts, broadening the successful applicability of the VLA.

Fig. 5: Scaling with number of corrections. On CoffeeMug, OOPSIERECOVER rapidly reaches an 84% success rate with as few as 8 corrections, while HG-DAgger∗ achieves only 28% despite using three times as many corrections.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.
bullets: Targets brittle VLA behavior in shifted, safety-critical real-world settings.
Probes latent layers of a VLA backbone with minimal inference overhead and supervises pre-failure trajectory segments.
Improves early detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline.
Maintains valid missed-detection and false-alarm bounds in up to 86% of unseen-task runs, versus at most 21% for baselines.
