papers.title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
papers.tldr: VLA-Tug is a lightweight, calibrated latent probe that detects and classifies impending VLA failures early under distribution shift, enabling real-time corrective steering.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.
bullets: Targets high VLA inference cost and distraction from redundant visual tokens, especially across multiple cameras and under distribution shift.
Uses segmentation-guided pruning to remove irrelevant patches, followed by saliency-guided attention biasing over retained visual tokens and language instructions.
On LIBERO-Spatial, removes 85% of scene-camera tokens while essentially matching unpruned success and improves OOD success by up to 7 percentage points.
Adds 7.8 ms per inference call for refinement and achieves up to 3.3× LLM-forward speedup at higher input resolutions.
Across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones, benefits are strongest in multi-camera settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-stage T3R pipeline. Stage 2 (biasing): Integrated Gradients over the instruction identifies salient words; an additive attention bias (𝛽=2.0) is injected into the middle decoder layers for action-token queries, steering attention toward salient text tokens and retained visual patches before the action chunk is decoded.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 2D vision-language pre-training and reliable 3D robotic manipulation.
Jointly trains action prediction with alignment between VLA visual features and a frozen 3D perception model.
Unifies heterogeneous robot datasets across embodiments, tasks, scenes, and geometric annotations.
Uses feature-dependent layer aggregation, partial depth/calibration, and probabilistic state dropout to improve spatial supervision and visual reliance.
Training-only auxiliary components enable direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights without changing inference.

papers.abstract: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.
bullets: Evaluates in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning across long-horizon manipulation tasks and three robot embodiments.
Uses harder initial conditions from existing benchmarks in an extensible MuJoCo-based framework with modular task, agent, and interface components.
GPT-6 Astra scores 49.8% versus Claude Fable 5.1 at 43.6%, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Most failures involve poor strategy selection or imprecise execution rather than scene misunderstanding; agents falsely claim success on 24–39% of subtasks.
A single in-context demonstration or self-revised prompt substantially improves Astra’s performance on a five-task subset.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Failure Breakdown for RoboARCade. Success requires correct visual reasoning, approach and precision. GPT-6 Astra generally performs best. More tries mainly improve approach and success. Visual reasoning changes little across agents. D: This plot breaks down agent behavior on subtasks it attempted. Stronger agents are more likely to succeed on later tries. When they get stuck, weaker agents fail more on approach, while stronger agents fail about as often on approach as on precision. Stronger models also make fewer incorrect success claims, though GPT-6 Astra still incorrectly claims success on 24% of subtasks.

This figure shows 20 of them. Tasks require combinations of visual understanding, precise control, memory, and multi-step planning. RoboARCade supports rendering with Blender for high-fidelity visual observations.

Figure 2: Different settings for robot control with FMs. Hierarchical VLA: a high-level VLM issues language subgoals to a VLA policy. Code-as-Policies: an FM generates a program that controls the robot through perception and action primitives. The FM is not involved during policy execution. Agentic robot control (ARC): the FM itself is the policy, observing the scene and issuing controller targets in a closed loop. This work focuses on the ARC setting.

Stronger models also make fewer incorrect success claims, though GPT-6 Astra still claims success on 24% of subtasks it did not succeed at.

papers.abstract: Enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to control humanoid robots requires both reliable whole-body interfaces and knowledge of how to use the body that carries over across tasks. We present HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command Humanoids), a harness in which perception returns the 3D position of any point the VLM selects in its image, and execution turns commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking, and gaze into whole-body motion with a learned tracker. We find that both measuring the scene and executing commands accurately raise task success. We then fine-tune a VLM on trajectories in which teacher policies solve five base tasks through HITCH, so that it learns how to operate the humanoid. Without task-specific trajectories, the fine-tuned model completes 51% of SIMPLE episodes and 42.5% of HumanoidArena episodes, and adding five trajectories per SIMPLE task raises its SIMPLE success to 95%. On a real G1, it carries a box and walks to a goal without real training data.
bullets: Addresses reliable perception, control interfaces, and transferable body-use knowledge for VLM-controlled humanoids.
Maps selected image points to 3D positions and converts pelvis, torso, hand, walking, and gaze commands into motion using a learned tracker.
Fine-tunes the VLM on teacher-policy trajectories covering five base tasks.
Achieves 51% success on SIMPLE and 42.5% on HumanoidArena without task-specific trajectories; five trajectories per SIMPLE task increase success to 95%.
Demonstrates real-world box carrying and goal-directed walking on a G1 without real training data.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview. Top left: in each turn, the agent πθ (Qwen3.8-27B) receives the instruction ℓ and the history ht of head-camera images and body states, and writes a response at that contains one call. Top right: the call goes to the harness. A perception call selects points in the image and returns their 3D positions in the observation frame O, measured from depth, together with the marked image. An execution call sets the body, hands, fingers, walking, and gaze; a planner turns it into a whole-body reference, which the HEFT tracker follows at 50Hz, and the call returns the next observation. Bottom: teacher code policies act through the same harness on five base tasks and six SIMPLE tasks. The agent is fine-tuned on their multi-turn trajectories and evaluated on new tasks without or with a few task trajectories, and on a real G1 in new scenes.

papers.abstract: Current language-guided 3D object placement typically predicts a rigid 6-DoF pose, ignoring the physical reality that indoor placements are dictated by contact. Consequently, predicted poses often float, interpenetrate supports, or fail to deform soft surfaces. We propose Deformable Contact-Aware Placement (DCAP), a framework that reframes placement as a drop-to-equilibrium process. Rather than predicting a static pose, DCAP constructs a semantic release state that specifies the drop location, object scale, and deformable components, allowing a coupled rigid-deformable simulator to settle the object under gravity and friction. This explicitly separates semantic intent from physical realization. Evaluated on a benchmark of 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases, DCAP significantly outperforms static baselines. On standard placements, it improves VLM Physics & Naturalness by 21.2 points and human preference by 26.5 points over the strongest raw rigid baseline, while reducing mean penetration depth by 72.3%. Compared to simulated rollout baselines, DCAP reduces residual speed by 72.1%. Ultimately, our results prove that physically accurate 3D placement requires modeling semantic intent and physical realization as strictly separate processes.
bullets: Targets floating objects, support interpenetration, and failure to deform soft surfaces in rigid 6-DoF placement.
Predicts a semantic release state—drop location, object scale, and deformable components—rather than a final pose.
Uses coupled rigid-deformable simulation with gravity and friction to realize the placement through drop-to-equilibrium.
On 2,063 prompt–asset–scene cases, it improves physics/naturalness and human preference while substantially reducing penetration and residual motion.
The approach separates semantic intent from physical realization; its scope is indoor placement involving contact and deformability.

papers.abstract: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.
bullets: Goal interpretation errors propagate through downstream planning and actions.
The method first fine-tunes an LLM to produce valid EAI symbolic goals.
CORE then learns to rank complete candidate outputs generated by the model.
Evaluated on household scenes from the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark with several open-source LLMs.
The approach outperformed prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge-graph baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Our two-stage generate-then-rank approach on an example record. Stage 1: given the instruction, scene objects, and task prompt, the fine-tuned LLM generates 𝐾 = 9 outputs, of which three are unique candidate goals; each is drawn as the dishwasher contents it specifies and written as node (N), edge (E), and action (A) goals. Stage 2: the candidates and their likelihoods are the input. Contrastive learning pairs the positive, the best candidate, with each negative, a lower-quality candidate; the ranking loss raises the positive’s score and lowers the negatives’, more strongly for the pair with the larger quality gap. The output is the candidate with the highest likelihood after training. Likelihood is the average per-token probability; changes are in percentage points.

papers.abstract: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.
bullets: Targets safe handling of handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, where robots must infer intent and manage physical contact.
Uses a lightweight two-camera RGB intent model to generate language prompts for a VLA policy; low-confidence predictions suppress motion.
Applies interaction-specific arm impedance profiles during contact and an independent latched voice-triggered safe-stop mechanism.
Evaluated four fine-tuned VLA models on a Unitree G1 using approximately 1,300 VR-teleoperated multimodal episodes.
Intent gating improved the best standalone model’s macro-F1 from 0.75 to 0.90, with 6.27 ms p95 intent-inference latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed human-aware VLA pipeline. (a) The perception module estimates the human partner’s interaction intent from two RGB camera views, filters uncertain predictions, and independently detects voice commands for safe stopping. (b) The on-robot VLA bridge converts a confirmed intent into a task prompt, predicts whole-body action chunks, and applies playback smoothing and finger-contact safeguards. (c) During deployment, task-conditioned arm-compliance profiles and the latched safe-stop mechanism supervise the SONIC whole-body controller, enabling safe and compliant handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs.

papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21-52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. Despite retaining knowledge of synonym referents, agents often fail to take the corresponding objects even after observing them, exposing a gap between referential knowledge and object binding. Partial observability further complicates binding, as referents may remain unseen or have already been encountered under different labels. To address this challenge, we propose BINDIntent, a training-free framework that probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates. Without additional training or LLM calls, BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5-49.1 percentage points (pp) with only 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. It also raises GiGPO-7B's overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/cau-hai-lab/ALFWorld-Para.
bullets: ALFWorld-Para shows paraphrased instructions reduce success rates by 21–52%, mainly because of object synonyms.
Agents often know synonym meanings but fail to bind them to the correct observed objects.
Partial observability makes binding harder when referents are unseen or previously labeled differently.
BINDIntent uses semantic proximity and estimated persistence to probabilistically match expressions with observed labels.
It improves synonym-paraphrase success by 17.5–49.1 percentage points with 0.4 ms CPU overhead per step; GiGPO-7B’s overall success rises from 61.8% to 77.4%.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D. Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Concertina Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/Traly/concertina
bullets: Addresses the decoupling of cognition and manipulation in existing vision-language-action policies.
Encodes each control timestep as a continuous latent action token and generates trajectory blocks through the shared Transformer.
Applies physical-coordinate supervision and the same corrupt-and-reconstruct process used for multimodal pretraining.
Uses 0.21% active action projections in a 4.46B-parameter model, with no separate action-generator layers.
Reports 98.15% success on LIBERO, 85.9% on LIBERO-Plus, and 4.142 completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Action Interface Audit across representational, computational, and parameter coupling. (a) Physical action error span (p05–p50–p95) and structural decoding fragility under singletoken substitutions: continuous coordinates (Concertina) preserve unit error geometry (EGC = 1.0×, 0% invalid), whereas 256-bin quantization induces a 25.1× error span and compressed DCT+BPE tokenizers (FAST+, MolmoAct2-FAST) suffer 82.2% and 77.9% invalid trajectory shapes while perturbing 30/30 steps on valid decodes. (b) Normalized Jacobian singular value spectrum (σi/σ1) of Concertina’s continuous action encoder ∂Eϕ(a)/∂a ∈ R2560×20 across pretraining updates, maintaining a full-rank 20D manifold (effective rank 18.63/20, Spearman ρ = 0.86–0.93). (c) Layerwise emergence of cross-time trajectory coupling (NLR, |t− t0| ≥ 6) across the 36-layer BARD-VL-B4 backbone versus 0.0% for the position-wise interface (Dψ ◦ Eϕ) alone. (d) Action-Specific Capacity Ratio (ASCR) across VLA families, showing that Concertina uses 78×–167× fewer action-specific parameters (0.21%) than external-expert architectures (16.5%–35.1%).

Figure 2: From decoupled VLAs to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). Comparison of four architectural routes to robot manipulation: (A) OpenVLA quantizes coordinates into discrete vocabulary tokens (language-objective VLA); (B) π0 delegates continuous trajectory generation to a separate flow-matching action expert (separate-objective VLA); (C) Dream-VLA retains a shared diffusion VLM backbone but switches to a flow-matching objective for continuous control (switchedobjective VLA); (D) Concertina instantiates an eVLM that preserves both the shared diffusion VLM backbone and its native masked block reconstruction operator over continuous latent action tokens.

Figure 3: Blockwise horizon partition, physical action coherence, and cumulative recipe progression. (a) Regular-LIBERO suite-level and overall success over 200 episodes (40 tasks × 5 episodes, Wilson 95% CIs) at fixed 2,400-step finetuning budgets, showing consistent gains across all four suites (38.5% → 73.0% overall). (a) Shared-hidden gradient cosine between the main relative-action objective and auxiliary absolute-action objective across eight fixed windows is −0.891 (99% of action slots < 0), reducing combined-vs-main alignment to +0.474 (auxiliary/main norm ratio 0.88×). The token-risk head predicts log reconstruction error from detached hidden states; candidate slots are committed in order of confidence, and optional refinement rounds remask and update low-scoring positions when the predicted score improves.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses vision-language-action and robot manipulation with a unified diffusion VLM.

papers.abstract: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.
bullets: Addresses open-world interactive navigation where obstacles may need to be moved rather than avoided.
Uses explicit VLM affordance reasoning before planning to choose actions such as swiping, picking up, or avoiding objects.
Handles context-dependent cases, such as pushing an empty cart but avoiding one carrying fragile glassware.
Evaluated on a mobile manipulator in real indoor and outdoor environments.
Improves real-robot success by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline, without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MessyNav: A framework for zero-shot open-world interactive navigation. MessyNav consists of an Affordance Reasoner that infers object interactability from an RGB image using a VLM to evaluate both robot-centric physical feasibility and object-centric interaction safety. For example, it will label a cart with a laptop as non-interactive while labeling a wheeled crate with a bin as interactive. Given the object affordance labels, a Task Planner then sequences manipulation and navigation actions from an open-language skill library containing a simple set of motion primitives (pick up, swipe left, swipe right) and a LiDAR-based navigation stack (move to) that we find can tackle a wide range of interactive navigation scenarios. Finally, the generated plan is executed by grounding object references in 3D coordinates using VLM keypoint identification, semantic segmentation, and depth-based deprojection.

Figure 4: Explicit affordance reasoning improves context-dependent task planning. In this scene, a suitcase supporting a stack of books is inherently unstable, while the black cart holding a single book can be safely cleared. [Left] MessyNav reasons about affordances before planning, correctly labeling the suitcase as non-interactive and the cart as interactive, and swiping the cart aside to clear the path. [Middle] vlm-planner-only plans directly from the image without an explicit affordance stage and incorrectly decides to swipe the unstable suitcase. [Right] closed-set-planner assigns fixed category-level affordances that misclassify the suitcase as interactive, leading to an unsafe plan.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results across Environments. We deploy MessyNav in varied settings to test its zero-shot capability. The robot successfully reasons about affordances and executes interactions across different lighting conditions, environments, and object types.
Figure 7: Example Open-Vocabulary Keypoint Detection. We use gemini-2.5-pro [36] to detect keypoints of objects specified by the task planner through language queries.
Figure 6: Hardware: We deploy on the TidyBot++ holonomic mobile manipulator [18] with two cameras and a LiDAR for perception. An onboard laptop runs the autonomy stack.

Figure 9: MessyNav’s failure breakdown compared to the strongest baseline. Sankey diagrams of trial outcomes for MessyNav (left) and vlm-planner-only (right) over 15 real-world trials. MessyNav succeeds on 10/15 trials versus 6/15 for vlm-planner-only. While most of vlm-planner-only’s failures are planning failures in which vlm-planner-only decides to interact with non-interactive objects (7 of 9), MessyNav reduces these to 2, showcasing the importance of explicit affordance reasoning.

Figure 3: MessyNav reasons about context, not just object category. In this cluttered scene, closed-set-oracle assigns affordances by category alone, misclassifying the rolling cart as interactive (ignoring the glassware it carries) and the suitcase as interactive (ignoring its fragile sticker). In contrast, MessyNav reasons at the instance level. It treats the cart and the glass stemware as a single fragile unit and reads the sticker on the suitcase as a contextual cue, correctly labeling both as non-interactive.

Table 3: Scaled-Up Offline Planning Results. We evaluate high-level planning performance across 55 real-world scenes in 5 environments, with 15 repeated trials per scene, assuming perfect low-level execution. MessyNav outperforms the strongest baseline from the real-world evaluation overall and under well-lit conditions, while nighttime remains challenging for both methods.

Table 1: Affordance Reasoning Results. MessyNav outperforms geometric and closed-set baselines, highlighting the importance of context-dependent affordance reasoning.

Table 5: Composition of the Affordance Reasoning Benchmark. Our benchmark spans diverse environments, lighting, clutter, and obstacle sizes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/STAR.
bullets: Addresses a late-layer grounding gap in vision-language-action models, where action representations may lose task-relevant visual information.
Applies an exponential moving average to late-layer residual updates so later representations inherit object-aware directions from earlier layers.
Adapts the mixing strength using recent proprioceptive states, applying more conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly.
Improves late-layer object awareness and raises average task success by 4.0 percentage points on robot manipulation benchmarks.
Requires no model updates or architectural changes; its scope is pre-trained VLAs and the evaluated manipulation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models now grade robot videos, and text placed beside the frames can change their verdicts. On clips where the robot is losing progress, we add one log line saying the robot is making progress. Across Gemini, Qwen and GPT judges, this flips correct verdicts to progress 10 to 35 percentage points more often than a neutral line does. A one-line warning that the log may be wrong removes most of this effect. Selected fake "task complete" claims flip half of Qwen's correct verdicts, against a tenth for unrelated log lines. They have no detectable effect on Gemini.
bullets: Adding a false progress log beside videos where the robot is losing progress causes more verdict reversals than a neutral log across Gemini, Qwen, and GPT judges.
A one-line warning that the log may be incorrect largely mitigates this influence.
Fake “task complete” claims reverse about half of Qwen’s correct verdicts, versus about a tenth for unrelated logs.
Gemini shows no detectable response to the selected fake completion claims.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A fake progress line flips correct verdicts 10 to 35 points more often than a neutral line in all three judges; selected fake “task complete” claims fool Qwen, with no detectable effect on Gemini. Each dot is the rate at which a correct Falling verdict turns to Rising, minus the same rate for the control: a neutral sentence (left) or an unrelated log line (right). Bars are 95% CIs. Only intervals the judge gets right on the frames, both forward and reversed. Numbers in Table 1.

Figure 1: One fake “task complete” log line flips Qwen’s correct verdict. Task: hand the pen from the left to the right arm, then place it in the blue plate; the right arm never takes the pen. On the frames alone, Qwen answers Falling (losing progress): “the right arm remains open and does not grasp it”. With the log “Successful completion confirmed: the pen was . . . transferred to the right arm, and placed in the blue plate”, it answers Rising (making progress): “the execution log confirms the successful completion of the task”. Example chosen for visual clarity.

A completion claim counts only if a second call with it also answers Rising. The completion-claim attack used all Falling intervals for Qwen and a random 80 for Gemini.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
authors: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu, Ziqi Huang, Tianqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Ziyi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Hanming Deng, Quan Wang, Lei Yang, Lewei Lu, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Dahua Lin, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Problem: Fixed visual encoders may discard action-critical details such as local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes.
Method: Tokenizes images with lightweight patch convolutions and jointly processes visual tokens with language across the backbone.
Action generation uses a flow-matching expert conditioned on visual representations from multiple depths.
Controlled comparisons find native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts; scaling alone does not close the gap.
Layer-wise probing and evaluations under distribution shifts indicate that useful control signals often emerge before the final visual layer.

Figure 3: Data quality filtering. Illustrative checks cover implausible joint readings, unreliable channels, action outliers, corrupt episodes, and camera calibration, removing only affected data. Joint and projection checks are source-specific; episode retention is determined in the final corpus pass.

Figure 2: NEO-VLA: pixels in, continuous actions out. Previous and current multi-view observations preserve their aspect ratios within a fixed token budget and enter patch embedder shared across time and views. The visual path uses no vision transformer, autoencoder, or vector-quantised codebook. Shared MLPs embed camera intrinsics and rotations, while state MLPs embed previous and current robot states. These tokens join a structured prompt describing control frequency, embodiment, frame reference, and task instruction. A separate, narrow, randomly initialised action expert jointly attends to cached prefix keys and values from selected backbone layers and its own action-token keys and values. Its suffix embeddings combine projected noisy actions and flow time τ with additive step, frame, and identity embeddings. Both arm blocks and the body block share temporal rotary offsets 0–29, with identity embeddings distinguishing the blocks. Trained by flow matching, the expert predicts a velocity field that covers both arm and body action chunks.

Figure 1: Three VLA designs: encoder-based vs. encoder-free backbones, and discrete vs. continuous actions. (a) A separate visual encoder converts pixels into image features, which are consumed by the language backbone together with text tokens; actions are generated as discrete tokens. (b) The same encoder-based visual interface is retained, while a separate action head predicts continuous actions conditioned on the backbone. (c) NEO-VLA removes the separately pretrained visual encoder: a lightweight patch embedder maps pixels directly into the backbone token space, while text tokens enter the backbone jointly. A narrow action expert then reads cached keys and values from selected backbone layers and predicts a flow-matching velocity field.

papers.abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.
authors: Fei Lin, Tengchao Zhang, Ziyang Gong, Xiaotong Yu, Bohan Zhang, Yifan Zhou, Qihao Yang, Ji Dai, Dong Li, Yining Jiang, Qinghua Ni, Jun Huang, Qiang Zhang, Yue Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Yonglin Tian, Fei-Yue Wang, Xue Yang

papers.abstract: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

papers.abstract: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.
bullets: Studies self-repair for simulated robot manipulation using repeated program generation after scene resets.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.

papers.abstract: Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.
authors: Xingchen Zou, Maonan Wang, Kemou Jiang, Jie Li, Yiqi Chen, Xi Chen, Hai Yang, Yuxuan Liang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of structured-state pipelines and idealized simulator imagery in visual traffic signal control.
SynTra-V generates photorealistic, multi-view surveillance data with semantic auditing to preserve control-critical traffic geometry and movements.

papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.
authors: Albert Wilcox, Frank Chang, Nhi Nguyen, Aishani Chakraborty, Jeremy A. Collins, Vaibhav Saxena, Benjamin Joffe, Siddharth Karamcheti, Animesh Garg
bullets: Evaluates in-distribution performance plus four distinct generalization axes: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition.
Uses MESA-Gen, an improved MimicGen-based pipeline, to generate tasks and demonstrations at scale.
Releases single-arm MESA and BiMESA, a large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization.
Across seven baseline methods, the strongest model reaches 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, leaving substantial room for improvement.
MESA rankings broadly agree with RoboArena scores, suggesting relevance beyond simulation.

papers.title: MESA: An Evaluation Framework for Compositional, Semantic, and Spatial Generalization in Robotics
papers.tldr: MESA is a reproducible robotics benchmark that isolates spatial, object, category, and compositional generalization, revealing substantial weaknesses in current language-conditioned policies.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: VLA training can provide action information through expert-loss gradients, discrete action-token supervision, or both.
The study independently varies gradient routing and action-token supervision in autonomous driving and robot manipulation.
With action-token supervision, insulation is competitive in open-loop driving; without it, coupling lowers trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%.
When trained jointly from the start, coupling improves closed-loop route progress by approximately 17% with action tokens and 40% without them, while also improving manipulation performance.
The benefit of insulation depends on supervision and evaluation setting rather than being universally protective of VLM capabilities.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates gradient coupling, insulation, and action-token supervision in VLA training, directly relevant to vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
papers.tldr: Gradient coupling from the action expert to the VLM can substantially improve VLA control, especially when action-token supervision is absent, challenging gradient insulation as a default.

papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.
authors: Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Targets latency in large vision-language-action models caused by sequential reasoning and control.
Uses a high-capacity VLM to asynchronously update semantic memory and a lightweight vision-action expert to produce actions at a higher frequency.
Trains the action expert to handle stale semantic memory and execution delays from asynchronous processing.
On Franka tasks, reports 18% higher success and 20% shorter execution time in quasi-static settings, with 3–5× baseline performance in dynamic simulation.
Runs the VLM at 10× lower than its nominal frequency without significant performance loss, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision-language-action (VLA) models promises smaller and faster VLA deployments. However, when analyzing existing VLA quantization works, we realised that it is hard to reason about the performance of the suggested quantization method compared to existing, similar, or in many cases, simpler PTQ methods. We present LoopQ, a closed-loop benchmark that compares multiple quantization policies on the same checkpoint, layers and engine, varying only the method and the kernels. We evaluate RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant and QuantVLA on four VLAs with more than 180,000 episodes of LIBERO and LIBERO-plus, compare against QVLA's reported results on the same layers, and benchmark whether the four public VLA-quantization releases can be reproduced. We benchmark the methods on an NVIDIA H100, an L4, and a Jetson AGX Thor. Our results show that while quantization reliably saves memory, 2-3x for real low-bit models, VLA-specific PTQ methods underperform compared to simpler generic baselines. At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA, plain RTN matches the calibrated methods, and plain AWQ matches the success QVLA reports for itself. Standard LIBERO hides the losses that do exist: configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5-4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Speed is a weaker story. At batch 1 on the H100, no quantized pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT configuration is faster than its 16-bit model (1.06-1.58x slower on library kernels); only the L4 with int8 kernels gains (4-14%), the Thor is slower on every 4-bit configuration, and the engine alone changes latency by 2.1x. Profiling explains why: pi0.5's quantized backbone is compute-bound, while its memory-bound action expert, 63% of GPU time and 13% of the parameters, stays in 16 bits.
authors: Syed Umer Bukhari, Magnus Almgren, Ahmed Ali-Eldin
bullets: Evaluates RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant, and QuantVLA under controlled conditions: same checkpoints, layers, engines, and varying only methods and kernels.
Covers four VLAs, over 180,000 LIBERO/LIBERO-plus episodes, and NVIDIA H100, L4, and Jetson AGX Thor hardware.
At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ, and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA; standard LIBERO can hide 1.5–4.3-point losses revealed by LIBERO-plus perturbations.
Quantization consistently reduces memory, but speedups are hardware- and kernel-dependent; some configurations are slower than 16-bit models.
Profiling attributes limited speed gains partly to a 16-bit, memory-bound action expert that accounts for most runtime in pi0.5.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.
authors: Yihang Liu, Yiming Chen, Mingzhe Zheng
bullets: Addresses whether multimodal robot agents must repeatedly reinterpret visual observations during interaction.
Represents object-part geometry with typed, evidence-aware symbolic references grounded in calibrated RGB-D.
Provides compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after actions, while refreshing only locally observed state.
Supports offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution with visual reasoning invoked on demand.
The abstract reports improved multi-step manipulation completion and substantially fewer repeated multimodal queries.

papers.abstract: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.
authors: Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Saimouli Katragadda, Yuze Du, Zijun Sha, Guoquan Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-level VLA planning and the physical safety requirements of real-world legged-robot navigation.
Combines a high-level VLA planner with state estimation, in-situ 3D perception, and signed distance fields to produce executable trajectories.
Uses a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with discrete exponential barrier-function constraints for collision avoidance under stated assumptions.
The platform-agnostic system is compatible with different VLM/VLA models and is evaluated on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
Real-world experiments demonstrate versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language navigation.

papers.abstract: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

Across four LIBERO suites and three seeds, TIF reaches a 76.25% mean success rate, 3.00 percentage points above existing-trajectory training.
On real-robot videos, clean completion among selected trajectories rises from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.

papers.abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
authors: Shresth Grover, Andrey Kolobov, Dhruv Shah
bullets: Limited-demonstration fine-tuning can improve nominal success while harming robustness to appearance, object, and instruction variations.
RAFT uses two stages: low-rank adapter training on task-relevant reasoning annotations, followed by policy fine-tuning on action demonstrations with the adapters frozen.
On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves 75.0% out-of-distribution success versus 27.9% for plain fine-tuning.
On a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, RAFT reaches 70.0% mean success versus 36.0% for the strongest baseline.
RAFT improves performance under visual, object, and instruction shifts, while increasing attention to annotated regions and later-layer object-identity probe accuracy.

papers.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
authors: Kailing Li, Ruoxuan Zhang, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun
bullets: Covers diverse 3D-game tasks including navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery.
Organizes demonstrations into complete tasks with overall instructions, ordered subgoals, local skill instructions, visual observations, and keyboard-mouse actions.
Uses a vision-language pipeline to detect objective or interaction-target changes, ground navigation goals in visual waypoints, and compose task instructions.
Explicit stage boundaries connect task progression with low-level control and skill transitions.
Annotation quality was evaluated through model verification and human inspection; an audit of 500 trajectories achieved a 95.8% pass rate.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the AceAction data construction pipeline. Gameplay from direct collection and public datasets is annotated with skill- and waypoint-based subgoals. Adjacent subgoals within each trajectory are composed into task-level instructions, followed by annotation and alignment validation. Two models then verify visual grounding and action consistency, retaining only samples approved by both at every annotation level. A sampled human audit further assesses data quality.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.
authors: Zihao Feng, Qingzhao Zhang, Chunyu Xia, Bo Yu, Z. Morley Mao, Ramesh Govindan
bullets: Reasoning text and physical actions can diverge at their shared text/action interface.
The text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) identifies directions that strongly shift actions while minimally affecting text.
Across driving and manipulation VLAs, TNAS perturbations shift actions more and cause less text drift than text-gradient perturbations.
In driving, TNAS attacks caused new collisions with identical rationales in 52.6% of full-image scenes and 35.1% of localized-patch scenes, versus 4.55% for unguided attacks.
TNAS improved rationale preservation and reduced text drift while maintaining comparable action changes across both models.

papers.abstract: A mobile manipulator asked to "put the toys away in the toy box" must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute. Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task. We present FEIJOA, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction. An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill's preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill's effect from observations before and after execution. On 103 open-ended grounding queries, FEIJOA resolves 94.2% exactly, compared with 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation. Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trials, 13 were caused by the robot's physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent's reasoning. Project website: https://williamshen-nz.github.io/feijoa/.
authors: Aditya Agarwal, William Shen, Sahit Chintalapudi, Lucy Cai, Nishanth Kumar, Aidan Curtis, Travis Manderson, Tom\'as Lozano-P\'erez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between prebuilt scene representations and task-specific concepts needed to interpret user instructions.
Uses a language-model agent to iteratively query and inspect grounding results from posed RGB-D scans.
Checks skill preconditions, samples reachable base poses, and verifies outcomes using before-and-after observations.
Resolves 94.2% of 103 grounding queries exactly, versus 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation.
Completed 35 of 50 Spot trials; most failures were due to physical skills rather than grounding or reasoning.
