papers.abstract: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.
authors: Ruijie Zhang, Jiayin Zheng, Yequan Zhao, Liyan Tan, Ziyue Liu, Zhengyang Wang, Kunpeng Song, Nathan Zhao, Jian Yao, Yin Zhang, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Downstream action models can concentrate sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of pretrained VLM representations, especially under representation–task mismatch.
Finding: Counteracting this sensitivity concentration benefits control across tested backbone–head combinations.
Method: AdaIE is a parameter-free interface mechanism that reweights pretrained representations based on evolving downstream sensitivity during training.
Results: It improves simulation success rates by up to 5.28 pp and 1.68 pp on two benchmarks, with an average 19 pp gain across five real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: The approach also improves performance for diffusion policies and world models.

papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

papers.abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.
bullets: Learns behavior together with spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry and estimating hand motion from each video.
Aligns geometry and hand motion at a shared scale using a 3D hand-size prior.
Uses gated residual fusion to ground a pre-trained vision-language model in geometry, while predicting future geometry and wrist/finger actions.
Generates finger motion conditioned on predicted trajectories of both wrists.
Pre-training on reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over hand-motion-only pre-training; the method also reports gains on simulated and real-world bimanual tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Real-world rollouts. SpatialDex on Spray Plant, Unzip Bag, and Sweep Trash with Wuji hands and Tianji arms, which involve tool actuation, a deformable object, and coordinated two-hand sweeping. Each row runs from the initial frame on the left to task completion on the right.

Fig. 1: SpatialDex reconstructs scene geometry and estimates hand motion from RGB-only human videos and aligns them at a shared video-level scale to jointly supervise policy pre-training. The policy maps RGB-D observations to bimanual dexterous actions and is adapted to specific tasks through fine-tuning on robot demonstrations. The lower panel shows the six bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks for real-world evaluation.

Fig. 3: 3D-grounded visuomotor policy. Reconstructed geometry enters the policy in two roles. As an input, depth samples from each image patch are encoded jointly in 3D and pooled back to their patches, so that the geometry grid g arrives on the same token grid as the visual features x and is fused into f through two gates and a residual whose weight warms up from zero, leaving the priors of the pre-trained VLM intact. As a target, a training-only predictor estimates future scene geometry from the shared context, which requires the representation to retain spatial structure that the action losses alone do not demand. From the same context, a wrist expert predicts both wrist trajectories and a finger expert predicts finger actions conditioned on them.

papers.abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel
bullets: Combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers.
Supports multiple teleoperation and robot-free interfaces for scalable human demonstration collection.
Uses a unified whole-body controller and shared policy-learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations.
Adds hierarchical, language-conditioned visuomotor control for long-horizon tasks.
Demonstrates behaviors involving dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained manipulation couples instruction grounding, local visual precision, and sustained execution. We present FineCraft, a framework that adapts pretrained models for fine-grained manipulation in the MetaFine Challenge. A task-routed mixture of policies selects independently adapted DINOv2-DiT or pretrained $π_{0.5}$ policies through a common observation-action interface. Local visual features help identify the instructed object parts, demonstrations and expert continuations teach the required actions, and new observations guide replanning during execution. FineCraft ranks fourth with an overall score of $0.878$, exceeding the published reference on all five tasks. Official results and local diagnostics characterize performance across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation. Code is available at https://github.com/eqcy/FineCraft

Evaluates robustness across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.
bullets: Benchmarks latency sensitivity across tasks, object speeds, execution modes, and VLA policies.
A 100 ms latency can nearly halve success on moving-target tasks, with effects varying by task and policy.
Latency sensitivity reflects task-specific needs for precision and continuous motion.
Asynchronous execution recovers some success by overlapping inference and action, but requires more frequent inference.
An empirical model predicts task success from limited calibration data with 5.7–7.8% RMSE and supports system-specific configuration selection.

papers.abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model jointly learns subtask planning, task-relevant object grounding, and 3D point flow prediction in an end-to-end way. By processing heterogeneous data in a shared 3D point flow space, PointPilot is able to absorb demonstrations from different embodiments. Extensive simulative and real world experiments validate our method. Notably, we demonstrate zero-shot embodiment generalization with PointPilot. A single trained policy can be deployed on previously unseen embodiments and successfully complete manipulation tasks without any additional fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets generalization across embodiments, camera poses, scene layouts, and manipulation modes.
Represents only task-relevant objects, including grippers, in a unified 3D coordinate space rather than modeling the full scene.
Jointly learns subtask planning, object grounding, and 3D point-flow prediction from sensor observations and language instructions.
Supports closed-loop, fully automatic action execution without a separately trained action expert.
Simulated and real-world experiments validate the approach, including zero-shot deployment on previously unseen embodiments without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can handle noncritical stages of long-horizon manipulation yet fail during short precision-critical phases. Lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) specialists can address these failures without directly applying RL to the full VLA, but retain auxiliary controllers and switching mechanisms at deployment. We study how to transfer their capabilities into a single flow-matching VLA. Direct imitation of specialist rollouts can reproduce action jitter and leave the VLA unprepared for states encountered during its own execution. We introduce REPAIR, a value-guided distillation framework that combines offline initialization with on-policy refinement. At each critical-phase observation, REPAIR queries the corresponding specialist for multiple action candidates and weights them using its critic to construct a supervision distribution. A shared weighted flow-matching objective trains the VLA first on observations from specialist-assisted rollouts, then on observations collected through its own execution. Specialists provide supervision without taking control during on-policy collection and are removed at deployment. Across six real-robot tasks with 30 evaluation trials per task, REPAIR achieves 100% success on all six tasks, with lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.
bullets: Targets short, precision-critical phases where VLAs often fail during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses specialist critics to weight multiple candidate actions within a shared flow-matching objective.
Combines offline training on specialist-assisted rollouts with on-policy refinement on the VLA’s own observations.
Avoids reproducing action jitter and reduces distribution mismatch from direct imitation.
Achieves 100% success across six real-robot tasks and lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.
bullets: Addresses failures of Markovian VLA models on tasks requiring working memory and persistent context.
Uses factorized event detection with event-triggered updates to maintain task-relevant language history.
Evaluated on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks with 56 variants, including five inter-episode tasks.
Improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 78% subtask success on compositional generalization.
Uses up to 4.5× less memory and runs 2.5× faster than a keyframe baseline at long horizons.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall Architecture of HeLM. The High Level Policy (HLP) integrates language memory with a pretrained VLM, which switches between a ‘detect mode’ that monitors events and an ‘update mode’ that updates these events into language memory. The Low Level Policy (LLP), a pretrained VLA, executes action commands generated by the HLP.

Figure 1: Example of non-Markovian task. Due to architectural limitation, a vanilla VLA loses track after pressing the red button and presses it again. HeLM successfully executes the task by storing progress in language memory, allowing the HLP to guide the LLP correctly.

Figure 4: The Real-World Evaluation Suite of HeLM. Our tasks are categorized into two types based on their temporal memory requirements. (Top) Intra-episode tasks (A1–A5) evaluate working memory within a single instruction. (Bottom) Inter-episode tasks (E1–E5) assess episodic context across task boundaries.

In contrast, Keyframe-HLP fails to detect termination in A1, A4 (denoted by ⋆), while the baselines PCMB-π0 and Naı̈ve-π0 (denoted by ⋆⋆) fail both sequencing and termination across all trials. Under strict task success, HeLM retains 81.3%, while KeyframeHLP drops to 29.3% and both PCMB-π0 and Naı̈ve-π0 drop to 0%. papers.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.
bullets: Standardizes policy serving and evaluation protocols across locally operated robots at 124 sites.
Evaluates five VLA policies and three frontier agents across four embodiments using open and fine-tuning tracks.
Frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies in open-world trials, but all systems struggle with reliable completion.
Fine-tuning changes model rankings substantially across embodiments; Open Track rankings poorly predict adapted performance.
Partial-progress metrics and active matchmaking provide more informative and trial-efficient evaluation than success rates and uniform sampling.

papers.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models now act in a closed loop, yet their safety is evaluated one variation at a time: robustness benchmarks perturb the scene while assuming instantaneous inference, and real-time execution methods study inference delay in nominal scenes. We argue that physical safety is not a property of the model alone, but emerges from how variations in the physical environment, the model, the computing platform, and execution interact in closed loop. We formalize this as cross-layer variation propagation across these system layers and use an interaction contrast to measure when joint variation creates more risk than the sum of its parts. In 4,000 paired closed-loop episodes of the pi0.5 vision-language-action model on LIBERO, a 400 ms inference delay raises the safety-violation rate by 3.5 percentage points under the training viewpoint but by 37 percentage points under a 60-degree camera shift: 33.5 percentage points (95% CI: 25-43) more than the two effects combined. We close with a research agenda toward predictable physical intelligence: predicting when variation becomes risk, and adapting compute, power, and control accordingly.
bullets: Existing evaluations often test scene variation and inference delay separately, missing their closed-loop interaction.
The paper formalizes cross-layer variation propagation and measures excess joint risk with an interaction contrast.
Across 4,000 paired LIBERO episodes using pi0.5, a 400 ms delay was far more harmful under a 60° camera shift than under the training viewpoint.
The results motivate predicting when variation becomes dangerous and adapting compute, power, and control accordingly.

papers.selection_reason: Studies closed-loop safety of vision-language-action robot models, fitting the VLA subtopic.
papers.title: When Delay Meets Drift: Physical Safety of Robot Foundation Models Is a Cross-Layer Problem
papers.tldr: Robot foundation-model safety depends on interacting environment, model, hardware, and execution variations—not on any single factor in isolation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD
bullets: Diffusion driving VLAs repeatedly run the backbone during denoising, but scenes differ in the decoding needed for reliable trajectories.
Late-layer features can support useful readout after one backbone sweep, while early-layer features benefit more from continued refinement.
A scene-conditioned readout MoE combines layer-specific predictions, and an adaptive policy adds native decoding only when needed.
Across two VLAs on Waymo E2E and nuScenes, the method improves planning quality, reduces trajectory error, and achieves up to 6.0× end-to-end speedup on Waymo E2E.
papers.selection_reason: Scene-adaptive readout and decoding for diffusion driving VLAs, improving planning quality while cutting inference cost; fits VLA and efficiency.
papers.title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
papers.tldr: A scene-adaptive framework reduces diffusion driving VLA inference cost by selecting where to read trajectories and how much to decode per scene.

papers.abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9$\times$ the success, 5.4$\times$ the generalization, and 3.9$\times$ the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8$\times$ faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.
bullets: Addresses the discontinuity of policies that predict discrete actions directly.
Uses a neural ODE to learn an action vector field and integrates actions from the previous action at deployment.
A diversity head supports multimodal behavior by randomizing the field direction.
Evaluated across visuomotor policies, VLA/WAM action heads, and model-based RL on diverse real-world robotic tasks.
Reports strong gains over flow matching in early IL training, faster action generation, smoother motion, and the highest success rate across 14 real-world tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Novel ODE-based action-dynamics policy for robot learning, directly relevant to manipulation and VLA.
papers.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
papers.tldr: ODE Policy learns continuous action dynamics with neural ODEs, producing smoother and faster robot behavior across imitation learning and reinforcement learning tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.
bullets: VLA-generated actions lack guaranteed safety in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes.
Standard CBF-QP filters enforce local safety but can divert the robot from its task trajectory without providing recovery guidance.
The method detects blocked short-horizon action chunks and generates entry-exit-rejoin routes around obstacles.
These routes softly guide the CBF-QP objective, while safety constraints remain hard.
On SafeLIBERO, it improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess over AEGIS.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair. The method uses the VLA action chunk to estimate a nominal future trajectory and detect obstacle-induced blockage. When the nominal trajectory is blocked, it generates an entry-exit-rejoin route around the obstacle and adds the selected route to the CBF-QP objective as soft guidance. The CBF constraint remains hard, so the repaired action preserves safety while following a recoverable route toward task completion.

papers.abstract: This report presents GatedVLA, our entry for the Physical AI AV (PAI-AV) track. Our learned vision-language-action (VLA) policy pairs the driving-pretrained Qwen-Drive-1.0-4B vision-language model with a layer-wise flow-matching action expert that outputs a 2.5 s horizon of acceleration and curvature controls, augmented with a soft visual mask applied to the expert's cross-attention. Compared to an identically trained baseline, the masked policy achieves comparable overall open-loop error while reducing error on left turns. In local closed-loop evaluation across the same 150 scenes (two rollouts per scene), the visual mask increases the mean scene score from 0.479 to 0.517 (paired difference +0.038, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.018, +0.093], wins/losses 37/26, sign test p = 0.21). Incorporating a rule-based automatic emergency braking (AEB) module at deployment further increases the mean score to 0.599 (+0.082, CI [+0.023, +0.143]) and reduces the mean number of scenes with at-fault collisions from 34.0 to 11.0.
bullets: The policy predicts 2.5-second acceleration and curvature control horizons using a layer-wise flow-matching action expert.
A soft visual mask on the expert’s cross-attention maintains comparable open-loop error while reducing left-turn error.
Across 150 scenes, visual masking raised the mean closed-loop score from 0.479 to 0.517, though the improvement was not statistically conclusive.
Adding deployment-time automatic emergency braking increased the mean score to 0.599 and reduced mean at-fault collision scenes from 34.0 to 11.0.

papers.abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.
bullets: Addresses the dependence on proprietary frontier models that limits further RUA training research.
Introduces a unified harness for training and evaluating open-weight robot-use agents.
An out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39 and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks.
Analysis across model generations, families, and sizes identifies four general capabilities linked to effective robot use.
The work suggests future RUA training should develop these capabilities jointly.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, yet deployed robots waste time in two ways that are independent of model capability: they halt while the next chunk is inferred, and they move at the speed of slow, cautious demonstrations. Existing remedies remove one loss each, and stacking them fails, because asynchrony and speed-up each change the correspondence between planned progress and executed motion. We present Path-preserving Time Scaling (PTS), a training-free execution layer for frozen action-chunking policies built on one principle: the robot's motion is a time reparameterization of a reference path, and the path changes only in response to new observations. A path layer decodes every replan deterministically in one step and enters it at the progress consumed during inference. A time layer sums the planned increments, keeps the arm at 1x while the gripper moves, and caps the rate by the actuator's linear range and by chunk feasibility under latency. We show that misaligned entry and stochastic sampling add a bias and a variance to the continuation error, and derive a break-even success rate that states when speeding up pays off. On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs under injected inference latency, PTS raises task throughput over the strongest deployable baseline by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA while matching or improving the success rate, is best on all six model-suite combinations, and exceeds zero-latency 1x execution. Against asynchronous 1x execution with the same one-step decoder, the time layer alone adds 28% and 38%. On LIBERO-Dynamic it improves on stop-and-wait execution by 38% and is comparable to asynchronous 1x execution.
bullets: Addresses two deployment bottlenecks: robot pauses during action-chunk inference and follows unnecessarily slow demonstration speeds.
Uses a path layer for deterministic one-step replanning with latency-aware path entry, plus a time layer that scales motion while respecting gripper behavior, actuator limits, and chunk feasibility.
Explains continuation error from misaligned replanning and stochastic sampling, and derives when speed increases are worthwhile.
On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs, PTS improves throughput by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA over the strongest deployable baseline while matching or improving success rate.
Also improves throughput on LIBERO-Dynamic, indicating scope beyond the primary benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on VLA model execution and latency, directly matching Vision-Language-Action.
papers.title: Same Path, Less Time: Training-Free Fast Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models under Inference Latency
papers.tldr: PTS is a training-free execution layer that lets frozen vision-language-action policies run faster without sacrificing task success by preserving planned paths while adapting timing to inference latency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.
bullets: Addresses the limited role of VLMs in diffusion-based vision-language-action models, where they usually provide only static conditioning.
Feeds noisy action latents, visual observations, and language instructions into the VLM at every denoising step.
Uses gated cross-attention to dynamically guide the action expert and supervises the VLM to recover clean action latents.
An adaptive step-size schedule balances task performance with inference latency.
Achieves the highest average success rate among evaluated π₀.₅-based methods on RoboDojo and improves results on RoboTwin 2.0 and four real-world bimanual tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Joint VLM-action denoising for VLA models; directly advances embodied action generation.
papers.title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
papers.tldr: JADE jointly denoises robotic actions with a vision-language model and action expert, improving out-of-distribution performance and reducing sampling steps.

papers.abstract: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting manipulation to changing garment geometry and appearance.
Uses NOCS-textured garment meshes to provide canonical surface cues to a pretrained vision-language-action model.
Fine-tunes the model on human demonstrations and corrections, then filters autonomously generated rollouts by task success.
Re-renders successful trajectories with randomized appearances for training policies that use only RGB observations.
Generated data improves RGB-policy performance over original human data across evaluated garment splits and appearances, though unseen-garment generalization remains difficult.

papers.selection_reason: Simulation platform and learned policy for bimanual garment manipulation, fine-tuning a vision-language-action model on human demonstrations to generate training data.
papers.title: ClothDojo: Learned Data Generation and Benchmarking for Bimanual Garment Flattening and Folding
papers.tldr: ClothDojo is a simulation and data-generation platform that creates diverse closed-loop trajectories to train more effective RGB policies for bimanual garment flattening and folding.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks. Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga
bullets: Addresses the large execution gap between high-level VLM decisions and physical robot control.
Combines explicit task beliefs, tool calls or synthesized Python programs, calibrated 3D sensing, dual-arm control, and a unified robot gateway.
Uses paused visual trajectory previews and runtime checks for tolerances and grasp bounds, enabling interruption and discrepancy-based recovery.
Achieves 57.7% success on RoboDojo and 73.2% on RoboCasa365 with a frozen, zero-shot harness.
Remains robust under scene randomization, though the abstract does not specify limitations beyond its evaluated settings.

Every physical motion passes through the admission gateway A, which returns a receipt and a new observation. Bottom: Closed-loop execution on hang_mugs: (1) localization, (2) grasp preview, (3) execution, and (4) placement on the rack.

Figure 1 Auriga completes manipulation tasks zero-shot within a single episode. A general-purpose model plans and acts through a shared harness, with no target-task exploration, demonstrations, or resets. The model localizes targets by multi-view triangulation, complemented by depth and point-cloud estimates (1), and reviews candidate motions before they are executed (2). The harness verifies each execution and stops when an action fails (3); the model then revises its plan and recovers from the current state (4–5) until the task succeeds (6).

Figure 5 The three nested loops of Auriga within one episode. The stage loop runs inside A and stops execution when a declared condition is violated; the model closes the action and belief loops. Deliberative calls extend the evidence record without advancing the world.

Figure 6 Preview and verification in two rounds, drawn on the head-camera image. In the first round, the previewed gripper path moves to the object, closes on it, and lifts it to a checkpoint placed by the model, where the robot pauses and the model receives a fresh wrist view (inset 1). The measured path follows the preview until a finger lands on the basket rim while the object is lowered. Once the gap exceeds the tolerance, the harness stops the arm and reports with a fresh view (inset 2), so the gripper does not open. In the second round, the model previews a revised motion from the stop that lifts clear of the rim and lowers into the basket, where the gripper opens (inset 3). The rim contact and the second round are illustrative.

Figure 2 Planning, execution, and recovery within a single tower-building episode. From left to right, the model grounds the task in visual and geometric observations, constructs a plan, and builds the tower through direct tool calls and generated programs. Action previews and execution feedback support a preview–execute–verify loop. After a failed grasp, the model inspects the scene, updates its plan, and regrasps the object to complete the tower. The harness provides measurements and execution checks; the model selects actions and recovery strategies. The scene is never reset.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses embodied manipulation using a task-agnostic agent harness that integrates vision-language models with robot control, closing the planning-execution gap.
papers.title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: Auriga is a task-agnostic robot-control harness that substantially narrows the gap between vision-language planning and reliable zero-shot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $τ$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between roughly 1 Hz scene-semantic updates and 20–50 Hz reactive control.
Caches VLM context and combines it with high-frequency visual features from a compact robot-video-pretrained encoder.
Conditions the flow-matching action expert on cache age and trains it with realistic cache-age histories and staleness-mimicking pixel corruption.
On LIBERO, achieves 95.2% success at a 1 s semantic refresh and 94.5% at 2 s, versus 96.3% for a frequency-matched anchor.
Adds zero-latency chunk-boundary correction and a verdict gate that freezes execution under instruction–scene mismatch.],

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Leap-VLA overview. Slow system: the VLM runs at fslow over a token sequence that appends, after the prompt and the observation, the chain-ofthought region; it produces the cached context C and the chain-of-thought-supervised anchor features, and its reasoning region is emitted as the structured output shown. Because attention is causal, the prompt-region features the expert consumes are unchanged by the appended block (Sec. III-B). Fast system: the flow-matching expert runs at ffast, consuming C and fresh fast-stream features through one pluggable token-block interface: image tokens from the frozen motion-aware encoder (dual-frame, robot-pretrained with reconstruction, optical flow, and depth). The measured cache age τ conditions the expert via AdaRMS, proprioception enters as a dedicated input token, and the control rate f is passed to the action head; training samples τ from the physical episode history.

Fig. 5. Task-perturbation generalization on LIBERO-PRO (libero goal). Top: the original task “put the wine bottle on the rack”, which appears in the training data—our model completes it. Bottom: only the goal is changed (“Put the wine bottle on the stove”); the scene and objects are identical. Our model still executes the new instruction, whereas VLA baselines score 0.0–6.8% on this perturbation dimension (ours: 20.4% averaged over the four suites, 8.4–49% per suite). Both rows are successful episodes re-recorded with the evaluation protocol of Table IX (asynchronous deployment: semantic anchor refreshed at each 0.5 s re-plan, fast stream and measured cache age updated every control step); frames are keyframes sampled from the 100 ms-interval agentview replay.

Fig. 7. Qualitative real-robot rollouts on the four platforms of Fig. 6. Each row shows five keyframes of one episode (start, approach, grasp, transport, final state) sampled from the onboard camera stream, one task per row: sorting blocks by color and packing workpieces into a box (Realman, rows 1–2); four-piece continuous dual-arm pick-and-place (Realman, row 3); pick-and-place of a workpiece (Dobot Atom, row 4); color-based sorting and word spelling with letter cubes (Galaxea, rows 5–6); placing a bottle into a marked target zone (in-house humanoid, row 7). All keyframes are sampled from successful autonomous segments of the policy rollout; in the interactive task (row 7) a human only hands over and re-stands the bottle between cycles, which is not shown.

Fig. 13. Failure analysis on LIBERO-PRO task perturbations (libero goal). Rows 1–3: under task-perturbed instructions, the characteristic failure is semantic interference—the policy reverts to the behavior of the trained task. Asked to turn the stove off, it turns the burner on (row 1); asked to put the wine bottle on the stove, it carries the bottle back to the trained rack goal (rows 2–3). Row 4: on the unperturbed original task, failures are motor-level instead (the grasp slips and the bottle is dropped). Perturbed-instruction failures therefore reflect instruction generalization rather than manipulation competence. These modes are systematic rather than cherry-picked: 2/2 recorded failures of “turn off the stove” turn it on, and 2/6 recorded failures of the wine-bottle task revert to the rack.

Fig. 9. The eight boundary windows with the largest uncorrected-vs-corrected contrast, one per episode (two LIBERO-Goal tasks, 200-trajectory evaluation; Table VI). Each panel shows the per-step 6-DoF displacement around one boundary (step 0 = first executed step on the new chunk; each method aligned to its own nearest boundary); the title gives the boundary displacement of all three executions (no-correction/guidance/nudge). Both corrections remove most of the boundary spike; soft-nudge consistently more.

Fig. 11. Environment-perturbation generalization on LIBERO-PRO. Each pair shows the same task in the original environment (top) and in an unseen perturbed environment (bottom): the light table is replaced by a dark wooden one, with background and lighting changed as well. Our model completes the task in both settings—placing the book into the rear compartment of the caddy (rows 1–2) and the tomato sauce into the basket (rows 3–4). Episodes are successful takes re-recorded with the evaluation protocol of Table IX; frames are keyframes of the 100 ms-interval agentview replay.

Fig. 14. Representative failures on LIBERO-plus for the two weakest perturbation categories of our model: extreme lighting (Light, 53.5%) and unseen table textures (Background, 55.6%), both at difficulty L5. Rows 1–2 (dim lighting): the policy reaches and manipulates the bowl but fails to complete the placement—the bowl is knocked beside the plate (row 1), or the bowl is never extracted from the cabinet (row 2). Rows 3–4 (dark table texture): the policy manipulates the distractor bowl next to the plate while the target bowl remains on the ramekin (row 3), and the grasp on the can fails so that it never reaches the basket (row 4). All episodes run to the step limit without a success.

Fig. 2. Fast-stream pretraining objective. A dual-frame pair (ot−δ, ot) is fused into a 6-channel input at the stem; a ∼49% row/column strip mask is applied jointly to both frames (pair-level tube masking), and the visible patches go through the compact encoder. Three lightweight decoders share the encoded features: the reconstruction decoder fills in both frames’ masked patches, the optical-flow decoder predicts the dense ot−δ→ot motion of masked patches, and the depth decoder predicts per-pixel depth for each frame. Panels show a held-out RoboTwin sample; decoder outputs are the training-time ground truth (WAFT flow, Depth Anything V2 depth, and the raw frames).

Fig. 3. Chunk-boundary analysis over the seam events of the 200-trajectory evaluation behind Table VI. (a) Displacement at the boundary step, aligned over all boundary events (mean ± 95% CI; maxima 0.120 / 0.078 / 0.070; the double spike reflects the 10-step chunk cadence). (b) Boundary events paired by ordinal position, corrected vs. uncorrected displacement (log–log); the median corrected/uncorrected ratio is 0.60 for RTC guidance and 0.52 for soft-nudge.

Fig. 6. Real-robot deployment platforms. From left to right: Realman dual-arm workstation, Galaxea dual-arm workstation, Dobot Atom mobile dual-arm humanoid, and our in-house humanoid upper body. All policies run on-board on the same Leap-VLA checkpoint layout; only the embodiment config differs per platform.

Fig. 8. Left: false execution under instruction–scene mismatch—each row is one rollout at increasing time fractions, instruction quoted above; the instruction refers to absent objects, yet the policy grasps an unrelated plate (top) or knocks over a bottle (bottom). Right: a consistency-gated policy freezes on a feasible instruction (“open the middle drawer of the cabinet”, t=0/50/97%): the negatives-only policy executes correctly, while behind a CoT-verdict gate misjudged as inconsistent the policy freezes for the entire episode (0/20 feasible tasks under gating vs 6/20 without)—a property of scene-imbalanced gate supervision, not of gating itself: after scene-balanced retraining the gate passes 20/20 feasible tasks and matches the ungated policy.

Fig. 12. Language-perturbation robustness on LIBERO-PRO. Each pair shows the same task from the same initial state under the original instruction (top) and a paraphrase (bottom): a telegraphic rewording (“put book in rear compartment of caddy”, rows 1–2) and an elliptical one (“place salad dressing in basket”, rows 3–4). The executed behavior is essentially unchanged and both episodes succeed, indicating the policy follows the task semantics rather than surface word patterns.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Leap-VLA, a VLA model that decouples a low-frequency VLM backbone from a high-frequency action expert, directly addressing the efficiency of vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
papers.tldr: Leap-VLA enables high-rate robot control by reusing low-rate VLM semantics while adapting to cache staleness with fresh visual input and age-aware action prediction.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained robotic manipulation requires instruction grounding, robust perception, and precise contact control. We describe our submission to the MetaFine Open Competition at CoRL 2026. Five independently trained models use a common architecture with frozen DINOv2 and CLIP encoders, trainable language-conditioned feature modulation, and task-specific action heads. We improve demonstrations through contact-aware grasp filtering, instruction-matched data, and expert correction of insertion failures. At inference, task-dependent strategies include photometric test-time augmentation, stochastic action averaging, and uncertainty-triggered replanning. Our submission achieves an official overall score of 0.914 and ranks third among 15 teams. We analyze the models and their task-specific behavior.
bullets: Targets instruction grounding, robust perception, and precise contact control for fine-grained manipulation.
Uses five independently trained models with frozen DINOv2 and CLIP encoders, trainable language-conditioned feature modulation, and task-specific action heads.
Improves demonstrations via contact-aware grasp filtering, instruction-matched data, and expert correction of insertion failures.
Applies task-dependent test-time augmentation, stochastic action averaging, and uncertainty-triggered replanning.
Evaluates task-specific model behavior; scope is the MetaFine Open Competition setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of our approach. Frozen DINOv2 and CLIP encoders provide language-conditioned visual features through trainable FiLM modules. A multimodal Transformer drives action heads that produce end-effector targets for T1–T4 or joint-space actions for T5.
Figure 2: Task-dependent effects of replanning. Episode success rates with and without uncertaintytriggered replanning for (a) T4 block placement and (b) T5 letter insertion.
Table 2: Official MetaFine evaluation results. Scores are rounded for display.

papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned robotic manipulation with task-specific action heads, directly fitting VLA and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Task-Specialized Language-Conditioned Models for Fine-Grained Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: A task-specialized, language-conditioned robot-learning system combines frozen visual-language encoders with targeted data and inference strategies to achieve a 0.914 score and third place in the MetaFine Open Competition.

papers.abstract: Simulation-based VLA evaluation often treats matching task, seed, and episode identifiers as sufficient evidence that two policies faced identical test conditions. Under specific vectorized reset and autoreset conditions, different termination timing can change subsequent initial-state assignment, so the same episode index need not mean the same test state. We present an evaluation-integrity framework for paired comparison - invariants I1-I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker - and a controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study with emulated controllers. Four evidence levels are kept separate: (A) mixed-horizon Sync wave-1 IDs [20, 5, 22, 7] vs [4, 5, 6, 7]; (B) homogeneous separate-job Sync control (16 cells, 0 ID/fingerprint mismatches); (C) Async+Freeze batch-size map differences (12 I3 mismatches; bs=8 incomplete; mechanism unisolated); (D) a synthetic McNemar illustration only. Controllers were emulated and no real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. We recommend checking declared/resolved init-state identity and provenance before paired statistics. We do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.
bullets: Vectorized reset and autoreset behavior can make identical task, seed, and episode identifiers refer to different states when termination timing differs.
The framework defines invariants I1–I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker.
A controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study found no mismatches in a homogeneous separate-job control, but identified 12 map mismatches in an Async+Freeze batch-size comparison.
The study used emulated controllers and did not complete a real-VLA shared-vector experiment.
The authors do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses test-state integrity and provenance in paired simulation-based evaluation of Vision-Language-Action models.
papers.title: Verifying Test-State Identity in Paired Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Paired VLA evaluations can compare different initial test states despite matching episode IDs, so state identity and provenance must be verified before statistical comparison.

papers.abstract: Vision-language action (VLA) models excel for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet their tendency to over-invoke chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning mirrors a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as deliberate reasoning can slow or mislead human judgment in routine tasks, excessive CoT in VLA incurs unnecessary compute overhead and can paradoxically degrade planning performance. Recent research tackles this via adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity by selectively triggering CoT for complex scenes while responding directly to routine ones. While prior adaptive methods rely on implicit adaptation, recent work shows that explicitly optimizing the route between CoT and direct responses yields superior performance, assuming scene-difficulty annotations which are labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity. We explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved without any scene-difficulty labeling. We introduce STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring two key components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 demonstrate that STEER is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in both planning quality and the Pareto front of inference efficiency.
bullets: Targets over-reasoning, which can increase inference cost and hurt planning in routine driving scenes.
Uses uncertainty-aware rollout to calibrate routing diversity to the model’s uncertainty.
Applies cross-route advantage credit assignment to learn routing from environmental rewards rather than subjective annotations.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 show competitive planning quality and inference-efficiency trade-offs with state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of STEER. STEER is built on an autoregressive vision-language model that takes a front-view driving image together with structured driving context as input, and generates a textual future ego trajectory as output. It formulates adaptive reasoning in autonomous driving as an explicit routing problem, where an initial decision selects either a reasoning route or a direct route before trajectory generation. The framework is trained in three stages: (1) driving-centric pretraining for domain adaptation, (2) route-balanced supervised fine-tuning to preserve support for both valid routes, and (3) route-aware policy optimization to learn the routing preference directly from task rewards, without any scene-difficulty labels.

Figure 2: Route-aware policy optimization in STEER. For each prompt, STEER first inspects the initial routing distribution to estimate routing uncertainty. When the routing decision is uncertain, the model performs route-contrastive rollout by explicitly sampling both the reasoning and direct routes under the same prompt; otherwise, it falls back to standard on-policy rollout. During optimization, STEER applies a standard content advantage to all response tokens and adds a cross-route advantage at the initial routing position, jointly optimizing response quality and route preference.

Figure 3: Prompt-level route comparison. For each prompt, we compare the trajectory produced by the route selected by STEER (blue) with the counterfactual alternative route (red). In the top case, explicit reasoning yields safer obstacle clearance. In the bottom case, STEER correctly avoids over-reasoning and selects the direct route, which better follows the road geometry compared to the perturbed reasoning alternative.

papers.selection_reason: Directly targets vision-language-action models for autonomous driving with adaptive reasoning to reduce over-thinking and improve planning efficiency.
papers.title: STEER: Route-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: STEER enables autonomous-driving VLA models to adaptively choose between CoT reasoning and direct responses without costly scene-difficulty labels.

papers.abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
bullets: Addresses the need to retain motion history and earlier visual evidence missing from current observations.
Trains memory with temporal supervision from predicted future visual features.
At execution, uses spatially normalized prediction discrepancies to selectively update the visual state.
Improves success from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO and 14.4% to 83.8% on RMBench M(1).
Also improves general manipulation and spatial-perturbation robustness, with 7.7 ms mean inference overhead on an NVIDIA H800.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation and overview of PREM. (A) Current observations alone can miss recent motion and earlier task-relevant visual evidence. (B) PREM uses future prediction to supervise memory learning and prediction discrepancy to regulate visual-state updating. Figure 2: PREM architecture. (A) PREM compares the cached prediction with observed visual features at each spatial location to compute prediction discrepancy. (B) The spatially normalized discrepancy regulates how much of the candidate visual-state update is incorporated. (C) An actionconditioned predictor predicts the next visual features from the incoming visual state, observed visual features, and latent action representation. The prediction objective supervises memory learning. The cached prediction provides a reference for subsequent visual-state updating.

papers.selection_reason: Recurrent visual memory regulated by prediction for VLA robot manipulation policies.
papers.title: PREM: Prediction-Regulated Memory for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: PREM improves robot manipulation by using action-conditioned future predictions to learn and regulate visual memory updates.

papers.abstract: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.
bullets: The challenge evaluates fine-grained manipulation under visual changes, language instructions, and behavioral precision across five simulated tasks.
The solution uses one 19M-parameter policy per task, a separate instruction classifier, and simulator-generated demonstrations from a privileged scripted teacher.
Failure analysis showed that near-perfect teachers can teach memoryless students poorly through pauses, fixed habits, and missing recovery examples.
Making demonstrations more imitable improved letter insertion from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32% more data, and ultimately to 0.88 using the same architecture.
The team’s overall score was 0.947, earning second place and motivating practical lessons about demonstration design and evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. Top: offline data generation with a privileged teacher and takeovers (Sec. 3). Bottom: the student policy (Sec. 2), one control network per task plus a shared instruction classifier. For T5, a second image stream sees a gripper crop at about twice the resolution.
Table 1: Official results (task score: mean of P, U, B; overall: mean over tasks). Episodes: training episodes per task (ours: teacher demonstrations and takeovers; π0: planner demonstrations).

Table 2: T5 development. Local: successes in 80 clean episodes (same seeds in every row). Official: leaderboard T5 score. The network is unchanged from t5 c on (t5 a: centre instead of gripper crop, fewer auxiliary targets); t5 j was fine-tuned from t5 g, the others trained from scratch.

papers.selection_reason: Fine-grained robot manipulation via imitation learning with a VLA model and per-task policies.
papers.title: Learning from an Imitable Teacher: Competition Solution for the MetaFine Challenge
papers.tldr: Team Friday achieved second place in MetaFine by training compact task-specific policies on deliberately imitable teacher demonstrations, substantially improving precise manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.
bullets: Per-token goal-word edits steer π₀.₅-LIBERO without changing the instruction text.
At layer 0, BatchTopK swaps redirected up to 20/20 rollouts in one scene, while random-feature swaps redirected none; results varied across scenes and layers.
Word-selected Matryoshka edits generally did not outperform random swaps, and SAEs were not necessary: a scaled difference-in-means vector also redirected behavior.
Edits remained effective through layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity; patching camera tokens extended effectiveness to layer 13.
The study is a simulated proof of existence and an initial characterization of the depth limits of goal-redirection edits.

papers.selection_reason: SAE-based goal steering in a robot foundation model (pi0.5) via instruction-token edits; directly relevant to robot policy and VLA research.
papers.title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$
papers.tldr: Swapping SAE features for a single goal word can redirect π₀.₅’s simulated robot behavior toward an alternative task, with effectiveness depending on feature type, layer, and token coverage.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to adapt pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs). We investigate the problem of behavioral steering: adapting a VLA's execution style to preferences such as carrying objects higher. To investigate how little trainable capacity such steering requires and how much pretrained capability can be retained, we freeze an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and optimize TinyLoRA adapters with 8 to 384 trainable parameters using either policy-gradient RL (GRPO) or evolutionary search (CMA-ES). With just 256 trainable parameters, we raise carry height by 120 mm on trained tasks at 92% success and by 74 mm on a held-out task at 80% success. By rescaling the learned update, we can tune the trade-off between style gains and capability retention without retraining. Increasing adapter capacity generally improves this trade-off, retaining more pretrained capability at comparable style gains. The choice of optimizer also depends on capacity, with CMA-ES being competitive at low parameter counts, while GRPO offers better trade-offs as capacity grows. These findings show that extremely low-dimensional updates can steer pretrained VLA behavior, with adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling offering practical control over adaptation and retention.
bullets: Studies behavioral steering, such as making a robot carry objects higher, without updating the full policy.
Freezes an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and trains TinyLoRA adapters with 8–384 parameters using GRPO or CMA-ES.
With 256 parameters, carry height increases by 120 mm on trained tasks and 74 mm on a held-out task, with 92% and 80% success respectively.
Adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling control the trade-off between behavioral change and capability retention.
CMA-ES is competitive at very low capacities, while GRPO provides better trade-offs as capacity increases.

Each curve is a single trained update rescaled by α (§3.4). The large marker is the trained update, the small markers are its rescalings, and color is the parameter count. Dotted line: unsteered held-out success at 0.96.

papers.selection_reason: Steering pretrained VLA policies with tiny adapters via RL and evolutionary search, directly relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Behavioral Steering of Vision-Language-Action Models in the Low-Parameter Regime
papers.tldr: Extremely small adapters can steer a pretrained vision-language-action model’s behavior while largely preserving its original capabilities.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.
bullets: Uses successful and failed rollouts with an Action-Confidence Alignment squared margin-ranking loss.
Updates OpenVLA-7B through low-rank adapters without an auxiliary failure detector.
Pairs observations at similar normalized elapsed times, which may not reflect equivalent physical progress.
On 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence reaches 0.7392 ± 0.0480 AUROC over three seeds.
Mean task success falls from 58% to 55%; safety benefits and improved control are not established.

ACAL adapts LoRA parameters using native action-token confidence. At test time, observed-prefix confidence supplies a failure-ranking score without a separately trained detector.
