papers.abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.
bullets: Addresses the need for intuitive, adaptable cobot programming as shop-floor tasks and environments change.
Uses a three-stage pipeline: teach workflows, abstract them into skills, then apply those skills to new situations.
Evaluated on a collaborative structure-building task with open- and closed-model agents in self-play and cross-model setups.
Skill abstraction improved task success rates and reduced interaction cost.
A preliminary human-in-the-loop study indicates the approach can also handle human instructions.

papers.abstract: Deformable linear objects (DLO) pose a coupled perception and control challenge: their slender geometry makes precise localization difficult, while their deformations depend on object-specific physical properties. To address this challenge, we propose PS-DLO, a property- and spatially aware DLO manipulation policy. First, contrastive image-text learning maps the initial observation to categorical descriptions of DLO properties, providing explicit physical and structural priors for action generation. Second, SAM3 extracts mask-guided features from future observations, which are distilled into the policy's action expert to encode task-relevant DLO regions and their subsequent configurations. We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, training a shared multi-task policy for each embodiment. PS-DLO achieves an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.0 percentage points. In generalization experiments, PS-DLO achieves higher success rates than the baseline in six of seven visual-shift conditions on butterfly-knot untying. These results demonstrate that combining object-property priors with future spatial supervision improves multi-task DLO manipulation and robustness to visual variation.
bullets: Addresses the coupled perception and control challenges caused by DLO geometry and object-specific deformation.
Uses contrastive image-text learning to infer categorical physical and structural properties from the initial observation.
Uses SAM3 mask-guided features from future observations, distilled into the action expert to highlight relevant regions and configurations.
Evaluated across nine real-world tasks on single-arm and bimanual platforms with shared multi-task policies.
Achieves 68.9% average success, 20.0 percentage points above the strongest baseline, and outperforms it in six of seven visual-shift conditions for butterfly-knot untying.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PS-DLO. The framework consists of DLO property extraction and future spatial knowledge distillation. The property extractor maps the initial observation to a categorical property description for policy conditioning, while the distillation branch uses SAM3-guided features from future observations to provide spatial supervision for the action expert through a teacher–assistant scheme. Training proceeds in three stages: contrastive propertyextractor adaptation, teacher pretraining with auxiliary action supervision, and joint training with teacher–student alignment.

Fig. 3. Representative execution sequences of real-world DLO manipulation tasks. The upper three rows show straightening, elastic-rope hooking, and knot untying on the bimanual PiPER platform. The lower two rows show thick-rope threading and lifting and long-rope wrapping on the single-arm Franka Research 3 platform. The tasks cover five DLO property dimensions: bending stiffness, extensibility, topology, thickness, and length. Frames are arranged chronologically from left to right.

Fig. 1. Property and spatial challenges in DLO manipulation. (b) Image downsampling degrades fine details of slender DLO while bulky objects remain visually salient, making interaction-relevant regions difficult to localize. These complementary challenges motivate PSDLO, which combines object-property conditioning with future spatial representation supervision to guide action learning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer knowledge from large-scale pretraining into robot control, but their manipulation performance remains sensitive to changes in observation conditions, which recent work addresses by fine-tuning the visual module on target-domain data. However, it remains unclear how such adaptation affects robustness beyond the target condition, as existing robustness benchmarks only evaluate models without fine-tuning and adaptation studies only report the target gain. Measuring this cross-dimension effect requires separating target gains from off-target changes, isolating adaptation effects from architectural differences, ruling out generic forgetting, and comparing tuning choices. Therefore, we introduce VLA-Retain, a benchmark that compares five open VLA models, tuned on Camera-view or Sensor-noise data, with their own base checkpoints on LIBERO-Plus dataset spanning seven perturbation dimensions. Our study reveals four findings. First, targeted vision tuning is not local, and its target gain does not predict retention. Mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model--domain configurations. Under Camera-view tuning, X-VLA gains $69.4$ percentage points on the target but loses $4.6$ points on average elsewhere, whereas OpenVLA-OFT gains $39.3$ and $1.4$ points, respectively. Second, these regressions are not explained only by performance loss on the same tasks without perturbations. Third, broader training coverage raises overall gain over target-specific training but does not eliminate dimension-level regressions. Fourth, tuning strategies are model-dependent, as DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain to $+1.2$ points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's to $-23.1$. Overall, these findings show that target-domain success alone is insufficient and highlight cross-dimensional retention as a key criterion for targeted VLA adaptation.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark comparing five open VLA models before and after tuning on camera-view or sensor-noise changes across seven LIBERO-Plus perturbation dimensions.
Targeted tuning is not reliably local: mean off-target performance decreases in 8 of 10 model–domain configurations.

Retention strategies have model-dependent effects, improving X-VLA but substantially hurting OpenVLA-OFT in the reported comparison.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.
authors: Pengfei Zhou, Yixing Ma, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Zhenglin Wan, Hexin Wang, Wangbo Zhao, Yang You

papers.abstract: Automated endoscope guidance reduces the need for continuous manual camera control during minimally invasive surgery. However, the desired camera motion depends on the surgeon's immediate intentions and cannot always be inferred from the visual operative scene alone. We propose to automate the task using language-conditioned behavioral cloning; we define 6 clinically relevant guidance behaviors and collect 235 subtask demonstrations. In preliminary phantom experiments, our policy achieves 100% success on focus, overview, and stop, 80% on search-tip and follow-tip behaviors, and 50% on horizon leveling. These results demonstrate the feasibility of learning heterogeneous surgeon-requested camera behaviors with a single visuomotor policy, while the observed failure modes motivate future work on adding temporal context for more demanding guidance tasks.

bullets: Endoscope motion depends on the surgeon’s immediate intentions, which may not be inferable from vision alone.

Preliminary phantom results show perfect success on focus, overview, and stop; lower success occurs for search-tip, follow-tip, and horizon leveling.
Failures suggest that temporal context may be needed for more demanding guidance tasks.

papers.abstract: Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by the scarcity of diverse, robot-executable data and by the difficulty of jointly learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control. We present Movens-5M, constructed from raw Internet videos through clip generation, quality filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery, and physical refinement with humanoid retargeting and execution verification. It contains 15 million human-motion sequences and 5 million physically executable humanoid-motion sequences spanning over 10,000 hours, aligned with text, RGB video, speech, and music. Building on this data, we introduce Movens-Zero, a scalable understanding-generation-execution architecture that supports joint learning across modalities and real-time closed-loop execution. Task-mixed flow-matching training jointly optimizes a single action expert across seven generation tasks, enabling direct motion generation from text, speech, music, and video. Multimodal Real-Time Chunking connects overlapping chunks under continuously updated instructions and robot states for continuous closed-loop execution. We further introduce Movens-Intent, a four-track benchmark with 8,192 expert-verified condition-motion pairs across text, speech, music, and video. Experiments show consistent gains across all four modalities when scaling execution-verified data from 1% to 100% and action-expert capacity from 64M to 911M parameters, while demonstrating that data quality and cross-modal supervision improve generation and execution.

papers.abstract: LLM-based robotic agent systems can generate programs for robot control, yet their generalization to new tasks often depends on elaborate scaffolding. Expanding their skill repertoires alone offers limited guidance on how to assess new capabilities or identify what remains beyond their reach. We introduce META-Robot, a framework that couples self cognition with capability scaling by expanding the criteria through which an agent evaluates and develops its skills. At its core, action-level predicates make execution outcomes explicit and available for LLM reasoning. The agent uses these assessments to identify its own limitations, extend relevant evaluation criteria, and guide the structured expansion of its skills. Proprioceptive feedback further grounds this process in the robot's physical state, enriching the evidence available for self-cognition. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate stronger overall task performance, generalization to new tasks, continued expansion of skills and evaluation criteria, and effective use of non-visual proprioceptive signals.
authors: Xuanzhi Feng, Zeyu Liu, Weiheng Gao, Xinchen Li, Jiankun Tang, Fangqi Zhu, Quanxin Shou, Hao Chen, Zhengyang Yan, Hualei Zhang, Junhao Li, Zhiyao Wu, Jie Zhang, Song Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generalizing to new tasks without relying on elaborate scaffolding.
Uses action-level predicates to make execution outcomes explicit for LLM reasoning.
Combines self-assessment, adaptive evaluation criteria, and structured skill expansion.
Uses proprioceptive feedback to ground self-cognition in the robot’s physical state.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots show improved task performance, task generalization, skill and criterion expansion, and effective use of non-visual signals.

figures.caption: Figure 1: META-Robot starts from a task description. Its framework consists of three components: (1) Loop Execution Agent, which generates programs and predicates, evaluates execution evidence, and repairs failures; (2) Proprioceptive Signal Orchestration, which supplements insufficient visual observations with physical feedback; and (3) coupled Predicate and Skill Libraries, which consolidate validated criteria and repairs for cognitive and capability scaling.

Figure 2: META-Robot Loop Execution Agent. Given a task description, the agent (1) decomposes it into executable subtasks and initial conditions; (2) jointly generates the task program and action-level predicates; (3) executes each skill while collecting task-relevant evidence; (4) evaluates predicate transitions to determine whether execution should continue or be repaired; (5) locally corrects and re-executes the failed skill, missing evidence routine, or verification check; and (6) performs system-level repair and full-task validation, consolidating validated predicates and skills for reuse. This procedure is repeated to form a closed execution–evaluation–repair loop.

Figure 3: Proprioceptive Signal Orchestration Mechanism Example: in thin-towel grasping, torque change provides a contact cue, while gripper feedback and a lift check verify successful acquisition to complement insufficient visual evidence during execution and verification. Validated signal usage is then consolidated into a reusable skill together with corresponding action predicates, jointly expanding sensing, execution, and verification capabilities

papers.abstract: Inserting an unseen part requires sub-millimetre precision and the correct orientation of keyed features. Current zero-shot agentic manipulation methods built on vision-language models (VLMs) produce spatial outputs that are far too coarse for this. We propose to let a VLM build a sketch model of the task, i.e., a few geometric primitives and two mate frames, which a VLM agent measures with geometric tools in multi-view depth and which a standard planner and compliant controller execute. Because a sketch describes the parts independently of their placement, the robot needs to build it only once per task. A sketch memory stores each agent run and transfers the stored sketch to later placements by point-cloud registration, so that the VLM is called only for unfamiliar parts. After grasping the part, the robot inspects both mating faces at close range and corrects the sketch by shape matching. On 69 simulated insertion episodes, our method inserts 88% of the parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test, while ReKep and MOKA with the same VLM insert none. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing one stored run inserts as many parts as calling the agent in each episode, and it produces the sketch in 3.4 s instead of about 90 s.
bullets: Targets sub-millimetre insertion of keyed parts, where existing VLM-based agents produce overly coarse spatial outputs.
A VLM builds a task sketch with geometric primitives and mate frames; geometric tools, a standard planner, and compliant control execute it.
The robot refines the sketch by inspecting mating faces at close range and shape-matching them after grasping.
A sketch memory transfers prior sketches to new placements via point-cloud registration, invoking the VLM only for unfamiliar parts.
In 69 simulated episodes, SketchMate achieved 88% strict-kinematic insertion versus 0% for ReKep and MOKA; reuse matched fresh agent calls while reducing sketch creation from about 90 s to 3.4 s.

papers.abstract: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending "if no task is given do not move" to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.
authors: Minsu Jang, Jae-Woo Choi, Youngwoo Yoon, Dohyung Kim
bullets: Across six checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation, robots moved in every episode with empty instructions.
Five checkpoints often completed tasks not specified by the instruction, including under meaningless or wrong-task inputs.
On two GR00T checkpoints, instructions selected the executed task but did not determine whether motion began.
A textual prefix failed to suppress starts; an action-chunk similarity gate succeeded on non-task inputs in five of six checkpoints.
Fine-tuning prevented task completion on non-task inputs but did not reliably suppress motion or handle infeasible instructions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and suppresses unintended starts in VLA policies, directly relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
papers.tldr: VLA policies may start and execute tasks even without a valid instruction, while a simple action-similarity gate suppresses starts more reliably than prompting or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to follow a language-specified person under occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. We show that improving tracking persistence can simultaneously increase safety violations. Using a compact 0.6B vision-language-action (VLA) tracker with a frozen backbone, we update only the planner head with proximal policy optimization (PPO). PPO improves success and following rates across all three EVT-Bench settings, but increases the collision rate on distracted tracking because episodes that previously ended in target loss can instead end in contact. We introduce TRACE, an execution-time target-state risk gate that preserves the learned policy and intervenes selectively. A lightweight risk head processes 84 cues, including candidate boxes, identity margins, a learned range-and-bearing probe, and the policy's commands. When the calibrated risk exceeds a threshold, TRACE rescales the translational component of the next waypoint while leaving yaw unchanged. The executed action is identical to PPO's on more than 98% of steps. In paired evaluations on identical episodes, TRACE reduces the distracted-tracking collision rate by 3.96 percentage points, while further improving success and following rates. Matched slowdown controls without target-state timing do not reproduce this improvement. Concurrent evaluation reproduces a collision reduction of 3.77 points, compared with 0.29 points for identical-arm null pairs, indicating that the effect exceeds evaluation variability. These results show that target-state-aware execution can recover the safety cost of policy post-training with minimal intervention.
authors: Mingyang Lyu, Gongce Cao, Yiyang Jia, Lu Jia, Erliang Lin, Yuhao Zhang, Yinqian Sun, Pin Lyu, Feifei Zhao, Bo Wang
bullets: PPO improves tracking success and following rates but increases collisions in distracted tracking because some target-loss episodes become contact events.
TRACE uses a calibrated risk head over 84 visual, geometric, identity, and action cues to detect risky executions.
When risk is high, it rescales only the next waypoint’s translational motion and leaves yaw unchanged; actions remain unchanged on over 98% of steps.
On paired evaluations, TRACE reduces distracted-tracking collisions by 3.96 percentage points while further improving success and following; concurrent evaluation shows a 3.77-point reduction.
The approach targets safety-cost recovery after policy post-training, with matched slowdown controls failing to reproduce the improvement.

A positive label is a step inside the K-step window preceding a collision termination. Ranking is strong at every window; the raw sigmoid is badly calibrated as a probability at every window. We therefore report the output as a risk score.

Per run the calibrated gate is not uniformly better than PPO (Table 7), and its paired deltas did not reproduce under concurrent evaluation (see below).

papers.selection_reason: VLA tracker with risk-aware execution-time intervention for embodied tracking.
papers.title: TRACE: Target-State Risk-Aligned Conditional Execution for Embodied Tracking
papers.tldr: TRACE adds a selective, target-state-aware execution gate that reduces collisions from a PPO-trained embodied tracker while preserving its tracking improvements.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
bullets: Evaluated 281 policies from seven families across about 1,700 trials of RJ45 grasping and insertion with a five-fingered hand.
Observation and action representations dominated optimizer and sampling choices.
For point-cloud policies, cropping, robot-base coordinates, and encoder normalization each improved success by 70–100 percentage points.
Absolute actions improved vision-language-action insertion success by up to 70 percentage points; decomposition, multi-view sensing, and recovery data appeared beneficial but were not isolated.
Only five of 67 offline metrics correlated reliably with success, and only within one policy family, so real-robot evaluation remains necessary.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates imitation learning policies for dexterous manipulation, including VLA policies.
papers.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Large-scale real-robot evaluation shows that representation choices—not standard optimization settings—most strongly determine dexterous imitation-learning success, while offline metrics provide only limited guidance.

papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.
authors: Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Yilei Jiang, Dongming Wu, Jiaxu Wang, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Addresses the gap between CaP agents relying on frontier models or VLAs and small open VLMs failing at robot manipulation.

Uses GPT-6 Astra-generated synthetic trajectories for SFT, followed by multi-turn RL.
Introduces a privileged physical critic that assigns credit to individual requests based on their effect on predicted task success.
CaPtain-4B improves from 55.4% to 73.8% held-out LIBERO success, reaches 78.5% on LIBERO-PRO, and transfers to other simulators and a real robot.

papers.abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.
authors: Xiaoyi Zhang, Haoqing Wang, Xinjie Zhang, Xiang Ming, Xing Wang, Senqiao Yang, Kaichen Zhang, Zhaoyang Jia, Andong Tan, Xinjiang Wang, Jinghao Guo, Yifei Shen, Xiao Li, Peng Zhang, Xun Guo, Jiahao Li, Shicheng Zheng, Jinglu Wang, Zongyu Guo, Wenxuan Xie, Bin Li, Yan Lu

papers.abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.
bullets: Provides a prompt-driven pipeline for generating diverse drawing trajectories in simulation and on real robots.

Demonstrates reactive drawing with a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm under human intervention.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark with controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean–perturbed rollouts, and simulator-grounded stage-aware failure analysis.
Evaluates GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts.
Robustness varies across tasks and perturbations, and greater severity does not always cause monotonic performance degradation.
Perturbations with identical end-to-end success degradation can produce different failure-depth profiles, revealing where execution breaks down.
Motivates reporting outcome degradation, paired-outcome sensitivity, and failure progression jointly; code is publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of RoboCasa-Shift. RoboCasa-Shift evaluates VLA robustness on selected long-horizon RoboCasa tasks under controlled single-factor distribution shifts with multiple frozen severity levels. Strictly matched clean-perturbed rollouts enable counterfactual comparison under shared task conditions, while robustness is characterized jointly through end-to-end task outcomes and stage-aware semantic execution diagnostics. Representative findings illustrate that aggregate success rates can mask substantial episode-level outcome changes, similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to different failure locations, and severe visual corruption can shift failures toward earlier stages of task execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of StageTracker. (a) A long-horizon task is represented as an ordered sequence of semantic subgoals, each associated with a simulator-state predicate. (b) During rollout, StageTracker evaluates the current predicate, records the completion step when it is first satisfied, and advances to the next subgoal. Completed subgoals are latched, allowing the tracker to report the deepest semantic progress reached and the first incomplete subgoal for failure localization.

Fig. 2: Pipeline of RoboCasa-Shift. (a) Task Suite. Candidate RoboCasa tasks are filtered through clean-competence screening to construct the formal evaluation suite. (b) Controlled Shifts. Selected tasks are evaluated under four singlefactor distribution shifts with calibrated and frozen severity levels. (c) Counterfactual Pairing. Clean and perturbed rollouts share the underlying task conditions and policy seed and differ only in the target shift. (d) Diagnosis. RoboCasa’s official task outcome is complemented by stage-aware semantic diagnostics of execution progress, first incomplete subgoal, and subgoal reach.

Fig. 8: Representative severity calibration examples. Rows correspond to the four perturbation factors, and columns show the clean condition (L0) and three calibrated severity levels (L1–L3). Illumination progressively darkens the scene, camera orientation changes the third-person viewpoint, robot base initialization perturbs the initial base position and yaw orientation, and Gaussian blur progressively reduces visual sharpness. For base initialization, the inset provides a schematic top-down view, where the black and orange markers represent the nominal and perturbed base poses, respectively, while the straight and curved arrows indicate planar displacement and yaw rotation. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor and are not assumed to be physically equivalent across factors.

Fig. 9: Task-wise distributions of first incomplete semantic milestones among perturbation-induced failures. Each subplot corresponds to one formal task. For each perturbation factor and severity level, the stacked bar shows the distribution of first incomplete milestones g1, . . . , gK among strictly matched S→F transitions, where K depends on the task. Trackercomplete official failures, in which all tracked milestones are reached but RoboCasa’s official task-success criterion remains unsatisfied, are reported separately without assigning a first incomplete milestone. The proportions are calculated over all S→F transitions in the corresponding task and condition. The annotation above each bar indicates the number of transitions n; conditions without such transitions are marked as n = 0.

Fig. 7: Representative matched replays at different semantic failure depths. Each case compares a strictly matched clean– perturbed rollout pair that shares the same task instance, initial simulator state, episode metadata, and episode-level policy seed, while differing only in the target perturbation. The two rows show the clean and perturbed executions, respectively, and the columns present selected frames spanning the execution process. Checkmarks and crosses indicate whether the corresponding tracked semantic subgoals are completed, while the final annotation reports the official task outcome. These examples provide a qualitative view of how perturbations can change execution depth and failure location, complementing the aggregate stage-aware statistics in Figure 6.

Fig. 5: Task-level robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Each cell reports the paired success-rate degradation ∆SR for one task and perturbation condition, computed from 20 matched episode pairs. Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition, while negative values indicate a higher success rate under the shifted condition for the corresponding finite paired sample. The task-level breakdown reveals heterogeneous severity responses that can be obscured by macro aggregation.

Fig. 10: Representative counterfactual outcome transitions under camera orientation at L1. Case A (StackBowlsCabinet) shows a success-to-failure (S→F) transition, whereas Case B (PreSoakPan) shows a failure-to-success (F→S) transition. Within each case, the clean and perturbed rollouts share the same task instance, initial simulator state, and episode-level policy seed, differing only in the target camera-orientation perturbation. Columns show selected frames from the initial, intermediate, and final stages of execution, with the final outcomes determined by RoboCasa’s official task-success criterion. These examples illustrate opposite episode-level outcome changes under the same perturbation condition, despite zero aggregate success-rate degradation at L1.

Fig. 4: End-to-end robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Macro-averaged paired success-rate degradation ∆SR is shown for the four distribution-shift factors, with each factor evaluated at three frozen severity levels (L1– L3). Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals obtained from paired bootstrap resampling. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor, and equal level indices across different factors do not imply physically equivalent perturbation magnitudes.

Fig. 6: Stage-aware execution depth of perturbationinduced failures. Each marker summarizes strictly matched clean-success-to-perturbed-failure (S→ F) transitions under one perturbation factor and severity level. The vertical position indicates the mean normalized subgoal progress of the corresponding S→F cohort, marker size represents the number of transition events, and marker color denotes the fraction of failures occurring before the first tracked semantic milestone. The annotated n gives the number of transitions in each condition. Gray lines connect L1–L3 within the same perturbation factor only to visualize the within-factor severity trend and do not encode an additional quantity. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor and are not assumed to be physically equivalent across factors.

TABLE IX: Complete counterfactual outcome transitions across all perturbation conditions. Each row contains 80 strictly matched clean–perturbed episode pairs, categorized into four mutually exclusive outcomes: success-to-success (S→S), success-to-failure (S→F), failure-to-success (F→ S), and failure-to-failure (F→F).

TABLE VI: Task-specific semantic subgoal specifications. Each gk denotes a task-specific diagnostic milestone. The criteria were frozen before formal perturbation evaluation. For WashLettuce, thresholds refer to the simulator washed time counter.

TABLE XI: Condition-level statistics for perturbationinduced failures. Statistics are computed over strictly matched clean-success-to-perturbed-failure (S → F) transitions. The policy-side comparison shows that uncontrolled inference randomness breaks repeatability, whereas sharing the episode-level policy seed restores consistent action sequences.

papers.abstract: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals. Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning. To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning. With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.
bullets: Addresses costly, limited humanoid demonstrations and the mismatch between human egocentric video and robot embodiment.
Uses VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller plus hand-control signals.
Trains in three stages: egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning.
Bridges embodiment gaps with simulated pseudo-proprioception and re-rendered arm appearances.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena; adapted egocentric data improves real-world Unitree G1 pick-and-drop success.

papers.abstract: Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feed-forward VLA models, which ignore long-horizon context and hierarchical visual-language representations.
Injects pretrained VLM key-value features into an adaptive mixture-of-experts action module.
Uses asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and DINOv2 historical-frame features for dynamics-aware temporal conditioning.
Applies covariance-structured flow matching on an Action Dynamic Manifold to model coupled robot actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with ablations supporting the proposed components.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PRIME W0 architecture.

(2) NTP / task-specific pre-training: with DAT action tokens, the VLM learns visuomotor next-token prediction over instruction–observation–action sequences. (3) DiT Pretrain: the VLM is frozen while the MoT / Adaptive MoE flow-matching action expert is trained with world-model conditioning to denoise continuous actions (and associated state tokens). (4) SFT: both the VLM and the action expert are jointly fine-tuned end-to-end, optionally with action-prefix tokens that shorten the denoising trajectory at inference. papers.abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying aerial perception, language grounding, reasoning, and control without offboard computation.
Uses a shared vision-language representation, a compact waypoint-generating action expert, temporal memory, and action priors.
Trains on approximately 70,000 simulated navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction–response pairs.
Runs onboard at 10 Hz on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, producing 12-waypoint action chunks.
Transfers zero-shot to physical flight, achieving a 48% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data.

papers.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.
authors: Baiqiao Yin, Zhongang Cai, Ruisi Wang, Qiwei Liang, Lei Yang, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Evaluates four capabilities: spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained manipulation requires a robot policy to follow instructions, remain robust to visual variations, and translate predicted actions into precise robot control. We present Demonstration Expansion and Execution Design (DEED), a framework for adapting a pretrained vision-language-action policy to the five MetaFine tasks through structured demonstration expansion and execution design. DEED generates demonstrations for different instructions from the same initial scene and renders each physical trajectory under different camera positions and lighting conditions while preserving its original states and action targets. A hierarchical sampling strategy balances instructions, trajectories, and visual conditions during supervised adaptation. At deployment, DEED converts predicted action chunks into robot commands using inverse kinematics, gripper mappings selected for each task, and closed-loop replanning. DEED achieves an official Overall score of 85.55%. Fixed-policy evaluations show that performance varies with execution horizon, denoising budget, and gripper mapping.
bullets: Targets instruction following, visual robustness, and precise action execution in five MetaFine tasks.
Expands demonstrations across instructions, camera positions, and lighting while preserving states and action targets.
Uses hierarchical sampling for supervised adaptation of a pretrained vision-language-action policy.
Executes action chunks with inverse kinematics, task-specific gripper mappings, and closed-loop replanning.
Achieves an official Overall score of 85.55%; performance depends on execution horizon, denoising budget, and gripper mapping.

papers.abstract: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring robot experience across heterogeneous embodiments and execution frequencies.
Pretrains a shared latent function space using action reconstruction and consistency across different temporal sampling views.
Connects this space to a world model conditioned on observations, language instructions, and the robot’s current state.
A single decoder produces end-effector actions for any queried time, separating shared dynamics from task-specific action selection and temporal sampling.
The abstract describes a unified transfer framework but reports no quantitative experimental results or explicit limitations.

Training Stage B connects observation-conditioned latent prediction to the learned function space using latent and physical reconstruction supervision. At inference, current multimodal observations and visual features condition latent prediction; the function decoder combines the predicted latent with physical query times and observed context to produce embodiment-specific control commands.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Rongxing Ding, Hongyu Qu, Kehong Wu, Xudong Wang, Fan Zhang, Xinguang Xiang, Xiangbo Shu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-term dynamics, long-term goals, and their relevance to current actions in VLA models.
Jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goals using a Hierarchical Dependency Mask.
Structures future latent representations across horizon, viewpoint, and spatial dimensions for fine-grained retrieval.
Adaptively retrieves future information according to evolving action representations during denoising.
Evaluated on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The overview of HIFOR. (a) We augment the VLA with hierarchical foresight prediction and action-guided world retrieval, enabling the Action Expert to leverage future information during action generation. (b) Hierarchical Foresight Prediction (§3.4) predicts short-term, milestone, and goal futures through hierarchical dependency modeling. (c) Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling (§3.5) organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions. (d) Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval (§3.6) selectively retrieves action-relevant future information through denoising-aware factorized attention to guide action generation.

papers.abstract: Building general game agents requires both high-level task reasoning and low-latency action control in rapidly changing visual environments. These capabilities favor models with substantially different computational profiles, making them difficult to realize within a single model. In this work, we present TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner-controller framework that connects task-level planning with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control. A vision-language task planner decomposes a high-level goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions and is optimized through supervised learning and dependency-aware GRPO. The hidden states of special goal tokens that terminate each atomic instruction provide continuous goal embeddings that are cached and reused across control steps. A causal Transformer controller combines the embedding of the active goal with recent observations to predict discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions and continuous camera motion at every game step. We train the system in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. Experiments in Minecraft show that TaskFrame is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and that in closed-loop evaluation the agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines.

A causal Transformer controller predicts keyboard, mouse-button, and camera actions from goals and recent observations.
Trained through planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment.
In Minecraft, it is competitive on instruction decomposition and achieves higher closed-loop combat success than evaluated baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner–controller agent that separates task-level planning from frame-level control. (A) Task Planner. A vision–language model decomposes a high-level goal (e.g., “collect oak logs across the river”) into an ordered sequence of atomic goals, each terminated by a special goal token. The hidden states at these tokens are cached as goal embeddings z1, . . . , zk. (B) Frame Controller. A per-frame autoregressive policy. Each frame consumes the active goal embedding zj , an action-query token ain, a SigLIP image token ot, and the action at, which only later frames attend to. A causal Transformer aggregates them into the action-output token aout, which is decoded into discrete keyboard and mouse-button presses and continuous camera motion. The planner runs once per high-level goal, while the controller acts at every game step.

papers.abstract: Choosing a robot action model requires evidence about task capability, adaptation cost, deployment requirements, and the reliability of reported conclusions. Success rates alone offer limited guidance to researchers with different computing budgets and goals. We propose RoboSeed, a multidimensional evaluation framework for vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAM), within a continuing program to train, evaluate, and openly release robot models with verifiable evidence for model selection. The framework defines five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence. It maps empirical measurements and audit criteria to 0-100 profiles using fixed normalization anchors, with balanced, training-constrained, and deployment-constrained preference settings. Interface and protocol checks establish when comparisons are appropriate. Missing measurements remain explicit, incomplete aggregate scores are withheld, and weighted input coverage identifies evidence gaps. We apply the framework to representative VLA and WAM models, drawing on local training, released-weight evaluation, task-level audits, and an evaluation-system study. The results reveal budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language and visual task interfaces. Reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence support extension to additional models. The study provides dimension-level assessments and priorities for further measurement, while incomplete serving traces and heterogeneous protocols preclude overall numerical rankings.

Finds budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language- and visual-task interfaces.
Provides reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence, but does not produce overall rankings because serving traces and protocols are incomplete or heterogeneous.

papers.abstract: Agentic robots must turn a high-level goal into actions while keeping the physical conditions needed for future steps valid. A completed action does not ensure that its effects will persist: a later disturbance can invalidate support that the remaining plan still assumes. We present LOGIV, a graph engineering framework for agentic robot execution that uses an explicit task graph to connect symbolic planning, observation-based verification, and embodied action. LOGIV compiles a validated plan into condition-support and resource-ordering edges, checks their physical validity during execution, and uses dependency tracing to determine what must be restored after a failure. Repair is constrained by retained unfinished actions, and the combined continuation is symbolically validated before execution resumes. The framework operates above existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Model (WAM) policies without adding trainable components. Across 20 dual-arm tasks from RoboTwin~V2 and BiCoord with three execution backbones, LOGIV improves mean task success without injected disturbances by 10.67 and 15.33 percentage points, respectively. Under predefined perturbations, it achieves higher task completion and condition restoration than three adapted recovery baselines for every backbone on both benchmarks. On three real-robot tasks, successful trials increase from 12/30 to 17/30. These results support explicit, continuously checked task dependencies as a practical interface for reliable agentic robot execution.

Works above existing VLA and WAM policies without adding trainable components.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) policies write a reasoning trace and then decode the action from it. A wrong trace yields a wrong action, and even a correct-looking trace can mislead the plan. Existing remedies ask whether the reasoning is right. We ask how strongly it should steer. CoC-CFG applies classifier-free guidance between the policy's context and the same context without the reasoning span. One weight per Euler step attenuates or amplifies the reasoning, and w=1 recovers the original policy. We treat the choice of this weight as a Markov decision process whose action values are measured, not bootstrapped. With the expert frozen and the noise fixed, applying a weight for one step and finishing the plan under the current controller returns that weight's value exactly. Q-adaptive guidance fits these values with small critics and improves the controller conservatively. In the Alpasim driving simulator it outperforms every fixed weight and online RL (SAC, GRPO) in open loop, and in closed loop it passes 262 of 300 scenes, against 252 for the original policy. On held-out frames of the Waymo end-to-end driving benchmark, its first three stages outperform every fixed weight, four adaptive-guidance methods, SAC and GRPO. On the hidden test set, a frozen Alpamayo 1.5 with rule-based camera and vehicle conversions and Q-adaptive guidance sets a new state of the art among published methods: 8.135159 rater feedback score, against 8.079 for the best published method.
bullets: Problem: A reasoning trace can be incorrect or misleading, so treating it as uniformly trustworthy may produce poor actions.
Method: CoC-CFG adjusts reasoning influence separately at each Euler step by interpolating between policy contexts with and without the reasoning span.
Method: The guidance weight is formulated as an MDP action; its value is measured exactly by applying it for one step and completing the plan with the current controller.
Contribution: Small critics fit these measured values to produce conservative, adaptive guidance without bootstrapping.
Results: The method outperforms fixed-weight and online-RL baselines in simulator and benchmark evaluations, including 262/300 closed-loop scenes and a reported 8.135159 hidden-test score.

papers.abstract: Generating interactive 3D assets from a single image requires realistic appearance, fidelity to the depicted object, and plausible physical behavior. Yet detailed geometry alone does not determine how an object should move or deform. We introduce PhysAg3D, which couples 3D generative models with agentic reasoning and tool use. A vision-language agent first infers semantic parts, candidate interactions, and physical priors from the image; a 3D generator then produces a textured whole-object mesh from the same image. A hierarchical interaction representation links these revisable priors to mechanisms and the generated surfaces they control, organizing interaction construction and refinement. Guided by this representation and observations of the mesh, the agent uses geometric and physical tools to construct parts, joints, deformable regions, and surface bindings while retaining useful generated geometry and materials. Rendered interactions and execution measurements guide targeted revisions within a fixed budget. The framework accommodates both rigid articulation and compliant deformation. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks demonstrate detailed, image-aligned assets with plausible interactions. Ablations support bounded refinement and source-surface preservation. Project Page: supra-3d.github.io/PhysAg3D.
authors: Bi'an Du, Fanpeng Meng, Jiemin Fang, Chen Yang, Pufan Li, Daizong Liu, Qi Tian, Wei Hu
bullets: Targets single-image 3D asset generation with realistic appearance, visual fidelity, and physical interactivity.
A vision-language agent infers semantic parts, possible interactions, and physical priors, while a 3D generator creates a textured whole-object mesh.
A hierarchical interaction representation connects inferred priors to mechanisms and mesh surfaces for iterative construction and refinement.
Geometric and physical tools add rigid joints, deformable regions, and surface bindings while preserving useful generated geometry and materials.
Evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks show detailed assets with plausible interactions; ablations support bounded refinement and source-surface preservation.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) increasingly couple internal visual or world representations with action generation, making their world-to-action pathways a critical yet poorly understood source of robustness. We investigate when perturbations to these internal representations actually become behaviorally consequential, and uncover a pronounced mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across visual K/V routes, while larger representation displacement does not reliably imply stronger control failure. Our analysis attributes this mismatch to the action-conditioned readout, where keys determine where action queries read and values determine what content they receive. This motivates an action-facing view of vulnerability, in which the effect of a perturbation depends on how it is routed into action generation rather than on representation-space magnitude alone. We instantiate this view with Tail-AV, a short-probe signal for identifying vulnerable routes, and operationalize it in PASA-KV, which selects action-facing K/V targets before training a fresh task-shared attack. Experiments across multiple WAM systems and a physical robot validate readout-informed target selection, demonstrate strong closed-loop attacks, and reveal substantial system-level differences in resistance.
authors: Zhongbo Wu, Jiakai Huang, Zheng Zhang, Siyu Xu, Kaixiang Chen, Xiaohong Liu, Shan You, Chang Xu, Tao Huang
bullets: WAM robustness can differ sharply across visual K/V routes, even when representation perturbations are similarly large.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes action-facing visual routes in world action models, revealing readout-informed vulnerabilities relevant to action-conditioned world models.
papers.title: PASA-KV: Attacking Action-Facing Visual Routes in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PASA-KV finds and attacks the visual key/value routes that most directly influence action generation, showing that perturbation impact depends on action-facing readout rather than representation displacement alone.

papers.abstract: Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) to guide action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them. We introduce CoRAct, a consequence-grounded reasoning-to-action alignment framework that explicitly aligns reasoning and action through reward-guided optimization in action noise space. CoRAct formulates two physically grounded ECoT components as verifiable signals: movement specifies intended motion, while waypoints encode expected spatial consequences. A unified Mixture-of-Transformers jointly models ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction. For candidate actions generated from sampled noise, CoRAct computes alignment rewards based on movement consistency and agreement between predicted outcomes and specified waypoints. These rewards guide group-relative optimization of the initial noise distribution, steering action generation toward consistency with intended actions and expected consequences. Experiments across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements in task success, generalization, and reasoning-execution alignment over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. CoRAct also grounds externally provided ECoTs in executable behavior, enabling zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios by leveraging knowledge from powerful vision-language models. Project page and dataset: https://onlyxingxingzyx.github.io/CoRAct/
authors: Yixue Zhang, Wenke Xia, Kun Wu, Wenbo Yu, Pei Ren, Junnan Nie, Di Hu, Zhengping Che, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between implicit ECoT-conditioned action generation and explicit reasoning–action alignment.

A unified Mixture-of-Transformers jointly models reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction.
Reward-guided optimization in action-noise space steers candidate actions toward consistent consequences.
Experiments on RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation show improved success, generalization, and reasoning–execution alignment; external ECoTs support zero-shot adaptation.

papers.abstract: Predicting where to grasp and how to move is fundamentally a geometry problem. Vision-language models treat it as language generation instead. They tokenize spatial coordinates into text and decode them autoregressively. This mechanism ignores spatial structure and truncates continuous precision. Errors compound across coordinate tokens during decoding. In this paper, we show that compact off-the-shelf VLMs with 0.5-2B parameters already encode rich spatial information in their intermediate hidden states. Autoregressive decoding is the dominant bottleneck for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends additionally on feature depth and decoder architecture. We expose the latent spatial information with a lightweight, geometry-compatible prediction head that attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction and refines it via cross-attention over the visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone. We evaluate on ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K. Our 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60% and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline. It approaches RoboBrain on trajectory prediction (0.251 vs 0.191 DFD) at 3.8x higher throughput. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Dimity Miller, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
bullets: Problem: Tokenizing coordinates as text loses continuous spatial precision and causes autoregressive error accumulation.
Method: Attach a lightweight head to a frozen VLM, using intermediate features, instruction-conditioned queries, and cross-attention to regress boxes and waypoints directly.
Contribution: Separates geometric prediction from language decoding without modifying the VLM backbone.

Results: On ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K, the 2B model reduces trajectory error by over 60%, improves affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline, and achieves 3.8× higher throughput than RoboBrain while approaching its trajectory performance.
Scope: Affordance prediction also depends on feature depth and decoder architecture.

Two independent FFNs decode the query into continuous outputs: affordance boxes (L1+GIoU loss) and trajectory waypoints (L1+startpoint+endpoint loss). No gradient flows into the VLM.

papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.
