papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
authors: Qingyuan Cai, Bo Zhang, Yongzhen Huang, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of robot data and the human–robot embodiment gap.

Reports consistent gains over no-pretraining baselines on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions, but their large weight footprint challenges deployment on memory-constrained onboard platforms. Ultra-low-bit quantization reduces this footprint, yet preserving task performance and controlling weight recovery costs remain challenging. We propose Action-Guided Quantization, which combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets. Per-channel calibration compensates for quantization error, while a uniform bitwidth within each matrix preserves regular layouts. Bit-dependent grouped lossless coding reduces resident weight storage, and block-wise recovery limits temporary buffers. On LIBERO, AGQ achieves 92.7% task success at W3, exceeding AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively, and retains 70.5% success at W2.5. An asymmetric configuration, denoted W1.5$^{*}$, uses W4 vision weights and a parameter-weighted average of 1.5 bits for language weights. With lossless coding, it achieves $6.10\times$ complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/Qiuxu00/AGQ
authors: Xuhong Qiu, Zhuoyu Wu, Qiawei Zheng, Wenhui Ou, Wenqi Fang, Rapha\"{e}l C. -W. Phan
bullets: Targets the large memory footprint of vision-language-action models on onboard, memory-constrained robots.
Allocates matrix bitwidths under storage budgets using action sensitivity and a proxy for weight recovery cost.
Uses per-channel calibration, matrix-uniform bitwidths, lossless coding, and block-wise recovery to reduce storage and recovery overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 92.7% success at W3 and 70.5% at W2.5; W3 exceeds AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points.
A W1.5* configuration with lossless coding provides 6.10× compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success.

papers.abstract: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50s, 1.72$\times$ faster than the default policy's 6.02s while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.
authors: Seungyong Moon, Deokjae Lee, Hansang Lee, Munkhtselmeg Battsengel, Youngin Kim, Seonghyeon Yun, Sungjin Jeon, SongEun Kim, Jeongmin Park, Hyun Oh Song
bullets: Teleoperator timing can vary across demonstrations and cause policies to learn operator-specific speeds rather than task-relevant motion.
The method predicts a distribution of execution speeds from the task instruction, motion path, and path images; a selected quantile defines each demonstration’s new clock.
One speed prior trained on robot and handheld demonstrations can retime demonstrations across tasks without fitting a separate acceleration model per task.
A real-time optimal-control layer tracks policy action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace.
Across 120 RoboLab tasks, learned retiming improved success and reduced jerk by up to half; a real robot stacked cups in 3.50s with 29/30 successes.

papers.tldr: A learned speed prior retimes robot demonstrations to task-appropriate, consistent pacing, improving motion smoothness and enabling faster execution without reducing success.

papers.abstract: Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and kinematically feasible for the target robot. Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space. The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning. Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being generated. We present EmbodyHOI, which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object. Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without retraining. On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite. Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human-space HOI generation and humanoid robot execution, which can cause contact failures and poor policy learning.
Integrates a differentiable inverse-kinematics solver into the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI generator.
Uses embodiment-aware gradient feedback and jointly optimizes humanoid positioning relative to the object; the same generator transfers across robot embodiments.
On ARCTIC trajectories, wrist error drops from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm, while task success increases from 68% to 79% for G1 and from 62% to 76% for H1-2.
Outperforms post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection for policy training, despite those alternatives achieving lower IK energy.

We then retarget the guided sample and train a PPO tracking policy on it with decoupled arm and hand rewards. Changing the robot changes only the IK module.

papers.abstract: Generalization in multi-arm collaboration can be studied as composing familiar atomic skills in new ways across arms. However, existing evaluations offer limited insight into which training and architectural choices support this ability under different coordination requirements. We introduce \textbf{ACG-Bench}, a benchmark for \emph{Arm-wise Compositional Generalization} that provides a common testbed for studying skill recomposition in dual-arm policies. It contains 23 task--condition pairs across 8 task families, with 6 in-domain conditions and 17 unseen compositions covering reordering, synchronization, their combination, and cross-task composition. All methods receive the same per-arm atomic prompts, and success requires achieving the task goal while satisfying physical milestones and specified order or timing constraints. Using $π_{0.5}$ as a common vision-language-action backbone, we compare representative data-augmentation and architectural strategies with shared source data and a common evaluation protocol. Our architectural study examines arm-token grouping, skill-specific LoRA adapters (SkillLoRA), and arm-wise attention (AWA), highlighting the complementarity of skill-conditioned parameters and attention structure. Combining these choices yields \textbf{AE-VLA}, which achieves 21.53\% generalization success in simulation, compared with 2.94\% for Single $π_{0.5}$, 3.06\% for MA-VLA, and 5.53\% for two independently controlled $π_{0.5}$ policies. On physical SO101 robots, AE-VLA reaches 39.00\% mean success across five unseen conditions, compared with 10.00\% for the strongest baseline. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing dual-arm policies that generalize beyond fixed training routines.
bullets: Introduces ACG-Bench: 23 task–condition pairs across 8 task families, including 17 unseen compositions.
Evaluates policies using shared per-arm atomic prompts and requires both task success and physical order/timing constraints.
Studies arm-token grouping, SkillLoRA adapters, and arm-wise attention, finding their design choices complementary.
Combining these components in AE-VLA achieves 21.53% simulation success versus 2.94% for Single π₀.₅ and 39.00% mean success on physical SO101 robots versus 10.00% for the strongest baseline.
Scope: the study focuses on dual-arm compositional generalization under the benchmark’s specified conditions and protocols.

papers.abstract: Adapting a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to a new robot, environment, or task requires demonstrations that are collected locally and often discarded. Federated learning is a promising approach to exploiting such distributed demonstrations by learning a shared policy. However, whether it can adapt large pretrained VLAs remains an open question, and a lack of reproducible benchmarks for pretrained VLAs and reusable training frameworks makes existing results difficult to compare. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study of federated fine-tuning of three modern pretrained VLA policies on the 40 simulated tasks of the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, and on six real-world tasks in two real-robot experiments, with demonstrations collected across two and three sites, respectively. Our study analyzes the key choices in this setting, spanning multiple federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and evaluation under distribution shift. Based on the study, we derive a series of lessons, including the dominance of the federated scope over the choice of aggregation algorithm and the difficulty of matching centralized fine-tuning on physical robots, where cross-site heterogeneity is stronger than simulation captures. We also highlight opportunities for federated VLA learning, such as the ability to match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data, to remain at least as robust as centralized fine-tuning under distribution shift, and to personalize, with each client federating part of the policy and keeping the rest local, which helps where the policy's pretraining is weak but leaves no usable global model. We open-source \decentvla{}, the model- and runtime-agnostic testbed behind the study, to facilitate future research and fair comparisons in federated VLA learning.
bullets: Evaluates three pretrained VLA policies on 40 simulated LIBERO tasks and six real-world tasks across multiple sites.
Studies federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and robustness under distribution shift.
Finds that the federated parameter scope matters more than the aggregation algorithm.
Federated learning can match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data and remain comparably robust to distribution shift, but matching centralized performance on physical robots is difficult.
Personalized federation can help when pretraining is weak, though it does not produce a usable global model.

Every client composes a policy backend (the VLA) and an execution backend (the FL runtime) independently, so the same loop runs in-process or over Flower [18] or NVFlare [19].

papers.title: An Empirical Study and Open Testbed for Federated Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: A systematic study shows how federated fine-tuning can adapt pretrained vision-language-action policies across distributed robot data, while introducing an open, reproducible testbed for future research.

papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.
authors: Minghao Zhu, Bohan Hou, Kun Xiang, Zixuan Wang, Yinzhou Tang, Yifei Yang, Zhikai Wang, Tianyi Zhang, Kehan Li, Haoyu Zhao, Siteng Huang, Leigang Qu, Sicong Leng, Dongchi Huang, Mingxiu Chen, Shijian Lu, Yue Wang, Xiaodan Liang, Zhenyu Zeng, Deli Zhao, Chengju Liu, Jianfei Yang, Xin Li

An agentic reinforcement-learning extension selectively uses video predictions to reason about unobserved states and interaction outcomes.
A world-action extension translates the model’s understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control.
The model achieves the highest average embodied-understanding score among evaluated unified multimodal models and improves Rynn-VP by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano.
Its extensions improve Rynn-GEU by 6.0 points over direct reasoning and achieve 51.5% success on selected RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7% average success across three real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified embodied model combining video-language reasoning, spatial understanding, visual planning, and robot control spans multiple configured topics.
papers.title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
papers.tldr: RynnUnify is a 16B unified embodied model that combines physical-world understanding, long-horizon visual planning, and robot control through interleaved video-language reasoning.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $\pi$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $\pi$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.
bullets: Targets brittleness when robot actions enter states poorly covered by training data.
Trains a small failure-prediction head on outcome-labeled rollouts using the frozen VLA’s internal representations.
When failure risk crosses a threshold, it pauses control, backtracks the arm, and returns control to the unchanged policy.
Adds only 0.48–0.88% to model parameter counts.
On LIBERO-Long, reduces failure rates by 19–48% and improves success by up to 7.4 percentage points; gains are smaller on easier suites, while all tested MetaWorld configurations improve.
papers.selection_reason: Lightweight failure recovery for frozen VLA policies directly targets embodied vision-language-action systems.
papers.title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
papers.tldr: Backtrack helps frozen vision-language-action models recover from predicted failures by retracing recent motions and retrying, without retraining or recovery demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.
authors: Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Obaidullah Zaland, Monowar Bhuyan
bullets: Human corrections vary in modality, urgency, behavioral scope, and privacy sensitivity across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments.
Naively shared updates may improve mean performance while suppressing rare safety interventions or causing unsafe behavior on other robots.
Corrections should retain their context and uncertainty when determining what to share.
Each candidate update should be evaluated in the receiving robot’s closed loop before deployment.
The paper proposes counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda; it reports no experimental results.
papers.selection_reason: Federated adaptation of VLA policies and safety across embodiments is directly relevant to embodied AI and VLA.
papers.title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
papers.tldr: Federated sharing of human corrections for VLA robots requires context-aware, closed-loop safety checks and privacy evaluation rather than optimizing average task success alone.

papers.abstract: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.
authors: Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang, Yuanwei Liu
bullets: GRPO assigns one trajectory-level advantage to every action, so recovery attempts in failed rollouts may be penalized with preceding errors.
The method uses success-probability and policy-score martingales to characterize stopping points where removing later gradients has zero conditional expected effect.
A LoRA-fine-tuned VLM identifies the last visible error without observed recovery in complete rollout videos and retains feedback only through that interval.
For retrospective boundaries, the work analyzes changes in gradient expectation and variance relative to ideal stopping conditions.
Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 report higher success rates than full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves GRPO for vision-language-action policies, directly relevant to VLA and robot policy learning.
papers.title: When to Stop Penalizing Actions? Martingale GRPO for VLA Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MART-GRPO truncates failure feedback at VLM-detected error boundaries to avoid penalizing potentially useful recovery actions while preserving the expected GRPO gradient under ideal stopping.

papers.abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Hongwen Li, Yiding Yu, Zhuang Fu, Siqi Ding, Zhengyuan Chen, JianGuo Chen, Hanyue Zhao, Tianyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses shot-to-shot NBI ion-source tuning when hidden operating conditions evolve and responses are nonstationary.
Combines deterministic extraction of physical and visual features, two-layer trajectory/knowledge memory, MLLM action generation, and independent feasibility checks.
In chronological replay of 455 shots across four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols outperformed waveform images alone for quality classification.
Retrieved context improved agreement with historical action directions, while visual evidence had model-dependent effects.
Demonstrates engineering feasibility for supervised sequential tuning on five ion sources; scope is limited to supervised operation and the evaluated platforms.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal agent for sequential physical instrument control with memory and action constraints; fits VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Adaptive Control of Scientific Instruments with Nonstationary Responses through Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: A physically grounded multimodal agent enables supervised, sequential tuning of nonstationary scientific instruments, achieving an 86.80% beam-extraction rate across 409 executed shots.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.
papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded memory for VLM-based robot planners that selectively retrieves frames, relevant to embodied memory, VLA, and token efficiency.
papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.tldr: LogLook improves robot-planning memory by grounding it in execution logs and letting the model selectively inspect frames and demonstrations, reducing visual context while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions. However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects. We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skill-conditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation. MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skill-query tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head. On the CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences. Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.
authors: Jiachi Yang, Zhiyi Xu, Hongquan Zhang, Xin Tan, Zhizhong Zhang, Jingyu Gong, Yuan Xie
bullets: Addresses insufficient modeling of primitive skill choice and object contact/movement in vision-language-action policies.
Uses skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts adapters with skill-query tokens and routing biases in the language-model backbone.
Converts affordance heatmaps into patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial priors for the action head.
Achieves an Avg. Len of 4.65 on CALVIN ABC→D long-horizon cross-scene evaluation and is validated in real-robot sequence experiments.
Scope includes robustness to real perception and control noise; broader limitations are not specified in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces skill-conditioned LoRA-MoE and trajectory-affordance priors for multi-skill VLA manipulation, directly in scope.
papers.title: MAST-VLA: Skill-Conditioned Adaptation with Trajectory-Affordance Priors for Multi-Skill Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: MAST-VLA improves generalist robot manipulation by conditioning both skill selection and action trajectories for multi-skill execution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are typically pretrained on broad, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuned on a comparatively small dataset tailored to a specific target robot. Such adaptation recipe is now widely established, achieving its most mature results on fixed-base arms due to their static base dynamics and consistent reference frame. Mounting the same arm on a quadruped extends the workspace to the entire floor, but fundamentally changes the embodiment: rather than controlling the arm in isolation, the policy must jointly coordinate base navigation, body posture, and end-effector motion. In this work, we study the practical demands of this embodiment change across data collection, model adaptation, and inference design to achieve closed-loop loco-manipulation on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm. We report the choices that made this real-robot deployment feasible, namely model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions, together with a study tailored to a pick-and-place task, separating data coverage from model capacity. We show that expanding demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%, and incorporating secondary skills (such as pushing rather than grasping) introduces new behavioral modes without degrading baseline performance. Finally, closed-loop real-world experiments show how dataset composition shapes success and failure, validating the pipeline for more complex loco-manipulation.
authors: Giovanni Minelli, Antonio Langella, Giovanni B. Dessy, Lorenzo Amatucci, Giulio Turrisi, Victor Barasuol, Claudio Semini
bullets: Studies the embodiment shift from fixed-base manipulation to coordinated navigation, posture, and end-effector control on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm.
Examines practical deployment choices across data collection, model adaptation, and inference, including model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions.
Finds that broader demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%.
Shows that adding secondary behaviors such as pushing introduces new modes without degrading baseline grasping performance.
Validates the pipeline in closed-loop real-world pick-and-place experiments and analyzes how dataset composition affects success and failure.
papers.selection_reason: Deploys a VLA policy on a legged manipulator for loco-manipulation, directly matching vision-language-action and robot manipulation interests.
papers.title: From Tabletop to Walking Bot: Deploying a VLA Model on a Legged Manipulator Robot
papers.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates a practical pipeline for deploying VLA models on a quadruped-mounted arm, showing that demonstration coverage and multimodal skills are key to effective closed-loop loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state. Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes. We further develop a VLM-based interpretation pipeline to generate behavioral descriptions of these patterns and validate their correspondence to feature activations on held-out intervals.
authors: Christian A. Rogers, Qian Lin, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of diagnosing why vision-language-action robot policies succeed or fail.
Uses sparse autoencoder representations of OpenVLA activations to identify outcome-predictive information.
Links individual SAE features to specific stages and recurring behavioral patterns in task outcomes.
Localizes temporal intervals with significant feature-activation changes to identify relevant behaviors.
Uses a VLM-based pipeline to describe these patterns and validates the descriptions on held-out intervals.
papers.selection_reason: Uses VLA activations to predict and interpret robot task failures; directly relevant to VLA models and robot learning.
papers.title: Do VLAs Know They Will Fail? Interpretable Success and Failure Patterns in Physical AI Systems
papers.tldr: Sparse autoencoder features in VLA activations can predict impending robot-task failures and help explain the behaviors associated with success or failure.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/
authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: Problem: Solver depth and open-loop execution horizon are usually tuned independently, creating a responsiveness–stability trade-off.
Method: Jointly adjust numerical sampling depth and execution horizon, using coarse integration as an implicit regularizer during extended open-loop execution.
Key insight: Numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, reducing compounding drift.
Results: The approach consistently improves task success and substantially lowers inference latency across simulated and real-world manipulation settings and multiple VLA backbones.
Scope: Coarse integration can hurt precision during rapid replanning, so its benefit depends on the execution horizon.
papers.selection_reason: Reveals a training-free coupling between execution horizon and sampling depth in flow-matching VLA policies, improving task success across robots.
papers.title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Coupling solver depth with execution horizon lets flow-matching VLA policies trade numerical precision for improved stability and lower-latency robotic control without retraining or architectural changes.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks. In our experiments, adding TTT and training on paired data at the current scale did not lead to consistent target selection based on demonstrations. Under the tested settings, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations. When demonstrations were reduced to single-frame cues, real-robot execution still showed a preference for cups at fixed positions. We document the implementation, training configurations, and observations to support further inspection and replication.
authors: Qiangong Zhou, Jiafeng Liang, Yimin Dong, Yang He, Hongxiang Li
bullets: Targets long-horizon robot tasks that require retaining information from human demonstrations.
Adds TTT with fast-weight context memory to InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5, using paired demonstrations and robot trajectories.
Studies memory transfer, truncated backpropagation, training objectives, gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization across video and image cues.
At the tested scale, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations.
In real-robot tests with single-frame cues, behavior still favored cups at fixed positions, suggesting limited cue use.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, integrating Test-Time Training (TTT) for action generation conditioned on human demonstrations.
papers.title: TTT in VLA Models: Exploring Training with Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: This study integrates Test-Time Training into VLA models to use human demonstrations, but finds no consistent demonstration-conditioned target selection under the tested settings.

papers.abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo
authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Behavior cloning is limited by costly, narrow demonstration data and insufficient coverage of successful states.
A privileged, latent-conditioned RL generator uses a parallel reverse curriculum and success-gated diversity objective to discover multiple solution modes.
Generated behaviors are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for imitation learning.
Across four manipulation tasks, downstream success rises from 40% to 62% in simulation and from 39% to 78% on a real robot.
The approach is evaluated with a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection.
papers.selection_reason: Uses RL to generate diverse demonstrations for downstream imitation learning and VLA policies, directly relevant to robot manipulation and VLA.
papers.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: DiscoDemo uses reinforcement learning to generate diverse, successful robot demonstrations that substantially improve downstream visuomotor imitation learning.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.
authors: Yan Shi, Kehua Chen, Jiarui Qi, Yihong Tang, Haichen Liao, Yinhai Wang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in MLLM-based driving, where committing to one interpretation can cause premature errors.
Uses particle-filter-inspired belief tracking: a VLM propagates, scores, and resamples diverse scene hypotheses as observations arrive.
On Bench2Drive, improves Driving Score from 68.50 to 81.37 and Success Rate from 41.36% to 54.09%.
Shows the largest gains in ambiguous situations, including unsignalized intersections and oncoming-traffic interactions.
Also improves interactive behaviors such as merging, emergency braking, and giving way.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop MLLM-based autonomous driving with belief tracking directly fits embodied navigation and vision-language-action.
papers.title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriveMind improves closed-loop autonomous driving by maintaining and updating multiple scene hypotheses across frames instead of reasoning from scratch each time.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language-action (VLA) model is fine-tuned with its trainable weights in bfloat16 (bf16) and no fp32 master copy, AdamW writes each update straight into bf16, silently rounding away any update smaller than 1/512 of a weight. In 9 of 12 open VLA codebases a default or documented recipe trains this way, 4 on full weight matrices, including LeRobot's SmolVLA default and its $\pi_0$/$\pi_{0.5}$ guides. In our LIBERO runs without the copy, a probe every 100 steps finds at least 79% of updates to bf16 weights erased. On the Hugging Face Hub, 99% of sampled full-weight SmolVLA fine-tunes store the action expert in bf16, and 84% of recent $\pi_{0.5}$ fine-tunes with a training configuration set the bf16 flag. On LIBERO-Object, with rules fixed in advance, an fp32 copy raises success over LeRobot's storage from 4.3% to 49.3% for SmolVLA and from 5.1% to 80.9% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at a ten-times lower learning rate, where both models are undertrained, and from 89.0% to 97.7% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at its default rate. For SmolVLA at its default rate it adds 10.2 points with open-loop 50-action chunks but only 4.2 when re-planning every 10 actions. In these five comparisons and two more against SmolVLA with every trainable weight in bf16, every run with the copy beats every run without it (p < 0.05); all gaps but the 8.7- and 4.2-point ones clear our 10-point threshold. The fix is to keep the trainable weights in fp32 during training, a one-line change for SmolVLA in LeRobot.
bullets: bf16 rounding removes updates smaller than 1/512 of a weight when no fp32 master copy is used.
This issue appears in documented or default recipes across 9 of 12 surveyed open VLA codebases.
A probe found at least 79% of updates erased in LIBERO runs without an fp32 copy.
Using fp32 training weights improved reported LIBERO-Object success across SmolVLA and π₀.₅ comparisons, including gains up to 76.6 percentage points.
The proposed fix is to keep trainable weights in fp32 during training; for SmolVLA in LeRobot, this requires one line.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies a training-precision pitfall in VLA fine-tuning and a simple fix, directly relevant to vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Full-Weight VLA Fine-Tuning Without an fp32 Master Copy Silently Erases Most Updates
papers.tldr: Training full-weight VLAs directly in bf16 can silently erase most optimizer updates, while keeping an fp32 copy substantially improves LIBERO success.

papers.abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.
authors: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma, Yue Su, Cai Zhou, Xiuwei Xu, Tianle Zhang, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of robot demonstrations and noisy action labels from egocentric videos.
Jointly learns visual future prediction and action generation in a vision-language-action framework.
Uses reliability-conditioned corruption and weighted regression to reduce the impact of unreliable action supervision.
Distills action-relevant structure from clean future observations into representations trained with corrupted futures.
Shows steeper scaling than a baseline, with 20.5% lower real-world open-loop action MSE and an 8.1-point RoboCasa few-shot success improvement at 30,000 pretraining hours.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action framework that scales policy learning with noisy egocentric human videos, combining reliability-aware action learning and future-representation distillation.
papers.title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
papers.tldr: EgoForesight scales robot policy learning with noisy egocentric video actions by weighting supervision by reliability and learning from demonstrated future outcomes.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation, requiring robots to regulate not only motion but also how they yield to external forces, has emerged as the next frontier for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing VLAs output purely kinematic commands, degrading performance on real-world contact-rich tasks. In this paper, we introduce CompVLA, a unified VLA framework that jointly predicts motion and stiffness matrix from RGB and language inputs. Our approach augments the conventional architecture with a dedicated Compliance Expert, which outputs time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles executed via geometric impedance control. We demonstrate that CompVLA achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks, outperforming both vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines, with ablations confirming each component is essential.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of VLAs that produce only kinematic commands and cannot regulate responses to external forces.
Adds a dedicated Compliance Expert to predict time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles.
Executes predictions through geometric impedance control for contact-aware behavior.
Achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks against vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines.
Ablations indicate that each component is essential to the framework.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model jointly predicting motion and compliance/stiffness for contact-rich manipulation directly targets embodied robot policy learning.
papers.title: CompVLA: A Variable Compliance Vision-Language-Action Model for Contact-rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: CompVLA enables vision-language-action models to perform contact-rich manipulation by jointly predicting robot motion and variable compliance from visual and language inputs.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
bullets: State hallucination occurs when a VLA acts as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.
The failure is associated with reduced attention to task-relevant visual regions and activation of specific sparse autoencoder features.
SOUL unlearns hallucination-related policy knowledge while retaining features associated with successful behaviors.
Experiments across simulated and real-world settings and multiple VLA architectures reduce hallucinated failures and improve task success.
The approach is evaluated specifically for state hallucination and aims to preserve existing manipulation capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses state hallucination in vision-language-action robot policies using sparse-feature unlearning.
papers.title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: SOUL selectively removes sparse features linked to state hallucination in vision-language-action policies, reducing these failures while preserving manipulation ability.

papers.abstract: Generative robot policies can represent diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting pretrained policies to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance remains challenging. Existing inference-time steering methods typically apply gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which can be computationally expensive for real-time control. We propose INSPO, which formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. By optimizing the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, INSPO searches the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. The optimization includes a regularization term that encourages solutions to remain consistent with the policy's input distribution and is solved online using population-based particle optimization. We evaluate INSPO on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while comparing favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance in diverse generative robot policies.
Optimizes policy input noise while evaluating constraints on the resulting state trajectory, preserving the policy’s behavior space.
Uses distribution-consistency regularization and online population-based particle optimization.
Evaluated on state-, image-, and vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial.
Improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while achieving lower runtime than gradient-guided generation.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time steering of one-step generative robot policies via noise-space trajectory optimization; applies to VLA policies and manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Safe Real-Time Policy Steering via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization for One-Step Generative Policies
papers.tldr: INSPO enables real-time constraint-aware steering of one-step generative robot policies by optimizing their input noise instead of repeatedly modifying actions or generation steps.

papers.abstract: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.
authors: Yunfei Xie, Howard H. Qian, Shiyi Lan, Kaiyu Hang, Chen Wei
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating robotic foundation models through closed-loop rollouts.
Extends the Platonic Representation Hypothesis to embodied models by treating motion trajectories as an additional modality.
Measures representation–motion alignment without training and correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families.
Can help screen promising vision-language model backbones before costly conversion or fine-tuning into vision-language-action models.
Provides representation-level insight into success patterns in vision-language-action and world action models, though the abstract does not establish causality.
papers.selection_reason: Offline metric for embodied policy success directly fits embodied AI and VLA/robot learning evaluation.
papers.title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
papers.tldr: Sensorimotor Alignment (S²) is a training-free offline metric that gauges embodied model quality by measuring how closely sensory representations match the geometry of physical motion.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $\pi_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj, Edward W. Duan, Junwon Seo, Prithwish Dan, Wei-Chiu Ma, Andrea Bajscy, Preston Culbertson
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable runtime monitoring of VLA policies without continuous human supervision.
Trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate execution progress and flag deviations.
Evaluated with the open-source π₀.₅ VLA on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Competitive with or better than VLM-based monitors and methods trained with failure data for task-failure detection.
Scope: focuses on monitoring execution progress using internal activations rather than preventing failures directly.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Progress Probes P2, a lightweight method for runtime monitoring of VLA models using internal activation probes, enabling inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Progress Probes use lightweight linear probes of a VLA’s internal activations to detect when manipulation tasks are going off-course, avoiding external VLM monitors.

papers.abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.
authors: Yufeng Liu, Bohao Fan, Juntu Zhao, Xinyi Wang, Hang Yu, Wenzhuan Luo, Yingzhi Wang, Qinghai Li, Yingdong Hu, Junliang Guo, Richard Wang, Dequan Wang, Yang Gao, Cheng Ma
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable stopping after success and recovery or replanning after failure without fine-grained progress labels, external monitors, or complex architectures.
Represents status with stop and failure dimensions appended to each action chunk, distinguishing ongoing, successful, and failed execution.
Builds successful, failed, and recovery trajectories to provide complementary supervision without frame-level annotations.
Controls signal–action interactions and denoises status signals faster, allowing cleaner status estimates to guide later action generation.
Real-world manipulation experiments show accurate status prediction and consistent policy-performance improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Echo, a framework for VLA models that couples task status signal learning with action generation to improve execution robustness.
papers.title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
papers.tldr: Echo jointly denoises task-status signals and robot actions so a single VLA can recognize success or failure and use that information to guide execution.

papers.abstract: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.
authors: Ziyi Jiao, Heng Zhang, Drishti Regmi, Xiaokang Ye, Lianhui Qin, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Introduces 20 Unreal Engine maps across five categories targeting equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies.
A single VLM controls both players from top-down images using high-level actions, while the engine handles navigation.
Evaluates four VLMs using task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance, and API expenditure.
The strongest evaluated model, gpt-6-astra, reaches 26.2% mean order completion.
Shared notebook memory has mixed effects across models, improving some and reducing scores for others.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language agents controlling simulated players through high-level actions in a cooking environment, fitting embodied vision-language-action evaluation.
papers.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
papers.tldr: DuoCook benchmarks how well vision-language models plan and coordinate two agents in visual cooking tasks with shared resources and time constraints.

papers.abstract: Agentic robot systems combine language-model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision of a {\pi}0.5 policy. A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions. The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval. On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT-as-Policy ({\pi}0.5 + GPT-6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.
authors: Tao Lin, Yuxin Du, Haoxiao Wang, Zile Zhong, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the overhead of reviewing every action chunk in familiar robot-task situations.
Uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes for a fast execution path, plus targeted supervision for error recovery.
Keeps the vision-language-action policy frozen and generates actions from current observations.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use fell 57.2% on average and mean episode time decreased from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes.
Mean success rose from 80% with GPT-as-Policy to 97.19% with FastHarness on the evaluated tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FastHarness, an experience-driven framework for scheduling supervision in Vision-Language-Action policies to reduce overhead and improve success rates.
papers.title: FastHarness: Experience-Driven Review Scheduling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: FastHarness adaptively reduces GPT supervision for robot policies by learning from past execution outcomes while preserving recovery support for failures.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $\pi_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.
authors: Huixin Xu, Ziya Yu, Peng Li
bullets: Existing VLA policies often over-rely on wrist views and fail to adapt view selection during manipulation.
The method predicts future interaction intent from historical actions to guide stage-aware multi-view routing.
It coordinates global and local observations according to the current manipulation stage.
On RoboTwin 2.0, it improves average success by 10.10 percentage points over π₀.₅.
In real-world tests, success rises from 71.7% to 85.0%; the modules can be integrated into existing VLA architectures.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model with future-intent-guided multi-view routing for robotic manipulation; directly fits embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FocusVLA improves robotic manipulation by using predicted future intent to dynamically route global and local camera views across task stages.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
bullets: Addresses non-Markovian manipulation scenes where important visual cues disappear or leave view.
Uses SAM3 to track objects and select key event frames within an adaptive memory budget.
An action expert reads selected frames via cross-attention alongside object tokens encoding appearance, geometry, and time.
Introduces HuMeGo, a benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
Raises success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot; also improves SIMPLE tasks from 70.2% to 86.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLA humanoid manipulation, relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: WholeBodyMem improves humanoid loco-manipulation by selectively remembering task-relevant object events from before the robot acts.

papers.abstract: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.
authors: Zecong Tang, Zian Guan, Yuncheng Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Bo Dai
bullets: Addresses the gap between native visuomotor control and high-level planning in open-ended games.
Uses a capability-aware harness with structured memory, VLM subtask planning, and a policy-coupled completion detector.
A single VLA perceives through vision and acts via native keyboard-and-mouse inputs across subtasks.
Improves control reliability with regime-specific normalization, separate mouse-token embeddings, and staged training with world knowledge, imitation, and reinforcement learning.
Reports 85.0% on MineStudio Bench, 37.4% average success on OpenHA, and successful long-horizon crafting tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical VLA agent with native keyboard-mouse control and VLM planning for open-world games.
papers.title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
papers.tldr: HiSTEVE combines hierarchical planning, structured memory, and a single vision-based native-control VLA to perform long-horizon tasks in open-world Minecraft.
