papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models bring an appealing form of explainability to a safety-critical domain, since a system that can state the reasons for its maneuvers offers the transparency that deployment and public trust in autonomous driving demand. These models read the world into language before they act on it, describing the scene and reasoning over it in text that ranges from chain-of-thought to multi-stage question answering on the way to a trajectory. That framing quietly assumes two separable properties, namely that the trajectory follows the generated reasoning and that the generated reasoning tracks the causes that actually produce the trajectory. To thoroughly investigate these properties, we apply causal, counterfactual interventions to four driving VLAs across different benchmarks. First, we perturb the models' own reasoning and show that altering its meaning produces small trajectory changes relative to blanking the same models' camera inputs, a pattern that persists across benchmarks and model architectures. We then construct scene-level counterfactuals through photorealistic removal of key objects named in the models' reasoning and analyze whether the generated reasoning and trajectories track these changes. Overall, our findings indicate that the reasoning these models present to account for their resulting driving behavior is weakly coupled to that behavior itself, pointing to limits on the explainability these systems are intended to provide.
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Saad Wazir, Thao Do, Seongah Kim, Hyeontaek Hwang, Tolcha Yalew Kidane, Daeyoung Kim
bullets: The study tests whether driving VLAs’ actions follow their generated reasoning and whether that reasoning reflects the causes of their actions.
Causal interventions perturb the models’ reasoning, while separate experiments remove objects referenced in that reasoning from the scene.
Changing the reasoning causes relatively small trajectory changes compared with removing camera inputs, consistently across benchmarks and architectures.
Scene-level counterfactuals assess whether both reasoning and trajectories respond to changes in relevant objects.
The results question whether generated reasoning provides faithful explanations for driving behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Directly investigates reasoning-action coupling in driving vision-language-action models via counterfactuals, fitting embodied VLA research.
papers.title: Measuring the Reasoning-Action Coupling in Driving Vision-Language-Action Models through Counterfactuals
papers.tldr: Counterfactual tests across four driving VLAs show that their textual reasoning is only weakly connected to the trajectories they produce, limiting its value as an explanation.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu
bullets: Pixel prediction quality can misalign with policy utility: lower next-frame MSE may yield worse policy gradients.
DRILL uses bilevel optimization to update the world model based on returns after an inner GRPO update from imagined rollouts.
DRILL-VWI is a rollout-free surrogate that weights errors by policy visitation, GRPO advantage, and model confidence.
DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.
papers.selection_reason: Trains action-conditioned world models to improve VLA policies via imagined rollouts, directly relevant to world models and embodied policy learning.
papers.title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
papers.tldr: DRILL trains world models to produce useful policy-learning signals rather than merely predict pixels, improving downstream VLA policy performance.

papers.abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Shuchang Liu, Jinsong Lin, Yidong Zhang, Xizi Wang, Ho Yin Chim, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses navigation in compliant, contact-rich environments where support changes tip motion.
Queries the global image for the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target, then predicts bending and insertion commands from their representations.
Introduces the VLCA dataset with demonstrations, action samples, spatial entries, and remaining-route records.
Achieves 97.5% tip localization, 94.8% waypoint localization, and 76.25% success across 1,920 physical trials.
Offline action imitation and physical task completion produce different rankings: GRU-BC has lower MAE but only 1/240 physical successes.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language policy for contact-aided endoscope navigation with semantic grounding in global images fits embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
papers.tldr: EBV-CAN uses a cached bird’s-eye image, live endoscopic views, and motor state to ground language instructions for contact-aware endoscope navigation.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
authors: Shivakanth Sujit, Luca Nunziante, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Kai Arulkumaran
bullets: Flow-matching VLA policies typically require iterative ODE integration, which limits deployment control frequency.
Across six flow-matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale.
Multi-step integration provides little or no consistent inference advantage in the studied setting.
The finding depends on models having sufficient training and capacity.
Large VLAs can use single-step inference directly, without distillation, retraining, or auxiliary objectives.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study showing one-step Euler integration suffices for large flow-matching VLA policies, improving deployment latency.
papers.title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
papers.tldr: For sufficiently trained, high-capacity flow-matching VLA policies, one-step Euler inference performs about as well as multi-step sampling while enabling much lower-latency control without retraining.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.
authors: Shiyang Zhang, Miao Yang, Zhengda Li, Yang Shao, Ruifang Zhai, Hui Peng, Peng Song
bullets: Addresses the limited multi-task capacity of lightweight VLAs that rely on one dense action expert.
Replaces action-expert FFNs with parallel experts and a token-level router, activating only one expert per token at inference.
Adds a tunable shared expert to balance pretrained capability retention with task-specific specialization.
On four LIBERO task suites, achieves an 84.25% average success rate versus 82.75% for SmolVLA and 76.5% for OpenVLA-7B.
Maintains comparable inference efficiency with approximately 500M activated parameters and 800M stored parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse MoE vision-language-action model for multi-task robot manipulation fits embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: SmolVLA-MoE: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SmolVLA-MoE improves efficient multi-task robotic manipulation by using sparse, token-routed experts in the VLA action module.

papers.abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
authors: Yi Loo, Siddhant Shrivastava, Minh Long Pham, Malika Meghjani
bullets: Addresses the limited study of VLA-based collaboration among robots and humans.
Uses decentralized collaborative planning to generate executable multi-robot task plans.
Converts these plans into collaborative demonstrations for decentralized VLA fine-tuning.
The resulting models match the task performance of models trained on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
papers.selection_reason: Automated generation of multi-robot collaborative demonstrations for VLA model finetuning directly targets embodied VLA and manipulation.
papers.title: Co^2Gen: Collaboratively Generating Task Plans for Decentralized Multi-Robot and Human Collaboration
papers.tldr: Co^2Gen automatically generates decentralized multi-robot collaboration plans and demonstrations for training VLA models, achieving performance comparable to models trained on human-teleoperated data.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Tactile sensing exposes physical contact information important for robust and dexterous manipulation.
Mechanics-driven methods interpret tactile signals using contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning to form state representations and guide actions.
Data-driven methods learn tactile representations and manipulation policies from data, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models.
The paper surveys tactile sensing fundamentals and developments across both perspectives.
It identifies open challenges and future opportunities for broader, more robust tactile-enabled robotics.
papers.selection_reason: Review of tactile-based manipulation covering mechanics-driven and data-driven approaches, including imitation learning, RL, VLA models, and predictive models.
papers.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
papers.tldr: This review traces tactile robotic manipulation from mechanics-based reasoning to data-driven learning and outlines challenges for scalable, generalizable, and robust systems.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
authors: Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
bullets: WAMs use future video representations to guide action prediction without costly iterative video denoising.
FRED self-distills representations predicted from noise using representations from ground-truth future observations as targets.
Historical observations provide temporal context for more accurate future representation prediction.
Across real-world manipulation tasks, FRED outperforms competing WAMs, especially on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks.
For skills shown only in human videos, FRED reaches 50.0% task success versus 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
papers.selection_reason: Improving future video representations for world action models directly fits world models and embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
papers.tldr: FRED improves efficient World Action Models by self-distilling better single-step future video representations with temporal context, substantially boosting long-horizon, zero-shot, and human-to-robot generalization.

papers.abstract: Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment. Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 \cite{MOLMO} on pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/LocoPilot
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting demonstrations that coordinate legged-base and manipulator motion while preserving robot-specific observations and commands.
Uses a leader arm and two handheld controllers to teleoperate a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 with a 6-DoF Piper L arm and onboard cameras.
Estimates interaction forces without a dedicated force/torque sensor and provides passivity-constrained haptic feedback.
Records synchronized multimodal data with a unified 11D action interface shared between teleoperation and deployment.
Demonstrates the full pipeline on multiple tasks, including physical pick-and-place deployment after fine-tuning MolmoAct2 without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a teleoperation and data-collection framework for loco-manipulation policy learning, including VLA fine-tuning and physical deployment.
papers.title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
papers.tldr: LocoPilot enables one operator to collect and deploy loco-manipulation policies on a quadruped by simultaneously controlling its base, body, arm, and gripper with bilateral haptic feedback.

papers.abstract: Embodied VLMs can execute increasingly complex manipulation tasks, yet execution errors can leave the environment in states that require replanning for recovery. Existing recovery methods either rely on inference-time mechanisms with fixed policies or learn from failure examples and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes. To enable recovery learning through verifiable interaction, we introduce the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors. We further construct ERR-Bench, a benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states for evaluating recovery capability and execution reliability. We then propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation, and use it to train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM. Evaluation on ERR-Bench reveals a mismatch between task progress and execution reliability across diverse VLMs. AGT-GSPO improves ERR-VLM by 10.25 percentage points in Strict Success Rate for error-free completion and 22.95 percentage points in Recovery Rate, while ablations and zero-shot transfer further validate the effectiveness of our method.
bullets: Introduces ERR-Env, which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors for recovery learning.
Introduces ERR-Bench with held-out nominal, intermediate, and error-state tasks to evaluate recovery and execution reliability.
Proposes Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO, combining turn-level progress/error rewards with action-grouped advantage estimation.
Trains a compact 2B ERR-VLM; on ERR-Bench, it improves Strict Success Rate by 10.25 points and Recovery Rate by 22.95 points.
Finds that task progress and execution reliability can diverge across VLMs; ablations and zero-shot transfer support the method’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Trains an embodied VLM for manipulation error recovery via online RL, directly fitting robot learning and vision-language-action.
papers.title: Replan for Error Recovery: Training Embodied VLMs through Verifiable Interaction with Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO
papers.tldr: AGT-GSPO trains embodied VLMs to recover from execution errors through verifiable interaction, substantially improving both reliable task completion and recovery.

papers.abstract: Dual-process agents pair a fast policy with a slow deliberative model. In real-time settings the slow model usually runs continuously; in turn-based agents and robot planners it is invoked on events such as uncertainty or a detected failure. We study a fast learned actor that takes every decision and hands control to a reasoning vision-language model only when a gate opens, while the game keeps running. We use closed-loop Doom and the new open "System One" typed-decision models, served through a common llama.cpp interface. On 900 held-out questions, (i) zero-shot decision models from 0.15B to 9B parameters choose to collect items 1.6-1.8 times more often than chance among their errors, in any option order, although the order changes some models' accuracy; (ii) accuracy, calibration and sensitivity (how well confidence separates right from wrong answers) are distinct: models of similar accuracy differ widely in AUROC, and the confidence of the most sensitive one tracks which kinds of situation it fails, not which answers are wrong; (iii) offline, deferring the least confident 30% of decisions to a reasoning model gains over random deferral in proportion to the actor's AUROC (rank correlation 0.87); with actor and rate chosen on held-out games the gain is +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] with doomLaya's option order and +0.08 [0.02, 0.14] with shuffled options, and reasoning carries about half of it; (iv) in closed loop (33 games, three seeds) no variant reaches the exit. Committing to plans, the reasoner's or a fixed explore rule's, opens more doors and makes an actor that stands still play; with the rule the agent dies more often. Told that some doors need keys, the reasoner takes ordinary doors for locked ones, which the state cannot tell apart; without that knowledge it goes back to collecting. We release code, prompts, data and logs.
bullets: The system combines a fast actor with a reasoning vision-language model that takes over when a confidence gate opens while the game continues.
Across 900 held-out questions, confidence quality—not accuracy alone—predicts the benefit of deferring decisions to the reasoning model.
Deferring the least-confident 30% outperforms random deferral offline, with gains correlated strongly with the actor’s AUROC; reasoning accounts for about half the gain.
In 33 closed-loop games across three seeds, no variant reached the exit, exposing failures in planning, exploration, and distinguishing locked from ordinary doors.
The authors release code, prompts, data, and logs.
papers.selection_reason: Studies a dual-process agent architecture (fast actor + slow VLM) in a closed-loop game environment, exploring the decision boundary for when to invoke reasoning, which is relevant to Vision-Language-Action models.
papers.title: System Switch: When Should a Fast Decision Model Stop and Think?
papers.tldr: A fast decision model can use confidence-based gating to selectively invoke slower reasoning, but this strategy shows offline promise and fails to reliably complete the closed-loop Doom task.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot learning, with performance improving as models and datasets scale. Scaling robot data collection, however, remains challenging because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning offers a way to train on decentralized robot data, but applying it to VLAs requires accounting for heterogeneous robot client data distributions. We present Co-VLA, which applies consensus optimization using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers~(ADMM) to federated VLA training. We show that the same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with both fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters. The name Co-VLA reflects both consensus and collaboration: clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing their data. Our experiments demonstrate that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. The project website and videos of our real-world experiments are available at https://embodiedvision.github.io/co-vla/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling robot data collection when data are distributed across robots, tasks, and locations.
Applies consensus optimization with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to federated VLA training.
Supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters.
Experiments show performance comparable to centralized training in both training settings.
Scope: designed for heterogeneous client data while keeping local robot data private to each client.
papers.selection_reason: Training vision-language-action models with federated consensus directly targets VLA policy learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Co-VLA: Consensus-based Federated Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Co-VLA uses ADMM-based consensus optimization to train vision-language-action models collaboratively across heterogeneous robots without centralizing their data.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
authors: Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Botong Zhang, Boning Shao, Jing Wang, Ruijie Zheng, Yuvan Sharma, Runyu Lu, Jiaming Liu, Renrui Zhang, Roei Herzig, Yutong Bai, Ken Goldberg, Danfei Xu, Yuke Zhu, Guanzhi Wang, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Trevor Darrell
bullets: Addresses the gap between predictive world action models and agentic systems with reusable, code-based skills.
Uses a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture with coupled code, video, and action generation streams.
Represents skills as parameterized programs while using code to structure multi-step prediction and control.
Introduces automated trajectory curation that aligns robot and human videos with programs and builds reusable skill libraries.
Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual tasks report improved task performance, language following, semantic reasoning, and robustness over VLA and WAM baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agentic world action model coupling code-based planning with joint video and action prediction for robot manipulation, directly fitting embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: Agentic World Action Models
papers.tldr: AW-0 unifies code-based planning, future video prediction, and robot action generation to make world action models more compositional, reusable, and grounded in physical dynamics.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.
authors: Likui Zhang, Zhe Zhu, Zhihao Zhan, Yibo Bai, Hanlin Wang, Dongwei Li, Bin Wang, Tianle Zhang, Xiaodan Liang, Liang Lin
bullets: Addresses sparse, delayed, and biased credit assignment in RL post-training for complex VLA manipulation tasks.
SAPO prevents failed atomic subtasks from contaminating credit across task boundaries while preserving within-subtask learning.
BATE adapts task sampling and exploration incentives according to individual subtask mastery.
A Real2Sim2Real pipeline supports transfer from simulation-based online RL to physical robots.
Reports gains over PPO on LIBERO-LONG, CALVIN ABC-D, and real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: RL post-training for VLA manipulation with atomic subtask credit assignment and sim-to-real transfer.
papers.title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: AtomicRL improves long-horizon VLA robot manipulation by assigning credit at atomic-subtask boundaries and adaptively targeting learning bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.
authors: May Espinola, Qifan Zhang, Yu Xiang
bullets: Evaluates six frontier models across three reasoning-effort levels using 1,800 LIBERO-10 episodes.
Models control the robot from visual observations and proprioception via structured tool calls for end-effector poses and gripper commands.
GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest reported success rate at 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%.
Higher reasoning effort generally improves performance, but gains vary by model and increase inference cost.
Models perform better on object placement than on precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks frontier AI models on LIBERO-10 robot manipulation tasks using a closed-loop framework.
papers.title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks
papers.tldr: A unified closed-loop benchmark finds that frontier AI models can perform some LIBERO-10 manipulation tasks without task-specific training, but remain unreliable on precise and multi-step actions.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our \href{https://sp-hlm.github.io/}{\textcolor{blue}{project page}}.
authors: Zhaohui Yang, Quanbao Lin, Chengqi Shi, Zhenglang Weng, Jicheng Lin, Boyu Chen, Tengjie Zhu, Guanzhu Ren, Jiahao Xu, Yang Feng, Xiaokang Yang, Yao Mu
bullets: Addresses the interface challenge between high-level task policies and coordinated whole-body control.
SP-VLA predicts five task-critical poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions.
SP-MGM reconstructs coordinated full-body motion from sparse targets using two-stage distillation.
SP-GMT combines explicit pose targets with an implicit motion prior to track whole-body motion.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show improved tracking, coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches.
papers.selection_reason: Presents SP-HLM, a framework for humanoid loco-manipulation using sparse-pose-driven interfaces and VLA models.
papers.title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: SP-HLM enables humanoid loco-manipulation by combining vision-language-predicted sparse body poses with learned full-body motion priors for real-time whole-body control.

papers.abstract: Geometric structure is essential for robotic manipulation and understanding the 3D world. Most VLA models rely on 2D representations of current observations, while geometry-aware approaches often require additional 3D information. However, geometry inferred independently from individual observations is often discarded rather than accumulated into a persistent task representation. Our key insight is that action generation needs a compact, task-relevant geometric abstraction that can be continuously updated, rather than a complete, renderable 3D reconstruction at every step. We introduce GeoMem-VLA, a VLA framework that internalizes explicit 3D supervision into dedicated geometric tokens and maintains them as temporal memory for action generation, without directly aligning the VLM's native visual embeddings with the teacher feature space. During training, a frozen geometry foundation model supervises learnable GeoPlan tokens through a geometric flow-matching objective over the current scene point map and future end-effector tracks. These tokens are integrated with the memory of observation representations, where historical information is retrieved, adaptively fused with current observations, and consolidated to retain event frames as the task progresses. At inference, the policy retrieves historical representations and fuses them with the current working representation to predict actions, without invoking the 3D teacher or explicitly reconstructing the scene. After benchmark-specific downstream adaptation, GeoMem-VLA achieves 98.9% average success on LIBERO and 91.10% / 91.24% on RoboTwin's clean/randomized settings. Across five real-world tasks, GeoMem-VLA achieves 78.0% average success. These results suggest that internalizing and remembering 3D scene understanding is a promising approach to robot control.
authors: Qinfan Zhang, Yifan Luo, Haoyuan Shi, Guanlin Liu, Han Dong, Haozhe Shan, Yong Dai, Xiangcong Ren, Xiaozhu Ju
bullets: Addresses the loss of accumulated geometric information in VLA models that primarily use current 2D observations.
Learns dedicated GeoPlan tokens from frozen geometry-model supervision over scene point maps and future end-effector tracks.
Retrieves, fuses, and consolidates geometric and visual memories across time without requiring 3D reconstruction or the teacher model at inference.
Reports 98.9% average success on LIBERO, 91.10%/91.24% on RoboTwin clean/randomized settings, and 78.0% across five real-world tasks.
Scope: performance depends on benchmark-specific downstream adaptation and is evaluated on the reported simulation and real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework with 3D geometric temporal memory for robot manipulation; directly fits embodied action and memory.
papers.title: GeoMem-VLA: Internalizing 3D Scene Understanding into Temporal Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: GeoMem-VLA equips vision-language-action models with compact, temporally persistent 3D geometric memory for improved robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language perception has achieved impressive progress in aligning natural language with visual observations, yet grounding high-level semantics into part-level physical interaction remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose UniRAP, a unified model for inferring part-level physical affordances and mapping language instructions to actionable geometric representations. UniRAP formulates this problem as a conditional multimodal generation task, integrating visual inputs, textual instructions, and optional prompts into a shared spatiotemporal representation space through a unified interface token mechanism. To predict executable contact geometry, we introduce a Unified Affordance Decoder (UAD), which jointly performs object detection, part-level affordance segmentation, and 4-DoF interaction pose estimation by leveraging intermediate segmentation features. In addition, we propose a curriculum-based transfer training strategy that progressively adapts the model from general visual parsing to interaction-aware perception, improving data efficiency under limited textual annotations. Experiments show that UniRAP achieves state-of-the-art performance on referring expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction pose estimation, while maintaining strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic video scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of UniRAP as a unified perception framework for language-guided physical manipulation.
authors: Linfei Li, Ruining Hu, Lin Zhang, Zhong Wang, Fengyi Zhang, Ying Shen, Binqiang Wang, Xin Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of grounding high-level language and visual semantics into part-level physical interactions.
Uses a conditional multimodal generation framework with a unified interface-token mechanism for visual inputs, instructions, and optional prompts.
Introduces a Unified Affordance Decoder for object detection, affordance segmentation, and 4-DoF interaction-pose estimation.
Applies curriculum-based transfer training to improve data efficiency with limited textual annotations.
Reports state-of-the-art results across referring-expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction-pose estimation, with strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic videos.
papers.selection_reason: Unified language-guided part-level affordance reasoning and interaction pose estimation, directly relevant to embodied vision-language-action and manipulation.
papers.title: UniRAP: Towards Unified Part-level Physical Affordance Reasoning and Actionable Perception
papers.tldr: UniRAP unifies language-guided part-level affordance reasoning with actionable geometric perception for physical manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
authors: Johannes Keller, Albrecht M. Blo{\ss}e, Adrian Lindenmeyer, Thomas Neumuth, Daniel Schneider
bullets: Targets costly failures by identifying situations where a VLA policy lacks training knowledge.
Fits Gaussian-process conditional-variance heads on policy embeddings without regression targets, gradient updates, or policy changes.
On SmolVLA with LIBERO-10, performs competitively with two-policy ensembles for success correlation, demonstration acquisition, and supervisor referral.
Vision-language backbone heads reduce uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately 50× versus ensemble scores and lower setup costs.
Controlled perturbations show modality-specific heads detect unfamiliar inputs, while fused or decoder heads can identify unfamiliar combinations and improve within-task referral.
papers.selection_reason: Single-policy epistemic uncertainty for VLA policies supports assistance seeking and active robot learning.
papers.title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: Post-hoc kernel-variance heads estimate useful epistemic uncertainty for VLA policies from a single frozen policy, avoiding ensemble costs while supporting adaptive assistance and learning.

papers.abstract: During steady pouring, images and robot pose may remain nearly unchanged while transferred mass accumulates, making the return decision ambiguous for a whole-task vision-language-action (VLA) policy. We present FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from physical-completion estimation. A shared $\pi_{0.5}$ action expert learns approach, pour, and return with boundary-aware supervision. A target-independent estimator fuses visual, joint, wrist-wrench, and recurrent force-belief histories to maintain an estimate of transferred mass. The controller initiates return when this estimate plus predicted residual outflow reaches the requested mass. In coffee-pot/water experiments, FlowVLA achieves 13.1 g goal-balanced mean absolute error (MacroMAE), lower than all tested VLA baselines. Across all attempts, 53.7% both complete the task and finish within +/-10% of the requested mass. The same model interpolates to held-out 150/250-g targets without retraining. Independently trained models further evaluate the formulation in three additional container-fluid settings.
authors: Liwen Yang, Yutian Zhang, Jiaqi Zhai, Li Yang, Tutian Tang, Qiwei Shan, Yancheng Bi, Qiankuan Shangguan, Yangkun Zhu, Ce Hao, Dong Wei, Qiaojun Yu, Dibo Hou
bullets: Addresses ambiguous return timing when visual and pose cues remain nearly unchanged during pouring.
Separates motion generation from physical-completion estimation using a shared action expert and multimodal history-based mass estimator.
Initiates return when estimated transferred mass plus expected residual outflow reaches the target.
Achieves 13.1 g MacroMAE in coffee-pot/water experiments, with 53.7% of attempts completing within ±10% of target mass.
Interpolates to unseen 150/250-g targets without retraining and is evaluated across three additional container-fluid settings.
papers.selection_reason: VLA policy for robotic pouring with physical completion estimation, relevant to VLA and manipulation.
papers.title: FlowVLA: Learning Flow-Aware Physical Completion for Quantitative Robotic Pouring
papers.tldr: FlowVLA improves robotic pouring by estimating transferred mass and using predicted residual flow to decide when to stop.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.
authors: Tingwen Du, Haoyu Guo, Hanxue Zhang, Xuanxu Wang, Junting Dong, Chao Gao, Mingfei Han, Tao Lu, Mulin Yu, Chunhua Shen, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Targets non-Markovian manipulation tasks where progress, past outcomes, partial observability, and errors affect future decisions.
Uses an editable harness around a high-level VLM, paired with a fixed VLA executor for low-level control.
Maintains task context from observations and execution feedback to guide later plans.
Self-evolves by proposing and evaluating harness revisions through environment rollouts before held-out testing.
On RoboMME, autonomous self-evolution improves overall success from 44.38% to 51.38%.
papers.selection_reason: VLA-based robotic manipulation with self-evolving memory harness for history-dependent tasks.
papers.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
papers.tldr: SERA turns a high-level vision-language model into a self-evolving robotic agent that uses execution history to improve long-horizon manipulation planning.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/
authors: Qinghang Liu, Conglin Wang, Zongsheng Li, Boyong He, Han Gao, Pengcheng Wang, Tao Sun, Lige Liu, Chang Liu
bullets: Targets the heavy reasoning burden of retrieving and interpreting history during execution.
Uses hierarchical memory: a short-term visual buffer, semantic-event memory, and executable subtask list.
A high-level VLM converts streaming observations into subtasks, then selects relevant subtasks for a low-level VLA policy.
Trains memory updates with staged supervision expansion and task-grounded self-labeling.
Achieves 56.05% success on RoboMME and 60.83% overall success across four real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical memory with VLM-generated subtask lists for vision-language robot manipulation fits embodied memory and VLA control.
papers.title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
papers.tldr: PAL improves long-horizon robot manipulation by planning future-relevant subtasks into executable memory before action time.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history. We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
authors: Josh Qixuan Sun, Xiaoying Xing, Yurun Chen, Huaiyuan Weng, Wentao Zhu, Mark Crowley
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic for instruction-action binding at route forks.
Builds 3,252 matched contexts by pairing instructions that share the traveled route but specify different branches.
Keeps the agent state and navigation history fixed while comparing actions, action likelihoods, and visual attribution.
Finds that higher navigation success does not necessarily indicate more faithful instruction following.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic method for instruction-action binding in navigation VLAs, directly relevant to vision-language navigation.
papers.title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
papers.tldr: NavBind tests whether navigation VLAs’ actions truly respond to instructions rather than relying on visual cues or history.

papers.abstract: Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and development. We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation. To automatically determine intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots during policy execution. After a rollout fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots, starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four post-training methods, RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO, across seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Relative to a fixed-interval snapshot baseline, the Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts by 75.0% and increases recovery success from 93.4% to 98.9%. Using SimPT, we develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting and low-pass filtering of value predictions. This refinement increases the overall success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. In real-robot HIL post-training, it increases the success rate from 72% to 96% across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. These results demonstrate the utility of SimPT for exploring and developing VLA post-training algorithms.
authors: Caicheng Wang, Zipeng Ye, Zhexuan Zhou, Zilong Huang, Xi Zhang, Yuchen Xie
bullets: Addresses the cost of human supervision and repeated real-robot testing during VLA post-training.
Integrates policy rollouts, corrective trajectory collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation.
Uses an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph with privileged simulator state and stable snapshots to choose recovery points.
A CuRobo-based expert recovers failed rollouts, while SimPT compares RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO across seven RoboTwin tasks.
The Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts and improves recovery success; the proposed RECAP-CF-LPF refinement also improves simulated and real-robot success rates.
papers.selection_reason: Simulation framework for intervention-based VLA post-training with automated recovery and evaluation.
papers.title: SimPT: An Automated Simulation Framework for Intervention-Based VLA Post-Training
papers.tldr: SimPT automates intervention-based VLA post-training in simulation, enabling more efficient recovery data collection and supporting improved policy refinement before real-robot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (FLEX), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot's internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate FLEX on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/
authors: Audrey Lee, Nathaniel Dennler, Ilia Sucholutsky, Andreea Bobu
bullets: Robot demonstrations show what to do but may not clarify which task features matter, causing misaligned representations.
FLEX iteratively edits representations using three operations: add missing features, generalize overly specific ones, and mask irrelevant ones.
Evaluated on 2D navigation, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation, and real-robot demonstrations with naturalistic language corrections.
All three editing operations are needed for interactive scenarios; FLEX achieves higher normalized reward than compared editing baselines while preserving compact, transferable representations.
papers.selection_reason: Language-guided iterative refinement of robot task representations for adaptive behavior in navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Flexible Language-Guided Representation Editing for Adaptive Robot Behavior
papers.tldr: FLEX lets robots refine task representations through natural-language corrections by adding, generalizing, or masking features, improving adaptive behavior across simulated and real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.
authors: Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So, Monroe Kennedy III
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable robot-learning data without depth sensors, robot hardware, or restricting augmentation to demonstrated objects.
Tracks object 3D poses using DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats and aligns photograph-based digital object “cousins” to demonstrated objects and functional regions.
Maps the human hand motion to feasible robot grasps and generates demonstrations in IsaacSim or MuJoCo.
Generates over 2,000 episodes in about two hours and supports training from one human video per task.
Across two real robots and four tasks, policies trained on generated data match or exceed teleoperation-trained policies across diverse object instances.
papers.selection_reason: Pipeline generating robot demonstrations from a single human RGB video via semantic augmentation; directly relevant to learning from human video and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
papers.tldr: Real2Sem2Real converts a single monocular human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across diverse object instances for training manipulation policies.

papers.abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu, Xihang Yu, Wei Dai, Bashar Kabbarah, Haoyu Chen, Ishita Goluguri, Zhiyang Dou, Haonan Chen, Fangneng Zhan, Mengyu Wang, Wojciech Matusik, Antonio Torralba, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: Addresses latency when contact conditions change faster than visual policy updates.
Generates base action chunks from images, instructions, and retrieved history.
Uses a lightweight tactile editor to revise unexecuted actions using touch and cached visual memory.
Adds future-image and future-pressure prediction as training-only supervision for interaction-aware representations.
Reports 30% lower finger-joint MPJPE than the strongest reported baseline and approximately 50.0% average success across four real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: World-language-action architecture with tactile correction for dexterous manipulation and visual memory.
papers.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
papers.tldr: T-WLA uses shared visual memory and fast tactile residual corrections to adapt manipulation actions without rerunning the visual policy.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one. By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows. Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence discontinuous. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation. Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate's implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier. A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods. On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when action chunks are generated from stale observations during asynchronous inference.
Generates multiple candidate chunks from the inference-start observation, then selects one using a later pre-commit observation.
FlowRes scores candidates by comparing their implied flow direction with velocity predicted by the frozen VLA policy; no separate verifier is needed.
A pipelined implementation overlaps candidate generation and scoring, adding no control-step delay on evaluated hardware.

At a four-step delay, average success improves by 15.0 points over RTC on Kinetix, 5.2 points over single-candidate execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and from 60% to 82% on three real-robot tasks over naive asynchronous execution.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free framework to improve VLA policy robustness against inference delay by selecting action chunks using pre-commit observations.
papers.title: PACT-VLA: Speculative Action-Chunk Verification with Pre-Commit Observations
papers.tldr: PACT-VLA uses delayed observations to verify and select complete action chunks, improving asynchronous VLA control without additional training or control-step latency.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models' embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model's capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon across instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
All models perform strongly on instruction following and spatial reasoning, but general manipulation is consistently weaker.
Astra leads instruction following and robustness; Opus leads spatial reasoning, manipulation, and overall performance in the tested configurations.
Harness design influences task success, planning cost, and execution time.
Astra case studies examine whole-body coordination, cross-embodiment manipulation, precision and dexterous manipulation, and real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-model evaluation of frontier multimodal LLMs for embodied robot control, including instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
papers.title: Frontier LLMs Enter the World of Robotics: A Cross-Model Evaluation on RoboColiseum
papers.tldr: A cross-model RoboColiseum evaluation finds that frontier multimodal LLMs understand robot tasks well but still struggle with reliable physical manipulation, with performance varying by model and harness design.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.
bullets: Addresses the implicit transition from scene and instruction representations to continuous actions in VLAs.
Uses a Masked Action Autoencoder to create horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens from expert action chunks.
A Bridge Module aligns task-relevant visual-language features with action latents, producing Bridge Tokens that initialize action generation.
At inference, Bridge Tokens are generated from observations and instructions without the autoencoder.
Improves evaluated models across LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and seven real-world tasks, including OpenVLA-OFT success rising from 51.4% to 65.0% and VLA-Adapter on LIBERO-Plus from 59.1% to 64.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation (Bridge Tokens) to improve continuous-action VLA models.
papers.title: PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: PAIR improves continuous-action vision-language-action models by learning an intermediate representation that connects visual-language perception to robot action generation.
