papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of processing redundant visual tokens during robotic control.
Trains a lightweight pruning policy with action-level consistency supervision, using full-context predictions as a teacher and ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision.
Keeps the base VLA model completely frozen, avoiding costly end-to-end fine-tuning.
On LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks, prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5× inference speedup.
Demonstrates a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VLA-ACL, a method for efficient visual token pruning in VLA models using action-level supervision without fine-tuning the base model.
papers.title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA-ACL efficiently prunes visual tokens in frozen vision-language-action models by learning which tokens preserve the model’s control actions.

papers.abstract: Active perception is essential for robotic manipulation when fixed viewpoints leave task-relevant information occluded or unobserved. However, enabling vision-language-action (VLA) models to reason across changing viewpoints and actively acquire informative observations remains challenging. We present ActiveScale, a framework that advances active perception through coordinated model, data, and hardware designs. Our model augments a VLA with historical video observations and explicit camera-pose supervision, using per-frame pose tokens and a lightweight prediction head to associate observations across viewpoints and support a coherent understanding of the scene. To learn from the camera motion naturally present in human activity, we introduce a scalable human--robot mid-training recipe using 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data, adapting the model to temporal inputs and pose supervision. We further introduce Active-perception Mobile-manipulation Platform (AMP), a robotic platform that supports active perception and mobile manipulation through single-operator teleoperation, enabling scalable collection of demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes and manipulation. Experiments demonstrate improved success rates on active-perception tasks, while ablation studies validate the contributions of camera-pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training. Together, these components provide an integrated foundation for studying and developing active perception in robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses occlusion and missing task information caused by fixed viewpoints in robotic manipulation.
Augments a vision-language-action model with historical video, per-frame camera-pose tokens, and pose supervision.
Uses 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data for human–robot mid-training on temporal inputs and camera motion.
Introduces AMP, a teleoperable platform for collecting demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes with manipulation.
Experiments report improved active-perception success rates; ablations support pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework for active perception and mobile manipulation with human-video pretraining, directly fitting embodied robot learning.
papers.title: ActiveScale: Scaling Active Perception for Robots across Model, Data, and Hardware
papers.tldr: ActiveScale improves robotic active perception by jointly scaling VLA modeling, training data, and mobile-manipulation hardware for viewpoint-aware manipulation.

papers.abstract: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank. To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost. UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (<=33.3%).
authors: Rahul Sajnani, Diego Romeres, Mingyuan Zhang, Kai Gao, Carl Qi, Baichuan Huang, Srinath Sridhar, Dylan Randle, Lillian J. Ratliff, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Jeroen Vanbaar
bullets: Learns shared representations across video, actions, and language, with each modality serving as both input and training target.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers backbone with synchronized modality-specific diffusion heads to generate actions and textual memory in one pass.
Re-consumes generated language on subsequent steps, creating a language-as-memory loop without an external memory bank or planner.
Introduces Flow Matching with Correction to improve recovery from perturbed action trajectories without inference-time overhead.
Reports gains on compositional manipulation, memory-dependent benchmarks, and a real-world Find-the-Item task; scope is demonstrated on these tasks and settings.
papers.selection_reason: A unified VLA model that integrates video, action, and language with a language-as-memory loop, directly relevant to embodied control and world modeling.
papers.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
papers.tldr: UniWALM unifies video, action, and language generation in one model, using language as memory to improve memory-dependent robot manipulation without a separate planner.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability. Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8\% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31\% to 99\%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.
authors: Ziyong Wang, Yupei Lin, Runxuan Huang, Liang Lin, Dongyu Zhang, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Studies whether general multimodal models can understand interaction physics and use tactile feedback to guide actions.
GPT-as-Tactile-Policy summarizes demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for assessing contact and correcting actions.
GPT-6-Astra combines these references with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate and adapt control commands.
Achieves 93.8% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks, with performance comparable to state-of-the-art policies.
On Insert Hole, tactile feedback raises success from 31% to 99%; analysis shows probing and contact-guided correction.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses vision-tactile-language-action models for contact-rich manipulation, outperforming specialized baselines without task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.title: GPT-6-Astra Understands Touch and Outperform Vision--Tactile--Language--Action Models
papers.tldr: GPT-6-Astra uses expert-guided tactile context and online contact feedback to perform contact-rich manipulation without robotics-specific pretraining or task-specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.
authors: Youwei Zhou, Bohan Hou, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lyu, Yifan Ye, Shilin Shan, Chen Guo, Jiaming Liu, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Shanghang Zhang, Jianfei Yang, Zhihe Lu
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation with a lightweight agent execution framework.
Probes depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding; the model demonstrates all three capabilities.
Tests five manipulation benchmarks across six capability dimensions, finding strengths alongside weaknesses in consequence-aware planning, precision, and coordinated motion.
Introduces LIBERO-GeoMotion, where GPT-6 Astra achieves 11.1% zero-shot success on geometry-constrained tasks; reported results also include 26.92% on RoboDojo and 76.0% on RoboTwin 2.0.
Real-world tests show simple zero-shot execution is feasible, but motion feasibility, physical safety, precise control, and inference latency remain deployment barriers.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation, probing depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile feedback.
papers.title: Large Multimodal Models for Direct Robot Control: GPT-6 as a Beginning
papers.tldr: GPT-6 Astra shows promising perception, learning, and tactile-feedback abilities for robot control, but struggles to convert semantic reasoning into precise, safe, and physically feasible manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $\pi_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
authors: Matteo Cercola, Katie Z Luo, Milan Ganai, John Alora, Simone Formentin, Marco Pavone
bullets: Existing VLA reasoning compresses alternative valid plans into one representation, limiting revision and control.
GPL models the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over choices such as objects, grasps, or routes.
Plans can be sampled for coverage, selected on request for steering, or reweighted using deployment outcomes without retraining.
In SimplerEnv, steering increased request-following executions from 0.48 to 0.94; native action-distribution guidance showed no reliable gain.
Explicit plans help most when they encode decision information not already determined by the observation.
papers.selection_reason: Represents VLA reasoning as a distribution over plan latents, enabling sampling, steering, and outcome adaptation without retraining.
papers.title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Generative Plan Latents let vision-language-action policies represent, sample, steer, and adapt multiple possible plans before acting.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy. To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.
authors: Jiatong Li, Jisheng Dang, Qiangqiang Ma, Bimei Wang, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Juncheng Li, Hong Peng, Bin Hu
bullets: Targets VLA failures caused by deviations from nominal task conditions, including object-position and instruction perturbations.
Uses Planner, Grounder, Verifier, and Correction Agents to parse tasks, bind references, monitor execution, diagnose failures, and select recovery actions.
Retains the pretrained VLA as the default action generator when no intervention is needed.
Demonstrates improved robustness across multiple VLA backbones on LIBERO-PRO, with state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-aware closed-loop multi-agent framework that improves VLA robustness at inference time for robotic manipulation.
papers.title: FIT-MAC: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FIT-MAC improves VLA reliability under perturbed instructions and object locations through a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent recovery layer at inference time.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.
authors: Byeonghun Bang, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Kangsan Kim, Youngwan Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Long-horizon computer-use agents are fragile because errors accumulate and actions can create unintended side effects.
Existing recovery approaches are limited by infeasible environment resets, costly long-horizon replay, or web-only rollback APIs.
ReTrace introduces Transition-Consistent Recovery, requiring identical downstream actions from recovered and target states to produce identical outcomes.
Its goal-oriented action replay framework systematically evaluates autonomous, model-based recovery after controlled error injection.
The study finds that agents possess latent recovery capabilities but fail to use them effectively; accurate recovery improves end-to-end performance.
papers.selection_reason: Study of model-based recovery for computer-use agents enabled by vision-language models, with evaluation methods transferable to embodied action agents.
papers.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay
papers.tldr: ReTrace evaluates how well computer-use agents recover from injected errors and shows that effective recovery is essential for reliable long-horizon task completion.

papers.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.
authors: Junha Song, Geonmo Gu, Jeongeun Park, Heejeong Nam, Lucas Maes, Byeongho Heo, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Trains one language-conditioned future predictor on simulation, robot trajectories, images, and videos.
Uses language to unify numerical actions and visual changes across heterogeneous data.
Achieves higher average MPC planning performance than domain- or task-specific latent world models.
With additional image/video data, planning robustness to action phrasing improves.
Matches an RAEv2 video-generation baseline with 6× lower training cost and 13.9× faster planning; its policy initialization enables competitive performance with up to 5.5× faster inference.

papers.title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions
papers.tldr: LaLa-World scales latent world models across domains by expressing actions and visual changes in language, enabling efficient planning and policy learning.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
bullets: RoboJudge-Bench evaluates MLLM judges on Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment using 800 human-annotated videos from 8 corpora, 10 generators, and varied hand embodiments.
Existing general-purpose and general-domain video judges show limited or inconsistent agreement with human judgments in embodied scenarios, especially for physical adherence.
RoboJudge-Train contains 12K videos with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales.
RoboJudge-9B is fine-tuned with supervised learning and reinforcement learning, achieving the highest reported agreement on the benchmark with a Pearson correlation of 0.719.
The trained judge also improves performance on external benchmarks and is used to evaluate video generation models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and model for evaluating embodied video generation using MLLMs, directly addressing the evaluation of embodied world models and video generation.
papers.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
papers.tldr: RoboJudge introduces a benchmark and trained 9B multimodal judge that better aligns with humans when evaluating the physical validity and instruction following of embodied video generations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.
authors: Zhan Yi, Yuchen Wang, Chao Li, Lei Hong, Boyuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of full future-image prediction and the loss of local detail in heavily compressed latent dynamics.
Predicts spatially structured future latent changes from visual and language inputs.
Uses change-aware supervision to emphasize regions expected to change most.
Feeds predicted future changes into action generation through a future-to-action interface.
Achieves 79.0% success on LIBERO-Long and raises CALVIN average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564, while updating 2.95% of parameters in the second training stage.

papers.title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
papers.tldr: PLaCA improves robot manipulation by predicting patch-level future latent changes and using them to generate actions.

papers.abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,
authors: Zhikang Chen, Yueqing Sun, Sen Cui, Ziang Ye, Yu Wang, Yan Feng2, Xierui Song, Yu Zhang, Tingting Zhu
bullets: Uses failure-driven diagnostic probing to determine when recovery hypotheses apply and refine future investigations.
Separates fast policy execution from a slower research loop that makes bounded harness revisions.
Accepts revisions only after matched sandbox comparisons show improvement; validated recoveries are reused across tasks.
Updates action- and knowledge-probing policies using immediate feedback and delayed episode-success credit.
Improves Minecraft task coverage and unseen-task completion over bare execution, fixed harnesses, and knowledge-only evolution.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts execution harnesses of frozen VLA agents in long-horizon Minecraft tasks, directly relevant to embodied vision-language-action research.
papers.title: KPHarness: Co-Evolving Knowledge and Probing for Long-Horizon Gaming Harnesses
papers.tldr: KPHarness improves long-horizon gaming by co-evolving recovery knowledge and active probing for a frozen vision-language-action model’s execution harness.

papers.abstract: Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. However, fine-tuning a flow policy against a learned value function is not trivial, because the policy generates its action over many flow steps. Adjoint matching offers a principled way to update the flow model itself by propagating value information from the final action back to each flow step, but it requires a vector--Jacobian product through the policy at every step, a cost that grows with the number of flow steps and the policy size. We observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal. Motivated by this finding, we derive a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time, eliminating the per-step vector--Jacobian products. We further find that controlling the critic's value at policy-generated actions is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. Based on these findings, we propose Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching (SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at those actions. SQAM's gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where its success rate exceeds that of the strongest baseline in each domain by 18 to 35 percentage points. To test whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we also fine-tune a vision-language-action policy on a real bimanual robot. SQAM improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.
bullets: Flow policies require value information to be propagated through many generation steps, making standard adjoint matching expensive.
The method uses a scalar adjoint that scales the final-action value gradient by flow time, avoiding per-step vector–Jacobian products.
SQAM adds a value penalty on policy-generated actions to control critic estimates.
On the four hardest OGBench domains, SQAM exceeds the strongest baseline by 18–35 percentage points in success rate.
It also improves over supervised fine-tuning across all three tasks in a real bimanual-robot evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: RL fine-tuning of flow policies and VLA policies for robot control; fits Embodied AI.
papers.title: Q-Learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching
papers.tldr: SQAM makes off-policy RL fine-tuning of flow policies cheaper by replacing costly per-step adjoint computations with a scalar approximation and stabilizing critic values at generated actions.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.
bullets: Verifier-guided test-time scaling selects among sampled action candidates to improve robot task success without collecting more robotic data.
Existing trajectory-level verifiers treat all states equally, despite only a sparse subset being important for distinguishing candidates.
DiVeR estimates state criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations and reweights verifier learning accordingly.
It requires neither step-level annotations nor additional environment interaction and adds negligible verifier inference overhead.
Experiments on LIBERO, RoboCasa, and a Franka Research 3 robot show consistent task-success improvements.
papers.selection_reason: VLA verifier learning for test-time scaling in robot manipulation; directly fits Embodied AI topics.
papers.title: DiVeR: Decision-Critical Verifier Learning for VLA Test-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: DiVeR improves VLA test-time action selection by training verifiers to focus on states where candidate actions differ most meaningfully.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.
authors: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang
bullets: RL with verifiable rewards provides task-level supervision but limited guidance for localizing visual-reasoning errors.
Privileged on-policy self-distillation adds token-level corrections, but these can be contaminated by linguistic priors, response style, or privileged-view effects.
Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG) validates corrections by comparing teacher outputs with evidence-present and evidence-degraded views.
VAG uses verifier-derived advantages as anchors and admits only directionally visually supported corrections.
Across six visual reasoning benchmarks, VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD, achieving new state-of-the-art average performance.
papers.selection_reason: Uses verifiable rewards and privileged visual grounding to train an RL policy with action corrections; relevant to multimodal policy learning and embodied control.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: VAG improves multimodal reinforcement learning by filtering self-distillation corrections to retain only those supported by visual evidence.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation.
authors: Jiaming Liu, Xinghao Zhu, Yiming Zhang, Shanghang Zhang, Yinxi Wang, Yichu Yang, Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Soha Pouya, Juekun Li, Yan Chang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language reasoning, which lacks fine-grained dynamics, and unstructured latent reasoning, which lacks reusable primitives.
Predicts future atomic action words and aligns their contextual representations with latent targets derived from future observations.
Builds a temporally structured space with visual and optional tactile variants to represent transitions between execution stages.
Reports 90.3% success on UniVTAC and 99.6% on LIBERO-Long, plus strong real-world performance with bimanual and dexterous hands.
Evaluations indicate generalization to unseen scenarios and long-horizon manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Structured latent reasoning with action words for robot manipulation, relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Physical Words: A Vocabulary for Structuring Latent Reasoning in Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: PhysWord structures latent robot-manipulation reasoning around atomic action words that connect language semantics with future physical dynamics, enabling strong long-horizon performance.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have enabled GPT-6 Astra to perform robotic manipulation through in-context learning. Yet contact-rich control and tactile perception are often regarded as strengths of specialist policies, leaving open whether Astra can directly understand and use tactile observations. We provide, to our knowledge, the first demonstration that Astra directly interprets vision-based tactile images and uses their contact cues for manipulation. Tactile RGB images enter through its existing visual interface, enabling few-shot closed-loop control on nineteen simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks with 210 sampled scene seeds per setting. With visuo-tactile input, Astra achieves mean success rates of 93.8% and 81.8%, exceeding the strongest reported specialist baselines in our comparison by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points, respectively. Vision-only performance also leads these baselines, reaching 76.3% and 80.6%. Trajectory analysis reveals active probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, alongside difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution. Our findings challenge the exclusivity of specialist policies in contact-rich manipulation and show that fine-grained vision can partially compensate for missing touch. They also identify vision-based tactile sensing as an interface for scaling contact understanding with foundation models and reveal signs of benchmark saturation. These results motivate joint visual-tactile pretraining, harder contact-rich evaluations, and physical-robot validation.
authors: Chen Yang, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Mu Xu, Jiansheng Fan, Chen Wang
bullets: Demonstrates direct interpretation and use of tactile contact cues, challenging the view that specialist policies are necessary for contact-rich control.
Evaluated on 19 simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks using 210 sampled scene seeds per setting.

Vision-only control also performs strongly, with mean success rates of 76.3% and 80.6%.

papers.title: GPT-6 Astra Is a Native Visuo-Tactile Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: GPT-6 Astra uses vision-based tactile images through its standard visual interface to perform strong few-shot, closed-loop contact-rich manipulation.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions. However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots. In this work, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that integrates task-specific demonstration collection and pretrained policy adaptation. A MuJoCo-based agricultural environment is developed with diverse tomato plant structures to support demonstration collection and controlled evaluation. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation, with a low-level controller used to execute robot actions. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and $\pi_{0.5}$, are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations. The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated. Results show that $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves higher task-performance scores than Octo and exhibits less degradation under distribution shifts. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating pretrained generalist policies with task-specific demonstration learning for agricultural manipulation.
authors: Hamid Hafezi, Javad Mohammadpour Velni, Mohammadreza Davoodi
bullets: Agricultural manipulation is difficult because of variable plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints.
The framework combines a MuJoCo tomato-plant environment, joystick-collected demonstrations, low-level control, and pretrained policy adaptation.
Octo and π₀.₅ are adapted first with simulated demonstrations, then fine-tuned using demonstrations on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
Policies are evaluated in simulation across in-distribution, shifted-viewpoint/spatial, and out-of-distribution settings, followed by real-robot experiments.
The study also examines how proprioceptive information affects policy performance.

papers.title: Robot Learning with Vision-Language-Action Models for Agricultural Manipulation
papers.tldr: A simulation-to-real framework adapts pretrained vision-language-action policies for agricultural reaching and grasping, with π₀.₅ outperforming Octo and showing greater robustness to distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots hold great promise as general-purpose agents in human-centered environments, yet adapting generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies to real-world humanoid loco-manipulation remains challenging. Unlike fixed-base or wheeled manipulators, humanoids must coordinate locomotion, posture, gaze, and dual-arm manipulation over a high-dimensional whole-body action space, where inaccurate base or waist motions can easily induce unstable and aggressive upper-body compensation. We propose HAF-VLA, a hierarchical action-flow framework for humanoid VLA control. Built upon a pretrained flow-matching VLA, HAF-VLA inherits the vision-language prefix encoder and action expert weights, and adapts them to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation with learnable stage embeddings and cross-stage KV-cache conditioning. Instead of generating the full action chunk in a single pass, HAF-VLA progressively denoises a shared whole-body action space: first locomotion and head commands, then waist refinement, and finally full-body manipulation. To preserve structural dependencies across stages, we introduce a cross-stage KV cache conditioning mechanism, enabling subsequent action generation stages to refine and augment their outputs based on the action representations from preceding stages. Experimental results across six real-world tasks demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances the performance of existing models in humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, demonstrating an effective pathway for adapting strong mobile-manipulation VLAs to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation.
authors: Langzhe Gu, Chengkai Hou, Meng Li, Xinhua Wang, Xinyuan Lv, Shuanghao Bai, Guangrun Li, Jingyang He, Ziluo Ding, Zhiyuan Xu, Ning Ding, Kuan Cheng, Jian Tang, Shanghang Zhang, Zhengping Che
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of coordinating locomotion, posture, gaze, and dual-arm actions in humanoid loco-manipulation.
Builds on a pretrained flow-matching VLA, retaining its vision-language encoder and action-expert weights.
Progressively denoises a shared whole-body action space: locomotion/head, waist, then full-body manipulation.
Uses learnable stage embeddings and cross-stage KV-cache conditioning to preserve dependencies between action stages.
Real-world experiments across six tasks show improved humanoid loco-manipulation performance for existing models.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical flow-matching VLA for humanoid loco-manipulation; directly fits VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: HAF-VLA: Hierarchical Action Flow Framework for Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Control
papers.tldr: HAF-VLA adapts pretrained vision-language-action policies to humanoid whole-body control by generating actions hierarchically from locomotion to manipulation.

papers.abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to $\pi_{0.5}$, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a $1.98\times$ full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.
authors: Shenli Zheng, Zhou Fang, Yuan Du, Yijiang Liu, Li Du
bullets: Targets costly VLA inference on resource-constrained robots, where aggressive compression can harm manipulation performance.
Prunes the LLM backbone’s hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions through pruning-aware tuning.
Uses post-pruning reinforcement learning for action-policy recovery.
On π₀.₅, reduces the language backbone by about 96% and the full model by about 67%.
Across four LIBERO suites, RL improves average success from 84.55% to 93.45%, with a 1.98× inference speedup.
papers.selection_reason: Structural pruning and RL-based recovery for vision-language-action models; directly relevant to VLA and robot manipulation, with an efficiency contribution.
papers.title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: SPAR aggressively compresses a vision-language-action model and uses reinforcement learning to recover—and improve—robot manipulation performance while substantially accelerating inference.

papers.abstract: Human-collected robot manipulation data often mix successful behavior with retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures. Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (AC-BC) can exploit such mixed-quality data, but only if the conditioning signal is both accurately constructed from offline trajectories and effectively incorporated into the policy's action-vector-field prediction. Existing pipelines can weaken this signal by thresholding estimator-derived advantage scores into noisy conditions, and by routing conditions through prompts that weakly affect the action vector field. We introduce ALIGN, a condition-aligned AC-BC framework for vision-language-action policies. ALIGN directly predicts categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injects them into a DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time. We evaluate ALIGN on deliberately mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging, each combining standard demonstrations with retry-heavy trajectories. ALIGN improves condition fidelity, strengthens conditional vector-field separability, and achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, compared with 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline. These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist.
authors: Zechen Wang, Zhenqi Qiu, Houlong Xiong, Suohang Zhang, Yiyu Ren, Wanting Xu, Hongfei Niu, Chengyang He, Ge Sun, Ran Cheng, Qian Zhu
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality robot demonstrations containing successes, retries, recoveries, and failures.
Predicts categorical pairwise conditions directly in the policy-facing label space instead of thresholding estimated advantages.
Injects conditions into a DiT action expert using AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time.
Evaluated on mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging.
Achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, versus 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline.
papers.selection_reason: AC-BC framework for VLA robot manipulation policies from mixed-quality data.
papers.title: ALIGN: Aligning Condition Estimation and Expression in Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning
papers.tldr: ALIGN improves advantage-conditioned behavior cloning by making quality conditions more accurate and more directly influence robot action prediction.

papers.abstract: Every driving scene is logged once, but driving is one-to-many: the scene determines which behaviors are feasible, while an instruction selects among them. A log records only the action taken, leaving no direct supervision for alternative feasible actions or instructions the scene cannot support. Consequently, a policy that ignores language and one that follows it without regard to scene constraints can fit the same data. We present Cartender, which learns from the drives not taken. Counterfactual Branching constructs matched and mismatched instruction-action pairs from real recordings without a simulator: a vision-language model proposes alternative futures and their selecting instructions, while unsupported instructions provide negative labels. A learned scene-language compatibility score regulates language conditioning in trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks generated candidates over a scene-based score. The branches are used for training; instruction following is evaluated by swapping instructions under identical recorded inputs and measuring behavior rather than agreement with generated targets. On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals achieves an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions. Across 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart. Compared with matched-only imitation using the same backbone, Cartender improves same-scene paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and RFS from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.
authors: Zhiwen Chen, Benjin Zhu, Yan Xie, Jun Ma
bullets: Driving logs show only the action taken, providing no direct supervision for feasible alternatives or infeasible instructions.
Counterfactual Branching uses a vision-language model to generate alternative futures and instructions, with mismatches serving as negative labels without a simulator.
A scene-language compatibility gate regulates language conditioning, while a reward-trained language residual re-ranks trajectory candidates.
On WOD-E2E, Cartender improves paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.

papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned driving with counterfactual learning and scene-language compatibility.
papers.title: Cartender: Verifiable Language-Conditioned Driving by Learning the Drives Not Taken
papers.tldr: Cartender enables verifiable language-conditioned driving by learning which alternative instructions and trajectories are feasible—or unsupported—from logged scenes.

papers.abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.
authors: Song-Li Wu, Chubin Zhang, Wenbo Ding, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses robotic photography requiring intent understanding, motion planning, and aesthetic image composition.
Uses PhotoCoT for structured camera-action planning within a Vision-Language-Action framework.
Applies Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization to align camera behavior with human preferences.
Introduces OpenPhotography, a dataset of language-guided robotic photography demonstrations for training and evaluation.
Real-world experiments show effective generalization to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex instructions.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework for autonomous robotic photography with language-guided camera control.
papers.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.tldr: RoboPhoto-VLA unifies visual understanding, language reasoning, and camera control to autonomously produce aesthetically preferred photographs across varied real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
authors: Hojin Jeon, Jimin Lee, Taekwan Kim, Nayoung Oh, Taeyoung Kim, Myungkyu Koo, Jinmo Koo, Joonwoo Ahn, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses temporal inefficiency caused by fine-grained actions learned from teleoperation data.
Uses shared-expert action decoders supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons.
Selects execution modes through quantizability guidance and a context-conditioned router.
Improves execution efficiency while maintaining success across three simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks.
Evaluated on multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive temporal action quantization for VLA robot policies; directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: PaceVLA adaptively varies action granularity in VLA policies to speed up robot manipulation without sacrificing task success.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao
bullets: Targets the learning burden and semantic-to-action gap in direct vision-language-action policies.
Models actionable state changes instead of reconstructing complete future states, reducing focus on static or irrelevant details.
Combines LT-Filter for local manipulation changes with GT-Anchor for coarse future-direction regularization.
Uses DDAR to inject the learned Delta into action denoising as a structured action-space seed.
Experiments report improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization.],
papers.selection_reason: Compact latent delta as actionable transition for VLA robotic manipulation; fits embodied VLA, robot learning, and latent-action world modeling.
papers.title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: VLDA learns compact, task-relevant state-change representations to bridge vision-language understanding and reliable robotic manipulation actions.

papers.abstract: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.
authors: Zhenqi Wu, Trung Tien Dong, Aditya Penumarti, Mohamed A. Fouad, Menna A. Fouad, Mingyang Mao, Jane Jaejeong Shin, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: Addresses the lack of training data for autonomous underwater robot operation by recording human pilots’ camera-based joystick control.
Provides 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, paired with camera images, joystick commands, language annotations, and inertial measurements.
Finds that simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and reduce the amount of real-world data needed for policy training.
Benchmarks seven imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies in closed-loop simulation; no policy completes more than one-fifth of episodes.
Reports that land-data pretraining gives large VLA models no advantage over smaller policies trained from scratch underwater.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a language-annotated underwater teleoperation dataset and benchmarks VLA and imitation-learning policies for autonomous robot control.
papers.title: AQUAACT: A Joystick-Level Underwater Teleoperation Dataset and Closed-Loop Benchmark
papers.tldr: AQUAACT introduces a language-annotated underwater teleoperation dataset and benchmark, showing that simulated demonstrations help real-world learning but current policies still struggle with autonomous underwater control.

papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.
authors: Yong Wang, Kecheng Zheng, Xing Zhu, Chao Xu, Yujun Shen, Shengze Cai
bullets: Targets the limited characterization of dexterous manipulation in existing robotic action models.
Covers five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long-horizon tasks, and memory.
Pairs every task with an out-of-domain variant to test robustness to controlled visual and spatial changes.
Includes two high-DoF hand embodiments and 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations totaling 6.25 million frames.
Provides unified-protocol baselines from evaluating seven recent Vision-Language-Action models.
papers.selection_reason: Presents BiDex-100, a comprehensive benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation and Vision-Language-Action models, directly supporting research in robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
papers.tldr: BiDex-100 is a 106-task simulation benchmark for evaluating bimanual dexterous manipulation across capabilities, robustness, embodiments, and data efficiency.

papers.abstract: Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision-language-action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zhe Liu, Yuxuan Zheng, Jinzhe Qin, Ziqi Gao, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between onboard inference latency and UAV motion during VLA control.
Uses B-spline trajectories initialized from expert demonstrations for continuous position and yaw references.
Fuses new predictions with active trajectories while preserving derivative continuity and limiting deformation.
Applies execution-aware GRPO to adapt the policy to deviations caused by asynchronous execution.
Achieves a 76.56% success rate on UAV-Flow and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations versus waypoint tracking.
papers.selection_reason: Presents AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous UAV flight. It addresses the latency mismatch in VLA policies through trajectory fusion and GRPO, demonstrating strong performance in language-conditioned flight.
papers.title: AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight
papers.tldr: AeroDASH enables smoother, continuous language-conditioned UAV flight by asynchronously adapting vision-language-action trajectory predictions to ongoing motion.

papers.abstract: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate seven models at multiple reasoning-effort settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget. However, these capabilities are improving rapidly: performance increases on our benchmark between July and September 2026 (inclusive) correspond to a performance doubling time of 44.5 days, while the best recorded execution rate increased by a factor of 4.4 and the lowest recorded execution cost fell by a factor of 6.2. These trends raise the possibility that the Bitter Lesson is coming to robotics; the capabilities of embodied general purpose LMs may one day be comparable to those of more specialized models.
authors: Christopher Leet, Achyutha Menon, Sravanthi Machcha, Sven Koenig, Tzu Kit Chan, Jay Chooi
bullets: Evaluates seven models across six RoboDojo manipulation tasks on physical robotic hardware.
Tests multiple reasoning-effort settings to systematically compare frontier models.
Current systems complete varied tasks but generally exceed practical action budgets.
Performance improved rapidly from July to September 2026, including a 44.5-day performance doubling time.
The findings suggest general-purpose embodied models could eventually approach specialized robotics systems, with associated safety risks.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically evaluates frontier multimodal LMs for direct robotic arm control. Provides performance metrics and trends relevant to the development of general-purpose embodied agents.
papers.title: The Bitter Lesson Comes to Robotics
papers.tldr: Frontier multimodal language models can control real robotic arms, but remain too imprecise and inefficient for practical manipulation—while improving rapidly.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.
authors: Sicheng He, Yi Pan, Qiuting Yu, Jiaming Huang, Qi Lu, Shuyan Wu, Hongyan Feng, Xuanyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Jie Zhang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Action tails retain useful denoising progress instead of being regenerated from fresh noise.
The framework combines tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided renoising/refinement.
It operates during inference with the underlying VLA model frozen.
Across 16 model–benchmark pairs, it reduces inference cost in every case, with up to 1.48× speedup.
Success rate improves in 14 pairs, by up to 15.08 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces adaptive action-tail reuse to reduce denoising steps and improve VLA control, directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
papers.tldr: VLA-Rolling reuses discarded action tails and adaptively allocates denoising to make vision-language-action control faster and more accurate.

papers.abstract: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.
authors: Sen Fang, Liwei Che, Dimitris N. Metaxas
