bullets: Addresses limited facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific deformation, and loss of fine visual detail in existing avatars.
Uses Shared Face Primitive Splatting for transferable expression control.
Applies Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting to learn a signer-specific virtual muscle layer, plus TunnelingNet-based super-resolution for identity-specific details.
Test-time modules are optimized once per signer; inference thereafter uses stored identity parameters while preserving interactive streaming.
Reports reductions of 71.4% in facial geometry error, 35.1% in body-boundary error across ten identities, and 24.2% in high-resolution RGB reconstruction error.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Stable Signer V3, a system for sign language production using 4D deformable primitive splatting. This directly connects visual and language understanding to physical actions (avatar generation), fitting Vision-Language-Action and 3D Vision.
papers.title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
papers.tldr: Stable Signer V3 enables interactive, high-resolution sign-language avatars with richer expressions, more accurate signer-specific motion, and finer appearance details using 4D deformable primitive splatting.

papers.abstract: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide an open-source VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation-action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Zhiqing Tang, Hanlin Zhao, Siu Hing Lui, Tao Yang, Jingsong Lin, Huxin Gao, Yeung Trevor, Raymond Tang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses scan-then-revisit target acquisition from partial observations in confined, deformable anatomy.
Adapts a pretrained vision-language-action backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands.
Combines initial, intermediate, and current images with language instructions to guide out-of-view search.
Introduces an open-source dataset of 1,050 episodes and approximately 262k observation-action pairs across six tasks.
Reports 93.3% success in cross-embodiment evaluation; expanding training data improved success from 40.0% to 90.0% in a controlled comparison.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned VLA policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy; relevant to VLA and robot manipulation.
papers.title: EndoVLA-OOV: Language-Conditioned Out-of-View Target Acquisition in Robotic Endoscopy
papers.tldr: EndoVLA-OOV uses language, visual history, and camera-control actions to reacquire previously observed targets in robotic endoscopy, achieving strong performance across challenging physical settings.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model's original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.
authors: Chaoran Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Chenglin Cui, Yazhe Wan, Taein Kwon, Changjae Oh
bullets: Directly matching VLA and 3D foundation-model features can cause severe rank collapse.
The proposed method aligns pair-wise relationships rather than enforcing point-wise feature equality.
It integrates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning without compromising original expressivity.
Experiments across public benchmarks, a new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation show robust spatial understanding across diverse tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Relational spatial alignment to inject 3D awareness into VLA models; directly relevant to VLA and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Relational Spatial Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: A relational alignment method injects 3D spatial awareness into vision-language-action models while preserving their representational expressivity.

papers.abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
authors: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying task-level planning with interaction-specific, state-dependent whole-body control.
Projects independently learned skill policies into the latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM).
Trains a single offline perceptive flow planner on aggregated closed-loop latent rollouts from multiple skills.
Introduces AH-BFM with adaptive horizons for both precise control and extended whole-body behavior.
Across three simulated tasks, achieves 42.0% mean success versus 11.6% for latent replay and 3.5% for kinematic planning; real-robot tests show transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering.
papers.selection_reason: Latent action-aligned planning for humanoid loco-manipulation using a behavioral foundation model; relevant to latent actions and robot learning.
papers.title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: FIBER enables one perceptive humanoid planner to coordinate diverse loco-manipulation skills by planning in an executable latent space that preserves low-level feedback.

papers.abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu, Kezhi Mao
bullets: Commodity RGB-D sensors produce missing, distorted, or incorrect geometry, causing a sharp performance drop in modern 3D policies.
NISE learns trustworthy spatial features using Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision with calibrated multi-view depth.
Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention propagates position uncertainty instead of treating corrupted 3D tokens as exact.
Simulated sensor-corruption benchmarks and real-robot tasks with transparent and reflective objects show improved noise robustness.
The approach targets deployment with imperfect commodity RGB-D sensors, beyond clean-depth evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial encoding for 3D manipulation policies robust to depth corruption; relevant to VLA, manipulation, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding for 3D Manipulation Policies under Depth Corruption
papers.tldr: NISE improves the robustness of 3D manipulation policies to realistic RGB-D depth corruption without sacrificing clean-depth performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5\% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA.
authors: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan, Yang Li, Tiange Fu, Xiaoyuan Fu, Guiyang Luo, Jinglin Li
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large VLA models for real-time autonomous driving.
Uses temporal scene variations and decision deviations to estimate scene complexity and model uncertainty.
Encodes this information into scene-aware tokens and specialized queries for budget-conditioned layer routing.
Dynamically selects layer combinations and active parameter ratios through end-to-end optimization.
On Bench2Drive, reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5% with negligible capability degradation.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-Language-Action driving model with dynamic layer routing for efficient inference, fitting embodied VLA and efficient AI.
papers.title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
papers.tldr: Scene-Adaptive VLA dynamically activates model layers according to driving-scene complexity, reducing inference computation while largely preserving driving and language performance.

papers.abstract: LIBERO has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating robotic manipulation policies. However, strong performance on LIBERO does not necessarily indicate robust embodied capabilities, as models may exploit benchmark-specific regularities rather than generalize to diverse operating conditions. In this work, we introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0, a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of embodied foundation models under distribution shifts. LIBERO-Pro2.0 encompasses 22 static perturbations and 20 runtime interventions across six dimensions: Condition, Environment, Observation, Execution, Robot State Configuration, and Language, yielding 1,648 validated shifted task instances. To support robustness-oriented learning, we further collect 39,390 training trajectories through model-generated and human demonstrations. All shifted task instances undergo six rounds of iterative human review and correction to ensure physical plausibility and task validity. We evaluate 17 representative robot policies spanning vision-language-action models, world-action models, and robustness-oriented policies. Our results reveal substantial robustness gaps across all evaluated paradigms: under runtime distribution shifts, the evaluated models exhibit an average performance drop of 26.5 percentage points, with individual drops reaching 32.5 points. These findings highlight the gap between nominal benchmark performance and robustness under distribution shifts, underscoring the need for systematic robustness evaluation of embodied foundation models.
authors: Xueyang Zhou, Yangming Xu, Qianjiang Li, Guiyao Tie, Junhao Wu, Ziheng Huang, Guowen Zhang, Zhijie Yuan, Di Wu, Duanfeng Chu, Pan Zhou, Lichao Sun, Yongchao Chen
bullets: Introduces 22 static perturbations and 20 runtime interventions across six shift dimensions, producing 1,648 validated shifted task instances.
Provides 39,390 training trajectories from model-generated and human demonstrations to support robustness-oriented learning.
Uses six rounds of human review to verify the physical plausibility and validity of shifted tasks.
Evaluates 17 robot policies and finds substantial robustness gaps, including an average 26.5-point performance drop under runtime shifts.
Shows that strong nominal LIBERO performance does not guarantee robust generalization to changed operating conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Robustness benchmark for embodied foundation models under distribution shifts, evaluating VLA and world-action policies.
papers.title: LIBERO-Pro2.0: A Benchmark for Evaluating the Robustness of Embodied Foundation Models
papers.tldr: LIBERO-Pro2.0 benchmarks how robust embodied foundation models remain when robotic manipulation tasks undergo diverse distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.
authors: Jinming Wang, Ruiheng Zhang, Yong Wang, Zipan Xiong, Keyuan Luo
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen VLA policies to learn from prior failures without updating the model.
Uses an external memory of stress-collected local-depth records to trigger translation-only projection corrections.
Keeps rotation and gripper commands unchanged while intervening on translations.
Primary CALVIN evaluation reduced a depth-based near-collision/stall proxy without changing task-success count, but an independent replication did not reproduce the effect.
Failure analysis highlights endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the absence of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline; physical safety improvement remains unestablished.
papers.selection_reason: External-memory retrieval wrapper for frozen VLA policies with empirical failure analysis; directly relevant to VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Retrieval-triggered Action Projection Adjustment for Frozen VLA Policies: An Empirical Study and Failure Analysis
papers.tldr: RTPC adds retrieval-based translation corrections to frozen VLA actions, but its apparent reduction in near-collision/stall events was not replicated or shown to be retrieval-specific.

papers.abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to participate effectively in social interactions is important for their integration into human-centered environments. Existing methods, however, typically map pre-generated speech directly to continuous motion trajectories but have limited awareness of complex social environments and lack explicit high-level semantic action planning. We introduce SocialCoAct, a unified agent-centered framework for VLM-based egocentric social co-action. We formulate egocentric social co-action as an end-to-end agent task and develop SocialCoAct-Agent, which transforms egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and atomic action sequences, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting behaviors in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate the VLM capabilities required by this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous egocentric recordings of natural multi-party interactions. The benchmark comprises 423 human-verified multiple-choice questions across three subtasks: Long Episode Understanding (LEU), Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU), and Coordinated Action Planning (CAP). Across a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, the highest overall accuracy is 77.54%, while accuracy on the hard subset reaches only 46.51%. Extended reasoning improves Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B by 19.62 and 17.02 percentage points, respectively, but reduces inference throughput by 53.6$\times$ and 20.2$\times$. Visual-input ablations further show that the benefits of visual context vary across models. SocialCoAct provides a foundation for developing and evaluating VLM-based humanoid agents that coordinate context-aware speech and action in complex social interactions. The codebase and benchmark will be made publicly available upon publication.
authors: Jiancong Ma, Kun Li, Jin Jiang, Shengcai Liao
bullets: Frames social co-action as an end-to-end agent task involving perception, dialogue, verbal response, and atomic action planning.
SocialCoAct-Agent maps egocentric observations and dialogue history to utterances and aligned action sequences, executable in simulation and on a humanoid robot.
SocialCoAct-Bench contains 423 human-verified questions covering episode understanding, speaker intention, and coordinated action planning.
Evaluated VLMs achieve up to 77.54% overall accuracy, but only 46.51% on the hard subset, indicating substantial challenges.
Extended reasoning improves some small VLMs but sharply reduces inference throughput; visual-context benefits vary by model.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based egocentric social co-action for humanoid robots.
papers.title: SocialCoAct: Enabling and Benchmarking Egocentric Social Co-Action for VLM-Based Humanoid Robots
papers.tldr: SocialCoAct introduces an egocentric VLM framework and benchmark for humanoid robots to understand social interactions and coordinate context-aware speech with physical actions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation. Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by modern policies. We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies. Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains with 300 Hz gaze synchronized with images, proprioception, and actions. We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets across the policy's visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping inference gaze-free. Across 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6%, with gains up to 25 percentage points. Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors. The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial (57.9% to 69.6%) and different VLA backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA manipulation.
authors: Anupam Pani, Wang Yuan, Qifan Wang, Yanchao Yang
bullets: Introduces a real-robot, multi-view gaze dataset with 12,000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains.
Synchronizes 300 Hz human gaze with images, proprioception, and actions, then transfers gaze targets across camera views.
Uses gaze as soft supervision to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training; inference requires no gaze.
Improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6% across 18 real-world tasks, with gains up to 25 percentage points.
Benefits transfer to LIBERO-Spatial and different VLA backbones; real gaze outperforms generic attention-shaping priors.
papers.selection_reason: Gaze-annotated manipulation dataset and attention regularization for VLA policies; directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: GazeAct: A Human-Gaze-Annotated Manipulation Dataset for Attention-Regularized Policies
papers.tldr: GazeAct uses synchronized human gaze to train gaze-free VLA policies with better visual grounding and manipulation success.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.
authors: Liang Su, David Chen, Jason Li, Kevin Guo, Teresa Lv
bullets: Targets real-time single-batch inference bottlenecks from kernel-launch overhead, data movement, and redundant recomputation across decisions.
Uses deep kernel fusion with launch overlap, an execution contract for cross-decision state reuse, and execution-state capsules for fast snapshot, restore, and fork operations.
Supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models through parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement.
Across evaluated policies and hardware, achieves 1.3–3.7× speedup at matched 16-bit precision and 3.38–12.66× over official eager implementations with reduced precision.
In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 reaches 94.04% success on Jetson AGX Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, near or above the reported FP16 reference.
papers.selection_reason: Low-latency inference engine for VLA and world action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
papers.tldr: FLASHRT-PAI accelerates physical-AI inference by optimizing the entire execution pipeline—not just individual kernels—achieving substantial speedups while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal. We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.
authors: Sungsu Kim, Vineet Bhat, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Ramesh Karri, Farshad Khorrami
bullets: Addresses multi-step robot manipulation under diverse and heavy clutter.
Orchestrates open-vocabulary detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing.
Uses action memory for long-horizon planning and outputs transferable grasp poses or 3D waypoints without task-specific training.
Achieves 89.1% average success in simulation and benchmarks, with an 88.8% success rate on a real robot arm.
Shows generalization across object classes, lighting, clutter levels, and from simulation to reality.
papers.selection_reason: A VLM agent orchestrating language-conditioned grasping and pushing in clutter, connecting visual-language understanding to physical manipulation actions.
papers.title: CLARO: Clutter Aware Robot Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Grasping using VLM Agents
papers.tldr: CLARO is a vision-language-model agent that combines perception, grasping, and pushing with memory to retrieve language-specified objects in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
authors: Yanjun Li, Jiarui Ye, Weiyu Guo, Zixiao He, Kangjie Ye, Dihan Wang, Yishuo Cheng, Zishang Xiang, Mingju Gao, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses WAMs’ difficulty distinguishing task-relevant changes from incidental visual changes.
Uses a frozen vision-language model to describe plausible task-progressing state changes between current and future frames.
Aligns encoded descriptions with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features alongside existing WAM objectives.
Adds no inference-time overhead because language components are used only during training.
Achieves 79.17% average success on HumanoidArena and improves real-world task success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Language-aligned whole-body World Action Models for humanoid loco-manipulation directly address embodied robot policy learning and vision-language-action.
papers.title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
papers.tldr: LANGUAGE-FORCING improves humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation by aligning future visual predictions with language-described task progress during training.

papers.abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
authors: Tao Lin, Yikeng Chen, Qiwei Liang, Zinan Xie, Zhengtu Liang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Targets the joint problem of selecting layers to remove and choosing recovery procedures after pruning.
Uses offline action-output interventions, evaluation history, and retained diagnoses to guide an LLM agent’s next pruning and recovery proposal.
Evaluates each proposed configuration on target tasks within a fixed search budget.
Across three VLA models and four LIBERO suites, removes 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining over 90% task success.
Reports inference speedups up to 2.50×; functional probes reveal action-sensitive layers that representation similarity may miss.],
papers.selection_reason: Agent-driven depth pruning of vision-language-action models to reduce inference cost, relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: AutoPruner uses an agentic closed-loop search to prune VLA model layers and recover performance, achieving substantial compression while preserving high task success and improving inference speed.

papers.abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.
authors: Kapalik Khanal, Biswash Khatiwada, Stephen Afrifa, Fan Wu, Ramesh Bahadur Bist
bullets: A reinforcement-learning policy controls the 13-joint lower body, while arm targets come from any compatible manipulation policy.
The framework combines locomotion and manipulation commands only at the robot interface, avoiding shared training or direct coordination.
The same locomotion checkpoint was paired on hardware with GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5 vision-language-action models.
In simulation, the robot tracked velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height without falls, with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m.
The approach remained robust to pushes and payload variation; an upper-body pose curriculum was crucial for survival and fall reduction.
papers.selection_reason: Decoupled humanoid loco-manipulation with RL locomotion and exchangeable VLA manipulation policies directly fits embodied robot learning and vision-language-action.
papers.title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: DUET decouples humanoid locomotion from manipulation so arm policies can be exchanged without retraining the balance controller.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable language-guided robot manipulation, but remain vulnerable to visual attacks that undermine user control over robot behavior. Prior studies optimize visual perturbations using fixed target supervision. However, the perturbation can change earlier actions and, in turn, the physical states reached later. As the attacked trajectory evolves, this supervision may no longer match the behavior needed at the states actually reached. Accurately matching these targets can therefore fail to advance the attacker-specified task. Even with suitable supervision, reducing average matching error does not ensure sustained task progress. The robot may still fail at a critical stage, and further updates can disrupt previously successful behavior. To address these limitations, we propose TRACO, a framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks through closed-loop optimization. Its Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds supervision for the states reached under attack to guide subsequent updates. Within this framework, Progress-Guided Selection focuses updates where progress stalls while maintaining supervision on the earlier behavior needed to reach that point. Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments show improved task-redirection success with TRACO, highlighting the security implications of closed-loop attack optimization.
authors: Chunjin Ye, Guanying Chen, Jianjie Huang, Jianhao Chen, Quanlin Chen, Hanjie Zhao, Haozhe Liang, Tieyun Qian, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Problem: Fixed target supervision can become mismatched as visual perturbations alter earlier actions and later physical states.
Method: Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds targets from attacked states, while Progress-Guided Selection concentrates updates where task progress stalls.
Contribution: A closed-loop framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks without relying solely on average matching-error reduction.
Result: Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments report improved task-redirection success.
Scope: The work highlights security risks for language-guided robot manipulation; the abstract does not specify real-world evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop visual attacks on VLA models for robot manipulation; directly relevant to embodied VLA and manipulation.
papers.title: Enhancing Visual Task-Redirection Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models via Closed-Loop Optimization
papers.tldr: TRACO improves visual task-redirection attacks on vision-language-action robots by adapting attack supervision and updates to the trajectory states actually reached.

papers.abstract: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.
authors: Hongcheng Gao, Alex Zhou, Jay Zhu, Zelin Zheng, Shijia Ge, Xiping Li, Di Wu, Yazhe Wang, Jianshu Zeng, Xuan Shangguan, Yongli Wang, Yexing Wan, Lingyu He, Zhiqi Jia, Sihang Wu, Xiao He
bullets: Controls a two-arm robot through a command line using three calibrated RGB cameras.
The agent analyzes failures and iteratively writes reusable observation-based tools for localization and control.
Tools use camera triangulation, known planes, and repositioned wrist-camera views to estimate object geometry.
Tools are developed on 10 layouts per task, frozen, and evaluated on 10 new layouts of the same seed.
Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, it reports 39.7% success and 48.0 progress; pushing is strong, while tight insertion is difficult.
papers.selection_reason: VLM coding agent controlling robot manipulation; fits embodied VLA and manipulation interests.
papers.title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
papers.tldr: HexaShell shows that a thin VLM coding-agent harness can achieve strong robot-manipulation performance, but precise physical contact remains the main bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
authors: Jiawei Geng, Zhenyang Liu, Yuzheng Wu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses failures caused by occlusion, clutter, and changing viewpoints in open-world manipulation.
Predicts task-related virtual camera motion and queries a geometry-conditioned world model to generate spatial priors.
Compresses the imagined prior into fixed memory and fuses it with live observations for diffusion-based action prediction.
Reports success rates of 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials.
The demonstrated robustness is scoped to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Active world-action model with trajectory-conditioned view imagination for manipulation; fits world modeling and VLA.
papers.title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: AWAM improves robot manipulation in cluttered and occluded settings by actively imagining task-relevant views along planned trajectories before acting.

papers.abstract: Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation-state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy's training distribution. We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity: under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to pi_0.5 reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%. We introduce ActiveAlign, a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates. A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning. At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with pi_0 and 72.7% with pi_0.5, outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively. Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90. These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.
authors: Jiawei Geng, Zhenyang Liu, Yuzheng Wu, Yongchong Gu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Problem: Camera repositioning can create first-frame observation and robot-state distributions unlike those seen during policy training, sharply reducing performance.
Method: A viewpoint module selects a camera trajectory; offline closed-loop alignment connects its endpoint to demonstrations and retains successful manipulation continuations for VLA fine-tuning.
Contribution: The adapted policy uses active perception without changing the VLA architecture and aligns training data with viewpoint-induced states.
Results: On 40 LIBERO tasks, success reaches 70.7% with π₀ and 72.7% with π₀.₅; real-world occlusion success rises from 35/90 to 83/90.
Scope: Gains are supported across controls and also observed with OpenVLA and GR00T N1, indicating the approach is not limited to one VLA.
papers.selection_reason: Active perception aligned with VLA policy training for manipulation; directly relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Look Before You Act: Bridging Active Perception and Vision-Language-Action Models via Observation-Aligned Data Adaptation
papers.tldr: ActiveAlign adapts vision-language-action policies to the states produced by active camera movement, substantially improving manipulation under occlusion and clutter.

papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
authors: Keyuan Luo, Yi Xie, Wanyun Ling, Yuanzhe Li, Ziyue Li, Zhuoqi Zeng
bullets: Introduces interventions at the retrieval interface, including target-fact substitutions, fact-preserving replacements, numerical perturbations, and exact replicas.
Separates decision correctness from motor execution success and evaluates within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory.
In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-ULP intervention changed 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while key-fact changes showed no clear extra effect over fact-preserving replacements.
ChainBench tests tasks requiring historical information absent from current observations.
Full memory increased ChainBench success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching oracle-decision performance under shared executions.
papers.selection_reason: Directly evaluates memory in vision-language-action robot systems, fitting VLA and embodied memory topics.
papers.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
papers.tldr: IMEP evaluates whether VLA systems genuinely use task-relevant memory, showing that memory can improve history-dependent decisions but aggregate success ablations are insufficient evidence.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.
authors: Jiajun Cao, Kai Tang, Bohua Zhang, Zezhong Qian, Ying Li, Xiaozhu Ju, Xiaobao Wei, Jiaming Liu, Yang Ding, Sixiang Chen, Yiding Sun, Siyuan Qian, Tinghao Wang, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Yi Zhang, Shilong Zou, Yong Dai, Jian Tang, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Uses semantic subtask progress to coordinate planning, action selection, execution monitoring, and transitions.
Combines a hybrid-expert VLM with a world-action model using mixture-of-transformer experts for video–action modeling.
Employs hierarchical visual memory and subtask-local value learning to preserve temporal context and learn from successful prefixes of failed trajectories.
Achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks, rising to 95.56% with OpenWAM-α.
Reaches 65% average success on three long-horizon real-robot tasks, versus 28.33% for π₀.₅ and 25% for Fast-WAM.
papers.selection_reason: Unified language-action-world model for long-horizon manipulation; strongly fits world modeling and VLA.
papers.title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
papers.tldr: LAW unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling to improve long-horizon robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.
authors: Yong Wang, Boyu Shen, Xinwei Zhang, Yizheng Li, Keyuan Luo
bullets: VLA models struggle with long-horizon tasks because limited temporal context hinders the accumulation and reuse of experience.
It proposes a taxonomy based on memory scope and persistence, covering five established paradigms and one emerging frontier.
Representative systems are compared by memory characteristics, architectural complexity, and open-source maturity.
The survey identifies a trade-off: greater architectural complexity generally corresponds to lower open-source maturity.
Key open challenges include efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolution.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of memory paradigms for long-horizon VLA models; directly relevant to embodied memory and VLA systems.
papers.title: From Sliding Windows to Self-evolving Lifelong Memory: A Dual-perspective Survey of Memory Paradigms for Long-Horizon Robotics VLA Models
papers.tldr: This survey organizes memory mechanisms for long-horizon robotics VLA models and highlights the trade-offs and challenges involved in building lifelong embodied agents.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
bullets: Addresses fragmented training data, multi-task interference, and conflicts caused by conventional model merging in VLA models.
Uses a nested hypernetwork conditioned on the target task to generate adaptive action-expert parameters alongside a frozen base VLA.
Stores task-specific compressed VLM residuals separately for flexible skill reuse and storage efficiency.
Across MetaWorld, ManiSkill, and CALVIN, it outperforms the strongest merging baseline by 41 percentage points on average.
Matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 percentage point on ManiSkill and substantially narrows the gap on CALVIN.
papers.selection_reason: VLA skill consolidation via nested hypernetwork for task-conditioned action-expert generation; directly relevant to embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: NestedVLA consolidates independently learned robotic skills by generating task-specific parameters instead of merging them, improving reuse while reducing interference.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.
authors: Zeyuan Ren, Guanxun Zhao, Qi Li, Hao Wang, Wenlong Liao, Keyi Luo, Xijing Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Jingye Cui, Qibin Gu, Zhichen Wang, Yucheng Hu, Liqiao Xia, Nan Bu, Zhengde Ma, Rankun Li, Xue Yang, Wende Xie
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between joint-space losses and the unequal physical impact of joint errors.
Uses differentiable forward kinematics to supervise tool-center-point and inter-arm relative poses during flow matching.
Adds global visual queries distilled from DINOv3 and local interaction queries guided by Grounding DINO attention.
Teachers are removed at inference, preserving a standard joint-space flow-policy deployment with a learned query pathway.

Experiments on simulated and real long-horizon bimanual tasks find complementary benefits: the full model suits in-distribution settings, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.
papers.selection_reason: Physics-grounded flow-matching and spatial grounding priors for bimanual VLA manipulation.
papers.title: GRASP: Global-Local Representation Alignment and Spatial-Physical Grounding for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: GRASP improves bimanual VLA manipulation by aligning joint-action learning with physical end-effector outcomes and focusing visual representations on relevant hand-object interactions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
bullets: Motivates unification of vision-language-action models and world-action models despite differing architectures, outputs, and objectives.
Represents models with conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels.
Connects pretraining and offline or online post-training to policy deployment.
Instantiates the framework for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
papers.selection_reason: Unified probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models covering VLA and world-action models; directly relevant to embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
papers.tldr: A stochastic-kernel formulation unifies diverse embodied foundation models by translating their outputs into task-conditioned robot policies.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies, high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored. We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments. On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over independently trained local policies by 16--40 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.
authors: Chenglong Zhang, Shuaijun Liu, Feiyang You, Shuyang Hao, Chengyu Wu, Ningxin Su
bullets: Targets coordinated multi-arm manipulation, where each arm retains local perception and action ownership.
Studies where interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how coordination should be learned.
Identifies complementary roles for shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction.
Reproduces the coordination design in a structurally different VLA architecture, suggesting backbone-agnostic applicability.

In physical experiments across four tasks, full interaction improves success over independent local policies by 16–40 percentage points; teams of three and four arms are evaluated in simulation and on hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-arm VLA coordination through learned interaction across complete vision-language-action policies.
papers.title: VLA-Fabric: Learning Interaction for Composable Multi-Arm VLA Agents
papers.tldr: VLA-Fabric enables multiple complete VLA policies—one per robot arm—to coordinate through learned interaction, substantially improving multi-arm manipulation success.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $\pi_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $\pi_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
authors: Khuyen Pham, Tran Nguyen Le, Edoardo Fazzari, Cesare Stefanini
bullets: Targets the repeated action-expert evaluations that make flow-matching VLAs costly for real-time robotic control.
Retains π₀.₅’s pretrained vision-language encoder and uses Mamba to model dependencies across noisy continuous-action sequences.
Compresses vision-language prefix tokens into a conditioning signal that gates and modulates Mamba blocks without repeated token-level cross-attention.
Uses a 10× smaller action expert and reduces denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment.
Improves mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three seeds, with gains also reported on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies; directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot manipulation with latency reduction.
papers.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: MambaAct replaces the transformer action expert in flow-matching VLA models with a compact Mamba-based expert, substantially reducing inference latency while preserving or improving manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $\pi_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $\pi_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $\pi_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $\pi_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $\pi_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $\pi_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $\pi_0$ solved a task on which unguided $\pi_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.
bullets: Motivation: Transfer frozen VLAs such as π₀ across robot embodiments without collecting demonstrations or changing policy parameters.
Method: Train a classifier on successful source- and target-body action chunks from a few calibration tasks, then use its gradient during each denoising step to guide π₀.

Result: On LIBERO with four modified controllers, average target-body success increased from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs; 11 of 12 improved, with 5 statistically significant after Holm correction.
Scope: Guidance is data-efficient in simulation and may support sim-to-real transfer where target rollouts are costly.
Limitation: It can be ineffective or harmful for weak or locked wrists when classifier data are insufficient or favor infeasible motions; guided data and retraining can partially address this.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the transfer of frozen VLA policies (like $	extit{$ ackslash$pi$_0$}) to new robot embodiments. It uses a lightweight classifier to guide the denoising process, a transferable technique for embodied AI.
papers.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
papers.tldr: A lightweight embodiment classifier can guide a frozen flow-based policy toward successful actions for a new robot body without demonstrations or policy updates, improving simulated transfer but struggling with poorly represented or infeasible dynamics.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.
authors: Victoria Smelova, Daniil Kazachkov, Georgiy Kazantsev, Iuliia Tsvetkova, Egor Cherepanov, Nikita Kachaev, Artem Latyshev, Aleksandr I. Panov, Alexey K. Kovalev
bullets: Addresses the cost and redundancy of retaining complete visual observation histories in long-horizon, multi-stage tasks.
Compares 35 plan-disagreement measures across autoregressive and flow-matching VLA policies, then validates selected signals on pretrained policies.
Uses plan-revision signals to trigger bounded visual-memory updates, with a robot-masked filter to suppress redundant frames.
Event detectors achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.981–0.997 in the reported evaluations.
The method preserved task-relevant observations until later decision points in 100% of evaluated episodes and showed transfer to real-robot replay data.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces RePlanMem-VLA, a method for selective visual memory in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. It uses replanning signals to trigger memory updates, directly addressing VLA policy limitations.
papers.title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: RePlanMem-VLA uses unusually large changes in a VLA policy’s rolling action predictions to selectively store task-relevant visual keyframes.

papers.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
bullets: Benchmarks robustness to 11 hardware/setup perturbation axes across four LIBERO suites, with five severity levels and 210 conditions.
Evaluates nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and statistical testing.
Pooled success decreases from 0.932 under nominal conditions to 0.767 at medium severity and 0.509 at the highest severity.
Robustness varies substantially by perturbation axis and action interface.
Training on visual perturbations does not address faults that do not alter camera images; fixed-parameter episode manifests are released.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language-action robot policies under hardware perturbations, directly fitting VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LIBERO-RIG shows that vision-language-action policies can degrade sharply under realistic robot hardware and setup changes, even when task visuals remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs. We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources. Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning. Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection. Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training. Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.
