The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023
bullets: Compliance is essential for contact-rich tasks but is not captured by common robot demonstration interfaces.
Four-channel bilateral teleoperation uses the leader arm to measure intended equilibrium separately from realized pose and force.
Per-axis, direction-dependent stiffness is recovered by regression without dedicated force/tactile hardware or manual annotation.
The resulting labels fine-tune a VLA to output stiffness alongside pose.
In a Franka Research 3 wiping task, commanded contact force rose from 6.4 N for normal wiping to 9.1 N for firm wiping; the policy was the only one of five to respond this way.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses VLA compliance learning and robot manipulation from teleoperation.
papers.title: Compliance for Free: Learning Identifiable Impedance via Bilateral Teleoperation
papers.tldr: Bilateral teleoperation makes operator stiffness identifiable from existing torque sensing, enabling free compliance labels that teach a VLA to adjust contact force to task instructions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
authors: Shaoyuan Xie, Zihan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Jiashu Qu, Xiaoqing Liang, Lingdong Kong, Junchi Lu, Henrik I. Christensen, Qi Alfred Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark jointly evaluating navigation following, conflict awareness, and adversarial robustness.
Predicts three navigation-compliance modes to separate conflict reasoning from action generation.
Uses navigation-conditioned world-model rollouts that simulate strictly following instructions to assess their safety.
Achieves 88.16 Driving Score and 68.64% Success Rate on Bench2Drive.
Improves closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 versus the best SimLingo variant.
papers.selection_reason: VLA for autonomous driving with navigation-conditioned world model dreaming; directly fits vision-language-action and interactive world models.
papers.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: SafeDriveVLA improves autonomous driving safety by reasoning about whether natural-language navigation instructions are safe to follow before generating actions.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
bullets: Addresses trajectory errors caused by action representations that are disconnected from visual dynamics.
Uses a visually derived motion scaffold plus a compact residual encoding for centimeter-scale corrections.
A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.
Reaches 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one denoising step, near its ten-step score at 3.29× higher end-to-end speed; also reports 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 on navhard.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VITAL, an action tokenizer that couples visual motion scaffolds with residual trajectory error encodings. This bridges visual dynamics and action planning, offering a novel approach to world-action models and latent action representations.
papers.title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
papers.tldr: VITAL derives action representations from visual motion and adds normalized residual corrections, enabling fast, precise driving decisions without predicting future images.

papers.abstract: Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act. We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken. After every recognized word, a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold tau set by the user, so 1 - tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object. Otherwise, it waits or asks. The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate, and evaluate. On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92 percent of the time when it commits at tau = 0.9, and needs 31 to 35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.
bullets: Addresses robots’ tendency to wait for complete instructions before acting.
Uses a fine-tuned text encoder to score scene objects word by word and commits when the best calibrated probability reaches a user-set threshold.
Supports waiting or asking when confidence is insufficient, with 1 − τ representing accepted error risk.
On instructions with unseen words, it commits correctly 1.6–2× as often as keyword matching and is at least 92% correct at τ = 0.9.
Runs in 31–35 ms per word on consumer GPUs and includes streaming, data-generation, training, calibration, and evaluation tools.
papers.selection_reason: Enables robots to commit to objects from partial spoken instructions, relevant to language-conditioned action.
papers.title: EarlyCommit: Calibrated Word-by-Word Commitment for Robots Acting Before You Finish Speaking
papers.tldr: EarlyCommit enables robots to choose the intended object before a spoken instruction ends by making calibrated, risk-controlled decisions after each word.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at: https://gr-bc.github.io
authors: Xiaoman Li, Zhiqiang Yang, Jiayu Hu, Jipeng Kong, Yang Zhang, Jingwei Zhang, Fangzheng Yan, Chunhua Shen, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality long-horizon demonstrations containing detours, failures, hesitations, and imperfect recoveries.
Builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over successful and failed intervention-assisted rollouts.
Uses reverse graph search to estimate minimal remaining steps and reweight chunks by their reduction in this potential.
Reuses recoverable segments and intervention paths without reward models, critics, progress predictors, trajectory comparisons, or progress labels.
Evaluated on four manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, reaching 91% success after a few offline iterations.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-based reweighting of action chunks for VLA post-training, relevant to robot manipulation learning.
papers.title: Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning with Human Interventions for Precise Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: GR-BC improves VLA post-training for precise manipulation by weighting action chunks according to their dataset-supported contribution to eventual task success.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.
authors: Peidong Wang, Ying Chang, Zhiming Ma, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng, Daqi Liu, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Daling Wang
bullets: Targets failures in pretrained vision-language-action models on unseen long-horizon tasks.
A coding agent first improves skills and the execution harness, then diagnoses persistent sub-step failures by retrying from saved states.
Fine-tunes only unreliable executor sub-steps using self-collected demonstrations and experience reused across tasks.
On 50 RoboCasa365 target tasks, success on unseen composite tasks increases from 4.6% to 13.8% without human demonstrations.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, uses 28% of GPU time and 22% of self-collected demonstrations while achieving slightly higher success.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive self-improvement for embodied VLA agents; fits VLA and adaptation/memory topics.
papers.title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: AdaRSI selectively improves an embodied agent’s skills, harness, or executor weights to recover from persistent failures, substantially improving long-horizon task success with less training cost.

papers.abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. Link for the webpage \href{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}
authors: Zeji Yi, Soham Dasgupta, Xinyang Zhang, Koushil Sreenath, Guannan Qu, Xi Chen, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Compares continuous and discrete single-step regression and multi-step flow policies in single-task and multi-task training, across simulation and real hardware.
Even naive uniform-bin quantization achieves comparable or better task success than continuous-action policies.
The key weakness of discrete policies is factorization error from product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions, rather than insufficient precision.
Iterative computation in discrete flows and classifier-free guidance improve responsiveness within predicted action chunks.
Geometric corruption processes inspired by continuous flow matching do not consistently improve discrete policies.
papers.selection_reason: Challenges continuous action parametrization in VLA policies, directly relevant to robot learning and action models.
papers.title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?
papers.tldr: Discrete action policies can match or outperform continuous controllers in robotic VLA tasks, with factorization—not action precision—as their main challenge.

papers.abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.
authors: Fucai Zhu, Xidong Zhang, Yichi Zhang, Yipan Wang, Fubo Wang, Zibin Wu, Kaiqi Li, Jianhao Jiao, Shihan Lu, Di Hu, Mengdi Xu, Siyu Zhu, Xiaoxiao Long, Yao Yao, Xun Cao, Zhuo Xu, Koichi Hashimoto, Qifeng Chen, Zhe Li, Jianfei Yang, Haofei Lu, Danica Kragic, Shuicheng Yan, Jianghua Duan, Michael Yu Wang, Weihao Yuan
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and inconsistent supervision of scalable tactile manipulation demonstrations.
Uses TacClaw, a tactile-enabled handheld interface that synchronously records vision, fingertip touch, and end-effector trajectories without a target robot.
Aggregates over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames across more than 1,000 task types and diverse real-world environments.
Provides trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and annotations for contact segmentation, subtasks, and spatial grounding.
Demonstrates cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Large-scale vision-tactile-language-action dataset for dexterous manipulation; directly supports VLA and robot learning from human demonstrations.
papers.title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: TacClaw-Infinity is a large-scale, quality-controlled vision-tactile-language-action dataset designed to enable dexterous manipulation and cross-robot transfer.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.
authors: Huailiang Ma, Yuxuan Li, Ziyi Zhao, Xinkai Wang, Mingyu Li, Xinyu Guo, Lifeng Zhu, Aiguo Song, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
bullets: Targets weak fine-grained object understanding in existing image-level VLA models, especially under layout, clutter, and background shifts.
Encodes observations into temporal object slots with separate representations for persistent identity and changing object state.
Routes VLM attention toward relevant object tokens using identity-guided modulation.
Trains an action-conditioned dynamics module to predict future object states, while avoiding future prediction at inference.
Improves generalization across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation with novel arrangements and backgrounds.
papers.selection_reason: Object-centric VLA framework for manipulation with future object state prediction; fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: ObjDream: Guiding Vision-Language-Action Models with Object-Level Understanding and Future State Prediction
papers.tldr: ObjDream improves VLA robustness by combining object-centric visual representations, identity-guided attention, and action-conditioned future state prediction for manipulation.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
authors: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang, Kai Hu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses underspecified task instructions that do not clearly specify the next physical interaction.
Uses a vision-language reasoner to infer the next local motion from instructions and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict video and action chunks.
Builds temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
Introduces Execution-Grounded GRPO to train motion descriptions for appropriateness and execution success while keeping the WAM fixed.
Achieves 39.6% task success with default instructions and 31.6% with vague instructions in RoboLab real-to-sim evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded atomic-motion reasoning for world action models; directly fits VLA, robot learning, and action-conditioned world/video prediction.
papers.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Atomic-WAM improves robotic action generation by grounding task reasoning in executable atomic-motion descriptions.

papers.abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.
authors: Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Hanjun Wei, Qinghao Zhang, Zhixi Cai, Shiwen Ni
bullets: The method reads action choices from hidden states of a frozen vision-language generator processing the goal and screenshot.
Heads predict the action type, select numbered visual targets, or choose text options and WRITE slots.
A confidence cascade uses head decisions when confident and otherwise falls back to generator decoding from the same forward pass.
Across seven offline test sets, heads controlled 12–64% of steps with performance within 1.4 points above or 0.3 points below the generator under a strict threshold.
A looser threshold improved WebArena success and used less than half the generated tokens, but results varied across benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Plug-in decision heads predict web-agent actions from hidden states, reducing generation; transferable to multimodal action models.
papers.title: Why Generate a Click? Plug-in Decision Heads for Web Agents
papers.tldr: Plug-in decision heads let web agents bypass text generation for many actions, reducing token use while maintaining or improving task performance.

papers.abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
authors: Bingao Chen, Lihan Zha, C. Karen Liu, Guy Tevet
bullets: Addresses the limited scene coverage of wrist cameras and the low-resolution detail of external views.
Predicts the next interaction region alongside each action chunk, then receives original-resolution crops plus full images.
Built on π₀.₅ in Single and Dual configurations using one or two external stereo cameras with RGB-D inputs.
On four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single and Dual achieve 70.8% and 77.1% success, compared with 52.1% for wrist-equipped π₀.₅.
Matches the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improves performance with distractors, cloth, and far-away objects.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model with learned foveation actions replacing wrist cameras for manipulation.
papers.title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
papers.tldr: FoveaVLA replaces a wrist camera with learned image foveation, enabling external-camera VLAs to recover fine manipulation details and improve real-world performance.

papers.abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $\pi_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
authors: Ziyan Liu, Jiting Liu, Weihong Zhong, Wenda Yu, Yeqiu Chen, Jason Li, Xiaojiang Peng, Shuyuan Hu, Kai Wang, Bo Zhao
bullets: Fixed shared parameters can struggle when different robot operations require competing updates.
MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank updates for both vision-language and action modules.
Coupled generators follow the policy’s dependency structure, letting vision-language updates influence action-side parameter generation.
The framework is trained with the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
It reports gains of up to 16.30% on LIBERO and Meta-World and up to 14% over π₀.₅ in real-world evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Contextual parameter generation for VLA robot policies, improving adaptation across interaction contexts.
papers.title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
papers.tldr: MorphAct dynamically morphs robot-policy parameters to fit changing interaction contexts, improving manipulation performance across simulated and real-world evaluations.

papers.abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
authors: Xiangyi Wei, Hanzhe Yao, Jingwen Shang, Zhenhong Wu, Yang Li, Changbo Wang
bullets: Targets costly data collection, limited capability reuse, and cascading failures in complete-trajectory learning.
Represents each manipulation unit with a local goal, initiation condition, and observable success/failure criteria.
Uses language and vision to sequence units, select policies from a frozen capability registry, and verify outcomes before proceeding.
Supports checkpoint reuse for equivalent units and composes heterogeneous policies without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
Evaluations on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks report higher complete-task success and verified progress, with better failure containment and lower error propagation than baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Compositional long-horizon manipulation framework using language, vision, and reusable policy units.
papers.title: MUCO: A Mani-Unit-Structured Manipulation Framework for Compositional Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
papers.tldr: MUCO decomposes long-horizon robot tasks into reusable, verifiable manipulation units and orchestrates compatible policies with retries and fallback to contain failures.

papers.abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.
authors: Qisen Ma, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Jiabing Yang, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: The study compares four integration paradigms: Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
World-representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, while 2D semantic representations provide robust gains across paradigms.
No paradigm is universally best; the decoupled MoT Future Expert performs competitively overall and is particularly robust out of distribution.
World modeling consistently helps standard VLM-based policies and improves action-only baselines, especially on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
Decoupled designs are more compatible with pretrained VLAs, with evaluation spanning in-domain, OOD, few-shot, long-horizon, dynamic, and real-world settings.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies world model integration in Vision-Language-Action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that world modeling improves vision-language-action policies, but its effectiveness depends on the representation, integration paradigm, and policy backbone.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$\pi$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$\pi$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$\pi$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $\pi_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$\pi$ also consistently outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun, Ping Luo, Yao Mu
bullets: Targets the high-dimensional, structured action space of bimanual VLA policies, where cross-hand interactions are often implicit.
Represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as separate, interleaved action tokens.
Uses learnable hand-identity embeddings and factorized RoPE to encode hand identity, sequence position, and shared control timing.
On five DexJoCo tasks, average success rises from 31.9% to 51.3% under rand-obj and from 18.3% to 32.3% under rand-full, compared with π₀.₅.
Also consistently outperforms π₀.₅ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Structured interleaved action representation for bimanual dexterous VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Coordi-π improves bimanual dexterous manipulation by explicitly modeling the two hands as coordinated action sequences rather than a single concatenated vector.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.
authors: Qi Chen, Yuwei Wu, Quan Chen, Kunpeng Gao, Jin Chen, Che Sun, Zhi Gao, Yunde Jia
bullets: Addresses the costly, poorly scalable need for task-specific robot demonstrations and retraining when adapting VLAs to novel tasks.
Builds a compact, phase-aware video representation using learned visual-token selection and task-relevant queries supervised by phase captions.
Conditions the pretrained VLA policy on the video and query representations to provide task-specific execution guidance while preserving its action-generation backbone.
Experiments on source and unseen target tasks show improved average performance across unseen target groups with comparable source-task performance.
The approach is scoped to cross-task manipulation adaptation guided by human videos; the abstract does not establish broader settings or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: One-shot human video-guided adaptation of VLA policies to unseen manipulation tasks without robot demonstrations.
papers.title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: CapPro adapts pretrained vision-language-action policies to unseen robot manipulation tasks using a single human demonstration video, without target-task robot data or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro
authors: Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Baekseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses failures caused by poor decisions about continuing versus intervening during VLA policy execution.
Uses a rollout-trained Critic to assess success prospects, choose intervention times, and select re-entry targets.
Applies Trajectory Retraction to return the robot to a selected point before resuming the same VLA with a fresh observation.
Evaluated with GR00T N1.7 and π₀.₅ in simulation and real-robot manipulation, improving success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points across the reported settings.
Also completes additional tasks when the available execution budget increases.
papers.selection_reason: Actor-critic rollout orchestration deciding when to intervene and where to resume for fixed VLA policies.
papers.title: ACRO: Actor-Critic Rollout Orchestration
papers.tldr: ACRO improves fixed vision-language-action policies by deciding when and where to intervene and resume execution, increasing task success under the same physical execution budget.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free action chunk and execution horizon selection that accelerates VLA inference while improving manipulation success.
papers.title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
papers.tldr: PICES accelerates VLA robot control by adapting both the selected action chunk and execution horizon using perturbation-based uncertainty cues, improving speed and success.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making hyperspectral distinctions usable by a pretrained model without retraining its visual encoder or action decoder.
Uses native-width residual enrichment based on each token’s normalized false-color reference, with projection, norm control, and validation-calibrated injection.
Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category-balanced accuracy increases from 0.812 to 0.883.
Own-token addition improves external category-probe reuse over pooled replacement (0.701 vs. 0.590) under identical residuals and scale.
Grouped tests recover within-category spectral shape, while spectral swaps indicate that own-token composition approximately doubles target-specific recovery after frozen decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, adapting frozen interfaces to hyperspectral data without retraining, a core interest in Embodied AI.
papers.title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
papers.tldr: SPECTRA-VLA transfers hyperspectral information into a frozen vision-language-action model by enriching each visual token with a calibrated, token-specific residual.

papers.abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
authors: Fan Huang, Dezhong Tong, Changyu Chen, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An
bullets: Evaluates one-shot generation versus ICMC on UR5e cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks in MuJoCo using o1 and o4-mini.
Trains an open-weight instruction policy with GRPO through a frozen code generator, averaging rewards from five programs per instruction.
Logged positive-reward rates increased from 31.6% to 35.3% over the reported five-step trajectory, but these rates were not always consistent with independently verified task success.
Audits found positive labels for geometric failures, including a case where all five rewards were 1.0 despite a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance.
Proposes independent evaluation against fixed task specifications to separate robot control from success assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned robotic arm control via code decomposition and reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control for Robotic Arms: Language-to-Code Decomposition and Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ICMC makes language-driven robot motion more traceable by separating instructions, parameters, and code, while exposing limitations in reward-based success evaluation.

papers.abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
authors: Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Introduces a unified simulation benchmark covering eight tasks, 1,600 synchronized demonstrations, and task-specific success criteria.
Compares a no-force baseline with six force-integration designs using a shared π0.5 backbone.
Prompt Fusion achieves 35.31% mean simulation success versus 23.25% for the baseline and improves all three task categories.
In real-world tests, Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion reach 63.00% mean success versus 40.00% for the baseline; only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
Predictive and temporal benefits are strongest for physical-property inference, while temporal designs underperform on assembly.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for force integration in VLA-based robotic manipulation.
papers.title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: ForceBench standardizes evaluation of six-axis wrist-force integration for vision-language-action policies, finding that Prompt Fusion performs best across diverse robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.
Failures primarily arise in task planning, navigation/base positioning, and local manipulation.
The proposed system adds demonstration-based planning, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment to a fixed subtask VLA.
Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-guided agentic interventions for long-horizon mobile manipulation with adaptive visual memory.
papers.title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
papers.tldr: Diagnosing bottlenecks across planning, navigation, and manipulation enables targeted agentic interventions that substantially improve long-horizon mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20\% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Keqiang Ren, Xuecheng Ye, Hanyu Liu, Zhihua Wang, Tao Jian, Yunsheng Ma, Jiayi Wen, Xinran Li, Zhigong Song
bullets: Addresses motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arms, and hands, plus error accumulation in long-horizon tasks.
Decouples the 29-DoF action space into hand, arm, and mobile-base branches within a Hierarchical Modular Framework.
Uses COMET cross-attention for inter-module coordination and vision-language-model task decomposition to limit temporal error propagation.
Adds full-palm 2D tactile sensing to represent distributed contact signals across modules.
On a physical 29-DoF robot, achieves over 20% higher task success than mainstream baselines across varied long-horizon tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Modular coordination policies for high-DoF whole-body mobile manipulation with tactile sensing.
papers.title: RoboSpan: Learning Modular Coordination Policies for High-DoF Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation with Teleoperation
papers.tldr: RoboSpan combines a high-DoF teleoperation platform with hierarchical modular policies to improve long-horizon, contact-rich whole-body mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time adaptation of VLA models via in-context RL; directly relevant to VLA and test-time/continual learning.
papers.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: VLRLA enables fixed vision-language-action models to adapt during deployment by learning from accumulated interaction history through in-context reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Jointly encodes task, execution stage, and future action continuations in both current-state queries and recorded experiences.
Uses predictive retrieval training and a corpus of 1,695,684 training anchors; introduces a 4,000-query benchmark with an 8,000-entry gallery.
Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.
papers.selection_reason: Unified VLA retrieval embeddings for robot in-context learning and task-local memory evolution.
papers.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
papers.tldr: Robota-Embed learns a unified vision-language-action retrieval space that helps robots retrieve useful past experience for in-context learning and task-specific evolution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points, against -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy's reliance on the instruction unchanged.
authors: Hanlong Li, Sihan Tan, Takeshi Ashizawa, Benjamin Yen, Kazuhiro Nakadai
bullets: Rewording instructions reduces base OpenVLA success by 38.0 points on LIBERO, despite using semantically equivalent commands.
Test-time prompt ensembling, paraphrase medoids, and confidence-based selection fail to recover the lost performance; aggregation mainly reduces variance while preserving paraphrase bias.
A wrong-instruction probe links paraphrase sensitivity to how much policy success depends on the instruction, with stronger policies losing a smaller fraction.
LoRA training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points versus −32.0 for a matched control, replicating across seeds and OpenVLA-OFT.
The robustness improvement transfers to withheld phrasings without changing the policy’s overall reliance on instructions.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of instruction paraphrase robustness in VLA policies directly addresses vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies
papers.tldr: VLA policies can be highly sensitive to instruction wording, and paraphrase aggregation does not remove this shared bias, whereas paraphrase-focused LoRA training substantially improves robustness.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
authors: Kyusong Lee, Heting Ying, Tiancheng Zhao
bullets: Targets the challenge of following the intended person in shared spaces with visual distractors.
Uses frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer, and waypoint prediction.
Trains in stages: vision-language alignment, multimodal reasoning, and tracking specialization.
On-policy refinement raises distractor-tracking success from 55.80% to 58.22% and reduces collision rate by 1.99 percentage points.
The study is preliminary and motivates further work on on-policy refinement for person following.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language waypoint policy for embodied tracking, relevant to embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
papers.tldr: VLX-Go improves robot person-following among distractors through staged vision-language learning and on-policy refinement.

papers.abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy's own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace's source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.
authors: Chang Liu, Sibo Tian, Litian Gong, Zhiwen Fan, Jiachen Li, Xiao Liang, Minghui Zheng
bullets: Targets product variation, prerequisite sequences, and precise contact-rich approaches in EoL disassembly.
Weights valid action chunks by progress toward the target and each trace’s source and outcome.
Trains policies under different weighting settings and selects among them using held-out validation.
On UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, PACER achieved 87/100 successful trials versus 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.
papers.selection_reason: Process-aware VLA policy learning from human corrections for robotic disassembly; fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: PACER: Process-Aware VLA Policy Learning from Human Corrections for Robotic Disassembly
papers.tldr: PACER improves robotic disassembly by using process-aware weighting of policy rollouts and human corrections during supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.
bullets: Addresses robustness challenges from extreme lunar illumination and deployment-time perceptual disturbances.
Uses an end-to-end vision-language-action policy mapping observations directly to rover control actions.
Trains with safety-aware expert demonstrations generated in a high-fidelity lunar simulation.
Performs competitively with a modular navigation baseline in closed-loop evaluation under unseen disturbances.
Adaptive execution horizons reduce inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates versus fixed horizons in evaluated scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end VLA policy for lunar rover docking; directly relevant to embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
papers.tldr: A vision-language-action policy enables robust autonomous lunar rover docking under unseen perceptual disturbances while reducing inference through safety-aware adaptive-horizon control.

papers.abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.
authors: Maria Attarian, Yifan Ruan, Claas Voelcker, Chenyang Cao, Amy Zhang, Peter Stone, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski
bullets: Compares supervised finetuning, critic-based steering, and offline RL across on/off-policy, offline/online, and optimal/suboptimal data scenarios.
Evaluates simulated LIBERO tasks and real Franka-robot tasks.
With offline failure data, critic-based steering outperforms supervised finetuning.
Offline RL-trained critics do not outperform simpler Monte Carlo-based critics.
Online critic-based steering is more sample-efficient than policy-gradient finetuning but reaches a lower performance ceiling.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of adaptation methods for VLA policies across data scenarios; relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Post-Training, Finetuning, and Steering:A Field Guide for Curating Training Data
